title: CS109 oral question bank
subject: CS109 oral question bank
system_prompt: You are an oral exam proctor for a university course.

questions.text: You are modeling an unknown coin bias θ. A student says, “If I have no prior opinion, I should use Beta(0,0), because that represents zero prior heads and zero prior tails.” Do you agree? Explain what prior would actually represent no prior preference in this course’s setup, and interpret its pseudo-counts.
rubric_items: Full credit: States Beta(0,0) is invalid or not used here because Beta parameters must be positive.; Identifies Beta(1,1) as the no-prior-preference choice.; Explains the pseudo-count interpretation as a−1 and b−1, giving 0 prior heads and 0 prior tails.
Partial credit: Identifies Beta(1,1) but gives a vague or incomplete reason.; Mentions uniform prior without connecting it to pseudo-counts.
Common mistakes: Saying Beta(0,0) is the correct uninformative prior in this course context.; Interpreting Beta(a,b) as a prior heads and b prior tails instead of a−1 and b−1.

questions.text: Suppose your prior on a coin’s probability of heads is Beta(4,3), and then you flip the coin 12 times and observe 9 heads and 3 tails. What is the posterior distribution, and how would you explain verbally what changed from prior to posterior?
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes posterior Beta(13,6).; Explains conjugate updating as adding successes and failures to parameters.; Interprets the posterior as both shifted and more concentrated due to more evidence.
Partial credit: Gets the posterior right but gives little interpretation.; Explains update idea but makes a small arithmetic slip.

Common mistakes: Using Beta(9,3) and forgetting the prior.; Adding 1 extra for successes/failures again even though the prior is already in Beta form.; Treating 12 trials as one count added to both parameters.

questions.text: A classmate says: “Conjugate means the posterior equals the prior, so choosing a Beta prior forces your beliefs not to change form or value after data.” Identify what is right and what is wrong in that statement, using the Bernoulli/Binomial setting.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes same family from same parameter values.; States the update Beta(a+n,b+m) or equivalent.; Uses Bernoulli/Binomial context explicitly.
Partial credit: Says the posterior is still Beta but does not explain why the original statement is partly wrong.; Mentions parameter updating without clearly defining conjugacy.
Common mistakes: Saying conjugate means prior and posterior are numerically identical.; Only repeating the definition without addressing the misconception.

questions.text: A startup is testing whether users click a new button. Before any experiment, the product manager says, “I think the click-through rate is about 30%, and my belief is as strong as if I had seen 20 past users.” Using the Beta pseudo-count interpretation from class, propose a reasonable prior and justify your parameter choice.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the pseudo-count interpretation correctly.; Sets 20 imaginary trials with about 6 successes and 14 failures.; Produces Beta(7,15) or an equivalent justified nearby integer choice if the student explains rounding.
Partial credit: Gets the success/failure counts right but forgets the +1 shift.; Chooses parameters with roughly 30% mean but does not connect to strength 20.
Common mistakes: Using Beta(6,14) directly under the course convention.; Making total pseudo-trials equal to a+b instead of a+b−2.; Ignoring the requested prior strength.

questions.text: Derive aloud why a Beta prior is conjugate to Binomial data, but do it at the level of proportionality rather than normalization constants. Start from a prior θ ~ Beta(a,b) and Binomial data with n successes and m failures. What kernel do you get for the posterior?
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes likelihood kernel θ^n(1−θ)^m.; Writes prior kernel θ^(a−1)(1−θ)^(b−1).; Multiplies exponents correctly to obtain θ^(a+n−1)(1−θ)^(b+m−1).; Identifies the posterior as Beta(a+n,b+m) and explains why constants can be ignored.
Partial credit: Understands the multiplication idea but is sloppy about constants or exponents.; States the final posterior correctly without fully showing the kernel derivation.
Common mistakes: Including the combinatorial term as if it changes the posterior family.; Dropping the −1 terms from the Beta exponents.; Confusing n trials with n successes.

questions.text: You see three candidate priors for a proportion θ: Beta(5,5), Beta(2,8), and Beta(8,2). Without drawing the exact curves, explain how their centers and shapes differ, and match each one to a belief statement about a process being roughly fair, likely small, or likely large.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies Beta(5,5) as symmetric near 0.5.; Correctly identifies Beta(2,8) as skewed toward 0 and Beta(8,2) toward 1.; Comments on concentration or strength of belief.
Partial credit: Gets the center directions right but says little about shape or concentration.; Correctly matches two of the three.
Common mistakes: Reversing Beta(2,8) and Beta(8,2).; Claiming Beta(5,5) is uniform.; Ignoring that support is on [0,1].

questions.text: In a medical trial, before any data are collected, you are told the treatment is believed to work about 80% of the time. Two scientists propose priors Beta(81,21) and Beta(5,2). Explain how both can be defensible even though they are different, and describe how their posteriors would differ after observing 14 successes and 6 failures.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains same mean but different strength.; Correctly interprets Beta(81,21) as much stronger than Beta(5,2).; Computes posteriors Beta(95,27) and Beta(19,8).; Explains how stronger priors resist change more.
Partial credit: Explains the strength distinction but does not compute both posteriors.; Computes posteriors correctly but gives weak interpretation.
Common mistakes: Claiming only one prior is valid because both have mean 0.8.; Comparing priors only by mean and not by concentration.; Forgetting to add observed failures to the second parameter.

questions.text: A student observes 8 heads in 10 flips and says, “So the posterior must be Beta(8,2), because those are the observed counts.” Critique this statement in two different ways depending on what prior was used.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that posterior depends on prior and data.; Under Beta(1,1), correctly gives Beta(9,3).; Explains that observed counts alone are not the posterior under the course convention.
Partial credit: Points out that a prior is missing but does not compute the corrected posterior.; Gives Beta(9,3) but does not explain why Beta(8,2) might sound tempting.
Common mistakes: Accepting Beta(8,2) as the posterior under a uniform prior.; Confusing likelihood with posterior.

questions.text: Suppose X is the number of successes in 25 independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p. State the distribution of X, give its expectation and variance, and then explain what changes and what does not if p itself is treated as an unknown random variable with a Beta prior.
rubric_items: Full credit: States X|p ~ Bin(25,p).; Gives expectation 25p and variance 25p(1−p).; Explains clearly that the Binomial model for data conditional on p stays the same while the prior/posterior describe uncertainty about p.
Partial credit: Gets the Binomial facts right but gives a vague explanation of the Bayesian part.; Explains prior/posterior uncertainty but omits expectation or variance.
Common mistakes: Saying X itself is Beta-distributed.; Replacing the Binomial model with Beta after introducing a prior.; Confusing the random variable X with the parameter p.

questions.text: In a class discussion, someone says the Beta distribution is appropriate for election vote share because it is “basically Bernoulli.” Give a more careful explanation of why Beta is a reasonable model for a two-candidate vote share, and also state one important limitation of that modeling choice.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains support on [0,1] and role as a model for an unknown proportion.; Distinguishes Beta from Bernoulli/Binomial rather than conflating them.; States a relevant limitation such as poor fit for multiparty settings.
Partial credit: Mentions that Beta models proportions but does not explain the Bayesian updating advantage.; States a limitation but does not distinguish Beta from Bernoulli clearly.
Common mistakes: Saying Beta is a discrete success/failure distribution.; Claiming Beta directly models individual votes rather than vote share uncertainty.; Ignoring the two-party limitation.

questions.text: A website owner uses a Beta(1,1) prior for the conversion rate θ. On day 1, they observe 3 conversions and 7 non-conversions. On day 2, they observe 4 conversions and 6 non-conversions. Explain two ways to update the posterior and show that they agree.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes sequential updates Beta(4,8) then Beta(8,14).; Correctly computes the one-step combined update Beta(8,14).; Explains why the two methods agree.
Partial credit: Gets one method right but not the other.; Explains additivity of counts without correct arithmetic.
Common mistakes: Resetting the prior on day 2 instead of using the day 1 posterior.; Adding total trials rather than separate successes and failures.

questions.text: For a Beta(a,b) distribution with a>1 and b>1, the mode is given in the notes. Use that formula to compare the prior mode and posterior mode when the prior is Beta(6,4) and you observe 8 successes and 2 failures. Interpret the result in words.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the correct mode formula.; Computes prior mode 5/8 and posterior mode 13/18.; Interprets the increase as evidence pushing belief toward larger θ.
Partial credit: Gets the posterior right but not the prior, or vice versa.; Uses mean instead of mode but gives a sensible qualitative interpretation.
Common mistakes: Using a/(a+b) instead of the mode formula when asked for mode.; Forgetting to update the posterior parameters before computing the mode.

questions.text: A student says, “If two Beta priors have the same mean, then they express the same prior belief.” Give a counterexample using priors from the course materials and explain what feature of the belief differs.
rubric_items: Full credit: Provides a concrete counterexample with same mean but different concentration.; Explains the difference in prior strength or imaginary sample size.; States clearly that same mean is not the same as same prior belief.
Partial credit: Gives the right intuition without a concrete example.; Provides a concrete example but does not explain strength.
Common mistakes: Equating center with full belief specification.; Discussing only means and not uncertainty/concentration.

questions.text: You are comparing two manufacturing lines. For line A, your prior is Beta(2,2) and you observe 18 defect-free items and 2 defective ones. For line B, your prior is also Beta(2,2) and you observe 9 defect-free items and 1 defective one. Without doing any integrals, compare the posterior beliefs about the two lines’ success probabilities and explain which line you are more certain about.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes posteriors Beta(20,4) and Beta(11,3).; Recognizes their centers are similar because the observed proportions match and priors match.; Explains that more total evidence makes line A’s posterior more concentrated and therefore more certain.
Partial credit: Gets both posteriors right but does not explain certainty.; Explains the qualitative difference without computing the exact posterior parameters.
Common mistakes: Choosing line A as better solely because it has more successes, ignoring differing sample sizes.; Claiming equal certainty because both empirical rates are 0.9.

questions.text: Explain the relationship among Bernoulli trials, the Binomial random variable, and the Beta prior in one coherent story. Your answer should make clear which object represents data, which represents a count summary, and which represents uncertainty about a parameter.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly describes Bernoulli as one trial and Binomial as counting successes over n trials.; Clearly states that Beta is a distribution on the parameter θ.; Integrates the three pieces into a coherent Bayesian story.
Partial credit: Gets each object mostly right but does not connect them well.; Mentions Beta and Binomial but is vague about which is data and which is parameter.
Common mistakes: Saying Beta is the distribution of the number of successes.; Confusing Bernoulli and Binomial.; Treating θ as observed data rather than an unknown parameter.

questions.text: A coin has prior Beta(3,7). You flip it once and observe a head. Then you flip it once more and observe a tail. Give the posterior after each step, and explain whether the final posterior depends on the order of these two observations.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly updates to Beta(4,7) then Beta(4,8).; Checks reversed order and shows the same final posterior.; Explains that only total successes and failures matter.
Partial credit: Gets the final posterior right but not both intermediate steps.; Explains order-independence qualitatively without verifying it.
Common mistakes: Adding both observations to the same parameter.; Thinking the order changes the final posterior.

questions.text: A scientist wants a prior that strongly favors a fair coin, while another wants a prior that is fair on average but weak. Give one example of each using Beta distributions, and explain how the two priors would react differently to seeing 8 heads and 2 tails.
rubric_items: Full credit: Provides one strong fair prior and one weak fair prior, both centered at 0.5.; Correctly updates both with 8 heads and 2 tails.; Explains the different sensitivity to data due to prior strength.
Partial credit: Provides reasonable priors but does not compute both posteriors.; Explains strength qualitatively without concrete examples.
Common mistakes: Choosing priors not centered at 0.5.; Thinking equal means imply equal updating behavior.

questions.text: Someone claims: “Because the Binomial variance is np(1−p), once we place a Beta prior on p the variance formula for the observed count X is still just n times the posterior mean times one minus the posterior mean.” Is that statement automatically valid? Explain carefully what is being mixed up.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the confusion between conditioning on fixed p and averaging over uncertain p.; States that Var(X|p)=np(1−p) applies conditionally.; Explains that parameter uncertainty adds extra variability beyond plugging in the posterior mean.
Partial credit: Says the statement is not automatically valid but gives only a vague reason.; Mentions conditional variance without clearly explaining the mismatch.
Common mistakes: Approving the plug-in argument without qualification.; Confusing posterior mean of p with a fixed true p.

questions.text: Why is it natural that Beta distributions are only used for parameters like probabilities or proportions, rather than arbitrary real-valued parameters? Answer by referring to support and interpretation, not just by citing a rule.
rubric_items: Full credit: Mentions support on [0,1].; Explains the relevance to probabilities/proportions.; Adds interpretation such as pseudo-counts or flexible shapes for uncertain fractions.
Partial credit: Mentions support but gives little explanation beyond that.; Gives a generally correct answer without tying to interpretation.
Common mistakes: Saying Beta can model any parameter because it is flexible.; Ignoring the support mismatch.

questions.text: A teacher says, “I will use Beta(1,1) for every problem because it is objective.” Give a nuanced response. In your answer, explain one advantage of that choice and one situation where a different Beta prior could be more appropriate.
rubric_items: Full credit: States an advantage of Beta(1,1) as a simple no-preference prior.; Explains that informative priors can be better when credible prior knowledge exists.; Gives a concrete example of an alternative prior and why it might be used.
Partial credit: Defends Beta(1,1) but does not discuss limitations.; Critiques the claim but does not name a specific alternative prior.
Common mistakes: Claiming Beta(1,1) is always the uniquely correct objective prior.; Rejecting all use of priors despite available prior knowledge.

questions.text: Suppose you start with Beta(a,b), then observe n independent Bernoulli trials with x successes. A student proposes the posterior Beta(a+x−1,b+n−x−1) because “the Beta density already has minus ones in the exponents, so you should subtract one when updating.” Explain why this reasoning is incorrect and give the correct posterior.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that the −1 terms belong to the prior exponents, not to an additional update step.; Correctly combines the prior and likelihood exponents.; States the correct posterior Beta(a+x,b+n−x).
Partial credit: Gives the correct posterior but weakly explains the exponent issue.; Explains exponent addition but makes notation slightly inconsistent.
Common mistakes: Subtracting 1 from the counts during updating.; Confusing Beta parameters with exponents directly.

questions.text: Imagine two analysts are using Beta-Binomial updating on the same sequence of data. Analyst 1 reports only posterior means, while Analyst 2 also emphasizes how concentrated the posterior is. Explain why Analyst 2 is giving a more complete Bayesian summary, using Beta priors as your language.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that mean captures center but not uncertainty.; Uses Beta examples or parameter-size reasoning to illustrate differing concentration.; Connects concentration to strength of belief or decision-making.
Partial credit: Says uncertainty matters but does not tie it specifically to Beta parameters.; Mentions concentration without giving a concrete comparison.
Common mistakes: Treating posterior mean as a complete description of Bayesian belief.; Ignoring the role of parameter magnitude in concentration.

questions.text: A startup is testing a new signup flow. Let θ be the probability that a visitor converts. Before collecting data, the product manager says, "I want a prior that reflects a 70% conversion belief, but only as strongly as if we had previously seen 8 imaginary visitors." Explain how you would choose a Beta prior, then suppose the team observes 9 conversions and 6 non-conversions. State the posterior and interpret what changed.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the pseudo-count interpretation a−1 and b−1 clearly.; Chooses a reasonable Beta prior consistent with 70% and strength 8, ideally Beta(7,3) or explicitly discusses rounding/integer approximation.; Correctly updates to posterior by adding observed successes and failures.; Interprets posterior as a compromise between prior belief and observed data.

Partial credit: Gets the update rule right but is vague on how the prior was chosen.; Identifies pseudo-count idea but mixes up whether to add 1 when converting counts to Beta parameters.; Chooses a close prior with correct reasoning even if numbers are slightly off due to rounding.

Common mistakes: Using Beta(5.6,2.4) without acknowledging the integer-parameter convention in the provided context.; Forgetting the minus-1 interpretation and using Beta(6,2) directly as 6 successes and 2 failures.; Updating to Beta(7+9,3+6) but being unable to explain why that update is justified.

questions.text: A classmate says: "If the medicine is believed to work 80% of the time, the prior must be Beta(80,20), because those parameters literally mean 80 successes and 20 failures." Critique this statement carefully. Use the pseudo-trial interpretation from class, and explain why more than one prior could reasonably encode '80% belief.'
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly identifies the a−1, b−1 pseudo-count interpretation.; Explains why Beta(80,20) is not literally 80 prior successes and 20 prior failures in this framing.; States that multiple priors can encode an 80% belief because prior strength is separate from central tendency.; Gives at least one valid alternative such as Beta(81,21) or discusses weaker/stronger alternatives.

Partial credit: Notices that there is an off-by-one issue but does not clearly explain the interpretation.; Says multiple priors are possible but does not connect that to prior strength.; Mentions Beta(81,21) but cannot explain why it is preferable under the given interpretation.
Common mistakes: Claiming Beta(80,20) is uniquely correct.; Confusing mode with mean without saying so.; Assuming any prior with mean 0.8 is equivalent regardless of concentration.

questions.text: Suppose θ has prior Beta(a,b), and then you run n independent Bernoulli trials with x successes and n−x failures. Without doing any normalization integrals, derive the posterior kernel aloud from Bayes' rule and explain exactly where conjugacy appears. Your answer should make clear which terms are treated as constants in θ.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes posterior as proportional to likelihood times prior.; Uses the binomial/Bernoulli likelihood kernel θ^x(1−θ)^(n−x).; Uses the Beta prior kernel θ^(a−1)(1−θ)^(b−1).; Combines exponents correctly to get Beta(a+x,b+n−x).; Explains that constants not depending on θ are absorbed into normalization.

Partial credit: Gets the final posterior parameters right but provides weak justification.; Shows the proportionality argument but mixes x and n−x notation slightly.; Recognizes conjugacy but does not explicitly identify which terms are constants in θ.

Common mistakes: Trying to keep the binomial coefficient as if it affects the posterior shape in θ.; Updating with Beta(a+n,b+x) or other parameter swaps.; Forgetting the prior exponents are a−1 and b−1, not a and b.

questions.text: Two analysts observe the same data: 12 coin flips with 9 heads and 3 tails. Analyst A uses a uniform prior Beta(1,1). Analyst B uses a prior centered at fairness with pseudo-count strength α on both heads and tails, as in Beta(α+1, α+1). Compare their posteriors conceptually, and explain what happens as α becomes very large. Do not just state formulas; interpret the effect of prior strength relative to sample size.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly states or describes both posteriors.; Explains symmetric prior as encoding belief in fairness with strength α on each side.; Clearly compares influence of prior versus data.; Correctly describes the large-α limiting behavior as prior domination toward 0.5.

Partial credit: Knows the update formulas but gives little interpretation.; Explains that larger α means stronger prior but does not connect it to the sample size of 12.; Understands fairness prior qualitatively even if one posterior parameter is off by 1.

Common mistakes: Saying a larger α makes the posterior more spread out rather than more concentrated.; Claiming both analysts must reach the same posterior because they saw the same data.; Treating Beta(α+1,α+1) as α total pseudo-trials instead of 2α.

questions.text: An election forecaster wants to model a candidate's two-party vote share in a state using a Beta distribution. Defend why Beta is a sensible choice in that setting, then identify one important limitation of the model and explain how that limitation could matter when communicating predictions to the public.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the support match: Beta models values in [0,1].; Connects Beta to uncertainty and Bayesian updating from prior plus polling data.; Identifies at least one substantive limitation such as multiparty inadequacy or prior dominance in sparse-data settings.; Explains why that limitation matters for interpretation or public communication.

Partial credit: States that Beta models percentages but does not discuss updating or uncertainty.; Names a limitation but does not explain its real-world consequence.; Gives a communication concern without tying it to a technical modeling issue.

Common mistakes: Saying Beta is appropriate for any election without qualification.; Ignoring that two-party framing is what makes success/failure natural.; Treating forecast output as objective truth rather than model-based uncertainty.

questions.text: A student says, “The Central Limit Theorem means that if I sample enough times, the original random variable itself becomes Normal.” Do you agree? Explain carefully by distinguishing the distribution of the individual observations from the distribution of a sum or average of iid observations.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that CLT concerns sums/averages, not the original variable.; Mentions approximate Normal distribution of sum and/or sample mean with correct mean/variance scaling.; Explicitly contrasts population distribution with sampling distribution.
Partial credit: Recognizes that sample mean becomes approximately Normal but gives incomplete distinction.; Gets the main idea right but omits assumptions like iid or finite variance.
Common mistakes: Saying the histogram of raw data must become Normal as sample size grows.; Confusing Law of Large Numbers with CLT.; Claiming the sum is exactly Normal for finite n.

questions.text: Let \(X_1,\dots,X_{10}\) be iid Uniform(0,1), and let \(S=\sum_{i=1}^{10} X_i\). Use the CLT to approximate \(P(S\le 10/3)\), but talk through the setup rather than just giving a number. Why is this approximation reasonably good even though n is only 10?
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes mean 1/2 and variance 1/12 for each Uniform.; Uses CLT to state \(S \approx N(5,5/6)\).; Sets up the standardized probability correctly.; Explains why n=10 can still work reasonably well.
Partial credit: Correct setup with minor arithmetic slip.; Correct Normal approximation but weak justification of accuracy.
Common mistakes: Using variance 1/6 instead of 5/6 for the sum.; Using the sample mean formula when asked about the sum.; Claiming CLT cannot be used because n<30.

questions.text: You often hear, “CLT only works once n is at least 30.” Use the example of sums of Uniform(0,1) variables to evaluate that claim. I want you to argue from the evidence in the example, not just from a memorized rule.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the hard threshold interpretation of n=30.; Uses the Uniform examples across n=2,5,10 to support the argument.; Explains that distribution shape affects convergence speed.
Partial credit: Says 30 is a rule of thumb but gives little support from the provided example.; Mentions symmetry or boundedness without connecting to approximation quality.
Common mistakes: Asserting CLT is invalid for n<30.; Saying CLT is always accurate for n>=30 regardless of distribution.

questions.text: A website receives 100 independent visits, and each visitor converts with probability 0.5. You want an approximate probability that at least 65 convert. Explain why a Normal approximation is appropriate here, and then explain why using 65 instead of 64.5 would systematically distort the approximation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies Binomial as sum of iid Bernoulli variables.; Justifies Normal approximation using large n and suitable np(1-p).; Explains continuity correction conceptually and applies 64.5 correctly.; Explains the direction of the approximation error if continuity correction is omitted.
Partial credit: Uses Normal approximation correctly but gives only a procedural reason for continuity correction.; Mentions discrete-to-continuous issue without explaining 64.5.
Common mistakes: Using Poisson approximation when p=0.5.; Using \(P(Y\ge 65.5)\) or no continuity correction.; Saying continuity correction is optional but not affecting interpretation.

questions.text: State the CLT in a way that would let you compute probabilities for a sample mean. Then explain how the mean and variance of the sample mean compare to the mean and variance of the original observations, and why that variance behavior makes intuitive sense.
rubric_items: Full credit: States approximate distribution of sample mean with correct parameters.; Correctly compares mean and variance of \(\bar X\) to those of \(X_i\).; Gives intuitive explanation for variance reduction.
Partial credit: Correct formula but weak intuition.; Explains standard error shrinkage but confuses variance and standard deviation.
Common mistakes: Saying variance of the mean is sigma squared times n.; Saying the sample mean becomes exact Normal for any n.; Confusing mean of sample mean with n mu.

questions.text: Suppose two independent groups each have sample size 20, and each group mean is approximately Normal by the CLT with mean 0.5 and variance \(v/20\). Without doing numeric table lookup, derive an approximate distribution for the difference in group means \(\bar X_1-\bar X_2\), and explain how you would use it to judge whether an observed difference is unusually large in a two-sided sense.
rubric_items: Full credit: Derives mean 0 and variance v/10 for the difference.; Uses independence to add variances.; Explains two-sided probability through \(|D|\ge k\) or equivalent.
Partial credit: Gets Normal form right but misses two-sided interpretation.; Correct mean with variance arithmetic error.
Common mistakes: Subtracting variances instead of adding them.; Using one-sided significance when the problem is two-sided.; Forgetting independence requirement.

questions.text: You are comparing two approximations for \(X\sim Bin(100,0.04)\): a Poisson approximation and a Normal approximation. Which would you choose first, and how would you justify that choice using the conditions and preferences given in the course material?
rubric_items: Full credit: Selects Poisson approximation.; Justifies using large n, small p, and \(\lambda=np=4\).; Explains why Normal is less compelling here due to skewness and p not mid-range.
Partial credit: Chooses Poisson with incomplete rationale.; Mentions np=4 but does not compare against Normal conditions.

Common mistakes: Automatically choosing Normal because 'Gaussian is always best.'; Claiming both are equally justified without discussing conditions.; Using continuity correction language with Poisson choice as if it were the main issue.

questions.text: A classmate claims, “Since a Binomial is a sum of Bernoulli variables and CLT says sums become Normal, we should approximate every Binomial by a Normal.” Diagnose what is right in that statement and what is missing or wrong.
rubric_items: Full credit: Acknowledges Binomial-as-sum-of-Bernoulli connection.; Explains asymptotic nature and need for favorable parameter regime.; Mentions continuity correction for probability approximation.
Partial credit: Explains condition on np(1-p) but omits continuity correction.; Gives continuity correction but not limitations of CLT.
Common mistakes: Saying CLT guarantees exact Normality.; Ignoring skewness when p is near 0 or 1.; Forgetting that Binomial is discrete.

questions.text: For \(S_5=\sum_{i=1}^5 X_i\) with iid \(X_i\sim Uniform(0,1)\), use the CLT to approximate \(P(S_5\le 5/3)\). Then compare your approximation qualitatively to the exact value given in class and explain whether the approximation is over or under.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses correct mean and variance for the sum.; Writes the standardized Normal approximation correctly.; Compares to the exact value and notes slight underestimation.
Partial credit: Correct setup with small arithmetic error.; Correct approximation but no comparison to exact value.
Common mistakes: Using sample mean distribution instead of sum distribution.; Incorrect variance aggregation.; Interpreting 'close' without directional comparison.

questions.text: The proof sketch in lecture mentioned characteristic functions and standardizing the sum. Without reproducing the proof, explain why standardization is essential and what it means that the standardized sum converges to the characteristic function of a standard Normal.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why raw sums cannot converge to a fixed shape without centering/scaling.; Describes subtracting mean and dividing by standard deviation.; Connects limit of characteristic functions to identification of the limiting distribution.
Partial credit: Knows standardization is needed but gives vague reason.; Mentions characteristic functions without explaining what convergence implies.
Common mistakes: Saying standardization is just for convenience rather than necessity.; Claiming the unstandardized sum converges to N(0,1).; Confusing characteristic function with density itself.

questions.text: An engineer says, “Our sensor reading is the sum of many tiny independent effects, so modeling it as Normal is reasonable.” Connect this statement to the CLT, but also give two reasons to stay critical instead of accepting the Normal model automatically.
rubric_items: Full credit: Connects 'sum of many effects' to CLT reasoning.; Provides at least two concrete caveats about the Normal model.; Shows modeling judgment, not blind rule-following.
Partial credit: Gives CLT connection with only one caveat.; States generic caution without linking to assumptions.
Common mistakes: Saying CLT proves all natural phenomena are Normal.; Ignoring dependence or skewness issues.; Confusing exact Normality with practical approximation.

questions.text: Suppose \(X\sim Bin(100,0.5)\). Derive the Normal approximation parameters directly from Bernoulli mean and variance, rather than quoting them. Then explain why the resulting approximation is centered at 50 and has standard deviation 5.
rubric_items: Full credit: Represents Binomial as sum of iid Bernoulli variables.; Correctly computes Bernoulli mean and variance.; Scales mean and variance correctly to get \(N(50,25)\).
Partial credit: Correct Normal parameters but insufficient derivation.; Minor slip in standard deviation while variance is correct.
Common mistakes: Using variance np instead of np(1-p).; Confusing variance and standard deviation.; Stating approximation without showing Bernoulli connection.

questions.text: A student uses the CLT for a sum of iid discrete random variables and says continuity correction is unnecessary because 'CLT already handles the approximation error.' Respond to that claim. In your answer, explain what continuity correction is trying to repair and when it matters most.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains discrete-to-continuous mismatch clearly.; States how continuity correction shifts thresholds by 0.5.; Discusses when the correction has the biggest impact.
Partial credit: Knows the rule but gives weak conceptual explanation.; Explains purpose generally but not specific threshold adjustment.
Common mistakes: Treating continuity correction as only a cosmetic convention.; Applying the wrong sign to the 0.5 adjustment.; Thinking it is needed for continuous original variables.

questions.text: A city tracks yearly flood counts. For one floodplain, a Poisson model with a very small annual rate is used; for the number of floodplains out of 10 that experience an extreme event, a Binomial model is used. Explain why CLT is not the first tool you would use here, and then describe a situation within this story where a Normal approximation via CLT might become reasonable.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why Poisson/Binomial are more natural here than CLT.; Notes rarity/skewness/small n as reasons Normal is poor initially.; Describes a concrete large-aggregation setting where CLT could become useful.
Partial credit: Correctly prefers Poisson/Binomial but gives limited CLT discussion.; Mentions 'many years' or 'many floodplains' without explaining why aggregation helps.
Common mistakes: Using Normal immediately for rare-event annual counts.; Ignoring skewness of low-rate counts.; Saying CLT is always the best approximation method.

questions.text: In the course summary, the CLT was stated for iid random variables with finite mean and variance. Explain why the iid structure matters for the formulas \(n\mu\), \(n\sigma^2\), and \(\sigma^2/n\), and what part of the conclusion you would be hesitant to trust if independence failed badly.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains role of identical distribution in common mu and sigma squared.; Explains role of independence in variance addition.; Mentions covariance and possible failure of the approximation if dependence is strong.
Partial credit: Knows independence matters but cannot explain variance formulas clearly.; Explains iid partially but not implications for CLT.
Common mistakes: Saying expectation also requires independence.; Ignoring covariance terms under dependence.; Assuming any dependent data still satisfy the same formulas.

questions.text: For iid \(X_i\sim Uniform(0,1)\), compare the CLT approximation quality for \(P(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \le n/3)\) at n=2 and n=10. I am not asking for a precise error bound; instead, explain from the z-score setup and the provided class numbers why the n=10 approximation is markedly better.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up mean and variance of the sum for general n.; Uses standardization and compares n=2 to n=10.; References the observed numerical closeness from class.; Explains improvement through increased Normality of the sum.
Partial credit: Compares the class numbers correctly but with weak z-score discussion.; Has the right qualitative conclusion with some formula slips.

Common mistakes: Claiming the threshold gets closer to the mean as n grows.; Using sample mean formulas incorrectly for the sum without adjustment.; Ignoring the class evidence and giving only a generic statement.

questions.text: You collect a sample of size n from an unknown population and want to use the CLT for the sample mean. The lecture notes say the CLT still holds in real life even when we do not know the population mean and variance. Explain what the theorem gives you, what unknown quantities remain, and why data collection is still useful.
rubric_items: Full credit: States what CLT says about sample mean distribution.; Identifies unknown mu and sigma squared as practical obstacles.; Explains that sample data are used to estimate these and enable inference.
Partial credit: Knows parameters may be unknown but gives limited explanation of why CLT still matters.; States sample mean is Normal-ish but omits parameter discussion.
Common mistakes: Saying CLT is unusable unless mu and sigma squared are known in advance.; Confusing the theorem itself with parameter estimation.; Claiming the CLT tells you the parameter values.

questions.text: Someone says, “Poisson approximation and Normal approximation are basically the same idea because they both replace a hard distribution by an easier one.” Compare them in a way that reveals an important difference in when each is appropriate.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that both are approximations but distinguishes their regimes.; Correctly characterizes Poisson for rare events and Normal for more balanced aggregated variation.; Explains that approximation choice depends on the shape/parameters.
Partial credit: Identifies one regime correctly but not the other.; Gives the main contrast without naming parameter conditions clearly.
Common mistakes: Saying both can always be used interchangeably.; Claiming Normal is always preferred regardless of p.; Ignoring the role of skewness or rarity.

questions.text: Why does the CLT help explain the prominence of the Normal distribution in practice, but not justify treating every bell-shaped dataset as evidence of a sum of iid effects? Give a careful answer that separates mathematical mechanism from modeling inference.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains CLT as one mechanism behind approximate Normality.; Rejects reverse inference from bell shape to iid-sum mechanism.; Separates mathematical explanation from empirical model selection.
Partial credit: States CLT explains Normality but gives weak caution against reverse inference.; Gives caution without connecting to mechanism.
Common mistakes: Assuming Normal-looking data prove independence or additivity.; Treating model fit as proof of generative process.; Saying CLT applies backward.

questions.text: Suppose \(\bar X\) is the mean of 15 iid observations from some population with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Using the CLT, describe the approximate distribution of \(\bar X\), and then explain how doubling the sample size would change the spread of that distribution.
rubric_items: Full credit: States approximate distribution \(N(\mu,\sigma^2/15)\).; Correctly updates variance and standard deviation when n doubles.; Explains that the center does not change.
Partial credit: Gets the variance scaling right but confuses variance and standard deviation.; States the form correctly with weak interpretation.

Common mistakes: Saying variance halves and standard deviation also halves.; Using sum distribution parameters instead of mean distribution parameters.; Claiming the mean changes when sample size changes.

questions.text: Imagine you are advising a team that wants to approximate a count distribution. They tell you only that the count is the sum of many Bernoulli trials. Ask them the minimum follow-up questions you would need to decide between a Normal approximation, a Poisson approximation, or neither, and explain why each question matters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Asks about n, p or probability regime, and independence/dependence.; Explains why each affects Normal vs Poisson suitability.; Acknowledges that neither approximation may be appropriate if assumptions fail.
Partial credit: Asks about n and p but not dependence.; Explains one approximation regime well but not the other.
Common mistakes: Choosing an approximation without asking about p.; Ignoring dependence or heterogeneous success probabilities.; Assuming CLT alone answers model choice.

questions.text: A student reports: 'I used the CLT for the sample mean, so I modeled \(\bar X\) as \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\).' Critique this statement. Why is it a serious mistake even if the student correctly remembered the center?
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the missing division by n in the variance.; Explains why averaging reduces variability.; States the practical consequence of overstating uncertainty.
Partial credit: Corrects the formula without much explanation.; Mentions standard error but not variance explicitly.

Common mistakes: Confusing the distribution of one observation with distribution of the sample mean.; Dividing standard deviation by n instead of sqrt(n).; Treating center as the only thing that matters.

questions.text: A classmate says, “The Central Limit Theorem means the original random variable becomes Normal once the sample size is large.” Respond to that claim using the distinction between the distribution of individual observations, the sum, and the sample mean. Then explain what assumptions are actually needed for the usual CLT statement discussed in class.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly rejects the statement that the original distribution becomes Normal.; Correctly distinguishes among distribution of Xi, distribution of the sum, and distribution of the sample mean.; States the approximate Normal parameters for sum and/or mean.; Mentions key assumptions: iid or at least independence with the standard course statement, and finite mean/variance.

Partial credit: Says CLT applies to averages or sums but does not clearly distinguish this from the original variable.; Mentions only one of sum or sample mean correctly.; Gives the right intuition but omits assumptions.
Common mistakes: Claiming the population itself becomes Normal.; Using the wrong variance for the sample mean, such as sigma^2 instead of sigma^2/n.; Forgetting the independence assumption.

questions.text: Suppose X1, ..., Xn are iid Bernoulli(p), so their sum X is Binomial(n, p). For n = 100 and p = 0.5, explain how you would approximate P(X \u2265 65) using the CLT, including whether a continuity correction is needed and why. Then contrast that with n = 100 and p = 0.04: if you had to choose between a Normal approximation and a Poisson approximation to the Binomial, which would you choose and why?
rubric_items: Full credit: Represents Binomial as a sum of iid Bernoulli variables and invokes CLT correctly.; States mean np and variance np(1-p).; Uses the continuity correction correctly for P(X \u2265 65) as P(Y \u2265 64.5).; Computes or describes the z-score setup correctly.; Gives a reasoned comparison between Normal and Poisson for n = 100, p = 0.04.

Partial credit: Gets the Normal parameters right but forgets the continuity correction.; Uses continuity correction but in the wrong direction.; Recognizes that p = 0.04 is a rare-event regime but gives only a partial justification for choosing Poisson or Normal.

Common mistakes: Approximating P(X \u2265 65) by P(Y \u2265 65) instead of 64.5.; Using variance np instead of np(1-p) for the Binomial.; Saying CLT always implies Normal is best, without discussing regime or the discrete correction.

questions.text: In lecture, the sum of iid Uniform(0,1) variables was used to test how good the CLT approximation is. A student says, “You should not use the CLT until n is at least 30, so using it at n = 2 or n = 5 is invalid.” Evaluate that statement carefully. Use the Uniform example to explain what is true, what is too rigid, and how symmetry of the underlying distribution affects the quality of the approximation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that n \u2265 30 is a rule of thumb, not a requirement of the theorem.; Uses the Uniform example to support the argument with comparative reasoning across n values.; Notes that approximation quality depends on the original distribution's shape, especially symmetry/skewness.; Distinguishes between 'allowed to approximate' and 'guaranteed exact.'

Partial credit: States that n = 30 is only a heuristic but does not explain why.; Mentions symmetry helps without connecting it to the Uniform example.; Describes the example qualitatively but omits the idea that CLT is still approximate.
Common mistakes: Saying CLT is invalid for all n < 30.; Saying CLT gives exact Normality for finite n.; Ignoring the role of the underlying distribution.

questions.text: You are comparing two independent groups, each consisting of 20 observations drawn iid from the same population with mean 0.5 and variance v. Let X-bar_1 and X-bar_2 be the two sample means. Use the CLT to give an approximate distribution for D = X-bar_1 - X-bar_2, and then explain how you would determine a threshold k such that observing |D| \u2265 k would be considered statistically significant at the 5% level in a two-sided sense.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the approximate Normal distribution of each sample mean.; Correctly derives D as approximately Normal with mean 0 and variance v/10.; Explains that independence implies variances add.; Correctly sets the two-sided significance condition and identifies the 97.5th percentile.

Partial credit: Gets the distribution of D mostly right but makes a minor variance slip.; Recognizes that the test is two-sided but uses the wrong quantile without explanation.; States k in terms of a z critical value but does not fully justify it.
Common mistakes: Using variance v/20 for D instead of v/10.; Using 1.645 instead of 1.96 for a two-sided 5% threshold.; Subtracting variances instead of adding them.

questions.text: A data scientist says, “Normal distributions are everywhere because most real variables are inherently Gaussian.” Give a more careful explanation, using the CLT, of why Normal models appear so often in practice. Your answer should distinguish between modeling a raw variable directly and modeling a quantity built from many contributions or a sample average.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses CLT to explain why sums/averages often look Normal.; Distinguishes aggregate quantities from raw variables.; Mentions that Normality of a raw variable may be an assumption rather than a theorem.; Provides at least one caveat or counterexample type, such as skewed or bounded data.

Partial credit: Mentions the CLT vaguely without connecting it to sums or means.; Says Normal is common in practice but gives limited nuance.; Provides caveats but does not tie them to the CLT explanation.

Common mistakes: Claiming CLT proves any real-world variable is Normal.; Failing to distinguish a sample mean from the underlying population variable.; Saying Normal is always the best model regardless of context.

questions.text: A student says, “Conditional expectation is just the usual expectation, except you compute it after plugging in Y=y. So E[X|Y=y] is a number, but E[E[X|Y]] makes no sense because you are taking expectation of an expectation.” How would you respond, and how does this connect to the law of total expectation?
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that E[X|Y=y] is a scalar for fixed y.; Explains that E[X|Y] is a function of Y, hence a random variable.; States or justifies E[X]=E[E[X|Y]].; Interprets the theorem as averaging conditional means over the distribution of Y.
Partial credit: States the theorem correctly but does not explain why E[X|Y] is a random variable.; Explains the difference between E[X|Y=y] and E[X|Y] but gives only an informal LOTe statement.
Common mistakes: Saying E[X|Y] is always a number rather than a random variable.; Confusing E[X|Y] with E[Y|X].; Treating the outer expectation as unnecessary duplication.

questions.text: A factory has two machine states. Let Y=0 denote normal operation with probability 0.8 and Y=1 denote misalignment with probability 0.2. The number of defects in the next hour is X, with E[X|Y=0]=1.5 and E[X|Y=1]=6. Without knowing the full distribution of X, compute E[X] and explain why your method is valid.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up E[X]=sum_y E[X|Y=y]P(Y=y).; Computes 2.4 correctly.; Explains that full distribution of X is unnecessary because of the law of total expectation.
Partial credit: Correct arithmetic with incomplete explanation.; Correct formula but minor arithmetic slip.
Common mistakes: Averaging 1.5 and 6 equally instead of weighting by probabilities.; Claiming independence is needed.; Using P(X|Y) notation incorrectly in place of expectation.

questions.text: Someone claims that linearity fails for conditional expectation unless the random variables are independent. They point to E[X+Z|Y=y] and say dependence between X and Z should break the rule. Is that claim correct? Defend your answer carefully.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that linearity holds even under dependence.; Gives the correct linearity formula for conditional expectation.; Explains that independence is not needed for expectation of sums.
Partial credit: States the result correctly but explanation is vague.; Mentions linearity of ordinary expectation and extends it informally to conditional expectation.
Common mistakes: Claiming dependence breaks linearity.; Confusing E[XZ|Y] with E[X|Y]E[Z|Y].; Saying all conditional expectation rules require independence.

questions.text: You roll two fair six-sided dice. Let X be the first die and let Y be the sum of the two dice. Without writing the full joint PMF table, explain how you would compute E[X|Y=8], and then use symmetry or conditioning to evaluate it. After that, explain how the law of total expectation predicts E[X] from these conditional means.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies the conditional sample space for Y=8.; Computes E[X|Y=8]=4.; Uses symmetry to state E[X|Y=s]=s/2.; Uses law of total expectation to recover E[X]=3.5.
Partial credit: Gets E[X|Y=8]=4 but does not connect to LOTe.; Uses LOTe correctly but symmetry argument is incomplete.
Common mistakes: Including impossible outcomes like (1,7).; Assuming X and Y are independent.; Claiming E[X|Y=s]=E[X]=3.5 for all s.

questions.text: Give an oral proof sketch of the law of total expectation in the discrete case. Start from E[E[X|Y]] and justify each step until you reach E[X]. I care more about the logic of the manipulations than about exact notation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from E[E[X|Y]].; Uses E[g(Y)] as a weighted sum over y.; Substitutes the conditional expectation definition.; Uses chain rule P(X=x|Y=y)P(Y=y)=P(X=x,Y=y).; Marginalizes to obtain E[X].
Partial credit: Knows the outline but omits one justification step.; States theorem with intuitive partition argument but not full algebra.
Common mistakes: Replacing P(X=x|Y=y)P(Y=y) with P(X=x)P(Y=y).; Forgetting to weight by P(Y=y).; Not recognizing E[X|Y] as a function of Y.

questions.text: A random variable Y takes values 1, 2, and 4 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3. Another random variable X satisfies E[X|Y=y]=2y+1. Compute E[X] without finding the distribution of X, and explain why this is an application of both conditional expectation and LOTUS.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes E[X|Y]=2Y+1.; Applies E[X]=E[E[X|Y]].; Uses linearity to compute 2E[Y]+1.; Computes 5.8 correctly.
Partial credit: Correct setup with arithmetic slip.; Computes E[Y] correctly but does not clearly connect to LOTUS/LOTE.
Common mistakes: Plugging in a single y instead of treating 2Y+1 as a random variable.; Averaging 2y+1 values without probability weights.; Thinking the formula requires independence.

questions.text: A classmate says, “Because conditioning gives you more information, E[X|Y=y] should always be larger than E[X].” Give a counterexample or a general argument showing why this statement is wrong.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that conditioning does not necessarily increase expectation.; Provides a correct counterexample or uses LOTe to refute the claim.; Explains that conditional means may be above or below the unconditional mean.
Partial credit: Gives an intuitive rebuttal without a precise example.; Provides example but explanation is incomplete.

Common mistakes: Arguing only from 'more information' without mathematics.; Confusing expectation with variance or uncertainty reduction.; Claiming conditional expectation is monotone in information in the sense of always increasing.

questions.text: A website shows either a simple layout or a premium layout. Let Y indicate the layout, with P(Y=simple)=0.7 and P(Y=premium)=0.3. Let X be time on page in seconds, and suppose E[X|Y=simple]=40 while E[X|Y=premium]=65. A product manager claims the expected time on page must be at least 65 because premium is the better layout. Critique that reasoning and compute the correct expectation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the manager's claim.; Uses weighted averaging of conditional means.; Computes 47.5 correctly.; States that the result lies between the conditional means.
Partial credit: Correct computation with weak verbal critique.; Good critique but arithmetic mistake.

Common mistakes: Taking the larger conditional expectation as the overall expectation.; Using equal weights instead of 0.7 and 0.3.; Saying the mean must exceed both because conditioning adds information.

questions.text: A student says: “If I know the function g(y)=E[X\mid Y=y], then I have not really learned anything about X itself, only about a new random variable g(Y). So there is no reason that E[g(Y)] should equal E[X].” Do you agree or disagree? Explain carefully using the discrete definitions of conditional expectation and the chain rule, not just by quoting the law of total expectation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that the claim is false/disagrees.; Explains that E[X\mid Y] is a random variable depending on Y.; Expands E[E[X\mid Y]] as a weighted sum over y.; Substitutes the definition of conditional expectation and uses the chain rule to get the joint pmf.; Marginalizes over y to conclude E[X].

Partial credit: Correctly states the law of total expectation without proof.; Gives an intuitive averaging explanation but omits one algebraic step.; Uses the chain rule or marginalization correctly but not both.
Common mistakes: Treating E[X\mid Y=y] as a constant unrelated to Y.; Saying E[X\mid Y]=E[X] for all Y.; Forgetting the weighting by P(Y=y).; Confusing P(X=x\mid Y=y) with P(Y=y\mid X=x).

questions.text: A box contains red and blue balls. First a random variable Y is generated, where Y is the number of red balls placed into a small sample you will inspect: P(Y=0)=1/4, P(Y=1)=1/2, P(Y=2)=1/4. Given Y=y, you then draw one ball uniformly from those two inspected balls, and let X be the indicator that the chosen ball is red. Compute E[X] in two different ways: first using conditional expectation given Y, and second by reasoning directly from linearity or weighted averaging. Then interpret what E[X] means in this setting.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes X as an indicator and interprets E[X] as a probability.; Computes E[X\mid Y=0], E[X\mid Y=1], E[X\mid Y=2] correctly.; Uses law of total expectation correctly to get 1/2.; Provides a second method using E[X\mid Y]=Y/2 and linearity to get the same answer.; Gives a correct interpretation of the result.
Partial credit: Gets the conditional expectations right but makes an arithmetic slip.; Uses only one valid method instead of two.; Identifies that E[X]=P(X=1) but gives incomplete conditioning steps.

Common mistakes: Treating E[X\mid Y=y] as y rather than y/2.; Averaging 0,1/2,1 equally instead of weighting by P(Y=y).; Assuming independence where none is needed.; Forgetting that the expectation of an indicator equals a probability.

questions.text: Two students are discussing conditional expectation. Student A says, “Because expectation is linear, E[X\mid Y=y]=E[X] for every y.” Student B says, “No, linearity means E[aX+bW\mid Y=y]=aE[X\mid Y=y]+bE[W\mid Y=y], but conditioning can still change the value.” Who is right? Defend your answer with a concrete example and explain what linearity does and does not imply.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies Student B as correct.; States the correct linearity property for conditional expectation.; Provides a valid counterexample showing E[X\mid Y=y] can differ from E[X].; Explains that equality with E[X] requires additional assumptions such as independence.

Partial credit: Correct conclusion but weak or incomplete example.; Good example but does not clearly separate linearity from independence.; States independence is relevant but does not articulate why.

Common mistakes: Agreeing with Student A because 'expectation averages things out'.; Giving the unconditional linearity rule instead of the conditional one.; Claiming dependence is required for conditioning to matter, instead of saying independence is sufficient for no change.; Using an example where E[X\mid Y=y] accidentally equals E[X] for all y and thinking it proves the general rule.

questions.text: A company tracks customer spending X and customer segment Y, where Y can be Budget, Standard, or Premium. The analyst knows only the conditional means: E[X\mid Y=Budget]=20, E[X\mid Y=Standard]=50, E[X\mid Y=Premium]=120, and the segment probabilities are 0.5, 0.4, and 0.1 respectively. Explain how to compute the overall expected spending E[X], and then explain why this calculation is valid even if spending behavior within each segment is highly variable and the joint distribution is otherwise unknown.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up E[X]=\sum_y P(Y=y)E[X\mid Y=y].; Computes the value 42 correctly.; Explains the weighted-average interpretation.; Justifies why full within-segment distributions are unnecessary for computing the mean.; Connects reasoning to law of total expectation rather than an ad hoc average.
Partial credit: Correct formula with arithmetic error.; Correct arithmetic but weak explanation of why the method is valid.; Good intuition but no explicit weighting by segment probabilities.

Common mistakes: Averaging 20, 50, and 120 equally.; Thinking high variance prevents computation of E[X].; Claiming the method requires X and Y to be independent.; Confusing E[X\mid Y] with P(Y\mid X).

questions.text: In a proof, someone writes E[X]=\sum_x\sum_y x\,P(X=x,Y=y), then claims this is ‘basically the same’ as \sum_y P(Y=y)E[X\mid Y=y]. Give a careful oral explanation of why these two expressions are equal. Your explanation should mention which step uses conditional probability, which step uses the chain rule, and which step uses marginalization or switching sums.
rubric_items: Full credit: Begins from one expression and transforms it systematically into the other.; Correctly invokes the definition of conditional expectation.; Correctly identifies the chain rule step converting conditional times marginal into joint.; Mentions switching the order of summation and marginalization.; Ends at E[X]=\sum_x xP(X=x).

Partial credit: Understands the overall equivalence but omits one named step.; Gives a mostly correct derivation with notation slightly imprecise.; Uses intuition about weighted averages without fully connecting to the joint pmf.

Common mistakes: Skipping from conditional to unconditional expectation without weighting by P(Y=y).; Using Bayes’ rule unnecessarily or incorrectly.; Marginalizing the wrong variable.; Treating x as if it depended on y in the summation step.

questions.text: A student says, “Conditional probability just means dividing by the thing you condition on, so it’s basically a computational trick.” Respond to that claim using the idea of sample-space restriction. Then explain why independence is exactly the special case where conditioning does not change the sample space in any meaningful way.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains conditioning as restricting the sample space to F; States and interprets P(E|F)=P(E∩F)/P(F); Connects independence to P(E|F)=P(E); Gives conceptual justification, not just formulas
Partial credit: Gives correct formula but weak interpretation; Mentions independence correctly without explaining why conditioning has no effect
Common mistakes: Saying P(E|F)=P(E)/P(F); Confusing independence with mutual exclusivity; Failing to mention that P(F) must be positive

questions.text: A university runs two entrance gates to a stadium. Forty percent of attendees use Gate A and sixty percent use Gate B. Security flags 5% of people at Gate A and 2% at Gate B for extra screening. A randomly chosen attendee was flagged. What is the probability they came through Gate A, and what does that number mean in words?
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines relevant events clearly; Uses law of total probability for denominator; Applies Bayes correctly; Interprets posterior in words
Partial credit: Correct setup but arithmetic slip; Gets denominator right but does not interpret result
Common mistakes: Using P(A|F)=P(F|A); Forgetting to weight by gate proportions; Conditioning on the wrong event

questions.text: Someone argues: “If a disease test is 99% accurate, then a person who tests positive has a 99% chance of having the disease.” Give a careful response using Bayes’ rule, and explain what extra information is missing from that statement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes P(+|D) from P(D|+); States need for prior/base rate; Mentions denominator includes all ways to test positive; Explains rarity effect qualitatively
Partial credit: Notes the conditional reversal but gives limited explanation; Mentions base rate without connecting to denominator
Common mistakes: Equating sensitivity with posterior probability; Ignoring false positives; Claiming accuracy alone is enough

questions.text: You flip a biased coin: with probability 0.7 it lands heads. If heads, you draw one card from Deck H containing 3 red and 1 black card. If tails, you draw one card from Deck T containing 1 red and 3 black cards. You observe that the card is red. What is the probability the coin landed heads, and how would you explain this as prior, likelihood, and posterior?
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies prior, likelihood, posterior correctly; Computes denominator via total probability; Obtains 0.875; Explains why posterior increases
Partial credit: Correct Bayes setup but arithmetic slip; Gets numerical answer with little interpretation
Common mistakes: Using 0.7 directly as posterior; Neglecting the tails-red path in denominator; Reversing P(R|H) and P(H|R)

questions.text: Derive Bayes’ theorem aloud starting from the definition of conditional probability, but do not just quote the result. Your derivation should make clear why the denominator is a normalization constant, and why the theorem requires positive probability for the conditioned events.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses both conditional-probability definitions correctly; Substitutes through the joint probability; Explains denominator as normalization; States positivity conditions and why they matter
Partial credit: States Bayes with a partial derivation; Gives formula but weak normalization explanation
Common mistakes: Claiming Bayes is independent of P(E); Failing to mention positivity assumptions; Treating normalization as optional

questions.text: A job candidate may come from one of three training programs: A, B, or C, with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2. The probability of passing a technical screen is 0.8 for A, 0.6 for B, and 0.3 for C. A candidate passed the screen. Compute the probability they came from program B, and explain how the law of total probability enters the calculation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes A, B, C as partition; Computes total pass probability correctly; Applies Bayes to get 0.28125; Explains role of total probability
Partial credit: Correct setup with arithmetic error; Computes P(P) but misinterprets final answer
Common mistakes: Dividing by 0.3 instead of P(P); Ignoring one of the programs in denominator; Assuming equal weighting among programs

questions.text: A student claims that if two events are disjoint, then they must also be independent because they “do not affect each other.” Evaluate this claim carefully, including any exceptional case.
rubric_items: Full credit: States claim is false except zero-probability edge case; Uses P(E∩F)=0 vs P(E)P(F) reasoning; Explains intuitive dependence
Partial credit: Says false but gives only intuition; Mentions formulas without exceptional case
Common mistakes: Confusing disjointness with independence; Ignoring zero-probability exception; Saying 'not affecting each other' implies disjointness

questions.text: A company’s spam filter uses the word “Dear” as one signal. Suppose 60% of all incoming emails are spam, 20% of spam emails contain “Dear,” and 1% of non-spam emails contain “Dear.” An email contains “Dear.” What is the probability it is spam, and why might someone initially guess the wrong direction?
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up Bayes correctly; Calculates denominator correctly; Gets posterior about 0.968; Explains misconception using likelihood comparison and prior
Partial credit: Correct formula with arithmetic slip; Gets answer but weak explanation of intuition
Common mistakes: Reporting 0.2 as the posterior; Ignoring non-spam contribution in denominator; Thinking a small likelihood automatically means a small posterior

questions.text: Explain the chain rule for three events by telling a story of information revealed sequentially. Then contrast it with the law of total probability, which combines mutually exclusive alternatives. I want to hear not just formulas but when each tool is the natural one to use.
rubric_items: Full credit: States chain rule for three events; States total probability over a partition; Explains sequential vs alternative-case viewpoints; Indicates when each is used
Partial credit: Provides formulas with limited interpretation; Explains one tool well but not the contrast
Common mistakes: Using chain rule where partitioning is needed; Thinking total probability requires independence; Forgetting disjointness in the partition

questions.text: A machine component is manufactured on one of two lines. Line 1 makes 30% of components and produces a defect with probability 4%; Line 2 makes 70% and produces a defect with probability 1%. If a component is found defective, compute the probability it came from Line 1. Then compare that posterior to the prior and explain the direction of the change.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correct Bayes setup; Correct weighted denominator; Computes about 0.632; Explains posterior increases because defect is more likely under Line 1
Partial credit: Correct setup but arithmetic error; States posterior is larger than prior without good explanation
Common mistakes: Using 0.04/(0.04+0.01) without priors; Confusing prior with posterior; Ignoring production proportions

questions.text: Suppose someone writes, for events E and F, 'Since P(E)=P(E|F)P(F), we can always recover unconditional probabilities by multiplying a conditional probability by the probability of the condition.' Diagnose the mistake and repair the statement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies P(E|F)P(F)=P(E∩F); Explains why this is not usually P(E); Repairs using law of total probability; Uses language of joint vs marginal
Partial credit: Spots that statement is wrong but not why; Mentions complement case without formula
Common mistakes: Saying formula is correct only if E and F independent; Forgetting the F^c term; Confusing intersection with conditioning

questions.text: You are told a game works as follows: first choose a bag by rolling a fair die. On 1–4 you use Bag X, on 5–6 you use Bag Y. Bag X contains 1 gold and 4 silver coins; Bag Y contains 3 gold and 2 silver coins. You draw a gold coin. What is the probability you were using Bag Y?
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses correct priors from die outcomes; Uses correct bag likelihoods; Applies Bayes to obtain 3/5; Explains evidence shifts belief toward Y
Partial credit: Correct setup with arithmetic slip; Gets answer but not interpretation
Common mistakes: Treating bags as equally likely; Using P(Y|G)=P(G|Y)=3/5 without Bayes; Ignoring Bag X in denominator

questions.text: In discrete and continuous settings, Bayes’ theorem appears with probabilities, PMFs, or PDFs. Explain what stays the same across all three versions, and what changes in interpretation when moving to continuous random variables.
rubric_items: Full credit: States common posterior-prior-likelihood-normalizer structure; Distinguishes events/PMFs/PDFs; Explains that densities at points are not probabilities; Mentions normalization role in continuous case
Partial credit: Knows formulas but weak interpretation of densities; Explains continuous case vaguely
Common mistakes: Saying P(X=x)>0 for continuous X in general; Treating a density value as a probability; Failing to mention normalization

questions.text: A hidden state Z can be 1, 2, or 3 with prior probabilities 0.2, 0.5, and 0.3. Given Z=z, a sensor reports success S with probabilities 0.9, 0.4, and 0.2 respectively. After observing success, rank the three posterior probabilities from largest to smallest and compute the exact posterior for Z=2.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes evidence 0.44; Computes posterior for Z=2 as 5/11; Ranks posterior probabilities via weighted likelihoods; Explains denominator is common to all categories
Partial credit: Correct ranking but numerical error; Correct posterior computation but no ranking explanation
Common mistakes: Ranking by likelihood alone and ignoring priors; Using priors alone; Forgetting to normalize

questions.text: A classmate says, “Since P(F|E)=P(E|F)P(F)/P(E), if P(E|F) is big then P(F|E) must also be big.” Is that always true? Give a counterexample structure or explain the conditions under which the intuition fails.
rubric_items: Full credit: States claim is false in general; Explains dependence on prior and normalization term; Provides or describes a counterexample structure; Distinguishes likelihood from posterior
Partial credit: Says false but explanation is vague; Mentions base rate without discussing denominator
Common mistakes: Assuming likelihood monotonicity guarantees large posterior; Ignoring prior rarity; Confusing P(E|F) with P(F|E)

questions.text: At a school, 15% of students are in the robotics club. Among robotics members, 70% know Python; among non-members, 20% know Python. A randomly chosen student knows Python. What is the chance they are in robotics, and what verbal explanation would you give a nontechnical audience?
rubric_items: Full credit: Correct Bayes setup; Correct denominator and posterior ≈0.382; Provides nontechnical interpretation balancing prior and likelihood
Partial credit: Correct setup but arithmetic slip; Correct number with weak interpretation
Common mistakes: Answering 70%; Ignoring non-members who know Python; Misreading 15% as posterior

questions.text: Suppose F1, F2, ..., Fk form a partition of the sample space. Explain how Bayes’ theorem and the law of total probability fit together into one coherent update procedure after observing event E. I want a response that emphasizes both the numerator and the denominator conceptually.
rubric_items: Full credit: States Bayes over partition elements; Uses total probability for denominator; Explains numerator as prior×likelihood; Explains normalization over competing hypotheses
Partial credit: Provides formulas without conceptual explanation; Explains numerator or denominator well, but not both
Common mistakes: Forgetting partition requirement; Treating denominator as arbitrary constant rather than total evidence probability; Not noting posteriors sum to 1

questions.text: A website has two traffic sources: ads and search. Thirty percent of visitors come from ads and seventy percent from search. The purchase rate is 12% for ad visitors and 4% for search visitors. If a random visitor made a purchase, what is the probability they came from ads? Then say whether purchases are disproportionately coming from ads relative to their share of traffic.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correct Bayes setup; Correct posterior 0.5625; Compares posterior share to prior traffic share; Interprets disproportionate contribution
Partial credit: Correct calculation without interpretation; Minor arithmetic error with correct setup
Common mistakes: Reporting 12%; Ignoring source proportions; Interpreting posterior as purchase rate

questions.text: A student says: 'If a medical test is 99% accurate, then a person who tests positive has a 99% chance of having the disease.' Give a careful response using conditional probability notation. Your explanation should distinguish between the probability the test is positive given disease and the probability of disease given a positive test, and say what extra information is needed to connect them.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly distinguishes P(positive | disease) from P(disease | positive).; States that the conditioning changes the sample space.; Uses Bayes' rule correctly and identifies the need for a prior/base rate and false positive information.; Mentions law of total probability for the denominator or explains how P(positive) is obtained.

Partial credit: Recognizes the two probabilities are different but gives only an informal explanation.; States Bayes' rule but does not explain the denominator.; Mentions prevalence/base rate without clearly connecting it to the formula.

Common mistakes: Claiming the two conditional probabilities are equal.; Ignoring false positives in the denominator.; Saying 'accuracy' alone is sufficient without clarifying prevalence or test characteristics.

questions.text: A website has two traffic sources. Forty percent of visitors come from ads and sixty percent come from organic search. Among ad visitors, 8% make a purchase; among organic visitors, 3% make a purchase. A visitor just made a purchase. Compute the probability they came from ads, and explain each step as a change from prior belief to posterior belief.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines events clearly.; Applies Bayes' rule with correct numerator.; Computes P(B) via law of total probability.; Obtains 0.64 and interprets it as posterior versus prior.
Partial credit: Correct setup but arithmetic error.; Gets numerator right but denominator incomplete.; Computes P(purchase) correctly but does not finish the Bayes step.
Common mistakes: Using P(A | B)=P(B | A).; Forgetting to weight by source proportions in the denominator.; Conditioning on the wrong event or reversing ad and purchase.

questions.text: You are told events E and F are independent. A classmate concludes that conditioning on E never changes any probability, so for every event G, P(G | E) = P(G). Is that conclusion valid? Give a careful argument, including either a proof under stronger assumptions or a counterexample showing why the statement as given is too broad.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that independence is pairwise and event-specific.; Explains that P(F | E)=P(F) only for events independent of E.; Provides a valid counterexample such as G=E.; Identifies the corrected statement: if G and E are independent, then conditioning on E does not change G's probability.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false but gives only an informal reason.; Mentions pairwise independence without a concrete example.; Provides a counterexample but does not connect it back to conditional probability.

Common mistakes: Claiming independence of one pair implies independence with all events.; Using G=F as the only example without explaining why that case is special.; Confusing mutual exclusivity with independence.

questions.text: A game works as follows: first flip a biased coin that lands Heads with probability 0.3. If Heads, you draw one card uniformly from deck H, which contains 3 red and 1 blue card. If Tails, you draw one card uniformly from deck T, which contains 1 red and 3 blue cards. You observe that the card drawn is red. What is the probability the coin landed Heads, and why is the law of total probability essential in your reasoning?
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines relevant events and target posterior.; Uses Bayes' rule correctly.; Computes P(R) with the law of total probability over Heads and Tails.; Gets 0.5625 and explains the denominator as combining mutually exclusive cases.
Partial credit: Correct conceptual setup but arithmetic error.; Finds P(R) correctly but does not finish posterior.; Uses an intuitive explanation of reweighting without full notation.
Common mistakes: Using only P(R | H) in the denominator.; Forgetting that Tails also can produce a red card.; Confusing P(H | R) with P(R | H).

questions.text: For three events A, B, and C with positive probability, derive an expression for P(A ∩ B ∩ C) using the chain rule, and then explain how you would rewrite P(A | C) if B and B^c form a partition of the sample space. I am not asking for numbers; I want the structure of the reasoning and why each factor or term appears.
rubric_items: Full credit: States a correct chain-rule factorization for P(A ∩ B ∩ C).; Recognizes B and B^c as a partition and decomposes A ∩ C into disjoint pieces.; Derives P(A | C)=P(A | B,C)P(B | C)+P(A | B^c,C)P(B^c | C).; Explains that conditioning on C changes the sample space but the same probability rules still apply.
Partial credit: Correct chain rule but incomplete conditional decomposition.; States law of total probability without conditioning on C explicitly.; Uses correct intuition but weak notation.
Common mistakes: Writing P(A | C)=P(A | B)P(B)+P(A | B^c)P(B^c), forgetting the conditioning on C throughout.; Dropping one of the partition terms.; Treating A, B, C as automatically independent.
