questions.text: A classmate says: 'For continuous random variables, the probability at a point is always zero, so the joint PDF value at a point is meaningless.' Do you agree? Explain carefully using the idea of probability as volume under a surface, and comment on what information the ratio of two PDF values can still convey.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that point probability is zero for continuous variables.; Explains that joint probabilities come from double integrals over regions.; Clarifies that the PDF is a density, not a probability.; Explains the local-neighborhood or ratio interpretation of PDF values.

Partial credit: Says PDF is not probability but gives no geometric explanation.; Mentions local likelihood informally without tying it to small regions.; Correctly rejects the statement but does not explain ratios.
Common mistakes: Saying f_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X=a,Y=b).; Claiming density values are meaningless because point probabilities are zero.; Confusing relative density with exact probability at a point.

questions.text: Suppose a proposed joint density is g(x,y)=cxy on the rectangle 0<=x<=1, 0<=y<=2, and 0 elsewhere. Without rushing to the final number, explain how you would determine c, and then describe in words what the shape of this density says about where probability is concentrated.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up normalization via a double integral over the support.; Correctly concludes c=1.; Interprets increasing density in both coordinates.; Distinguishes density concentration from point probability.
Partial credit: Gets c=1 but gives little reasoning.; Correct setup with minor integration slip but sound method.; Gives qualitative interpretation without mentioning support.
Common mistakes: Integrating over the wrong bounds.; Treating g(x,y) itself as a probability over the rectangle.; Forgetting that the density is zero outside the support.

questions.text: For the joint PDF f(x,y)=xy on 0<=x<=1 and 0<=y<=2, compute the marginal density of X and then use it to check whether X and Y are independent. I care more about the logic than the algebra alone, so explain what independence would require.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes f_X(x)=2x and f_Y(y)=y/2 on correct supports.; States the criterion f_{X,Y}=f_X f_Y.; Verifies equality on the support and concludes independence.; Mentions support appropriately.
Partial credit: Correct marginals but weak or incomplete independence check.; States independence criterion but only checks one marginal.; Minor arithmetic slip with otherwise correct logic.

Common mistakes: Claiming dependence because the formula contains both x and y.; Forgetting to specify where the marginals are nonzero.; Checking only whether the support is rectangular, without comparing densities.

questions.text: A student tries to get the marginal of X from a joint PDF by computing f_X(a)=integral from minus infinity to a of f_{X,Y}(x,y) dx. Diagnose the mistake. Then say what must happen to the other variable and why the operation for marginals differs from the operation for CDFs.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies confusion between marginal density and CDF.; Gives the correct marginal formula integrating over the other variable.; Explains that the target x-value is held fixed.; Contrasts region integration for CDFs with variable-elimination for marginals.
Partial credit: Provides correct marginal formula without diagnosing the conceptual error.; Says 'integrate over y' but does not explain why.; Mentions CDF vaguely but not the difference in bounds.
Common mistakes: Using cumulative bounds when asked for a density.; Integrating over the same variable being marginalized.; Confusing f_X(a) with P(X<=a).

questions.text: Explain how the joint CDF and joint PDF are related for jointly continuous variables. Then describe, in words, how you would recover P(a1<=X<=a2, b1<=Y<=b2) using either object, and why the two approaches must agree.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the joint CDF as a probability over a lower-left region.; States that the CDF is the double integral of the PDF.; States that the PDF is the mixed partial derivative of the CDF.; Explains rectangle probability via either double integral or corner-value inclusion-exclusion, and notes equivalence.

Partial credit: Knows one direction, such as integrating PDF to get CDF, but not the derivative relation.; Can describe rectangle probability using only one approach.; Uses correct intuition but imprecise calculus language.

Common mistakes: Saying the PDF is the ordinary derivative of the joint CDF in one variable only.; Forgetting that CDF is a probability and PDF is a density.; Using point evaluations of the PDF instead of region integrals.

questions.text: Let X be the fraction of a battery charge remaining at noon and Y be the fraction remaining at 6pm. A modeler proposes a joint density that is positive only when 0<=y<=x<=1. Without doing any heavy computation, explain what this support is encoding about the relationship between X and Y, and why such a support already suggests that X and Y cannot be independent unless something degenerate happens.
rubric_items: Full credit: Interprets the triangular support as a deterministic constraint.; Explains why the shape of support matters for independence.; Notes that independence typically corresponds to product structure over a rectangular support.; Mentions the degenerate-exception idea appropriately.

Partial credit: Recognizes that Y<=X implies some dependence but does not connect it to support geometry.; Explains the physical meaning but not the independence implication.; Mentions triangle vs rectangle without justification.

Common mistakes: Saying dependence can only be checked from formulas, not support.; Claiming any non-rectangular support automatically proves dependence without caveat.; Ignoring the meaning of y<=x in context.

questions.text: Suppose f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2 on the triangle 0<y<x<1 and 0 elsewhere. Find the marginal density of X, then describe verbally how its shape reflects the geometry of the support. After that, say whether X and Y are independent and justify your answer without relying on a slogan.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes f_X(x)=2x on 0<x<1.; Connects the marginal shape to varying slice length in the triangle.; Correctly concludes non-independence using factorization failure or support reasoning.; Keeps support conditions clear.
Partial credit: Correct marginal but weak geometric explanation.; States non-independence from triangular support alone.; Minor boundary omission with correct main reasoning.
Common mistakes: Integrating y over 0 to 1 instead of 0 to x.; Forgetting the density is zero outside the triangle.; Claiming X and Y are independent because the density is constant on its support.

questions.text: In one dimension, students learn that F(a)=integral from minus infinity to a of f(x)dx. In two dimensions, a student says the analogous statement should be F(a,b)=integral from minus infinity to a of f_{X,Y}(x,b)dx. Explain why this is wrong, and give the correct geometric picture for the joint CDF.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies that a line integral cannot produce the probability of a 2D event.; Gives the correct event for the joint CDF.; Describes the lower-left region and volume-under-surface picture.; Explains the source of the misconception from 1D analogy.
Partial credit: Provides the correct formula but weak geometric explanation.; Says a double integral is needed without saying over what region.; Recognizes the student forgot to integrate over y.
Common mistakes: Treating the joint CDF as a single integral.; Confusing CDF at (a,b) with marginal CDF of X evaluated at a.; Using boundary values of y instead of integrating over y<=b.

questions.text: Someone claims: 'If two continuous random variables have marginals f_X and f_Y, then the joint density must be f_X(x)f_Y(y).' Give a counterargument that does not depend on a specific exotic formula. Explain what extra assumption would make the claim true.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that marginals alone do not determine the joint distribution.; Explains that dependence structure is missing.; States independence as the extra assumption needed for factorization.; Uses a coherent qualitative example or comparison.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false and mentions independence, but gives little justification.; Provides an example intuition without stating the general principle.; Confuses correlation with independence but still rejects the claim.
Common mistakes: Assuming the product form always holds.; Saying equal marginals imply identical joint behavior.; Using independence as if it were automatic for continuous variables.

questions.text: You model the arrival times of two buses, X and Y, measured in minutes after 8am. Suppose the joint density is uniform over the square 0<=x<=10, 0<=y<=10. A student says the probability that the buses arrive within one minute of each other should be zero because that condition is 'basically a line.' Evaluate that claim carefully.
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes X=Y from |X-Y|<=1.; Explains that the band has positive area while the line has zero area.; Uses uniform-density area reasoning correctly.; Highlights the continuous-model point-probability issue.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false but does not clearly separate line vs band.; Uses geometric language without connecting to probability.; Correct intuition but no explanation of why zero probability applies only to the line.

Common mistakes: Treating 'close to equal' as the same as 'equal.'; Claiming any event defined by an equation has positive probability automatically.; Forgetting probability under a uniform joint density is area divided by total area.

questions.text: Suppose you know the joint CDF F_{X,Y}(a,b). Describe how to compute P(X>a, Y>b) using only CDF values and logic about complements. Then explain why your formula differs from simply taking 1-F_{X,Y}(a,b).
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies the relevant complement event.; Uses inclusion-exclusion properly.; Expresses result using F_X, F_Y, and F_{X,Y}.; Explains why 1-F_{X,Y}(a,b) is too large.
Partial credit: Knows 1-F_{X,Y} is not enough but cannot derive full formula.; Gets the right idea with set language but weak notation.; Minor sign error with otherwise solid reasoning.
Common mistakes: Saying P(X>a,Y>b)=1-F_{X,Y}(a,b).; Forgetting marginal CDF terms.; Confusing 'and' with 'or' in the complement.

questions.text: Give a careful oral explanation of the conditional density formula f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y). Since P(Y=y)=0 for a continuous variable, why is this not nonsense? Your answer should connect the formula to conditioning on a very small interval around y.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that exact point conditioning is replaced by a limit over small intervals.; Uses the joint and marginal densities in the approximation.; States the requirement f_Y(y)>0.; Mentions that the resulting conditional density integrates to 1.

Partial credit: Recites the formula correctly but gives only heuristic justification.; Says 'it is a density ratio' without explaining the small-interval logic.; Mentions P(Y=y)=0 but does not resolve the issue.
Common mistakes: Saying we literally divide P(X=x,Y=y) by P(Y=y).; Ignoring the condition f_Y(y)>0.; Confusing conditional density with conditional probability at a point.

questions.text: Let f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2 on 0<y<x<1 and 0 elsewhere. Find f_{X|Y}(x|y), and then interpret what this says about the possible values of X once Y=y is known. Do not stop at the formula; explain the support of the conditional density.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes f_Y(y)=2(1-y).; Derives f_{X|Y}(x|y)=1/(1-y) on y<x<1.; Explains that the conditional distribution is uniform on (y,1).; Emphasizes the conditional support restriction.
Partial credit: Gets the formula but not the support.; Correct support idea with algebra slip in normalization.; States 'uniform' without computing f_Y(y).
Common mistakes: Using the unconditional support for X instead of conditional support.; Forgetting that x must exceed y.; Producing a conditional density that does not integrate to 1 over x.

questions.text: A student argues: 'If the joint PDF integrates to 1, then any cross-section like f_{X,Y}(x,1) must also integrate to 1 over x.' Explain why this is false, and clarify the difference between a cross-section of a joint density and a marginal or conditional density.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that a fixed-y slice is not generally a probability density by itself.; Distinguishes cross-section from marginal and conditional density.; Mentions integration over y for marginals.; Mentions normalization by f_Y(y) for conditionals.
Partial credit: Says the claim is false but gives only one of marginal/conditional distinctions.; Uses geometric intuition without formulas.; Correctly notes that slices need not integrate to 1.

Common mistakes: Assuming every nonnegative function obtained from a PDF is itself a PDF.; Confusing f_{X,Y}(x,y) at fixed y with f_{X|Y}(x|y).; Thinking normalization of the full joint density forces all slices to normalize.

questions.text: Imagine X and Y are two measurements of a machine part taken by different sensors. The engineer only gives you the marginal densities f_X and f_Y and asks for P(X<Y). Explain why you generally cannot answer from the marginals alone, and describe two different dependence stories that could lead to different answers while keeping the same marginals.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that P(X<Y) depends on the joint distribution.; Explains why marginals alone are insufficient.; Gives two qualitatively different dependence scenarios with same marginals.; Connects those scenarios to potentially different values of P(X<Y).
Partial credit: Correctly says 'need the joint' but gives limited intuition.; Provides only one dependence story.; Talks about correlation vaguely without explaining event probability.
Common mistakes: Assuming P(X<Y) can always be found from separate distributions.; Treating same marginals as same joint distribution.; Equating lack of information with independence by default.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent with densities f_X(x)=2x on 0<x<1 and f_Y(y)=1/2 on 0<y<2. First build the joint PDF. Then set up, and if you can compute, the probability P(Y>X). Explain any region-splitting you use.
rubric_items: Full credit: Forms the joint PDF as the product x on the correct support.; Sets up the region Y>X correctly.; Uses appropriate bounds and computes 2/3.; Explains why no additional split is needed here.
Partial credit: Correct setup but incomplete computation.; Gets the product form right but uses wrong event bounds.; Correct region description without finishing arithmetic.
Common mistakes: Multiplying supports incorrectly.; Integrating y from 0 to x instead of x to 2.; Forgetting that X is limited to (0,1), not (0,2).

questions.text: Compare the formulas for obtaining marginals in the discrete and continuous cases. I do not want just the formulas; explain what stays conceptually the same and what changes when sums become integrals.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the shared idea of eliminating the other variable by aggregating over all its values.; Gives the discrete summation formula.; Gives the continuous integration formula.; Explains why sums become integrals in terms of mass vs density.
Partial credit: Provides both formulas but little conceptual comparison.; Explains conceptually but forgets one formula.; Uses correct intuition with imprecise terminology.
Common mistakes: Saying continuous marginals are obtained by summing.; Confusing marginalization with conditioning.; Ignoring the role of density versus probability mass.

questions.text: A researcher defines T=X+Y for two independent continuous measurements. Without invoking any formula you memorized, explain how the distribution of T is obtained from the joint distribution of (X,Y). Your explanation should make clear why the set x+y=t leads to integration rather than plugging into the joint PDF at one point.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that many pairs (x,y) map to the same sum.; Describes computing P(X+Y<=t) by integrating over the region x+y<=t.; Uses independence to justify product joint density when relevant.; Connects this reasoning to convolution or derivative of the CDF.

Partial credit: Knows the word convolution but cannot explain the geometry.; Describes the region idea without linking to the sum variable.; Says 'integrate over all possibilities' without specifying the constraint x+y<=t.
Common mistakes: Trying to compute the density of T by evaluating f_{X,Y}(t,t).; Ignoring that infinitely many pairs can have the same sum.; Confusing the line x+y=t with a single point.

questions.text: A classmate says: 'Because f_{X|Y}(x|y) is obtained by dividing by f_Y(y), conditioning on Y=y should become impossible whenever P(Y=y)=0.' Give a concise rebuttal that distinguishes probability from density and mentions the correct regularity condition.
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes P(Y=y) from f_Y(y).; States that the continuous conditional is based on a density ratio or limiting argument.; Gives the correct condition f_Y(y)>0.; Rejects the claim clearly.
Partial credit: States the formula but not the conceptual distinction.; Mentions density vs probability without the condition.; Says the claim is false but gives little explanation.
Common mistakes: Using P(Y=y) in the denominator.; Claiming conditioning on continuous values is impossible.; Failing to mention the positivity condition on f_Y(y).

questions.text: Suppose the joint CDF is given by F_{X,Y}(a,b)=ab^2 for 0<a<1 and 0<b<1, with the obvious boundary extensions outside that square. Determine the joint PDF on the interior, then derive the marginals, and decide whether X and Y are independent.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly differentiates to get f_{X,Y}(a,b)=2b on the unit square.; Computes marginals f_X(a)=1 and f_Y(b)=2b on the correct supports.; Checks independence via product of marginals or product of CDFs.; Acknowledges support boundaries appropriately.
Partial credit: Correct PDF but incomplete marginals.; Correct independence conclusion with one valid check only.; Minor derivative slip but overall reasoning is coherent.

Common mistakes: Differentiating only once.; Forgetting that a CDF must be differentiated with respect to both variables to get the joint PDF.; Assuming dependence because the PDF does not visibly contain x.

questions.text: Explain why a valid joint PDF can exceed 1 in some regions without violating probability rules. Then say what condition actually matters for validity, and contrast this with what must be true for the total probability assigned to the full support.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that density is not probability.; Says a valid joint PDF must be nonnegative and integrate to 1.; Explains probabilities come from integrating over regions.; Contrasts local height with total volume.
Partial credit: Knows PDFs can exceed 1 but does not explain why.; Mentions the normalization condition only.; Uses one-dimensional intuition without adapting to area/volume.
Common mistakes: Claiming any PDF value above 1 is invalid.; Confusing density with event probability.; Forgetting nonnegativity as a validity condition.

questions.text: An analyst estimates the waiting times X and Y for two independent service counters. She computes the marginals correctly but then says, 'Since they are independent, the conditional density f_{X|Y}(x|y) should equal f_Y(y).' Explain the error and state what independence really implies for conditional densities.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the variable mismatch in the student's claim.; States that under independence f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x).; Shows the cancellation argument using the factorized joint density.; Interprets the result as 'Y gives no information about X.'
Partial credit: Correct conclusion but weak explanation.; Uses the intuition of independence without formulas.; Recognizes that the answer cannot be f_Y(y) but does not provide the correct one.
Common mistakes: Saying conditional density equals the other variable's marginal.; Claiming independence makes all conditional densities uniform.; Mixing up x and y throughout the formula.

questions.text: A classmate says: "For continuous random variables, conditioning on Y=y is impossible because P(Y=y)=0, so the expression f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y) is just illegal." Do you agree or disagree? Explain carefully what conditional density means here, why the ratio is still meaningful when f_Y(y)>0, and what property you would check to confirm it is a valid density in x.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that the objection is based on confusing probabilities with densities.; Explains conditional density via local intervals or limiting argument, not by treating P(Y=y) as an ordinary denominator.; Gives the formula f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y) with condition f_Y(y)>0.; Checks normalization by integrating over x and obtaining 1.

Partial credit: Knows the formula for conditional density but gives only a vague justification.; Mentions that densities are not probabilities but does not explain the limiting idea.; Checks only that the function is nonnegative, without verifying integral 1.

Common mistakes: Saying conditional distributions do not exist for continuous variables because point probabilities are zero.; Claiming f_{X|Y}(x|y) is itself a probability at x.; Forgetting the requirement f_Y(y)>0.; Integrating the conditional density over y instead of x.

questions.text: Let the joint density be f_{X,Y}(x,y)=cxy on the rectangle 0<=x<=1, 0<=y<=2, and 0 elsewhere. Without skipping setup, determine c, then find the marginal density of X, and then compute P(X<=1/2, Y<=1). Finally, say whether X and Y are independent and justify your answer from the densities rather than from intuition.
rubric_items: Full credit: Normalizes correctly and obtains c=1.; Computes f_X(x) correctly with support specified.; Sets up and evaluates the rectangular probability with correct limits.; Justifies independence by showing f_{X,Y}=f_X f_Y on the support, not merely by saying the formula factorizes informally.

Partial credit: Gets c and the marginals right but makes an arithmetic slip in the probability integral.; States independence correctly but with incomplete support discussion.; Uses the right integrals but omits support restrictions.

Common mistakes: Using cxy directly without first normalizing.; Integrating with wrong bounds for y or x.; Concluding independence just because the density looks multiplicative, without checking marginals or support.; Confusing the joint CDF with the joint PDF.

questions.text: You are given a jointly continuous pair (X,Y), and someone asks for the joint CDF F_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X<=a,Y<=b). Explain two different routes to a probability such as P(a_1<X<=a_2, b_1<Y<=b_2): one using the joint PDF and double integration, and one using the joint CDF. Then explain how, in principle, the joint PDF can be recovered from the CDF, and what regularity idea makes that recovery reasonable.
rubric_items: Full credit: Describes the rectangle probability correctly using a double integral over the region.; Gives the inclusion-exclusion formula using the joint CDF.; States that the joint CDF is an integral of the joint PDF from -infinity in both coordinates.; Explains that the joint PDF is the mixed partial derivative of the joint CDF, with a mention of differentiability/smoothness or FTC intuition.

Partial credit: Knows one route well but is incomplete on the other.; States the mixed derivative formula without explaining why it is reasonable.; Makes a minor sign error in the inclusion-exclusion formula but shows the right idea.

Common mistakes: Using only F(a_2,b_2)-F(a_1,b_1) for a rectangle probability.; Taking only one derivative of the joint CDF instead of a mixed second derivative.; Treating endpoint inclusions as important for continuous variables.; Confusing marginal CDFs with the joint CDF.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent Uniform(0,1) random variables representing two independent delays, and you care about the total delay S=X+Y. Without quoting a memorized formula, derive the density of S by reasoning geometrically or via convolution, and explain why the answer changes at s=1. I want the setup and the shape, not just the final piecewise expression.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up convolution or equivalent geometric reasoning correctly.; Identifies the support of S as [0,2].; Derives the interval for x where both uniforms are valid.; Explains the piecewise result and why the breakpoint occurs at s=1.

Partial credit: Gives the correct triangular density but with weak derivation.; Uses geometry correctly but does not express the interval intersection clearly.; Gets the support and one branch correct but mishandles the other branch.

Common mistakes: Multiplying densities and concluding S is uniform.; Forgetting to restrict x and s-x to [0,1].; Giving the CDF when asked for the density, or vice versa.; Missing the breakpoint and writing one formula for all s.

questions.text: A student says: "If the ratio f_{X,Y}(10,3)/f_{X,Y}(5,3) equals 4, then the probability that X=10 and Y=3 is four times the probability that X=5 and Y=3." Critique this statement. Then salvage the correct intuition by explaining what kind of small-region comparison the ratio of joint densities does support.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly states that point probabilities are zero for continuous joint variables.; Distinguishes density values from probabilities.; Explains the valid local approximation using equal small rectangles or neighborhoods.; Connects the ratio of densities to relative likelihood in nearby regions, not exact points.

Partial credit: Recognizes that point probabilities are zero but gives only a vague replacement interpretation.; Mentions 'more likely near that point' without explaining equal-area neighborhoods.; Explains in one dimension only, without adapting to the joint setting.

Common mistakes: Saying the student's statement is exactly correct.; Replacing the point probability with density without any caveat.; Comparing neighborhoods of different sizes, which breaks the density-ratio interpretation.; Forgetting that the statement concerns a joint density in two dimensions.

questions.text: A student says: “For a continuous random variable, the probability at a point is given by the height of the PDF there, so if the graph reaches 2 at x=0.5 then P(X=0.5)=2.” Do you agree? Explain carefully what the PDF does represent, and contrast it with what a CDF represents.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that P(X=x)=0 for continuous RVs.; Explains that PDF values are densities, not probabilities.; Explains that probabilities are integrals/areas under the PDF.; Correctly describes CDF as a probability and PDF as derivative of CDF.
Partial credit: Says point probabilities are zero but gives weak explanation.; Mentions area under curve but does not distinguish PDF from CDF clearly.
Common mistakes: Claiming f(x)=P(X=x).; Saying PDF values must lie between 0 and 1.; Confusing density with cumulative probability.

questions.text: Suppose X has PDF f(x)=x/2 for 0≤x≤2 and 0 otherwise. Without just quoting a memorized fact, compute P(X≥1) in two different ways and explain why they agree.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up correct integral over [1,2].; Gets 3/4.; Provides a second valid method, such as complement or geometric area.; Explains agreement in terms of area/probability under PDF.
Partial credit: Correct integral setup with arithmetic error.; Correct answer from complement but no explanation of why it works.
Common mistakes: Using f(1) as the probability.; Integrating over the wrong interval.; Forgetting the PDF is 0 outside [0,2].

questions.text: A classmate claims that for a continuous random variable, P(X>a) and P(X≥a) may differ because one includes the boundary point and the other does not. Is that true? Give a precise justification using CDF language.
rubric_items: Full credit: States equality of P(X>a) and P(X≥a) for continuous RVs.; Justifies with P(X=a)=0.; Connects to the CDF, ideally showing both equal 1-F(a).
Partial credit: Correct conclusion with an intuitive but incomplete explanation.; Uses area intuition but does not mention point probability zero.
Common mistakes: Saying inclusion of endpoint changes probability.; Confusing continuous and discrete cases.; Writing 1-F(a) for one expression and leaving the other unresolved.

questions.text: An app records a user’s arrival time X in hours after midnight, modeled as Uniform(2,8). A product manager asks for the probability the user arrives between 3.5 and 6. Explain how you would compute it from the PDF and also by geometric reasoning, then give the result.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies uniform density 1/6.; Sets up or explains interval-length over total-length reasoning.; Computes 5/12.; Notes endpoint inclusion is irrelevant for a continuous RV.
Partial credit: Correct method but arithmetic error.; Uses geometric reasoning correctly without explicit integral.
Common mistakes: Using area of a rectangle with wrong height.; Dividing by 8 instead of 6.; Treating the endpoints as changing the answer.

questions.text: For X~Uniform(α,β), derive the CDF piecewise rather than quoting it. Then use your expression to compute P(a≤X≤b) for α≤a≤b≤β.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives correct piecewise CDF.; Derives it from integrating the PDF.; Uses F(b)-F(a) correctly.; Simplifies to (b-a)/(β-α).
Partial credit: Correct CDF with little derivation.; Correct probability formula but weak piecewise explanation.
Common mistakes: Using the PDF formula as the CDF.; Forgetting CDF saturates at 0 and 1 outside the support.; Using β instead of β-α in the denominator.

questions.text: A student sees the formula Var(X)=(β−α)^2/12 for a uniform random variable, but misreads the lecture note and says the variance must be (β−α^9)/12. In an oral exam, how would you convince them from first principles which form is correct, without relying only on memory?
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes the correct variance is (β-α)^2/12.; Derives E[X^2] and subtracts the square of the mean, or gives another valid derivation.; Uses a sanity check such as units/dimensions or translation invariance.
Partial credit: States correct formula with a plausible intuition but no derivation.; Partial derivation with algebra mistakes.
Common mistakes: Accepting the typo-like expression blindly.; Confusing variance with standard deviation.; Failing to square the spread term.

questions.text: A sensor lifetime T is modeled as Exp(λ=1), measured in minutes. Explain how to compute the probability the sensor fails within the next 2 minutes, and interpret your answer in words rather than only giving a formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the exponential CDF correctly.; Computes or states 1-e^-2.; Interprets it as a waiting-time probability or complement of survival.
Partial credit: Correct formula but weak interpretation.; Correct complement idea but does not identify the CDF.
Common mistakes: Using e^-2 directly for 'within 2 minutes'.; Confusing rate and mean.; Treating exponential like uniform over time.

questions.text: Someone says: “Since probabilities cannot exceed 1, the likelihood or density at a single observed point can never exceed 1 either.” Is that statement always true for continuous models? Explain carefully, including why this does not contradict the axioms of probability.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the claim is false for continuous distributions.; Explains density vs probability distinction.; Notes integrals over regions are probabilities.; Optionally contrasts with discrete PMFs.
Partial credit: Correct conclusion with limited explanation.; Mentions densities can exceed 1 but does not say why.
Common mistakes: Claiming every PDF value must be in [0,1].; Confusing point likelihood with event probability.; Ignoring the continuous/discrete distinction.

questions.text: Consider the function random_sum() that adds 1000 independent Uniform(0,1) samples. You are asked for P(total>501). Talk through an approximation strategy, including the distribution you would use, its mean and variance, and whether you expect the answer to be larger or smaller than 0.5 before doing any table lookup.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the sum of iid uniforms.; Uses mean 1/2 and variance 1/12 for each term.; Applies CLT to approximate with a normal.; Sets up z-score for 501 and notes probability is slightly below 0.5.
Partial credit: Correct CLT idea but missing variance.; Correct mean/variance but weak interpretation of tail direction.

Common mistakes: Using a uniform distribution for the sum.; Forgetting to add variances across independent terms.; Saying the answer is greater than 0.5 because 501 is 'close' to the mean without considering direction.

questions.text: Why is the CDF often a more convenient tool than the PDF for answering probability questions such as P(a≤X≤b)? Give an explanation that would convince someone who keeps trying to re-integrate from scratch every time.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines or describes the CDF correctly.; Explains interval probability via F(b)-F(a).; Mentions avoidance of repeated integration or easier tail calculations.
Partial credit: Says CDF is easier but gives only one of the main reasons.; Uses formulas correctly without interpretation.
Common mistakes: Calling the CDF a density.; Forgetting that the CDF is itself a probability.; Saying PDFs and CDFs answer exactly the same questions in equally direct form.

questions.text: A lab reports a measurement X that is normally distributed with mean 3 and variance 16. Without computing decimal values, express P(2<X<5) in terms of the standard normal CDF Φ, and explain each standardization step aloud.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies standard deviation as 4.; Standardizes both endpoints correctly.; Expresses probability as Φ(1/2)-Φ(-1/4), optionally with symmetry simplification.; Explains the transformation conceptually.
Partial credit: Correct expression but misses explanation of standardization.; Minor algebra error in one endpoint.
Common mistakes: Using variance 16 as the standard deviation.; Subtracting the wrong mean.; Forgetting the probability is a difference of CDF values.

questions.text: In one dimension, we often say f(x)=F'(x). Explain what this statement really means in probability terms, and what information is lost or gained when moving between the PDF and CDF.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly interprets F as accumulated probability and f as rate of accumulation.; States or implies the derivative/integral relationship.; Discusses what each representation is useful for.
Partial credit: States the calculus relationship correctly but gives weak probabilistic interpretation.; Mentions integration but not differentiation, or vice versa.

Common mistakes: Saying the PDF is the probability at x.; Treating derivative relation as purely symbolic with no probabilistic meaning.; Claiming no information difference between the two without nuance.

questions.text: A student writes P(X=x) for a continuous random variable and then starts listing 'the set of outcomes where X=x' just like in a discrete coin-flip example. What is the subtle but important distinction between a random variable, an event like {X=x}, and the probability of that event?
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes random variable from event.; Explains {X=x} as a set of outcomes.; Explains P(X=x) as probability of that event.; Notes the continuous-vs-discrete difference in point probabilities.
Partial credit: Makes the main distinction but omits the continuous-specific point about zero probability.; Correct language but no example or interpretation.
Common mistakes: Calling X itself an event.; Equating PDF value with P(X=x).; Assuming continuous variables cannot define events like {X=x}.

questions.text: A museum uses a normal model for a feature extracted from paintings. They say, “We chose a normal distribution because the feature is an average over many local brushstroke measurements.” Explain why this is a statistically reasonable modeling choice, and what assumption is hiding underneath that argument.
rubric_items: Full credit: Invokes the CLT or an averaging argument.; Explains that the average, not necessarily the raw data, is modeled as normal.; Mentions important assumptions such as many terms, approximate independence, finite variance.
Partial credit: Mentions CLT with limited assumptions.; Says 'many things are normal' without a proper averaging argument.

Common mistakes: Claiming every measurement must already be normal.; Ignoring the role of independence or finite variance.; Confusing the distribution of a sum/average with the distribution of one observation.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent continuous random variables with joint PDF f_{X,Y}(x,y)=g(x)h(y). Explain how you would verify from this factorization that P(X≤x, Y≤y)=P(X≤x)P(Y≤y), rather than just asserting it.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up the double integral for the joint probability.; Uses factorization of the integrand.; Identifies the resulting factors as the marginal CDFs.; Concludes independence via factorized joint CDF.
Partial credit: States the factorization result correctly but does not show the integral reasoning.; Uses PDF factorization directly with little explanation.
Common mistakes: Mixing up PDFs and CDFs.; Forgetting limits of integration.; Asserting independence without showing why factorization implies it.

questions.text: For independent continuous X and Y, is it enough to check that P(X≤x, Y≤y)=P(X≤x)P(Y≤y) for one particular pair (x,y)? Explain what 'for all x,y' is doing in the definition and why a single check is not enough.
rubric_items: Full credit: States one pair is insufficient.; Explains independence is a property of the whole joint distribution.; References the need for the condition to hold for all x,y.
Partial credit: Correct conclusion with a vague explanation.; Mentions coincidence at a point but not the full-distribution aspect.
Common mistakes: Thinking one successful numerical check proves independence.; Confusing independence of variables with one event equality.; Ignoring the quantifier 'for all'.

questions.text: You are given a continuous CDF F and asked for P(a≤X≤b). A classmate writes F(b)-F(a^-), worrying about whether the endpoints are included. In the continuous case, what should the answer be, and why is the endpoint issue less delicate than in the discrete case?
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives F(b)-F(a) for the continuous case.; Explains why endpoints do not matter via zero point probability.; Contrasts with discrete variables.
Partial credit: Correct formula but weak explanation.; Mentions endpoints don't matter without saying why.
Common mistakes: Using a left-limit adjustment unnecessarily.; Confusing continuous and discrete interval formulas.; Forgetting that CDF values are probabilities.

questions.text: A reliability engineer says the waiting time until the first failure is exponential, while the number of failures in a fixed interval is Poisson. They then claim that for λ=5, P(Poi(5)=0)=P(Exp(5)>1). Explain why this identity makes sense conceptually before you verify it algebraically.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the shared event: zero arrivals in [0,1] equals first arrival after 1.; Gives both formulas leading to e^-5.; Connects Poisson counts with exponential waiting times.
Partial credit: Verifies algebraically but gives weak conceptual interpretation.; States they are equal because formulas match, without the event explanation.
Common mistakes: Treating Poisson and exponential as unrelated facts.; Using P(T≤1) instead of P(T>1).; Not recognizing the unit interval connection.

questions.text: A student says: “If X1,...,Xn are iid, then their average always tends to a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 0 as n grows.” Identify everything wrong with that statement, and repair it into a correct version.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies that mean should be μ, not 0 in general.; Identifies variance of the average as σ^2/n.; States a correct CLT-style repair involving approximate normality for large n under assumptions.; Mentions finite variance or related assumptions.
Partial credit: Corrects mean and variance but gives only vague CLT statement.; Mentions standardization without clearly repairing the original claim.
Common mistakes: Saying the sample average itself converges to N(0,0).; Ignoring assumptions required for CLT.; Confusing the average with its standardized form.

questions.text: A modeling team says, “Since our random variable is continuous, we can answer every question by integrating the PDF directly.” Give a more nuanced response: when is direct integration natural, and when is it better to switch to the CDF or to a normal approximation?
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains when direct PDF integration is appropriate.; Explains when using the CDF is preferable.; Explains when a normal approximation is appropriate for sums/averages.; Frames tool choice as problem-dependent.
Partial credit: Gives two of the three tools with reasonable explanations.; Correct general sentiment but little detail.
Common mistakes: Insisting one representation is always best.; Ignoring the role of approximations.; Confusing CDF and PDF roles.

questions.text: Suppose X~Uniform(α,β). Without expanding every integral in full detail, explain how you would derive E[X]=(α+β)/2 from symmetry, and then give a second derivation using the PDF to confirm it.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses midpoint symmetry argument correctly.; Sets up the expectation integral correctly.; Simplifies to (α+β)/2.; Explains why the symmetry argument is legitimate for a uniform distribution.
Partial credit: Gets correct answer from integration but no symmetry argument.; Gives symmetry argument but no confirming calculation.
Common mistakes: Using (β-α)/2 instead of midpoint.; Forgetting density factor 1/(β-α).; Confusing expectation with range length.

questions.text: In an oral explanation, how would you persuade someone that random variables give a more powerful language than event-only probability when dealing with many similar outcomes, especially for continuous measurements?
rubric_items: Full credit: Contrasts binary events with multi-valued random variables.; Explains how RVs unify many related events.; Mentions statistics such as expectation/variance or tools such as PDF/CDF.; Connects the argument to continuous measurements.
Partial credit: Makes the event-vs-RV distinction but does not explain the practical payoff.; Mentions summaries like mean without showing why RVs are structurally helpful.
Common mistakes: Saying random variables are just events with different notation.; Ignoring continuous-variable motivation.; Failing to mention that RVs are functions on the sample space.

questions.text: You are handed a candidate function and told it is a PDF for a continuous random variable. In an oral exam, what checklist would you go through before trusting it, and how would that checklist change if the function is piecewise-defined on a bounded interval?
rubric_items: Full credit: Checks nonnegativity.; Checks total integral equals 1.; Explains how to handle piecewise support by summing integrals over pieces.; Notes that PDF values may exceed 1.
Partial credit: Mentions nonnegativity and normalization but little detail on piecewise handling.; Gives a correct but incomplete checklist.
Common mistakes: Thinking continuity of the function is required for validity.; Forgetting to include zero density outside the support.; Insisting the PDF must stay below 1.

questions.text: A student says: “For a continuous random variable X, the probability at a point is just the height of the PDF there, so if f(2)=0.7 then P(X=2)=0.7.” Respond to that claim carefully. In your explanation, distinguish the random variable X, the event X=2, the PDF, and the CDF, and explain what quantity the value 0.7 could represent.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly states that P(X=2)=0 for a continuous random variable.; Explains that PDF values are densities, not probabilities, and probabilities are areas/integrals.; Correctly distinguishes random variable vs event notation.; Mentions CDF as a probability-valued function and gives a correct interval-probability expression using CDF or integration.

Partial credit: Says point probabilities are zero but gives a weak or incomplete reason.; Mentions area under the curve but does not clearly distinguish PDF from CDF.; Distinguishes X from X=2 but does not connect this to continuous probabilities.
Common mistakes: Treating f(2) as P(X=2).; Saying the PDF must always be at most 1.; Confusing X with the event X=2.; Using CDF and PDF interchangeably.

questions.text: Suppose waiting time in minutes until the next cough in an exam room is modeled by Z~Exp(λ=1). Without just quoting a formula, explain how you would compute the probability that a cough happens within the next 2 minutes, and then interpret the result in words. Then compare that event to “no cough occurs in the first 2 minutes” and relate the two probabilities.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up the event correctly as P(Z≤2).; Uses the exponential CDF correctly to obtain 1-e^{-2}.; Interprets the probability in context as a waiting-time statement.; Correctly identifies the complement P(Z>2)=e^{-2} and relates the two.

Partial credit: Gets the correct numerical expression but gives little interpretation.; Uses complement reasoning correctly even if the CDF is not named.; Shows correct understanding of within 2 minutes versus after 2 minutes but makes minor notation slips.
Common mistakes: Using P(Z=2) instead of P(Z≤2).; Writing e^{-2} for the probability of a cough within 2 minutes.; Confusing rate λ with mean.; Forgetting complementarity.

questions.text: A program returns the sum of 1000 independent samples from Uniform(0,1). You are asked for the probability that the sum exceeds 501. Explain how you would approximate this probability without doing a 1000-fold convolution. Your answer should identify the distribution you use, justify why it is appropriate, compute the mean and variance of the sum, and say whether you expect the final probability to be above or below 0.5 before calculating.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the sum of i.i.d. uniform variables and invokes CLT with justification.; Correctly states mean 1/2 and variance 1/12 for each Uniform(0,1).; Correctly derives mean 500 and variance 1000/12 for the sum.; Writes the normal approximation in standardized form using Φ.; Interprets that the answer should be slightly below 0.5 because 501 exceeds the mean.

Partial credit: Uses CLT correctly but makes a minor arithmetic mistake in variance or standard deviation.; Gets the setup right but omits interpretation.; Correctly computes mean and variance but does not explicitly standardize.

Common mistakes: Using the distribution of one Uniform instead of the sum.; Forgetting the variance of Uniform(0,1) is 1/12.; Using the wrong CLT assumptions, such as requiring normal Xi to begin with.; Saying the probability is above 0.5 because 501 is 'close to' 500 without checking the direction.

questions.text: Consider two continuous random variables X and Y with joint PDF f_{X,Y}(x,y)=g(x)h(y) for all real x and y, where g and h are nonnegative functions. A classmate says, “That factorization is only an algebra trick; it does not prove independence unless you also check probabilities of every rectangle.” Do you agree? Explain carefully what must be true for the factorization to imply independence, and connect your reasoning to CDFs or probabilities of events like {X≤x, Y≤y}.
rubric_items: Full credit: States correctly that factorization of a valid joint PDF into single-variable functions implies independence.; Explains the needed validity condition: the factorization must hold over the support and define a proper joint density.; Connects the PDF factorization to either marginal densities or the joint CDF factorization.; Explains why rectangle probabilities then factor.

Partial credit: States the result correctly but gives only a sketch of why.; Mentions CDF factorization or marginalization but not both.; Recognizes that support issues matter but does not articulate them clearly.

Common mistakes: Thinking factorization is never sufficient.; Ignoring whether the density is valid over the support.; Confusing pairwise event independence with random-variable independence without tying it to CDF/PDF conditions.; Claiming independence requires checking infinitely many rectangles separately even after proving CDF factorization.

questions.text: Let X have PDF f(x)=x/2 for 0≤x≤2 and 0 otherwise. Compute P(X≥1) in two different ways, and explain why the two methods must agree. Then address a common concern: is there any difference here between P(X≥1) and P(X>1)?
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes P(X≥1)=3/4 by direct integration.; Provides a second valid method, typically complement or CDF, and gets the same result.; Explains conceptually why the methods agree.; States and justifies that P(X≥1)=P(X>1) because point probabilities are zero for continuous RVs.

Partial credit: Gets 3/4 correctly using one method but does not clearly provide the second.; Uses two methods but does not explain why they agree.; Knows strict versus non-strict inequalities are the same here but gives weak justification.

Common mistakes: Integrating over the wrong interval.; Forgetting the density is zero outside [0,2].; Treating P(X=1) as positive because f(1)=1/2.; Saying ≥ and > differ because one includes the endpoint.

questions.text: A student says, 'Whenever I see multiple steps, I should multiply, so choosing 3 club officers from 10 students is 10·9·8.' Explain carefully why that answer is not the number of ways to choose the officers if the roles are identical, and then explain when 10·9·8 would be the correct count.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly states that product rule counts ordered multistep assignments.; Explains overcounting by 3! when order does not matter.; Gives correct unordered count as binomial coefficient.; Identifies a scenario with distinct roles where 10·9·8 is correct.

Partial credit: Recognizes combination vs permutation but gives incomplete justification.; Mentions dividing by 3! without clearly explaining why.; Gives only formulas with little verbal interpretation.
Common mistakes: Saying 10·9·8 is always wrong.; Using binom(10,3) even when roles are distinct.; Claiming order 'sometimes matters' without tying it to the sample space.

questions.text: You roll two fair six-sided dice. Count the number of outcomes where at least one die shows an even number, and explain two different counting strategies that must agree.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses ordered-pair sample space of size 36.; Presents a valid complement method.; Presents a valid inclusion-exclusion method.; Explains agreement of the two methods.
Partial credit: Gets 27 with only one valid method.; Uses correct arithmetic but weak explanation of overlap.; Understands ordered pairs but not inclusion-exclusion.
Common mistakes: Counting only 18 by forgetting the second die can be even.; Adding 18+18 without subtracting overlap.; Treating outcomes like {2,5} and {5,2} as the same without justification.

questions.text: In the birthday problem with n labeled people, a classmate claims that the number of assignments with no shared birthday is simply binom(365,n), because we are choosing n different dates. Explain precisely why that is not compatible with the original sample space, and repair the argument.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the sample space as labeled assignments of size 365^n.; Explains why binom(365,n) counts unlabeled date sets.; Repairs by multiplying by n! or by using the product rule directly.; Connects to complement probability.

Partial credit: States the correct formula but does not explain mismatch of object types.; Explains labels matter but not why n! appears.; Gives only the product 365·364·... without conceptual justification.

Common mistakes: Claiming binom(365,n) is fine because birthdays are distinct.; Forgetting that people are distinguishable.; Using permutations in numerator but combinations in denominator inconsistently.

questions.text: A password consists of 8 characters: exactly 3 are letters A, exactly 2 are letters B, and the remaining 3 are all distinct digits chosen from 0 through 9. Digits may not repeat. Count the number of distinct passwords and explain where each factor comes from.
rubric_items: Full credit: Chooses the 3 distinct digits correctly.; Counts arrangements with repeated A and B using division by 3! and 2!.; Explains why digits are not divided out.; Provides a coherent product-rule interpretation.

Partial credit: Has the right general form but mixes binomial and permutation notation.; Counts arrangements correctly but forgets to choose digits.; Chooses digits as 10·9·8 without explaining equivalence to binom(10,3)·3!.
Common mistakes: Dividing by 3! for the digits even though they are distinct.; Using 10^3 instead of choosing distinct digits.; Treating repeated A's and B's as distinct.

questions.text: Suppose you must split 12 distinct students into three project teams of sizes 5, 4, and 3. Explain why the count is a multinomial coefficient, and then explain what would change if the three teams were unlabeled rather than labeled Team 1, Team 2, Team 3.
rubric_items: Full credit: States labeled-team count as 12!/(5!4!3!).; Explains the multinomial interpretation.; Recognizes that unlabeled makes no difference here because sizes differ.; Notes extra division would appear if equal-sized unlabeled groups existed.
Partial credit: Gets the formula but not the unlabeled subtlety.; Says 'multinomial' without explaining why.; Recognizes group labels matter but handles the unlabeled case vaguely.
Common mistakes: Dividing by 3! automatically for unlabeled groups even though sizes differ.; Using binom(12,5) only and stopping.; Confusing internal team order with team labels.

questions.text: A raffle draws 4 distinct winners from 75 tickets, and order of drawing does not matter. What is the probability that all 4 winners come from a particular block of 15 tickets? Then explain how you would compute the same probability if the raffle announced first, second, third, and fourth place so order did matter.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses unordered counting consistently for the first setup.; Computes favorable and total counts correctly.; Explains the ordered version with permutations.; States that both approaches agree if done consistently.
Partial credit: Gets one setup correct but not the other.; States formulas but does not justify why order matters or not.; Uses correct probability but weak explanation of sample space.

Common mistakes: Using binom(15,4)/75^4 despite no replacement.; Mixing ordered numerator with unordered denominator.; Assuming probability changes when switching descriptions of the same physical experiment.

questions.text: A student claims that the number of ways to arrange the letters in the word BALLOON is 7!, because there are 7 letters. Diagnose the overcounting and give the corrected reasoning aloud.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies repeated letters correctly.; Explains why swaps of identical letters do not create new arrangements.; Gives corrected count 7!/(2!2!).
Partial credit: Knows to divide by repeated counts but misses one repeated letter.; Gives formula without explanation.; Uses the right idea but incorrect arithmetic detail.
Common mistakes: Using 7!/2! only once.; Dividing by 4! because there are four repeated letters total.; Treating repeated letters as distinct positions.

questions.text: A university schedules 6 distinct guest speakers into 8 available time slots, with at most one speaker per slot. Count the number of schedules. Then compare that count to the number of ways if the university instead only cared about which 6 slots are used, not which speaker is in which used slot.
rubric_items: Full credit: Counts full schedules as binom(8,6)6! or equivalent.; Explains relation to permutations of distinct speakers.; Counts slot-only version as binom(8,6).; Clearly contrasts order/assignment versus selection.
Partial credit: Gets one count right but not the comparison.; Uses 8P6 without verbal interpretation.; Confuses choosing slots with ordering speakers.
Common mistakes: Using 8! for all 8 slots despite only 6 speakers.; Using binom(8,6) for the full schedule without assigning speakers.; Treating unused slots as indistinguishable objects to permute.

questions.text: Give a combinatorial proof, in words, of the identity binom(n,k) = binom(n,n-k). Your explanation should not just say 'the formula is symmetric'; it should describe one set being counted in two ways.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies a concrete set being counted.; Explains the bijection between chosen and unchosen elements.; Avoids relying only on algebraic formula symmetry.
Partial credit: States complement idea but not as a counting argument.; Uses formula manipulation only.; Gives an example but no general reasoning.
Common mistakes: Saying they are equal 'because factorials cancel' without combinatorial interpretation.; Confusing k-permutations with k-combinations.; Not specifying what the two counts refer to.

questions.text: How many 10-bit strings contain exactly four 1s, under the additional condition that the first bit and last bit are different? Explain your case split and why the cases are disjoint.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up the two endpoint cases correctly.; Counts each case with the correct binomial coefficient.; Explains disjointness and sums validly.
Partial credit: Correct case split but one coefficient wrong.; Correct total idea but weak explanation of why sum rule applies.; Attempts complement but without complete setup.

Common mistakes: Using 2·binom(8,3), ignoring asymmetry of the two cases.; Counting all strings with four 1s as binom(10,4) and stopping.; Forgetting that fixing a 1 at one end changes how many 1s remain to place.

questions.text: A menu offers 9 distinct toppings, and a pizza comes with exactly 3 different toppings. Compare the number of possible pizzas when the toppings are listed alphabetically on the receipt versus when the kitchen physically places toppings into three labeled sectors of the pizza. Why does one setup use combinations and the other use permutations?
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses combination count for unordered topping sets.; Uses permutation-enhanced count for labeled sectors.; Explains that the definition of an outcome determines the model.
Partial credit: Gets formulas but weak conceptual contrast.; Knows one is ordered and one unordered but does not explain why.; Counts sectors correctly after prompting.
Common mistakes: Using binom(9,3) in both cases.; Using 9^3 despite different toppings required.; Saying alphabetical listing introduces order that changes the pizza count.

questions.text: Someone counts the number of ways to place 7 identical balls into 3 labeled boxes as 3^7, arguing that each ball has 3 choices. Explain why that answer corresponds to a different model, and state the correct count for identical balls in labeled boxes.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why 3^7 corresponds to distinct balls.; Reframes the problem as counting occupancy counts.; Gives stars-and-bars answer binom(9,2).

Partial credit: States stars and bars result but weakly explains mismatch with 3^7.; Recognizes identical vs distinct issue without giving full count.; Gives correct formula in a different but equivalent form.
Common mistakes: Using 3^7 anyway because boxes are labeled.; Using binom(7,3) or similar without interpretation.; Forgetting that boxes may be empty.

questions.text: A 5-column game card is built by choosing numbers within each column from disjoint ranges of size 15. Four columns contain 5 numbers each, while the middle column has only 4 numbers because the center is free. Explain why the total number of cards is (15!/10!)^4·(15!/11!), and why replacing those factors by binom(15,5) and binom(15,4) would be incomplete.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes cells within a column are distinct positions.; Derives ordered counts for 5-cell and 4-cell columns.; Applies product rule across columns.; Explains why pure combinations undercount.
Partial credit: Correct formula with limited explanation.; Understands order matters but not why columnwise multiplication is valid.; Uses binom(15,5)·5! idea correctly but incompletely.
Common mistakes: Using binom(15,5)^4 binom(15,4).; Treating all columns the same despite free center.; Forgetting that row placement matters.

questions.text: Explain the difference between a generative process that is valid for the product rule and one that is not. Use the birthday problem's 'no shared birthdays' event as your example, and state the three properties you would want from the process.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the key properties of a valid generative process.; Applies them correctly to no-shared-birthday counting.; Explains why an unordered-date process is invalid in that context.
Partial credit: Describes the birthday process but omits one property.; Mentions 'no overcounting' without discussing coverage.; Understands labels matter but not the generative-process framing.

Common mistakes: Thinking any step-by-step procedure is automatically valid.; Ignoring the need for consistency with the sample space.; Assuming constant choices at each step is always necessary, rather than just product-rule-friendly.

questions.text: A committee of 6 is chosen from 14 people, but two particular people refuse to serve together. Count the number of valid committees in two ways: by subtraction from all committees, and by a direct case split. Explain why the answers must match.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes all-minus-invalid correctly.; Provides a valid disjoint case split.; Explains equality as counting the same set two ways.
Partial credit: Gets one method right but not the other.; Recognizes complement idea but not direct decomposition.; Uses inclusion-exclusion language vaguely without concrete counts.

Common mistakes: Subtracting binom(2,2)·binom(12,4) without explanation and then mishandling the rest.; Using permutations instead of committees.; Forgetting the 'exactly one of them' case in the direct split.

questions.text: How many ways are there to select 8 cards from a standard 52-card deck so that the hand contains exactly 3 hearts, exactly 2 spades, and the remaining 3 cards are from clubs or diamonds? Explain why the product rule applies here without overcounting.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the correct product of combinations.; Explains the categories are disjoint and exhaustive for the requirement.; Justifies why no extra factorial appears.
Partial credit: Correct formula but little explanation.; Understands suit-based splitting but omits why unordered selection is preserved.; Uses an equivalent choose-sequentially approach.
Common mistakes: Multiplying by 8! even though the hand is unordered.; Choosing the final 3 from 39 rather than 26.; Using multinomial with suits but forgetting the actual card identities.

questions.text: A student says, 'To count 4-digit PINs with no repeated digits, I can use binom(10,4) because I am choosing 4 digits from 0 through 9.' Explain what that count misses, and discuss one subtle issue involving leading zero.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that binom(10,4) ignores order.; Gives the ordered count for true PINs with no repetition.; Discusses the leading-zero distinction clearly.
Partial credit: Identifies order issue but misses leading-zero nuance.; Gets one of the two model counts correct.; Says 'permutation' without specifying what is being permuted.
Common mistakes: Using binom(10,4)·4! but then forgetting leading zero issue.; Treating PIN and 4-digit number as automatically the same.; Using 10^4 despite no repetition.

questions.text: Without doing algebraic simplification, explain why the formula for choosing k objects from n distinct objects can be derived from permutations by dividing out two sources of overcounting. Be explicit about what each division by a factorial corresponds to.
rubric_items: Full credit: Begins from permutation viewpoint n!.; Identifies both overcounting factors and their meanings.; Connects the quotient to unordered selection.

Partial credit: Knows the formula but explains only one factorial in the denominator.; Starts from choosing positions but does not articulate both symmetries.; Gives algebra but little interpretation.

Common mistakes: Dividing only by k! and forgetting the unchosen objects also vary.; Saying 'because order doesn't matter' without specifying where order was introduced.; Confusing permutations of n objects with permutations of k chosen objects.

questions.text: You have 12 distinct books and want to put them onto two labeled shelves, with 5 books on the top shelf and 7 on the bottom shelf, and order matters within each shelf. Count the number of arrangements, and then explain why your answer is not just binom(12,5).
rubric_items: Full credit: Chooses shelf membership and then shelf orders.; Obtains total 12! or equivalent.; Explains why binom(12,5) alone undercounts.
Partial credit: Correct count with weak interpretation.; Gets the choose-and-order structure partly right.; Recognizes shelves are labeled but misses internal order.
Common mistakes: Using only binom(12,5).; Multiplying by 2! for the shelves unnecessarily.; Treating bottom shelf order as irrelevant.

questions.text: How many 9-letter strings over the alphabet {A,B,C} contain exactly 4 A's, 3 B's, and 2 C's? Give two different counting explanations that lead to the same formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives both the repeated-permutation and sequential-position arguments.; Provides the correct formula 9!/(4!3!2!).; Explains why the two methods count the same objects.
Partial credit: One correct method only.; Correct formula but no second explanation.; Uses choose-position method with minor notational issues.
Common mistakes: Using 3^9, ignoring exact counts.; Using 9! with no division.; Choosing positions for A, B, C independently without accounting for overlap.

questions.text: A student wants the number of ways to distribute 10 identical candies to 4 children so that each child gets at least one, and says the answer is 4^10 because each candy chooses a child. Explain the model mismatch and derive the correct count.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why 4^10 is the wrong model.; Transforms the positive-count problem correctly.; Gives the stars-and-bars count binom(9,3).
Partial credit: Identifies identical-candy issue but incomplete derivation.; Uses stars and bars but forgets the at-least-one adjustment.; Correct formula with minimal explanation.
Common mistakes: Using binom(13,3) by forgetting the positivity condition.; Treating candies as distinct.; Forgetting that children are labeled.

questions.text: When using equally likely outcomes to compute probability as |E|/|S|, why is it dangerous to choose a sample space that tracks more detail than the event count does, or vice versa? Illustrate your explanation with an ordered-vs-unordered selection example.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that E and S must use the same elementary outcomes.; Explains the ordered/unordered mismatch clearly.; Gives a concrete example of consistent versus inconsistent counting.
Partial credit: Knows consistency matters but explanation is vague.; Gives an example without articulating the principle.; Focuses only on formulas rather than sample-space meaning.

Common mistakes: Thinking any numerator and denominator counts can be divided.; Saying order 'doesn't matter' without specifying in which model.; Assuming probabilities change when switching between equivalent consistent models.

questions.text: A research lab must assign 9 distinct samples into 3 labeled freezers so that the freezers receive 2, 3, and 4 samples respectively. Count the number of assignments. Then explain how the answer changes if the freezers with capacities 2, 3, and 4 are physically distinct but the order of samples inside each freezer is irrelevant.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives 9!/(2!3!4!) or equivalent sequential-choose expression.; Explains why labeled freezers matter.; Correctly observes no change when internal order is irrelevant because it was not counted initially.; Mentions what would change if internal slots were ordered.
Partial credit: Correct formula but weak interpretation.; Thinks there is a change but gives coherent reasoning about a different model.; Recognizes partitioning into labeled groups.
Common mistakes: Multiplying by 2!3!4! instead of dividing.; Dividing by 3! even though freezers are labeled and sizes differ.; Inventing internal order when the problem never included it.

questions.text: A classmate says: 'To count the number of ways to assign birthdays to 20 distinct students so that no two share a birthday, we should just choose 20 different dates out of 365, so the answer is 365 choose 20.' Explain carefully why that count is not compatible with the natural sample space for the birthday problem, and then give a correct count in two equivalent forms.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies that students are distinct and the sample space is person-labeled assignments.; Explains clearly why 365 choose 20 counts unordered dates and therefore is not the right event count by itself.; Provides a correct ordered count such as 365 × 364 × ... × 346 or 365! / 345!.; States an equivalent form 365 choose 20 times 20! and explains why it matches.

Partial credit: Gives the correct formula but weakly explains the mismatch with the sample space.; Recognizes ordering matters but does not explicitly connect it to distinct students.; Mentions multiplying by 20! without fully justifying why.
Common mistakes: Saying 365 choose 20 is correct because the birthdays are all distinct.; Using 365^20 for the no-match event.; Confusing ordered outcomes with unordered selections.

questions.text: You roll two fair six-sided dice. Let event A be 'at least one die shows an even number' and event B be 'the sum is 7.' Without listing all 36 outcomes one by one, compute the number of outcomes in A, in B, and in A ∪ B. Explain your counting strategy and where inclusion-exclusion enters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses ordered outcomes for two dice, with total 36.; Counts A correctly, ideally by complement, as 27.; Counts B correctly as 6 ordered pairs.; Computes the intersection correctly and applies inclusion-exclusion to get 27.; Explains why B is contained in A or equivalently why the intersection size is 6.
Partial credit: Gets the right counts but with limited explanation.; Counts A directly rather than by complement, but correctly.; Uses inclusion-exclusion correctly after a small arithmetic slip.
Common mistakes: Treating dice outcomes as unordered and using 21 total outcomes.; Counting only three sum-7 outcomes instead of six.; Adding |A| and |B| without subtracting the overlap.

questions.text: A research lab has 10 distinct students to assign to three project teams: Team A must get 4 students, Team B must get 3, and Team C must get 3. First count the number of valid assignments when the teams are labeled A, B, and C. Then explain how the answer would change if the three teams were unlabeled and only the group sizes 4, 3, and 3 mattered.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the labeled-teams case as a partition of distinct objects into groups of fixed sizes.; Gives 10! / (4!3!3!) or an equivalent sequential-choices expression and connects the two.; Explains why unlabeled teams require dividing by 2! for the two equal-sized groups.; Explicitly notes why division by 3! would be incorrect.

Partial credit: Gets the labeled count correct but is unsure about the unlabeled adjustment.; Recognizes some overcount in the unlabeled case but uses the wrong factor.; Uses choose notation correctly but does not simplify or interpret it.

Common mistakes: Using 10 choose 4,3,3 but not explaining what it means.; Dividing by 3! in the unlabeled case even though only two groups are interchangeable.; Treating the groups as ordered internally and multiplying by extra factorials.

questions.text: Someone claims that the number of ways to create a 5-card hand from a standard 52-card deck is 52 × 51 × 50 × 49 × 48. Give a careful critique of that statement. Then describe a counting process that would make that product correct, and explain how to convert it back to the usual hand count.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes ordered sequences from unordered hands.; Explains why the product counts each hand 5! times.; Gives the corrected count as 52 choose 5.; Describes a generative process with labeled positions under which the product is correct.

Partial credit: States that order does not matter but does not fully justify the 5! overcount.; Gives 52 choose 5 without connecting it to the ordered product.; Describes the ordered process but is vague about how to correct it.
Common mistakes: Saying the product is wrong because cards are not distinct.; Using 52 choose 5 times 5! as the final hand count.; Failing to specify what makes the ordered process ordered.

questions.text: A word game draws 7 letter tiles from a bag containing the multiset {A, A, A, B, B, C, D}. You are asked two different questions: first, how many distinct 7-letter strings can be formed using all the tiles; second, how many distinct 3-letter strings can be formed if you may use at most the available multiplicity of each letter. Explain why these are different kinds of counting problems, and compute both counts.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the first task as permutations with repeated letters and gives 7!/(3!2!).; Explains why the second task cannot be solved by the same single formula.; Breaks the 3-letter problem into valid multiplicity cases and counts each correctly.; Gets the total 43 and justifies exclusion of impossible cases like BBB or AAB with too many of an unavailable letter.

Partial credit: Gets the first count right but misses a case in the second problem.; Uses casework correctly but makes a small arithmetic error.; Recognizes repeated-letter issues but does not clearly separate the two tasks conceptually.

Common mistakes: Using 7! for the first part and ignoring repeated letters.; Using 4^3 for the second part and ignoring multiplicity limits.; Forgetting the AAA case or incorrectly including BBB.; Counting one-pair cases as unordered choices instead of ordered strings.

questions.text: A student says: 'Covariance tells you how strongly two variables are related, so if the covariance between height and weight is 255 in one dataset and 46 in another, the first pair must be more strongly related.' Do you agree? Explain using the effect of changing units, and say what aspect of covariance remains meaningful across unit changes.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that covariance magnitude is not directly comparable across unit changes.; Explains linear scaling effect: Cov(aX+b,cY+d)=ac Cov(X,Y), at least verbally.; Identifies that the sign of covariance is more meaningful than the raw magnitude.; Mentions correlation as the unitless measure for comparing strength.

Partial credit: Says covariance depends on units but does not explain why.; Mentions sign is meaningful but omits correlation.; Recognizes unit conversion issue but confuses covariance and correlation.
Common mistakes: Claiming covariance is unitless.; Saying translation changes covariance magnitude.; Treating larger covariance as universally stronger dependence.

questions.text: Let A and B be random variables with Var(A)=4, Var(B)=9, and Cov(A,B)=-3. Without assuming independence, compute Var(A+B) and interpret what the sign of the covariance did to the total variability of the sum.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the correct formula for Var(A+B).; Substitutes values correctly and gets 7.; Interprets negative covariance as reducing variance through cancellation.
Partial credit: Correct formula but arithmetic error.; Gets the sign effect right but forgets the factor of 2.; States variance is smaller but gives no explanation.
Common mistakes: Using Var(A+B)=Var(A)+Var(B) without checking independence/zero covariance.; Using Cov(A,B) once instead of 2Cov(A,B).; Interpreting negative covariance as making variance negative.

questions.text: A classmate argues: 'If two variables are dependent, then their correlation cannot be zero.' Give a counterexample or a reasoning path that shows why this is false, and explain what correlation zero actually rules out.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly rejects 'dependence implies nonzero correlation.'; Provides or describes a valid nonlinear counterexample such as Y=X^2 with symmetric X.; Explains why dependence still holds.; States that correlation 0 means no linear relationship / uncorrelated, not independence.

Partial credit: Gives the right conclusion but no valid example.; Mentions nonlinear dependence vaguely without explaining covariance 0.; Says uncorrelated does not imply independent but cannot justify it.
Common mistakes: Claiming correlation 0 implies independence in general.; Giving an example with nonzero covariance.; Saying 'dependent' means 'causal.'

questions.text: In a city, colder days tend to produce higher heating bills. Describe the sign you expect for the covariance between outside temperature and utility bill, and justify your answer using the centered-product definition of covariance rather than only intuition.
rubric_items: Full credit: States covariance is negative.; Uses the sign of (X-E[X])(Y-E[Y]) in both cold and warm cases.; Connects the expected product to negative average covariance.
Partial credit: Gets the sign right with only informal reasoning.; Uses EXY-EXEY correctly but does not interpret centered terms.; Explains only one side of the mean split.
Common mistakes: Saying covariance is positive because both variables are 'large' in winter.; Confusing temperature with lack of heating need.; Describing causation instead of covariation only.

questions.text: Suppose Y=aX+b with probability 1, where a>0 and both variables have nonzero variance. Explain why the correlation must be 1, not just positive. Then say what changes if a<0.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses covariance linearity to get Cov(X,Y)=a Var(X).; Uses sigma_Y=|a| sigma_X.; Derives rho=1 for a>0 and rho=-1 for a<0.; Emphasizes exact linearity, not approximate linearity.
Partial credit: States the correct result with incomplete derivation.; Knows adding b does not matter but mishandles absolute value.; Explains geometrically but not algebraically.
Common mistakes: Saying rho=a.; Forgetting standard deviations are nonnegative.; Claiming any positive slope gives correlation merely greater than 0 but not necessarily 1.

questions.text: You know Cov(X,Y)=5. Define U=3X-7 and V=-2Y+4. Compute Cov(U,V) and explain each step, especially which parts of the transformation matter and which do not.
