rubric_items: Full credit: Applies Cov(aX+b,cY+d)=ac Cov(X,Y).; Gets -30.; Explains why additive constants do not matter.; Explains sign flip from multiplying by a negative constant.
Partial credit: Correct numeric result with weak explanation.; Uses the one-variable rule twice but incompletely.; Forgets one scaling factor but otherwise reasons correctly.
Common mistakes: Adding constants into covariance.; Using 3+(-2) instead of 3·(-2).; Claiming covariance cannot be negative if original covariance was positive.

questions.text: Give an oral proof sketch of the identity Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]. I do not want only the formula; I want the expansion and the role of linearity of expectation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from centered-product definition.; Expands correctly.; Uses linearity of expectation correctly and identifies constants.; Arrives at E[XY]-E[X]E[Y].
Partial credit: States the formula but only partially justifies it.; Expands correctly but mishandles constants verbally.; Uses linearity without naming it.
Common mistakes: Writing E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] without independence.; Dropping one cross term.; Confusing covariance with variance.

questions.text: A student says: 'If Cov(X,Y)=0, then X and Y must be independent, because EXY=EXEY.' How would you respond? Your answer should distinguish a true implication from a false converse.
rubric_items: Full credit: States correctly that independence implies zero covariance / no correlation.; Rejects the converse.; Provides or references a valid counterexample.; Uses language of implication/converse clearly.
Partial credit: Gets the conclusion right but gives no example.; Says not always true but cannot explain why.; Mentions nonlinear relationship vaguely.
Common mistakes: Claiming EXY=EXEY is equivalent to independence.; Confusing dependence with causation.; Forgetting correlation requires nonzero standard deviations.

questions.text: An analyst computes the covariance between product price and demand and finds it positive in observational data. A manager concludes: 'Raising price causes demand to increase.' Critique this conclusion carefully, using what covariance and correlation can and cannot tell us.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects causal claim from covariance alone.; Explains covariance as association, not causation.; Mentions possible confounding or spurious correlation.; Notes correlation/covariance concern observed co-movement, not interventions.
Partial credit: Says 'correlation does not imply causation' with little explanation.; Mentions confounding vaguely.; Focuses only on unit dependence rather than causality.

Common mistakes: Saying positive covariance proves price increases demand.; Claiming causation can be inferred if covariance is large enough.; Treating observational association as experimental evidence.

questions.text: Let S=X1+X2+X3 where Var(X1)=1, Var(X2)=2, Var(X3)=3, Cov(X1,X2)=0.5, Cov(X1,X3)=-1, and Cov(X2,X3)=0. Compute Var(S), and explain why each covariance appears with a factor of 2.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the correct general formula.; Substitutes all terms correctly and gets 5.; Explains symmetry and double counting of off-diagonal pairs.
Partial credit: Correct setup with arithmetic slip.; Gets most terms but misses one covariance.; States factor 2 without explaining symmetry/double counting.
Common mistakes: Adding covariances only once without factor 2.; Assuming independence and dropping covariance terms.; Including Cov(Xi,Xi) separately in addition to variance terms.

questions.text: Why is Var(X) a special case of covariance? Give both the formula and the intuition in words, and then explain why this helps derive variance formulas for sums.
rubric_items: Full credit: States Var(X)=Cov(X,X).; Gives correct derivation from the definition.; Provides intuition in words.; Connects this identity to variance-of-sum expansions.
Partial credit: States the identity but not the intuition.; Gives intuition but not derivation.; Mentions sums vaguely without explaining Cov(X+Y,X+Y).

Common mistakes: Treating variance and covariance as unrelated formulas.; Writing Var(X)=E[X^2] instead of E[X^2]-(E[X])^2 without context.; Failing to connect covariance properties to variance expansions.

questions.text: Imagine a scatterplot where points lie almost exactly on a downward-sloping line. Without computing anything, explain what you expect for the sign and approximate magnitude of the correlation, and contrast that with what covariance alone cannot tell you from the picture.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies negative sign and magnitude near 1 for correlation.; Explains that correlation reflects near-perfect negative linearity.; Contrasts with covariance's unit dependence.; Notes covariance would be negative but not scale-comparable.
Partial credit: Gets sign right but not magnitude.; Mentions -1 without saying why exact -1 requires perfect linearity.; Discusses covariance vaguely.

Common mistakes: Saying covariance alone determines closeness to a line regardless of units.; Confusing strong negative with small negative number only.; Claiming any downward trend gives correlation exactly -1.

questions.text: A researcher finds correlation 0.95 between two time series and says: 'This proves a meaningful relationship between the phenomena.' Give a careful oral response that distinguishes statistical association, linearity, and the possibility of spurious correlation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that 0.95 indicates strong linear association, not proof of meaning or causation.; Mentions spurious correlation or common trends/confounders.; Distinguishes statistical association from substantive explanation.; Shows skepticism appropriate to observational data.
Partial credit: Says 'correlation is not causation' without elaboration.; Mentions spurious correlation but not why time series are risky.; Focuses only on sample size or only on causation.
Common mistakes: Accepting 0.95 as proof of causality.; Assuming high correlation excludes confounding.; Ignoring the linearity aspect of correlation.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent with finite variances. Show verbally how independence simplifies Cov(X,Y), and then use that to simplify Var(X+Y).
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses independence to state E[XY]=E[X]E[Y].; Concludes Cov(X,Y)=0.; Correctly simplifies Var(X+Y) to the sum of variances.; Makes clear the chain of reasoning.

Partial credit: Knows independent implies covariance 0 but cannot justify via expectation.; Gets variance sum formula right without explaining why.; Explains covariance part but forgets final variance result.
Common mistakes: Stating covariance 0 implies independence.; Using variance additivity without any condition.; Confusing pairwise independence with unrelated concepts.

questions.text: Can correlation change if we add constants or multiply by negative constants? Answer by discussing separately the transformations X* = aX+b and Y* = cY+d, and explain what happens to both covariance and correlation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States covariance transformation correctly.; Explains correlation invariance under shifts and positive rescaling.; Explains sign flip under negative scaling.; Separates effects on covariance from effects on correlation.
Partial credit: Gets covariance right but not correlation.; Says correlation is unitless without discussing negative scaling.; Understands shifts do not matter but not scale effects.

Common mistakes: Claiming correlation is unchanged even if one variable is multiplied by -1.; Claiming adding constants changes covariance.; Mixing up standard deviation scaling with variance scaling.

questions.text: You are shown four scatterplots: one perfect upward line, one perfect downward line, one circular cloud centered at the origin, and one parabola opening upward symmetric about the y-axis. For each, state whether the correlation is 1, -1, 0, or 'other,' and justify your choices aloud.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly classifies the four patterns.; Explains exact ±1 via deterministic linear form.; Explains why symmetric nonlinear patterns can have correlation 0.; Distinguishes no linear relationship from no relationship.
Partial credit: Gets the line cases right but struggles with the parabola.; Says the cloud is near 0 without mentioning symmetry.; Recognizes nonlinear dependence vaguely.

Common mistakes: Assigning nonzero correlation to the symmetric parabola solely because there is dependence.; Saying any clear pattern must have high correlation.; Forgetting that exact ±1 requires exact linearity.

questions.text: Suppose E[X]=2, E[Y]=-1, and E[XY]=0.5. Compute Cov(X,Y). Then explain whether this information alone is enough to determine the correlation, and what additional quantities you would need.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes covariance as 2.5.; States that correlation cannot be determined from this alone.; Identifies missing information: sigma_X and sigma_Y or the variances.; Notes the role of nonzero variance for defining correlation.
Partial credit: Gets covariance right but says too little about correlation.; Knows more information is needed but does not specify what.; Arithmetic slip but correct reasoning.
Common mistakes: Calling 2.5 the correlation.; Dividing by means instead of standard deviations.; Assuming covariance magnitude determines correlation magnitude.

questions.text: A student reasons: 'Because covariance is symmetric, Cov(X,Y)=Cov(Y,X), it follows that if X causes Y then Y causes X.' Identify the flaw in this argument and separate the mathematical symmetry from the interpretation of observed data.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies category error between symmetric association and directional causation.; Explains why covariance is mathematically symmetric.; States covariance provides no causal direction.; Uses intervention/mechanism idea or equivalent distinction.
Partial credit: Says covariance is not causation but gives little explanation.; Notes symmetry but does not connect it to the flaw.; Rejects the claim intuitively only.
Common mistakes: Suggesting covariance can reveal causal direction if large enough.; Equating association with mechanism.; Failing to explain the mathematical symmetry.

questions.text: A public-health analyst says handedness and musical ability have covariance near zero, so there is no relationship at all. How would you refine that statement to make it statistically accurate without overstating what zero covariance means?
rubric_items: Full credit: Rephrases near-zero covariance as near absence of linear association.; Avoids claiming complete independence or no relationship.; Acknowledges possible nonlinear relationships or other limitations.; Keeps interpretation cautious and data-centered.
Partial credit: Says zero covariance does not imply independence but does not rephrase clearly.; Mentions 'linear' but not why it matters.; Focuses only on causation instead of dependence.
Common mistakes: Saying near-zero covariance proves no relationship.; Treating covariance 0 and independence as equivalent.; Ignoring that 'near zero' is also a sample-size/context issue.

questions.text: Let T = X - Y. Derive an expression for Var(T) in terms of Var(X), Var(Y), and Cov(X,Y). Then interpret what happens when X and Y are strongly positively correlated.
rubric_items: Full credit: Derives Var(X-Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)-2Cov(X,Y).; Uses transformation properties correctly.; Interprets positive covariance as reducing variance of the difference.; Gives intuitive explanation of co-movement canceling in subtraction.
Partial credit: Correct formula with weak derivation.; Derivation mostly correct but sign error in interpretation.; States the effect qualitatively without formula.
Common mistakes: Writing +2Cov instead of -2Cov.; Claiming Var(-Y)=-Var(Y).; Saying positive correlation increases variability of the difference.

questions.text: Explain how the statement 'correlation measures linear relationship' should be understood carefully. In particular, contrast the meanings of rho=0, rho close to 1, and rho exactly 1.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains linear rather than general dependence.; Distinguishes rho=0 from independence.; Distinguishes rho close to 1 from rho exactly 1.; States exact ±1 correspond to deterministic linear relation.
Partial credit: Gets the broad idea but misses one case.; Says 0 means no relationship without qualifying linear.; Discusses strong association but not exactness of 1.
Common mistakes: Equating rho=0 with independence universally.; Equating high rho with causation.; Failing to distinguish exact from approximate linearity.

questions.text: Suppose a hidden variable K influences whether users like several different movie genres. Observationally, the genre-preference indicators are dependent. Explain why this kind of situation warns us to be cautious when interpreting covariance or correlation between any two observed preferences.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that latent K can induce observed dependence.; Connects this to caution in interpreting covariance/correlation.; Mentions conditional independence or shared cause structure.; Separates marginal association from direct relationship.
Partial credit: Mentions hidden variables vaguely.; Says correlation may be confounded but gives no mechanism.; Focuses only on causation without explaining induced dependence.
Common mistakes: Assuming observed correlation must be direct influence.; Ignoring latent-variable confounding.; Claiming conditional independence implies marginal independence.

questions.text: A city analyst records outside temperature X in degrees Celsius and household utility bill Y in dollars. She then converts temperature to Fahrenheit, X' = 1.8X + 32, and bills to cents, Y' = 100Y, and notices the covariance changed a lot. Explain, without doing heavy arithmetic, how Cov(X',Y') relates to Cov(X,Y), what happens to the sign, and why this makes raw covariance a poor scale-free measure of association.
rubric_items: Full credit: States or derives Cov(aX+b,cY+d)=ac·Cov(X,Y).; Explains that +32 has no effect and scaling by 1.8 and 100 changes only magnitude.; Correctly says the sign is unchanged here because both multipliers are positive.; Interprets why covariance is unit-dependent and therefore not a scale-free association measure.

Partial credit: Correct qualitative statement that covariance changes under rescaling but does not clearly express the product ac.; Identifies that constants do not matter but forgets to discuss sign or units.; Mentions correlation as unitless without connecting it to the scenario.

Common mistakes: Saying adding 32 changes covariance because it changes the mean.; Claiming covariance is invariant under unit conversion.; Confusing covariance with correlation and saying both remain numerically unchanged.

questions.text: Let S = X + Y for two random variables that are not assumed independent. A student says, 'The variance of a sum is always the sum of the variances.' Respond to this claim by deriving Var(S) from covariance properties, and then interpret what positive versus negative covariance would mean for the variability of S.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from Var(X+Y)=Cov(X+Y,X+Y) or an equivalent correct expansion.; Correctly derives Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+2Cov(X,Y)+Var(Y).; Explains the effect of positive and negative covariance on total variability.; Clarifies that independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not necessarily imply independence.

Partial credit: Gives the correct formula but with little derivation.; Derives the formula but does not interpret the sign of covariance.; States the independence caveat imprecisely but shows some awareness of it.
Common mistakes: Omitting the cross terms and asserting Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y) always.; Saying negative covariance makes variance negative.; Claiming zero covariance and independence are equivalent.

questions.text: A researcher says: 'If two variables have correlation 0, then they must be independent.' Give a careful response. Your answer should address which implication involving independence and correlation is valid, which converse fails, and use a concrete nonlinear example to justify your claim.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that 'correlation 0 implies independence' is false.; States the correct direction: independence implies zero correlation/covariance.; Uses a nonlinear counterexample such as Y=X^2 with symmetric X.; Explains why the example has zero correlation but is still dependent.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false and mentions nonlinear dependence, but gives no concrete example.; Gives an example but does not explain why covariance is zero.; Correctly states one implication but muddles converse and inverse language.
Common mistakes: Saying uncorrelated means unrelated in every sense.; Using a counterexample that actually has nonzero covariance.; Claiming dependence always produces nonzero correlation.

questions.text: Suppose a scatterplot of variables X and Y lies exactly on a straight line with positive slope, but the points are measured in very different units and have different spreads. Explain why the correlation must be 1, not just 'large and positive.' Then contrast this with a situation where covariance is positive but correlation is strictly less than 1.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that exact positive linearity Y=aX+b with a>0 implies correlation 1.; Explains the role of standardization/unitlessness in correlation.; Contrasts perfect linear relation with merely positive covariance.; Correctly places imperfect positive linear association at 0<rho<1.

Partial credit: Knows that a perfect line gives correlation 1 but does not explain why units do not matter.; Explains positive covariance versus positive correlation qualitatively but not the exact value 1.; Mentions normalization vaguely without connecting to the scenario.

Common mistakes: Saying correlation depends on the slope magnitude directly rather than on perfect linearity.; Confusing positive covariance with correlation 1.; Ignoring the condition that the points lie exactly on a line.

questions.text: You model a portfolio return as R = A + B, where A is the return from a tech stock and B is the return from an airline stock. Two analysts agree on Var(A) and Var(B), but disagree about dependence: one says the assets are independent, the other says they are strongly negatively correlated. Without plugging in numbers, explain how their predictions for Var(R) differ, what covariance term causes the difference, and why this matters for diversification.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes or states Var(A+B)=Var(A)+Var(B)+2Cov(A,B).; Explains the independent case as covariance zero.; Explains the negatively correlated case as reducing variance through a negative covariance term.; Connects the result to diversification/risk reduction in a portfolio context.

Partial credit: Knows negative covariance lowers portfolio variance but does not state the full formula.; States the formula but gives little interpretation of diversification.; Mentions independence but does not explain why covariance is zero under independence.

Common mistakes: Saying negatively correlated assets make variance negative.; Claiming independence and negative correlation are compatible descriptions of the same pair of assets.; Focusing only on expected returns rather than variance and covariance.

questions.text: A classmate says, "Deep learning is basically a completely different idea from logistic regression." Using the view from lecture that a neural network is many logistic regression units stacked together, explain what is the same and what is new when you move from logistic regression to a neural network with one hidden layer.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that both logistic regression and neural networks model conditional probabilities P(Y|X).; Explains that a neuron computes a weighted sum followed by a sigmoid/nonlinear activation.; Identifies stacking/composition through hidden layers as the source of added expressive power.; Mentions that hidden layers learn intermediate features or nonlinear transformations.

Partial credit: Says neural networks are built from logistic-regression-like pieces but does not explain P(Y|X).; Mentions hidden layers add complexity without explaining composition or nonlinearity.; Correctly contrasts single-layer vs multi-layer models but with limited detail.

Common mistakes: Claiming neural networks are generative models like Naive Bayes.; Saying the only difference is having more parameters, without discussing nonlinear composition.; Saying each neuron is literally an independent logistic regression fitted separately.

questions.text: Suppose you build a network with one hidden layer, but every hidden unit computes only a linear combination h_j = theta_j^T x, and the output applies a sigmoid to a linear combination of those h_j values. A student claims this is already a deep nonlinear model because it has a hidden layer. Do you agree? Reason it out algebraically and conceptually.
rubric_items: Full credit: Shows that composing linear maps yields another linear map.; Concludes the model reduces to logistic regression with an effective weight vector.; States that nonlinearity in hidden layers is what prevents collapse and creates added complexity.
Partial credit: Says the model is not more expressive but gives only intuitive justification.; Mentions linear layers collapse without explicitly tying it to logistic regression.

Common mistakes: Thinking any hidden layer automatically makes the model deep in a meaningful expressive sense.; Confusing number of parameters with functional complexity.; Saying multiple linear layers create polynomial decision boundaries.

questions.text: You have a binary classifier with 300 input features and one hidden layer of size 10, where every hidden neuron receives all 300 inputs and the output neuron receives all 10 hidden activations. Ignoring bias terms, count the number of trainable connection weights, and explain what each group of parameters represents.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes 3000 input-to-hidden weights and 10 hidden-to-output weights.; States total 3010 ignoring biases.; Interprets the role of both parameter groups in terms of feature extraction and final prediction.
Partial credit: Gets one of the counts right but makes a minor counting error.; Provides the total without explaining what the two groups do.
Common mistakes: Adding instead of multiplying for input-to-hidden weights.; Forgetting that each hidden neuron has its own separate weights.; Counting only hidden-to-output parameters.

questions.text: You are choosing between Naive Bayes, logistic regression, and a small neural network for a medical classification task with many binary features that are plausibly dependent. Explain why estimating P(X1, ..., Xn | Y) directly is problematic, how Naive Bayes avoids that, and why logistic regression or a neural network might be appealing despite requiring optimization.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why direct joint conditional estimation is intractable.; Describes Naive Bayes factorization via conditional independence.; Contrasts generative modeling of P(X|Y)P(Y) with discriminative modeling of P(Y|X).; Explains why dependence among features motivates logistic regression or neural networks.; Mentions optimization/parameter tradeoff for discriminative models.

Partial credit: Correctly compares Naive Bayes and logistic regression but omits why the full joint is hard.; Mentions feature dependence but does not connect it to model choice.; Describes neural networks as more flexible without tying them to discriminative learning.
Common mistakes: Saying logistic regression also requires conditional independence.; Claiming Naive Bayes directly models P(Y|X) only.; Ignoring the tractability argument for Naive Bayes.

questions.text: During training, a neural network lecture says "deep learning is maximum likelihood estimation with neural networks." Make that statement precise for binary classification. What objective is being optimized, and how does that connect to the predicted probability at test time?
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the network models P(Y=1|X=x; theta).; Identifies maximum conditional likelihood or log-likelihood as the training objective.; Gives or clearly describes the Bernoulli log-likelihood form.; Connects training objective to test-time probability prediction and thresholding.
Partial credit: Mentions MLE and thresholding but not the explicit likelihood/log-likelihood form.; Describes cross-entropy informally without linking it to maximum likelihood.

Common mistakes: Saying the network maximizes P(X,Y) rather than conditional likelihood.; Confusing training-time optimization with test-time argmax only.; Claiming MLE means minimizing squared error by default.

questions.text: Consider one binary-labeled training example. Your network predicts 0.9 for a true positive case and 0.9 for a true negative case in two different examples. Without doing heavy arithmetic, compare how each example contributes to the Bernoulli log-likelihood and explain what this says about how maximum likelihood rewards or penalizes confidence.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies log(0.9) for y=1 and log(0.1) for y=0 when y-hat=0.9.; Explains that the incorrect confident prediction gets much more heavily penalized.; Notes the distinction between likelihood-based training and simple 0/1 accuracy after thresholding.
Partial credit: Understands one case is rewarded and the other penalized but does not clearly connect to the log-likelihood form.; Mentions confidence matters but gives muddled sign interpretation.

Common mistakes: Treating both examples as equally good because both are above 0.5.; Forgetting that the y=0 term uses log(1-y-hat).; Saying likelihood only cares about final class labels, not predicted probabilities.

questions.text: A student says, "At test time, a neural network is doing something fundamentally different from logistic regression because it no longer outputs probabilities." Evaluate this statement for the binary classification setting described in lecture.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the network outputs a probability P(Y=1|X=x) in binary classification.; Explains that thresholding is a separate decision rule layered on top of the probability.; Contrasts single linear score in logistic regression with hidden-feature composition in neural networks.
Partial credit: Says the statement is false and mentions probabilities, but does not explain thresholding or the role of hidden layers.

Common mistakes: Confusing probability output with final hard label.; Claiming only logistic regression has a probabilistic interpretation.; Saying hidden layers eliminate the meaning of the final output as a probability.

questions.text: Imagine you train a neural network on a huge video dataset and later discover that some later-layer neurons respond strongly to cats, faces, or other high-level concepts. Explain why this phenomenon is plausible from the architecture and training objective, without appealing to biology or hand-waving.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains hierarchical feature composition across layers.; Connects emergence of high-level neurons to optimization for the prediction objective.; Avoids claiming neurons are manually programmed with semantic meanings.; Notes that useful intermediate representations can emerge from data and objective.
Partial credit: Mentions deeper layers learn more abstract features but does not tie this to training objective.; Correctly describes emergent features but in vague terms.

Common mistakes: Saying later-layer concepts appear because of a built-in semantic label for each neuron.; Explaining only by analogy to the brain with no machine-learning reasoning.; Claiming every neuron always corresponds to a human-interpretable concept.

questions.text: Compare Naive Bayes and logistic regression from the perspective of what probability distribution each model learns. Then explain why the lecture frames deep learning as an extension of logistic regression rather than of Naive Bayes.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies Naive Bayes as modeling P(X|Y)P(Y) and logistic regression as modeling P(Y|X).; Explains that neural networks directly model P(Y|X), so they extend the logistic-regression viewpoint.; Mentions conditional likelihood training and nonlinear feature composition.

Partial credit: Gets the generative/discriminative contrast right but does not explain why deep learning aligns with logistic regression.; Mentions direct probability modeling but not the specific distributions.
Common mistakes: Claiming Naive Bayes and logistic regression model the same distribution in different notation.; Calling neural networks generative here.; Failing to distinguish P(X|Y) from P(Y|X).

questions.text: Suppose a binary logistic regression and a one-hidden-layer neural network both produce an estimated probability for the same example, and both probabilities are below 0.5. Explain the decision rule each uses for classification, and then explain why the internal computation leading to that probability can still be very different.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the common thresholding rule at 0.5.; Explains logistic regression uses one linear score plus sigmoid.; Explains neural networks use hidden-layer nonlinear transformations before the final output.; Notes that same threshold does not imply same internal model or boundary.
Partial credit: Gets the thresholding rule right but gives only a vague comparison of internals.; Understands that neural networks have hidden layers but not why that matters.

Common mistakes: Claiming the threshold differs by model in the given lecture setup.; Saying a neural network’s output is not comparable to a logistic regression probability.; Ignoring the role of hidden activations.

questions.text: Why does adding hidden layers help with feature dependence in a way that Naive Bayes does not? Answer in terms of model assumptions and representation, not just "neural networks are more powerful."
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly names the Naive Bayes conditional independence assumption.; Explains that neural networks learn representations of feature interactions instead of assuming them away.; Frames the contrast in terms of model assumptions and representation, not vague flexibility only.

Partial credit: Notes Naive Bayes assumes independence and neural networks do not, but gives limited explanation of hidden representations.; Says neural networks can capture nonlinearities without tying this to dependence among inputs.
Common mistakes: Claiming logistic regression or neural networks require independent features.; Discussing only dataset size or compute cost.; Giving only a slogan like "deep networks are stronger."

questions.text: You are advising a team that wants to build a classifier for labeled images. One teammate points to the success of systems like AlphaGo and large image networks and concludes that any task should use the deepest model available. Give a careful answer that uses the course framing rather than hype.
rubric_items: Full credit: Acknowledges genuine successes of deep learning.; Places model choice in the supervised-learning pipeline rather than hype.; Explains that more depth/parameters increase expressive power but also training demands and complexity.; Rejects the blanket claim that deepest is always best.
Partial credit: Says deeper is not always better but provides limited reasoning.; Mentions data/compute needs without tying to course framing.
Common mistakes: Arguing solely from famous examples.; Claiming depth is always harmful or always beneficial.; Ignoring evaluation and task-specific model choice.

questions.text: A student argues that because each neuron is like a logistic regression, the hidden neurons in one layer can all share the same parameters without losing anything important. Is that right? Explain what would happen if all hidden neurons had identical weights.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that different hidden neurons need different parameters.; Explains that identical parameters produce identical activations for every input.; Concludes this collapses representational diversity and reduces the value of the hidden layer.
Partial credit: Says the claim is wrong but gives only intuitive explanation.; Mentions learning different features without explicitly noting identical outputs.

Common mistakes: Saying parameter sharing is always harmless because neurons are interchangeable.; Confusing this with convolutional weight sharing, which is not the issue in the given lecture context.; Claiming hidden units stay different just because they are in different positions.

questions.text: In Naive Bayes, the lecture emphasizes using sums of log-probabilities instead of products of probabilities at test time. Explain the numerical reason for that trick, and then contrast it with how optimization is framed for logistic regression or neural networks.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains underflow from multiplying many small probabilities in Naive Bayes.; States that logs convert products to sums and preserve the argmax.; Contrasts this with conditional log-likelihood optimization in logistic regression/neural networks.; Mentions the smooth gradient-based objective in discriminative models.
Partial credit: Knows logs help with numerical stability but does not clearly contrast the training roles across models.; Mentions underflow vaguely without explaining product-to-sum conversion.

Common mistakes: Saying logs change which class is predicted.; Claiming logistic regression is trained by multiplying P(X|Y) terms like Naive Bayes.; Ignoring optimization when discussing neural networks.

questions.text: The lecture says a neural network, like logistic regression, gets its intelligence from its parameters theta. Explain what that means operationally during training and prediction.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that architecture defines form, while parameters encode learned behavior.; States that training learns theta by optimizing likelihood/objective.; States that prediction uses the fixed learned theta to compute outputs for new inputs.
Partial credit: Says parameters matter but does not distinguish training from prediction.; Mentions learning weights without tying them to behavior or likelihood.
Common mistakes: Saying the architecture alone contains the intelligence.; Confusing parameters with training data points.; Describing training as memorizing labels without mentioning optimization.

questions.text: You are given a binary classification problem where the relationship between X and Y is strongly nonlinear. A teammate proposes to solve this by keeping logistic regression but just adding more linear layers before the final sigmoid. Another proposes hidden layers with nonlinear activations. Which proposal is principled, and why?
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects extra linear layers as insufficient.; Explains that composition of linear maps is linear.; Explains that nonlinear activations create extra expressive power and enable nonlinear boundaries.
Partial credit: Chooses nonlinear layers as better but without the linear-composition argument.; Mentions hidden layers help with nonlinearity in vague terms.
Common mistakes: Thinking depth alone guarantees nonlinearity.; Saying more linear parameters automatically fit nonlinear patterns.; Confusing output sigmoid with hidden nonlinearities.

questions.text: In a one-hidden-layer network for binary classification, explain why the chain rule is necessary to learn the input-to-hidden weights. Your answer should describe the dependency path from one early weight to the final log-likelihood, even if you do not compute derivatives explicitly.
rubric_items: Full credit: Describes the dependency chain: early weight -> hidden activation -> output score/probability -> log-likelihood.; Explains why direct differentiation requires chain rule through composed functions.; Identifies backpropagation as organized repeated application of chain rule.
Partial credit: Mentions chain rule and backpropagation but does not clearly describe the dependency path.; Explains only that there are many layers, without linking to the objective.

Common mistakes: Saying chain rule is needed only because there are many parameters, not because of functional composition.; Confusing backpropagation with gradient ascent itself.; Claiming early weights affect the likelihood directly without intermediate activations.

questions.text: Someone says, "Since neural networks are trained with MLE just like Naive Bayes can be, they are basically the same kind of model." How would you correct that statement?
rubric_items: Full credit: States that MLE is an estimation principle, not a model specification.; Contrasts Naive Bayes as generative and neural networks/logistic regression as discriminative.; Mentions differing assumptions or architectures despite shared MLE.
Partial credit: Says the models are different despite both using MLE, but without clarifying generative vs discriminative.; Mentions different architectures but not the probabilistic distinction.
Common mistakes: Equating training criterion with model family.; Claiming Naive Bayes directly models P(Y|X) in the same way.; Ignoring the role of independence assumptions in Naive Bayes.

questions.text: Why might a one-hidden-layer neural network be viewed as learning a new feature representation before doing classification? Explain this in terms of h, not in terms of vague metaphors.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines h as learned transformed features of x.; Explains each h_j as a nonlinear function of x.; States that the output layer classifies using h, so the network learns a representation before final prediction.; Mentions joint learning with the prediction objective.
Partial credit: Says hidden layers learn features but does not explain that the output works on h rather than raw x.; Correct but somewhat metaphorical rather than operational.

Common mistakes: Treating h as just an internal storage device with no modeling role.; Saying the hidden layer is precomputed independently of training objective.; Ignoring the nonlinear transformation aspect.

questions.text: A startup has labels for many observations and wants to "predict the class label given prior observations." Use the supervised learning pipeline from lecture to explain where a neural network fits, and name the roles of data, model, learning algorithm, testing, and evaluation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies data, formal model, learning algorithm, testing, and evaluation.; Places neural networks as one possible formal model in the pipeline.; Explains training as learning parameters from labeled data and testing as using them on new data.
Partial credit: Lists the pipeline components but with limited explanation of the neural network's role.; Explains training and testing but omits evaluation or model selection.
Common mistakes: Confusing testing with training.; Treating evaluation as part of the training labels themselves.; Skipping the formal model stage entirely.

questions.text: Why is a neural network with many parameters not automatically better than logistic regression, even though logistic regression is just one logistic unit? Give a reasoning-based answer that balances expressiveness and learnability.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that more parameters increase expressive power.; Explains tradeoffs: optimization difficulty, data demands, and potential over-complexity.; States that suitability depends on the task and feature relationship, not parameter count alone.
Partial credit: Says bigger models are not always better but gives only one side of the tradeoff.; Mentions overfitting or optimization vaguely without discussing expressiveness.

Common mistakes: Assuming parameter count alone determines performance.; Claiming logistic regression is obsolete because neural networks exist.; Arguing only from simplicity without acknowledging neural networks' extra power.

questions.text: Suppose you have a training set with binary labels and you can either maximize raw likelihood or maximize log-likelihood for your neural network. Explain why these lead to the same optimizer in principle, and why log-likelihood is still the preferred formulation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that log is monotone increasing, so argmax is unchanged.; Explains product-to-sum simplification across examples.; Mentions numerical/optimization convenience as the practical reason for using log-likelihood.
Partial credit: Knows the optimizer is unchanged but provides only one practical reason for the log form.; Mentions numerical stability without explaining why.
Common mistakes: Claiming the maximizer changes after taking logs.; Confusing maximizing log-likelihood with minimizing classification error directly.; Ignoring why sums are easier than products.

questions.text: You are designing a model whose output should be an expected future reward rather than a class probability. Use the lecture's contrast to explain why that problem is no longer ordinary classification, even if the internal function approximator is still a deep network.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that classification outputs probabilities for labels, while reinforcement-style outputs can be expectations of reward.; States that the same deep architecture can be used with a different target/objective.; Clearly distinguishes output interpretation from internal function approximator.

Partial credit: Notes that reinforcement learning is different because output is expectation, but gives limited explanation.; Mentions not everything is classification without specifying the probability-vs-expectation distinction.

Common mistakes: Assuming any deep network output is automatically a probability.; Confusing model architecture with learning objective.; Treating reinforcement learning as just multiclass classification.

questions.text: A classmate says: "Deep learning is a completely different statistical idea from logistic regression; neural networks are not really doing likelihood-based learning." Based on the course framing, explain why that statement is misleading. In your answer, connect logistic regression, hidden neurons, and the training objective, and explain what is new in a neural network compared with a single logistic regression classifier.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that both logistic regression and neural networks are trained via MLE / maximizing conditional likelihood.; Explains that a neuron is being framed as a logistic-regression-like unit.; Explains that hidden layers create compositions of nonlinear transformations, increasing expressive power.; Contrasts single linear score in logistic regression with stacked nonlinear units in a neural network.

Partial credit: Correctly says both model P(Y|X) but does not clearly connect to MLE.; Recognizes hidden layers add complexity but gives vague reasoning about why.; Says neural nets are many logistic regressions but does not explain what training objective remains the same.

Common mistakes: Claiming neural networks model P(X,Y) instead of P(Y|X) in this framing.; Saying the main difference is only that neural networks have more data, rather than more expressive parameterized structure.; Saying deep learning is not statistical or not likelihood-based at all.

questions.text: You are given a dataset of 300 binary medical features per patient and a binary disease label. A student argues: "Since naive Bayes already handles lots of features, deep learning must be preferable only because it has more parameters." Evaluate this claim by comparing naive Bayes, logistic regression, and a simple neural network in terms of what probability distribution they model, what assumptions they avoid or impose, and why a neural network might help when features interact.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies naive Bayes as modeling P(X|Y) and P(Y), and logistic regression / neural nets as modeling P(Y|X).; Explains the role of the naive conditional independence assumption.; Explains that logistic regression is limited by linear decision structure, while neural networks can learn nonlinear feature interactions via hidden units.; Explicitly rejects the simplistic claim that neural nets are better only because they have more parameters.

Partial credit: Gets the generative vs discriminative distinction right but gives weak explanation of feature interactions.; Mentions nonlinearities in neural nets without tying them to the medical-feature scenario.; Notes that naive Bayes uses independence assumptions but does not explain why that matters computationally or statistically.

Common mistakes: Saying logistic regression assumes feature independence.; Claiming naive Bayes directly models P(Y|X).; Reducing the comparison to parameter count only, without discussing modeled distributions or nonlinearity.

questions.text: Consider a binary classifier with d input features, one hidden layer of size h, and one output neuron, where every hidden and output unit is a logistic-regression-style sigmoid unit. Without plugging in numbers, explain how many connection parameters this network has, how the forward computation produces a prediction for one example, and why training requires the chain rule rather than the simpler gradient expression from ordinary logistic regression.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly gives d·h input-to-hidden parameters and h hidden-to-output parameters, with sensible treatment of biases.; Explains forward pass as hidden activations followed by output sigmoid yielding P(Y=1|X=x).; States that training still uses likelihood maximization.; Explains clearly why gradients for early weights require the chain rule/backpropagation through intermediate activations.

Partial credit: Counts parameters correctly but gives only a vague description of backpropagation.; Describes forward pass correctly but misses the interpretation as a conditional probability.; Mentions chain rule without explaining the dependence of output on earlier-layer weights through hidden units.

Common mistakes: Adding layers' parameters incorrectly, such as d+h instead of d·h+h.; Saying each hidden neuron shares the same parameters unless justified; the context says different parameters for every connection.; Treating hidden activations as final class predictions rather than intermediate features.

questions.text: A team builds a network with an input layer, several hidden layers, and an output sigmoid for binary image classification. One engineer proposes removing all hidden-layer nonlinearities while keeping the same layered architecture, arguing that depth alone should make the model more expressive. Do you agree? Give a verbal argument, using the course's comparison between a neural network and a linear network, for what happens to the effective model class.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that stacked linear layers compose to a linear map.; Connects that result to the final sigmoid, concluding the model is effectively logistic regression on a linear score.; Explains that nonlinear hidden activations are what create additional expressive power.; Uses the comparison between linear and nonlinear hidden layers, not just a memorized slogan.

Partial credit: Says 'no, it won't help' but gives only an intuitive answer without the composition-of-linear-maps argument.; Recognizes nonlinearities matter but does not connect to why layered linear maps collapse.; Correctly compares linear vs nonlinear networks but forgets the final output interpretation.

Common mistakes: Claiming more layers automatically imply more expressive power even without nonlinearities.; Confusing more parameters with a genuinely different function class.; Saying the final sigmoid alone is enough to make the whole deep linear network highly nonlinear in a way hidden layers preserve.

questions.text: Imagine you are training a deep binary classifier and, early in training, someone says: "At test time we just threshold at 0.5, so during training we should directly optimize the number of examples above 0.5." Explain why that is not the objective described in the course, what objective is used instead, and why that objective is especially natural when the network outputs an estimate of P(Y=1|X=x).
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes test-time thresholding from training-time objective.; Identifies MLE / conditional log-likelihood / binary cross-entropy as the training objective.; Explains why this matches the probabilistic interpretation of output as P(Y=1|X=x).; Notes why thresholded accuracy is a poor optimization target for gradient-based training: it discards confidence and is not smoothly optimized by gradient methods.

Partial credit: Names cross-entropy or likelihood correctly but gives weak reasoning about why.; Explains thresholding is for prediction, not training, but does not connect to probability modeling.; Mentions gradients vaguely without tying them to the objective.

Common mistakes: Saying the model is trained by counting how many outputs exceed 0.5.; Confusing the predicted label with the predicted probability.; Claiming MLE is only for logistic regression and not for neural networks.

questions.text: A city asks you to help design the decision rule for self-driving cars in rare crash scenarios. A policymaker says, "Just survey people globally, estimate the most popular moral preference, and encode that as the objectively correct rule." Explain why the probability framework from class does not by itself solve the ethical problem, even if the survey estimates are statistically precise.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains difference between descriptive and normative use of probability; Uses variation in Moral Machine preferences as evidence against a universal rule; States that statistical precision does not remove ethical controversy
Partial credit: Notes that cultures differ but does not connect to normative vs descriptive distinction; Says surveys can be biased without addressing the deeper ethical issue
Common mistakes: Claiming the majority preference is automatically ethical; Treating probability as a machine for deciding moral truth; Ignoring cross-group heterogeneity

questions.text: An autonomous-vehicle company reports that event A is "the car harms a pedestrian" and event B is "the car harms a passenger" in a simulated emergency. An executive says, "The probability of harm to either side is just P(A)+P(B)." Give a careful response using the probability rules, and explain what assumption would make the executive's formula valid.
rubric_items: Full credit: States inclusion-exclusion formula correctly; Explains mutual exclusivity as the condition for simple addition; Interprets double counting in the crash context
Partial credit: Gives the right formula but weak interpretation; Mentions overlap without naming mutual exclusivity
Common mistakes: Using independence instead of mutual exclusivity; Saying P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B) always; Subtracting P(A)P(B) without justification

questions.text: A company advertises its AI detector with the statement, "There is a 99% chance this essay was AI-written because our detector gave a positive result with p-value 0.01." Explain what is wrong with that statement, and describe what extra probabilistic ingredients would be needed to estimate the probability the essay was AI-written.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes p-value from posterior probability; Mentions Bayes' theorem and required components: prior and likelihoods; Explains base-rate dependence
Partial credit: Says p-value is not the same as probability of hypothesis but does not say what is needed instead; Mentions false positives only
Common mistakes: Interpreting p-value as P(hypothesis true | data); Ignoring prior probability of AI-written essays; Thinking low p-value alone proves authorship

questions.text: A university is considering a watermark-based policy for flagging student essays. Suppose H is the event "essay is human-written" and W is the event "essay contains the watermark pattern." Explain aloud how you would compute P(H | W), and then discuss one ethical danger of deploying the flag if administrators confuse P(W | H) with P(H | W).
rubric_items: Full credit: States Bayes formula correctly in this context; Expands denominator or otherwise explains normalization; Identifies confusion between likelihood and posterior as an ethical risk; Connects the error to wrongful flagging
Partial credit: Uses Bayes correctly but gives a vague ethical discussion; Mentions false accusations without explaining the probability confusion
Common mistakes: Equating P(W|H) with P(H|W); Forgetting the denominator; Ignoring the prior/base rate of human essays

questions.text: In a debate about AI-generated medical advice, one student says, "Probability is objective frequency, so talking about a prior belief that the advice is safe is unscientific." Another says, "Probability can represent a degree of belief that updates with evidence." Compare these views and explain which one better supports decision-making when evidence is incomplete.
rubric_items: Full credit: Accurately contrasts frequentist and Bayesian interpretations; Explains why Bayesian updating is useful under incomplete evidence; Notes that priors should be justified, not arbitrary
Partial credit: Gives the basic contrast but weak application to AI safety; Says Bayesian is better without discussing uncertainty updating
Common mistakes: Claiming one interpretation makes the other invalid in all contexts; Treating Bayesian probability as purely subjective guesswork; Ignoring the role of evidence updating

questions.text: A moderation team monitors two kinds of harms from an AI system on a given day: D = "it spreads dangerous misinformation" and B = "it expresses demographic bias." They know P(D)=0.08, P(B)=0.11, and P(D union B)=0.16. Compute P(D and B), and then explain why reporting only the two marginal probabilities could understate the ethical concern.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes 0.03 correctly; Uses inclusion-exclusion explicitly or correctly implicitly; Explains why overlap corresponds to compounded ethical harm
Partial credit: Gets the number right with little explanation; Discusses overlap qualitatively but arithmetic is off
Common mistakes: Adding 0.08 and 0.11 directly; Subtracting the union from one marginal only; Failing to interpret the joint event ethically

questions.text: A product team says, "Because our classifier has two errors, false positives and false negatives, they should add to 1." Is that statement always true? Answer carefully by defining the events and saying when such a complement relationship would and would not hold.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the claim is generally false; Explains that the rates are conditioned on different events/sample spaces; Gives a correct example of a true complement pair
Partial credit: Says they are not complements but explanation is vague; Mentions conditioning without a concrete example
Common mistakes: Saying all binary errors must sum to 1; Ignoring conditioning; Confusing false positive rate with 1-specificity but not explaining the distinction

questions.text: Suppose an AI-generated-text detector counts occurrences of a watermark-related word in a 10,000-word document. A colleague says, "We should always model the count as Poisson, because word counts are counts." Give a more nuanced answer comparing a Poisson model for short text with a Gaussian approximation for long text, and explain why the modeling choice matters ethically.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why Poisson can fit shorter, lower-count settings; Explains why Gaussian approximation can be appropriate for large documents; Connects model misspecification to ethical risk in enforcement
Partial credit: Mentions one model is more convenient but gives weak justification; Notes ethical stakes without linking to calibration
Common mistakes: Saying counts must always be Poisson; Claiming Gaussian cannot model counts at all; Ignoring document length regime

questions.text: In election forecasting, the course notes mention that reporting probabilities can influence voter behavior. Relate that idea to AI ethics: if a platform publicly reports a very high probability that its content-moderation model is fair, why might that itself be ethically problematic even if the estimate is statistically honest?
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies feedback effects of probability reporting; Transfers the election-polling ethical concern to AI fairness communication; Argues for communicating uncertainty and assumptions
Partial credit: Says probabilities can mislead without explaining behavior change; Discusses overconfidence but not feedback effects
Common mistakes: Treating forecasts as passive facts with no social effect; Assuming honesty alone removes ethical concern; Ignoring downstream decision-makers

questions.text: A safety auditor says an autonomous system avoids harm in 97% of simulated runs. Without doing new arithmetic, explain how you would express the probability that harm occurs in a run, and why this complement rule is useful but not sufficient for ethical evaluation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Applies complement rule correctly; States harm probability as 1 minus safety probability; Explains why aggregate probability alone is ethically incomplete
Partial credit: Gets 0.03 but no ethical interpretation; Mentions subgroup issues without clearly invoking complement
Common mistakes: Saying the harm probability is also 0.97; Forgetting events must be complements; Treating aggregate reliability as full ethical adequacy

questions.text: A hospital wants to infer whether an AI triage alert truly indicates a critical patient. You are told only that the system is highly accurate in trials, but not the prevalence of critical cases in the hospital. Explain why Bayes' theorem says prevalence matters, and describe the ethical consequence of ignoring it.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains role of prevalence/prior in Bayes updating; Connects rare-condition setting to many false positives; Describes concrete ethical harms from ignoring base rates
Partial credit: Mentions base rates matter but no clear Bayesian explanation; Gives ethical concern without linking to prevalence
Common mistakes: Assuming high trial accuracy guarantees high posterior certainty everywhere; Ignoring context-dependent prevalence; Confusing sensitivity with positive predictive value

questions.text: A regulator asks whether a generative model's "probability of harmful output" should be treated as a fixed property of the model or as a random variable reflecting uncertainty in our knowledge. Give a Bayesian answer and say why that distinction matters for governance decisions.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the probability itself can be modeled as a random variable under Bayesian reasoning; Explains distinction between point estimate and uncertainty about the true rate; Connects posterior uncertainty to governance choices
Partial credit: Mentions posterior uncertainty but not why governance changes; Gives a generic Bayesian description without applying it
Common mistakes: Saying probabilities can never be random variables; Confusing the random variable with observed outputs only; Ignoring limited-data uncertainty

questions.text: An AI company claims that two diagnostic subsystems fail independently. Let F1 be failure of subsystem 1 and F2 be failure of subsystem 2. Explain how independence changes the expression for P(F1 | F2), and then discuss why assuming independence without evidence can create ethical problems.
rubric_items: Full credit: States P(F1|F2)=P(F1) under independence; May also mention product rule for joint probability; Explains why unjustified independence can hide common-cause risk
Partial credit: Knows independence means 'does not change probability' but weak formula; Notes dependence may exist without giving ethical consequence
Common mistakes: Confusing independence with mutual exclusivity; Claiming independent events cannot occur together; Assuming independence because systems are separate modules

questions.text: A student says, "If event A is ethically worse than event B, then probability theory should assign P(A) greater than P(B)." Critique this statement using the axioms and the meaning of probability from class.
rubric_items: Full credit: Separates probability from moral severity; References the meaning or axioms of probability appropriately; States that rare but severe harms can have low probability
Partial credit: Says the statement is wrong but without linking to what probability means; Mentions severity vs likelihood in vague terms
Common mistakes: Equating importance with probability; Thinking the probability scale includes a moral ranking; Ignoring the event-frequency interpretation

questions.text: A firm uses rejection sampling to estimate the probability that a complex AI pipeline produces a harmful response under a certain user profile. Explain, at a high level, why sampling can help when exact inference is tedious, and then name one ethical risk if the rare profile of interest is badly under-sampled.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains sampling as approximation when exact inference is hard; Describes estimate via repeated simulated draws; Identifies under-sampling of rare profiles as an ethical fairness risk
Partial credit: Mentions Monte Carlo vaguely without explaining why needed; Notes rare events are hard but not the ethical implications
Common mistakes: Claiming sampling always gives exact answers; Ignoring variance or sample size; Assuming rare groups are unimportant because they are infrequent

questions.text: A content platform tracks two events for a generated post: U = "contains unsafe advice" and R = "was removed by moderation." The platform celebrates that P(R) is high. Explain why P(U | R) and P(R | U) answer different questions, and which one is more relevant if the ethical goal is to know whether harmful content is being caught.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes the two conditional probabilities; Identifies P(R|U) as the catch-rate question; Explains why confusing them can mislead policy
Partial credit: Knows they differ but muddles which is which; Gives one interpretation but not the ethical implication
Common mistakes: Swapping the conditioning event; Assuming the two conditionals are equal; Using a high removal rate P(R) as evidence harmful content is caught

questions.text: Why might a fairness claim based only on an overall average model score be statistically and ethically misleading? Use the course's emphasis on means, distributions, and subgroup variation rather than giving a purely legal answer.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why means can hide variation; Mentions subgroup-conditioned performance or tail risk; Connects hidden variation to ethical masking of harm
Partial credit: Says averages are incomplete but without statistical detail; Mentions fairness groups but not distributions
Common mistakes: Treating equal averages as equal fairness; Ignoring variance and tails; Assuming pooled data are always sufficient

questions.text: Imagine you are asked to defend a policy that suspends users whenever an AI abuse detector outputs a posterior probability above 0.8. What probabilistic and ethical questions would you ask before accepting 0.8 as a threshold? Focus on uncertainty, priors, and the consequences of false positives.
rubric_items: Full credit: Asks about priors/base rates and calibration; Raises subgroup comparability and uncertainty; Discusses false-positive costs and procedural protections
Partial credit: Focuses only on accuracy metrics or only on ethics; Mentions threshold choice but not posterior construction
Common mistakes: Treating 0.8 as universally meaningful without calibration; Ignoring prevalence differences; Assuming a high threshold automatically guarantees fairness

questions.text: A teammate says, "Since probabilities must sum to 1, if we make the probability of one harmful AI behavior smaller, the probabilities of all other harmful behaviors must get larger." Is that necessarily true? Clarify what sample space this claim is assuming and when the statement breaks down.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains need for mutually exclusive, exhaustive partition; States why overlapping events break the claim; Mentions probability can shift to non-harm events
Partial credit: Says 'not always true' but with weak explanation; Mentions overlap without discussing sample space
Common mistakes: Thinking all listed events automatically partition the sample space; Forgetting safe outcomes; Assuming one probability decreasing forces every other one upward

questions.text: You are comparing two versions of an AI tutor on average student rating. Version A and Version B each have many independent ratings, and you plan to compare the sample means. Explain why a normal approximation for the difference in sample means can be reasonable, and then state one ethical limitation of using only a significance threshold to decide deployment.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains CLT justification for means; States difference of independent normals is normal; Identifies an ethical limitation of significance-only decisions
Partial credit: Mentions CLT without connecting to difference of means; Critiques p-values generally without AI deployment context
Common mistakes: Assuming significance implies importance; Ignoring subgroup effects; Claiming normality is exact without conditions

questions.text: Suppose you observe 30 safe deployments and 20 unsafe deployments of an AI system, and a colleague says, "So the true safety probability is exactly 0.6." Give a Bayesian response that treats the safety probability as uncertain, and explain why that is ethically preferable in high-stakes settings.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects exact-certainty claim after finite data; Describes Bayesian distribution over the unknown probability; Connects uncertainty representation to cautious governance
Partial credit: Says 0.6 is only an estimate but does not mention distributional uncertainty; Mentions more data are needed without Bayesian framing
Common mistakes: Treating observed fraction as the exact true parameter; Confusing sample proportion with posterior certainty; Ignoring stakes when summarizing uncertainty

questions.text: A policymaker insists that any ethical AI standard must be universal, and therefore local variation in moral preferences is just noise to be averaged away. Using the self-driving-car context, argue for or against that claim in a way that separates statistical aggregation from value disagreement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Separates aggregation from normative legitimacy; Uses local/global variation as evidence of substantive disagreement; Explains why averaging does not automatically solve the ethical problem
Partial credit: States values differ but does not distinguish noise from disagreement; Argues for pluralism without referencing the context
Common mistakes: Treating disagreement as mere sampling error; Assuming universality follows from averaging; Ignoring whose values are excluded by aggregation

questions.text: A city asks you to design the decision policy for autonomous cars in unavoidable crash situations. A policymaker says, “Just use the most popular answer from the Moral Machine survey and call that the ethical standard.” Explain why that conclusion does not follow from the survey evidence, and distinguish carefully between a probability distribution over people’s responses and a normative ethical rule the car should implement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that survey frequencies are descriptive, not automatically normative.; Mentions cross-cultural or local variation as evidence against a single universal rule.; Correctly distinguishes probability as belief/frequency from ethical justification.; Raises at least one ethical policy concern such as fairness, minority protection, or legitimacy.

Partial credit: States that public opinion is imperfect evidence for ethics but does not clearly explain why.; Mentions disagreement in survey responses without connecting it to policy design.; Recognizes a difference between prediction and prescription but leaves it vague.

Common mistakes: Claiming the highest-probability response is therefore the correct ethical action.; Treating variability in responses as mere sampling noise rather than substantive disagreement.; Confusing probability of a response with moral correctness of that response.

questions.text: A university is considering a watermark detector for AI-written essays. Let H be the event “essay is human-written” and C be the event “essay is ChatGPT-written.” Suppose 90% of submitted essays are human-written, the detector flags 80% of ChatGPT essays, and it falsely flags 10% of human essays. If an essay is flagged, compute the posterior probability it was ChatGPT-written, and then explain why that posterior may still be a poor basis for accusing a student of misconduct.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines events clearly and uses Bayes’ theorem correctly.; Computes P(F)=0.17 and P(C|F)≈0.47.; Interprets the result as a base-rate effect.; Connects the quantitative result to ethical concerns about false accusations and evidentiary standards.

Partial credit: Correct setup but arithmetic error in denominator or final ratio.; Gets the intuition that flagged does not imply guilty, even if calculation is incomplete.; Mentions false positives but not the role of the prior prevalence.
Common mistakes: Answering 0.8 instead of the posterior 0.47.; Ignoring the prior and treating detector accuracy as guilt probability.; Mixing up P(F|C) and P(C|F).

questions.text: An ed-tech company says, “Our AI tutor predicts a 99% chance a student will fail the class, so intervention is ethically justified.” Another analyst replies, “That number alone is not enough.” Give two different probabilistic reasons the analyst could be right, and make sure at least one of them is not just ‘the model might be biased.’
rubric_items: Full credit: Provides two distinct probabilistic reasons the 0.99 may be insufficient.; At least one reason goes beyond generic bias language, such as calibration, base rates, conditioning, uncertainty, or intervention effects.; Explains clearly why the probability statement may not support the ethical decision claimed.

Partial credit: Provides one solid probabilistic reason and one vague concern.; Mentions bias correctly but gives limited probabilistic detail.; Recognizes that prediction and decision are different but does not elaborate.

Common mistakes: Saying 0.99 is always enough because it is numerically large.; Giving only non-probabilistic critiques with no connection to the meaning of the number.; Confusing uncertainty in prediction with moral certainty about intervention.

questions.text: A public health agency uses an AI screening tool to decide who receives a scarce follow-up test. Group A and Group B have different disease prevalences. A manager claims, “If the model uses the same threshold and the same posterior-risk formula for everyone, then the policy is automatically fair because probability rules are universal.” Do you agree? Use probability ideas to argue your position, and be explicit about the difference between mathematical consistency and ethical fairness.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the claim that universal probability rules imply automatic fairness.; Uses base rates or conditional probabilities to explain how the same threshold can create unequal error profiles.; Separates mathematical validity from ethical choice.; Mentions that fairness criteria may conflict or require normative judgment.

Partial credit: Recognizes that equal thresholds may not be fair but gives only intuitive explanation.; Mentions prevalence differences without linking them to conditional error rates or posterior probabilities.; Notes that ethics matters but does not distinguish it from probabilistic reasoning.

Common mistakes: Assuming same formula plus same threshold guarantees fairness.; Ignoring group prevalence entirely.; Claiming probability alone can determine the ethically correct fairness criterion.

questions.text: A company monitoring AI-generated content defines two events in a document: T = “the word ‘the’ appears unusually often” and O = “the word ‘of’ appears unusually often.” An analyst reports P(T)=0.30, P(O)=0.25, and P(T ∩ O)=0.12. First compute P(T ∪ O) and P(neither T nor O). Then explain why an ethics review board should care whether the company reports only P(T ∪ O) without also discussing dependence, uncertainty, and what those events actually mean for authorship.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes P(T∪O)=0.43.; Correctly computes P(neither)=0.57.; Explains that union of markers is not the same as probability of AI authorship.; Mentions at least one of dependence, estimation uncertainty, or ambiguity of the event definition.

Partial credit: Gets one probability correct but not the other.; Uses the right formulas but arithmetic slips.; Provides some ethical interpretation but does not connect it clearly to the event probabilities.
Common mistakes: Adding 0.30 and 0.25 without subtracting the overlap.; Treating P(T∪O) as the probability the text is AI-generated.; Ignoring that these are marker events, not authorship events.

questions.text: A student says: "Two events are independent whenever they do not overlap." Explain why this statement is usually false, and contrast it with the correct intuition for independence. Then describe the one special case in which disjoint events can still be independent.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that disjointness gives P(E ∩ F)=0.; States that independence requires P(E ∩ F)=P(E)P(F).; Explains why these conflict when both probabilities are positive.; Mentions the equivalent conditional-probability intuition P(E|F)=P(E).; Identifies the zero-probability exception.

Partial credit: Correctly says disjoint does not imply independent but gives incomplete justification.; Uses only the conditional form or only the product form without connecting them.; Mentions the zero-probability edge case vaguely.

Common mistakes: Saying disjoint events are independent because they 'do not affect each other.'; Confusing mutual exclusivity with independence.; Forgetting that P(E|F) is only meaningful when P(F)>0.

questions.text: You roll a fair die twice. Let E be the event that the first roll is 1, F the event that the second roll is 6, and G the event that the two rolls sum to 7. Determine which pairs among (E,F), (E,G), and (F,G) are independent, and then decide whether E, F, and G are jointly independent. Explain your reasoning aloud rather than just listing answers.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes P(E), P(F), P(G) correctly.; Checks all three pairwise intersections correctly.; Checks the triple intersection and compares to P(E)P(F)P(G).; Explicitly states that pairwise independence does not imply joint independence.

Partial credit: Gets pairwise results correct but forgets to test joint independence.; States the final conclusion correctly with incomplete probability calculations.; Correctly identifies G but makes a small arithmetic slip on one intersection.
Common mistakes: Assuming independent die rolls automatically make any derived events jointly independent.; Stopping after pairwise checks.; Computing P(G) incorrectly as 1/36 instead of 6/36.

questions.text: A classmate claims: "If two trials are independent, then any events built from those trials are independent too." Use the two-dice setup to evaluate this claim carefully. Your answer should make clear what is true, what is false, and why the wording matters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes independence of trials from independence of arbitrary events.; States the correct disjoint-subsets principle for independent trials.; Explains why the original claim is too broad.; Uses the dice example appropriately.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false but gives a vague reason.; Mentions that some derived events can be dependent without clearly explaining the role of overlapping trial information.; Uses an example but not a general principle.

Common mistakes: Saying any function of independent trials stays independent of any other function.; Thinking independence of underlying variables automatically transfers to all events.; Ignoring the disjoint-subsets condition.

questions.text: For two events E and F with P(F) > 0, explain why the statements P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) and P(E | F) = P(E) are equivalent. In an oral exam, I care less about symbolic manipulation than about whether you can explain what the cancellation means and when it is allowed.
rubric_items: Full credit: Shows both directions of the equivalence.; Uses the condition P(F)>0 explicitly.; Explains the conditional-probability interpretation in words.
Partial credit: Shows only one direction correctly.; Gives the equations but does not explain the need for P(F)>0.; States the intuition without the algebra.
Common mistakes: Cancelling by P(F) without mentioning the positivity condition.; Treating P(E|F)=P(E) as definition in all cases without caveat.; Confusing P(E|F)=P(F|E).

questions.text: A streaming company models a latent preference K = 'likes international emotional comedies.' Let A be 'liked movie 1' and B be 'liked movie 2.' Explain how it is possible that A and B are dependent overall, yet conditionally independent given K. Then tell me what kind of evidence in data would make this story plausible.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains marginal dependence via a common cause or latent variable.; Explains conditional independence using the factorization given K.; Connects observation of A to information about K and hence about B.; Describes what one would look for empirically.

Partial credit: Correctly describes either dependence overall or conditional independence, but not both clearly.; Uses the idea of a hidden variable without articulating the mechanism.; Mentions subgroup analysis vaguely.

Common mistakes: Saying conditioning can only reduce dependence, never create it.; Claiming dependence and conditional independence are contradictory.; Forgetting that the conditioning event creates a new sample space.

questions.text: A student writes, 'Conditional independence of A and B given E means P(A | B, E) = P(A).' Critique this statement carefully. If it is wrong, repair it and explain why the corrected form has to live entirely inside the conditioned-on world.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the proposed statement as incorrect.; Repairs it to P(A | B, E)=P(A | E).; Connects this to P(A ∩ B | E)=P(A | E)P(B | E).; Explains the 'new sample space' idea.
Partial credit: Says the statement is wrong but gives only the factorization or only the conditional form.; Repairs the statement but gives little explanation.; Mentions conditioning on E vaguely.
Common mistakes: Dropping the conditioning on E on one side.; Writing P(A|B,E)=P(A|B) as the conditional independence condition.; Confusing ordinary and conditional independence.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are discrete random variables. I tell you that for every x and y, P(X = x, Y = y) = P(X = x)P(Y = y).
