Explain how you would use that statement to justify the informal claim that 'knowing X tells you nothing about Y.' Then tell me what extra condition you need before you can write P(Y = y | X = x) = P(Y = y).
rubric_items: Full credit: States that factorization of the joint pmf is the definition of independence.; Explains the intuitive meaning in terms of no information gain.; Derives the conditional statement correctly.; Mentions the positivity requirement P(X=x)>0.

Partial credit: States the factorization correctly but does not articulate the intuition.; Mentions the conditional equality but forgets the positivity condition.; Explains 'knowing X tells you nothing' only informally.
Common mistakes: Assuming zero-probability values can be conditioned on.; Checking the factorization for only some pairs (x,y).; Confusing random-variable independence with zero covariance.

questions.text: For three events E, F, and G, why is it not enough to verify only P(E ∩ F ∩ G) = P(E)P(F)P(G)? Give a verbal argument and then state the full set of checks required for independence of three events.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the triple-product condition alone is insufficient.; Lists the three pairwise conditions and the triple condition.; Explains why mutual independence is stronger than a single equation.
Partial credit: Mentions pairwise checks are needed but does not state all of them.; Gives the right conclusion with limited explanation.

Common mistakes: Equating triple-factorization with full independence.; Thinking pairwise independence automatically follows from the triple condition.; Listing only pairwise conditions and omitting the triple condition.

questions.text: Imagine 10 independent coin flips. Let A be the event 'the first 5 flips contain exactly 2 heads' and B be the event 'the last 5 flips contain exactly 3 heads.' Without computing the actual binomial probabilities, explain whether A and B are independent and justify your answer using the structure of the trials.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies that the two events depend on disjoint subsets of independent trials.; States that this implies independence.; Explains why exact probabilities are unnecessary.
Partial credit: States the answer correctly with minimal reasoning.; Mentions independent flips but does not explicitly note the disjoint subsets.

Common mistakes: Thinking the fixed total of 10 flips creates dependence here.; Trying to argue from symmetry instead of the trial-structure principle.; Believing count events are automatically dependent.

questions.text: You are given a joint density f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 4xy for 0 < x < 1 and 0 < y < 1, and 0 otherwise. Explain how you would test independence without skipping the support issue. Then contrast this with the density f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 24xy on the region 0 < x, 0 < y, x + y < 1.
rubric_items: Full credit: Checks both algebraic factorization and support shape.; Concludes independence for 4xy on the square.; Explains why the triangular-support case is not independent.; States that support constraints can destroy independence.

Partial credit: Gets the conclusions right but underexplains the support issue.; Recognizes that the first factors into marginals.; Says the second is dependent because of x+y<1 but does not explain why that matters.
Common mistakes: Declaring independence in the triangular case just because 24xy factors.; Ignoring the support entirely.; Thinking any factorable formula implies independence.

questions.text: Give an oral explanation of the difference between pairwise independence and mutual independence for a collection of events. Your explanation should include why students often confuse them and one concrete consequence of making that mistake.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines pairwise independence correctly.; Defines mutual independence correctly.; Explains the common source of confusion.; States a concrete bad inference that can result.
Partial credit: Knows mutual independence is stronger but does not explain subsets clearly.; Provides only an example without the definitions.

Common mistakes: Saying pairwise independence and mutual independence are the same.; Checking only adjacent or selected pairs.; Thinking triple independence automatically implies pairwise independence without explicitly knowing the definition used.

questions.text: A medical researcher says: 'Symptom A and symptom B are independent in the population, so they will remain independent after conditioning on whether the patient has disease D.' Do you agree? Explain using the idea that independence can change after conditioning, and give an intuitive mechanism either way.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the blanket claim.; States that independence may change under conditioning.; Gives an intuitive mechanism for induced or removed dependence.; Shows awareness that additional assumptions are needed.
Partial credit: States that the claim is not always true but gives only one direction.; Uses a heuristic example without clearly identifying the logical issue.
Common mistakes: Assuming conditioning preserves independence automatically.; Claiming independence and conditional independence are interchangeable.; Thinking conditioning always reduces dependence.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent continuous random variables with CDFs F_X and F_Y. Explain why P(X < x, Y < y) = F_X(x)F_Y(y). I want you to justify both the event interpretation and the independence step, not just quote the formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes the event as an intersection.; Uses independence of events induced by independent random variables.; Correctly identifies the CDF terms.; Explains rather than merely states the formula.
Partial credit: Writes the correct formula with limited verbal explanation.; Explains only the CDF interpretation or only the independence step.
Common mistakes: Assuming P(X < x, Y < y) always factors without independence.; Confusing CDF with density.; Using ≤ versus < as if it mattered here without explanation.

questions.text: Someone says: 'If I know P(E | F) = P(E), then E and F are independent, no questions asked.' Is that statement always valid? Give the cleanest correction you can, including any hidden assumption that must be stated aloud in a rigorous answer.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the need for P(F)>0.; Explains the equivalence to the product definition when that holds.; Notes that otherwise the conditional statement may be undefined.
Partial credit: Mentions a positivity assumption but does not explain it.; States the equivalence without explicitly noting the caveat.
Common mistakes: Forgetting the definition of P(E|F) requires P(F)>0.; Thinking P(E|F)=P(E) is a universal definition with no conditions.; Treating zero-probability cases casually.

questions.text: For conditionally independent random variables X_1, ..., X_n given Y, explain why the joint conditional probability can be written as a product of individual conditional probabilities. Then say why taking logs of that product can be useful conceptually, even before doing any computation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the conditional factorization correctly.; Explains that Y=y fixes the conditioning context.; Explains the log transformation from product to sum.; Gives a conceptual benefit of additivity.
Partial credit: Writes the product formula but gives little interpretation.; Mentions logs turn products into sums without saying why that matters.

Common mistakes: Dropping the conditioning on Y=y from one or more terms.; Confusing conditional independence with unconditional independence.; Thinking the log changes independence rather than reexpressing the same factorization.

questions.text: A survey is sent independently to n people. Let A be the event that person 1 answers 'yes,' and let B be the event that the total number of 'yes' responses is exactly 1. Are A and B independent? Explain carefully, because many students overapply the phrase 'independent trials.'
rubric_items: Full credit: States that A and B are not independent.; Explains the overlap in trial information.; Uses the conditional reasoning that A changes what must happen among others.; Connects this to the correct interpretation of independent trials.
Partial credit: Gets the answer right but explains only that B uses more information.; Mentions dependent overlap without explicitly contrasting with disjoint subsets.

Common mistakes: Saying yes because each person's response is independent.; Ignoring that B includes person 1's response.; Using the wrong principle 'functions of independent variables are independent.'

questions.text: Suppose you want to show three events E, F, and G are independent. A student computes P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F), P(E ∩ G) = P(E)P(G), and P(F ∩ G) = P(F)P(G), then stops. Give a rigorous critique of this argument, and explain what additional calculation is needed and why.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the proof as incomplete.; Names pairwise independence as what has been shown.; States the missing triple-intersection condition.; Explains why the extra condition is logically necessary.
Partial credit: Says more is needed but does not clearly specify the missing condition.; References the pairwise-vs-mutual issue without full detail.

Common mistakes: Accepting the pairwise checks as sufficient.; Saying the triple condition follows automatically from pairwise independence.; Failing to distinguish 'independent in pairs' from 'independent as a collection.'

questions.text: In the conditional paradigm, many probability rules 'still hold after conditioning on E.' Explain what that means for independence statements. Why is it dangerous to remember formulas mechanically without recognizing that conditioning changes the sample space?
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the idea of conditioning as moving to a new sample space.; States the correct conditional independence factorization.; Warns against mixing conditional and unconditional terms.; Connects the idea to general probability rules holding under conditioning.
Partial credit: Mentions the new sample space but gives limited detail.; States the formula correctly without the conceptual explanation.

Common mistakes: Dropping the conditioning from one side of an equation.; Treating conditional independence as ordinary independence with an extra symbol.; Not realizing all formulas must be conditioned consistently.

questions.text: A student says: 'If X and Y are independent random variables, then for any events involving X and Y, dependence is impossible.' Diagnose the overstatement. What is the strongest correct version of the claim you can make from the independence of X and Y?
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the overstatement.; States the correct event-level consequence of random-variable independence.; Distinguishes X-only events, Y-only events, and mixed events.; Provides an illustrative type of event in each category.
Partial credit: Says the claim is too strong but does not articulate the corrected version precisely.; Gives examples without a general principle.

Common mistakes: Assuming any events derived from independent variables are independent.; Failing to distinguish single-variable events from joint events.; Thinking independence of variables is weaker than independence of their coordinate events.

questions.text: You observe two web requests sent to two different servers, and the system documentation says requests are independent trials. Let E be 'server 1 request times out' and F be 'server 2 request times out.' Then define G to be 'exactly one of the two requests times out.' Discuss which independence statements you can justify immediately and which require actual calculation or may simply be false.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies E and F as immediately independent.; Explains why G is a mixed event involving both trials.; States that E with G or F with G is not automatically independent.; Uses conditional reasoning or structure to justify likely dependence.
Partial credit: Gets the main conclusion right but with weak explanation of G.; Says G must be checked separately without explaining why.

Common mistakes: Assuming G is independent of E because the trials are independent.; Not noticing that G is defined using both trial outcomes.; Claiming all events in independent-trial experiments are mutually independent.

questions.text: Suppose events A and B are conditionally independent given E, and P(E) > 0. Starting from P(A ∩ B | E) = P(A | E)P(B | E), derive a formula for P(A | B, E) and interpret it verbally. Be explicit about what conditions you need to divide by something.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the conditional-probability definition within the E-conditioned space.; Derives P(A | B,E)=P(A | E).; Mentions the condition P(B | E)>0.; Interprets the result verbally.
Partial credit: Gets the algebraic result but omits the positivity assumption.; States the interpretation correctly with minimal derivation.
Common mistakes: Cancelling P(B|E) without checking it is positive.; Concluding P(A | B,E)=P(A) instead of P(A|E).; Forgetting that all probabilities are inside the conditioned-on world.

questions.text: A classmate says: "If two events are independent, they must be disjoint, because one event has nothing to do with the other." Respond to that claim carefully. In your answer, explain the difference between independence and mutual exclusivity, and give a concrete probability argument showing why confusing them leads to a contradiction unless a special edge case occurs.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that the claim is false.; Defines independence using P(E ∩ F) = P(E)P(F) or P(E|F) = P(E).; Defines disjointness as P(E ∩ F) = 0.; Explains that both can hold only if P(E)=0 or P(F)=0.; Articulates the intuition that independence is not the same as 'cannot happen together.'

Partial credit: Recognizes the claim is false but gives only an intuitive explanation.; Uses an example correctly but does not derive the general contradiction.; States one formal definition correctly but does not connect it to the other concept.
Common mistakes: Saying independent means events do not overlap.; Confusing 'does not affect probability' with 'cannot both happen.'; Forgetting the edge case where one event has probability 0.

questions.text: Roll a fair die twice. Let E be the event that the first roll is 1, F be the event that the second roll is 6, and G be the event that the sum of the two rolls is 7. Determine which pairs among (E,F), (E,G), and (F,G) are independent, and then decide whether E, F, and G are mutually independent. Explain your reasoning aloud rather than just listing answers.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes P(E), P(F), and P(G) correctly.; Checks each pair using intersection probabilities, not just intuition.; States that all three pairs are independent.; Checks the triple intersection against P(E)P(F)P(G).; Concludes correctly that pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.

Partial credit: Gets the pairwise checks right but forgets the triple condition.; States the final conclusion correctly with incomplete arithmetic.; Recognizes the distinction between pairwise and mutual independence even if one probability is misstated.

Common mistakes: Assuming pairwise independence automatically implies independence of all three events.; Computing P(G) incorrectly as 1/36 instead of 6/36.; Using only one pairwise check and generalizing.

questions.text: A student writes, "To show A and B are conditionally independent given E, it is enough to prove P(A|B,E)=P(A)." Evaluate that statement. If it is wrong, repair it and explain why conditioning changes the sample space in a way that affects both sides of the equation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the student's statement is incorrect in general.; Gives the correct condition P(A|B,E)=P(A|E) or P(A ∩ B | E)=P(A|E)P(B|E).; Explains that conditioning on E creates a new sample space.; Explicitly notes why P(A) is the wrong comparison.
Partial credit: Fixes the formula correctly but gives limited explanation.; Explains the new sample space idea without stating a formal criterion.; Recognizes that both sides need conditioning on E.

Common mistakes: Dropping the conditioning on E from one side of the equation.; Claiming conditional independence is the same as ordinary independence.; Forgetting the positivity condition when using P(A|B,E).

questions.text: Suppose a streaming platform tracks whether a user clicks on three different recommended movies, call the click events C1, C2, and C3. An analyst claims the clicks are independent because 'once we know the hidden preference type K, each click is generated separately.' Critique that claim carefully: what can be concluded about conditional independence given K, what cannot be concluded about unconditional independence, and why might dependence appear again after you average over users with different K values?
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes clearly between conditional and unconditional independence.; States the conditional factorization given K.; Explains why marginal dependence can arise from mixing over latent groups.; Uses the idea of a shared hidden cause to justify the dependence.; Optionally notes that the reverse phenomenon can also happen.

Partial credit: States that conditional independence does not imply unconditional independence without a clear mechanism.; Gives an intuitive explanation involving user types but no formal factorization.; Recognizes the role of hidden variables but does not connect it to updated beliefs after observing one click.

Common mistakes: Assuming independence given K automatically implies independence overall.; Confusing 'generated separately within a type' with 'generated separately in the population.'; Failing to distinguish events from random variables when discussing factorization.

questions.text: For two continuous random variables X and Y, a student says: 'If the joint density can be written as g(x)h(y), then X and Y are independent.' Is that always true? Answer using the role of the support, and apply your reasoning to this example: f(x,y)=24xy on the region x>0, y>0, x+y<1, and 0 otherwise.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that factorization alone is not enough unless it works over the entire support.; Explains the importance of the support being separable as a product set.; Applies that logic correctly to the triangular region x+y<1.; Concludes that X and Y are not independent.

Partial credit: Gets the final answer correct but only says 'because of the support' without elaboration.; Explains the support issue generally but does not tie it clearly to the specific example.; Notes the density is algebraically separable yet still dependent.

Common mistakes: Declaring independence solely because 24xy factors into a function of x times a function of y.; Ignoring the 0 otherwise part of the density.; Thinking independence is determined only by algebra and not by support.

questions.text: A student says: 'To show two discrete random variables X and Y are independent, it is enough to check one lucky pair of values, like P(X=1,Y=2)=P(X=1)P(Y=2).' Explain why that statement is wrong, and then give the correct definition in a way that distinguishes random variables from events.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the universal quantifier 'for all x,y'; Gives the factorization P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y); Explains that X=x and Y=y are events induced by the RVs; Explicitly rejects checking a single pair as sufficient

Partial credit: Mentions product form but omits 'for all x,y'; Correct intuition that knowing X gives no information about Y, without formal definition; Notes RVs are not events but does not connect to the definition
Common mistakes: Saying independence means only uncorrelated; Checking only one or a few value pairs; Treating X and Y themselves as events

questions.text: Someone claims: 'If random variables X and Y are independent, it is still possible that the particular events X=3 and Y=5 are dependent.' Do you agree? Give a careful verbal justification rather than just saying true or false.
rubric_items: Full credit: Answers 'disagree' or 'false'; Uses the assignment-event calculation P(X=3,Y=5)=P(X=3)P(Y=5); Explains that independence of RVs forces independence of such value events
Partial credit: Gets truth value correct with incomplete justification; Says 'knowing X tells you nothing about Y' but gives no event-level explanation

Common mistakes: Claiming variables can be independent while some assignments are dependent; Confusing dependence of values with dependence of variables; Giving only an example instead of a general reason

questions.text: Let X and Y be independent fair six-sided die rolls. Without listing all 36 outcomes one by one, explain how to compute P(X+Y=9) using independence, and interpret why the resulting expression is a sum of products.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes or explains the convolution-style sum; Uses independence to factor joint probabilities; Identifies the valid pairs summing to 9; Interprets 'sum of products' correctly
Partial credit: Finds correct answer by enumeration but does not connect to independence; Sets up sum correctly but makes minor arithmetic slip; Explains disjoint cases but not why product appears
Common mistakes: Multiplying the number of pairs by 1/6 instead of 1/36; Forgetting some valid pairs; Using independence without stating why it applies

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent discrete random variables with P(X=0)=0.7, P(X=1)=0.3 and P(Y=0)=0.4, P(Y=1)=0.6. Compute the distribution of S=X+Y, but spend most of your time explaining the setup and where independence is used.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies support {0,1,2}; Computes all three probabilities correctly; Uses disjoint-case decomposition for S=1; Explicitly invokes independence in joint-to-product step
Partial credit: Mostly correct distribution with one arithmetic error; Correctly sets up all sums/products but incomplete final probabilities; Gets endpoints 0 and 2 correct but mishandles S=1
Common mistakes: Forgetting both ways to get S=1; Assuming P(S=1)=P(X=1)P(Y=1); Not checking probabilities sum to 1

questions.text: For continuous random variables, a classmate says: 'Independence means P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y).' Explain what is wrong with that statement and replace it with a correct definition, including an equivalent PDF-based criterion when densities exist.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why point probabilities are inappropriate for continuous RVs; States CDF factorization definition; States equivalent PDF factorization when densities exist; Contrasts discrete and continuous cases

Partial credit: Gives PDF factorization but not the CDF definition; Correctly says point probabilities are zero but does not finish the definition; Uses informal 'knowing X tells nothing about Y' without formal criterion
Common mistakes: Using P(X=x,Y=y)=... for continuous RVs; Forgetting the 'for all x,y' condition; Confusing PDF values with probabilities

questions.text: You are told that a joint density has the form f_{X,Y}(x,y)=c·x·y on 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤1, and 0 otherwise. Explain how you would determine whether X and Y are independent. Do not stop at finding c; carry the reasoning through the factorization test.
rubric_items: Full credit: Normalizes correctly to get c=4; Finds both marginals correctly; Checks product equals joint on the support; Concludes independence with justification
Partial credit: Finds c correctly and states factorization idea but does not compute marginals; Computes marginals with minor algebra slip; Recognizes support matters but incomplete conclusion

Common mistakes: Forgetting to normalize first; Claiming any separable-looking expression implies independence without checking constants/support; Ignoring that factorization must hold on the whole support

questions.text: Let X and Y be independent Uniform(0,1) random variables. Explain how to derive the density of S=X+Y at a generic point α using convolution, and then describe in words why the answer changes at α=1.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up convolution integral correctly; Translates the indicator constraints into overlap of intervals; Derives the triangular piecewise density; Explains geometrically why the breakpoint is at 1
Partial credit: States correct final density without clear derivation; Sets up convolution but struggles with interval overlap; Explains shape qualitatively but not formula
Common mistakes: Integrating over all x without enforcing support; Getting the two linear pieces reversed; Forgetting density is zero outside [0,2]

questions.text: A colleague says, 'If two variables are independent, then E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]; otherwise that formula fails.' Respond to this claim, and contrast it with a formula that really does require independence.
rubric_items: Full credit: States linearity of expectation does not require independence; Provides a contrasting formula such as E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] or variance additivity; Explains the distinction clearly
Partial credit: Gets expectation statement right but no contrast; Mentions covariance vaguely without connecting to formulas; Knows one formula requiring independence but muddles expectation
Common mistakes: Saying expectation additivity needs independence; Confusing E[XY] with E[X+Y]; Claiming variance additivity always holds

questions.text: Explain why independence implies Cov(X,Y)=0, but the converse is not a valid definition of independence. Your answer should connect covariance formulas to what independence actually says about the joint distribution.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]-E[X]E[Y); Derives zero covariance from independence; Explains why the converse fails conceptually; Contrasts one-number summary with full joint factorization
Partial credit: States independence implies zero covariance without formula; Says converse is false but gives weak explanation; Confuses covariance and correlation but gets main direction right
Common mistakes: Claiming zero covariance implies independence in general; Not distinguishing full distributional property from moment condition; Forgetting E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] comes from independence

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent with Var(X)=4 and Var(Y)=9. Compute Var(X+Y), but then explain why the same numerical shortcut cannot be used blindly when independence is absent.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives 13; States the general variance formula with covariance; Explains independence makes covariance zero
Partial credit: Gets 13 but no explanation; States general formula but arithmetic slip; Mentions covariance informally without formula
Common mistakes: Always adding variances regardless of dependence; Subtracting instead of adding covariance term; Confusing variance of sum with square of sum of standard deviations

questions.text: You are given three random variables X, Y, Z. A student verifies that each pair is independent and concludes that the three are jointly independent. Is that logically sufficient? Explain what must actually be checked for independence of multiple random variables.
rubric_items: Full credit: States pairwise independence is insufficient; Describes the needed triple or all-subsets factorization; Mentions 'for all values' or all relevant subsets
Partial credit: Correctly rejects the claim but only vaguely says 'need more checks'; Knows there is a difference between pairwise and mutual independence but gives incomplete criterion
Common mistakes: Equating pairwise with joint independence; Giving only the pairwise conditions; Forgetting subset conditions in the multi-variable definition

questions.text: A researcher says a sample X1,...,Xn is 'iid' because all variables have the same mean and variance. Explain why that is not enough, and state what iid really requires. Then say one consequence of iid that is useful when studying sums or averages.
rubric_items: Full credit: States iid = independent + identically distributed; Says identical distribution means same PMF/PDF, not merely same mean/variance; Gives a valid consequence for sums/averages
Partial credit: Defines iid correctly but no consequence; Says same distribution and 'kind of independent' without precision; Gives CLT mention without explaining parameters
Common mistakes: Reducing iid to same mean and variance; Forgetting independence; Confusing identical distribution with equal parameter names only

questions.text: Let X1,...,Xn be iid with mean μ and variance σ². Without proving the CLT, explain how to get the mean and variance of the sample average X̄=(1/n)∑Xi, and then state the large-n normal approximation that is suggested by the lecture notes.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes E[X̄]=μ; Computes Var(X̄)=σ²/n; States approximate Normal(μ,σ²/n) for large n; Distinguishes where independence is used
Partial credit: Gets formulas right but no explanation; Correct mean and variance setup with minor notation issues; States CLT approximation but forgets variance scaling
Common mistakes: Saying the mean tends to 0; Using Var(X̄)=σ² instead of σ²/n; Thinking independence is needed for expectation additivity

questions.text: A student says: 'As n grows, the average of iid variables becomes Normal with mean 0 and variance 0.' Critique this statement carefully. Identify what part is right, what part is wrong, and what assumptions are being used.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies incorrect mean claim; States correct approximate mean and variance of sample average; Notes variance shrinks toward 0; Mentions assumptions like iid and finite variance
Partial credit: Corrects mean but not variance; Says CLT gives normality without parameters; Recognizes only that mean need not be 0
Common mistakes: Accepting the statement because variance goes to 0; Confusing sum and average; Saying the mean converges to 0 automatically

questions.text: Imagine a complicated total cost is modeled as X+Y, where X is the independent cost of materials and Y is the independent cost of shipping. Explain two distinct benefits of the independence assumption: one about distributional calculations and one about summary statistics.
rubric_items: Full credit: Names a distributional benefit via convolution/factorization; Names a summary-statistic benefit like variance additivity; Connects these to modeling a sum of simpler independent pieces
Partial credit: Gives only one benefit in detail; Mentions 'easier calculations' without specifics; Gets one formula right but no interpretation
Common mistakes: Claiming expectation additivity needs independence; Confusing convolution with simple addition of densities pointwise; Not distinguishing distribution calculations from moments

questions.text: Compare the discrete and continuous independence definitions for two variables. I do not want two isolated formulas; explain the common idea behind them and why the notation changes.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains shared factorization idea; States correct discrete formulation; States correct continuous formulation or equivalent PDF criterion; Explains why notation changes because point probabilities vanish
Partial credit: Gives formulas but weak comparison; Understands one case well but not the other; Uses intuition only, with no formal statement
Common mistakes: Treating continuous and discrete definitions as identical point-probability statements; Not mentioning the 'for all' aspect; Confusing CDF and PDF

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent and each has mean 1. Compute E[X+Y] and explain why your reasoning would still work even if the variables were dependent. Then say what additional information independence would give you about E[XY].
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes E[X+Y]=2; States linearity does not require independence; Uses independence to compute E[XY]=1
Partial credit: Gets E[X+Y] correct but omits product discussion; Knows E[XY]=1 under independence but not why; Mentions dependence irrelevance vaguely
Common mistakes: Saying E[X+Y] requires independence; Claiming E[XY]=E[X]+E[Y]; Confusing product with sum formulas

questions.text: A teammate tries to justify a CLT argument on a collection of random variables that all have the same distribution but may be dependent. Explain why 'identically distributed' alone is not enough for the standard iid conclusion about sums or averages.
rubric_items: Full credit: States identical distribution alone is insufficient; Explains dependence affects sum/average behavior; Gives an illustrative dependent example like Xi all equal; Connects to variance or CLT failure
Partial credit: Says independence is needed but gives no reason; Mentions covariance vaguely without example; Correct intuition but confuses CLT statement
Common mistakes: Claiming same distribution guarantees CLT behavior; Ignoring dependence in variance of sums; Treating iid as synonymous with same mean/variance

questions.text: You observe that a joint continuous density factors as f_{X,Y}(x,y)=g(x)h(y) for all real x,y. Explain why that is enough to conclude independence, and clarify any hidden conditions you are implicitly using.
rubric_items: Full credit: States factorized joint PDF implies independence; Mentions validity of the joint PDF and support-wide factorization; Connects to marginals or equivalent independence criterion
Partial credit: Knows factorization matters but gives weak justification; States independence from factorization without caveats; Mentions CDF criterion only
Common mistakes: Checking factorization at only some points; Ignoring support issues; Confusing product of arbitrary functions with automatically normalized marginals

questions.text: Let X and Y be any random variables with means 2 and 5. Without assuming independence, compute E[3X-2Y+7]. Then explain why this problem is easier than computing E[XY].
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes 3 correctly; Uses linearity of expectation explicitly; Explains why dependence is irrelevant here and relevant for E[XY]
Partial credit: Correct arithmetic with little explanation; Mentions linearity but not independence contrast; Explains E[XY] issue vaguely
Common mistakes: Trying to use independence unnecessarily; Computing 3X-2Y+7 pointwise rather than via expectation rules; Claiming E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] without assumptions

questions.text: Why do probability lectures often say that many useful formulas are 'sums of products' when independence is involved? Use one discrete example and one continuous example tied to sums of random variables.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains both the 'sum' and the 'product' roles; Gives a correct discrete example; Gives a correct continuous example; Connects both examples to independence
Partial credit: Only one example in detail; Good intuition but no formula; States formulas without interpretation
Common mistakes: Treating convolution as just ordinary multiplication; Missing the disjoint-case reason for the sum; Forgetting independence is what creates the product

questions.text: Suppose X1,...,Xn are random variables each with mean 1, but you are told nothing about independence. A student says you cannot conclude anything useful about the probability that X1+...+Xn is at least n. Explain why that is too pessimistic, using expectation reasoning rather than CLT.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the sum and computes its expectation as n; Uses contradiction: if S<n almost surely then E[S]<n; Concludes P(S≥n)>0; Avoids unjustified CLT use
Partial credit: Correct conclusion with incomplete contradiction argument; Knows E[S]=n but cannot finish the probability argument; Uses intuition about averages without rigorous link
Common mistakes: Invoking CLT or normality without assumptions; Assuming each Xi must equal 1 sometimes; Treating dependence as making expectation unusable

questions.text: A student says: “To prove two discrete random variables X and Y are independent, it is enough to check that P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y) for one or two representative pairs (x,y). If those work, the variables are independent.” Do you agree? Explain carefully what the definition actually requires, and contrast that with the idea that a single event like {X=1} might be independent of a single event like {Y=0}.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that independence of discrete RVs requires the product rule for every pair (x,y), not just selected examples.; Explains the distinction between random variables and events.; Clarifies that checking a few assignments can at most verify independence of those events, not of the variables overall.

Partial credit: Gives the correct formula but does not emphasize 'for all' values.; Recognizes that a single check is insufficient but gives a vague explanation.; Mentions event-vs-variable distinction without connecting it to the definition.
Common mistakes: Saying one representative pair is enough.; Confusing independence of RVs with independence of one event involving each RV.; Treating X and Y themselves as events.

questions.text: Let X and Y be independent Bernoulli random variables with parameters p and q. Define S=X+Y. Without listing all cases mechanically, explain how independence lets you derive the full distribution of S, and then use that distribution to compute E[S] in two different ways.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the convolution idea correctly for S=X+Y.; Derives all three probabilities P(S=0), P(S=1), P(S=2) correctly.; Computes E[S] both from the PMF of S and from linearity.; Explicitly comments on where independence is needed and where it is not.

Partial credit: Gets the PMF mostly correct but makes a small algebra mistake.; Computes E[S]=p+q correctly by only one method.; Uses case enumeration correctly but does not connect to convolution or independence.
Common mistakes: Forgetting the two disjoint ways to obtain S=1.; Claiming linearity of expectation requires independence.; Writing P(X=1,Y=0)=p(1-q) without stating this uses independence.

questions.text: A classmate argues: “If X and Y are independent, then surely X+Y and X must also be independent, because Y does not depend on X.” Is that true? Answer by reasoning from events or distributions, not by appealing to a memorized theorem. A simple concrete counterexample is acceptable if you explain it fully.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that the claim is false.; Gives a valid reason based on conditioning, events, or a concrete counterexample.; Explains why dependence appears because X+Y contains information about X.; If using a counterexample, computes or compares probabilities correctly.

Partial credit: States the claim is false but gives only intuition with no clear supporting argument.; Provides a counterexample but does not fully explain why it violates independence.; Shows that X+Y depends on X informally but without event/probability reasoning.

Common mistakes: Saying the claim is true because Y is independent of X.; Confusing independence of X and Y with independence of any functions involving them.; Giving an example where one variable is degenerate and drawing the wrong general conclusion.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent continuous random variables, each uniformly distributed on [0,1]. A triangular density is proposed for T=X+Y. Explain, without doing every integral from scratch, why the density must increase on [0,1] and decrease on [1,2]. Then state the density piecewise and justify why independence matters in the setup.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies convolution as the correct setup for the sum of independent continuous RVs.; Explains the overlap-interval geometry or equivalent reasoning for the piecewise form.; States the correct triangular density on [0,2].; Explains that independence is what allows factorization of the joint density into marginals.

Partial credit: States the correct density but gives weak justification.; Uses convolution correctly but does not clearly explain the changing limits/overlap.; Explains the shape qualitatively but omits the role of independence.

Common mistakes: Assuming the sum of two uniforms is uniform.; Forgetting the support is [0,2].; Using convolution without mentioning the need for independence.; Giving the CDF or PMF instead of the PDF.

questions.text: Consider three random variables X1, X2, X3. A student claims: “If every pair is independent, then the three variables are independent.” Give an oral response to that claim. Your answer should state the correct condition for independence of multiple random variables and explain why pairwise independence is not, in general, enough.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence in general.; Gives the correct full-independence condition for three or n variables.; Explains that all subsets, including the triple, must satisfy the product rule.; Clearly distinguishes pairwise from mutual independence.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false but only vaguely mentions 'stronger condition' without stating it.; States the n-variable factorization but does not contrast it with pairwise independence.; Explains the event version or variable version correctly, but not both.
Common mistakes: Claiming pairwise independence is sufficient.; Only checking the three pairwise products and ignoring the triple product.; Confusing 'identically distributed' with 'independent.'

questions.text: A student says: "For continuous random variables, the joint PDF at a point, f_{X,Y}(a,b), is the probability that X=a and Y=b." Do you agree? Explain carefully what the joint PDF does mean, and describe how you would use it to compute the probability that (X,Y) falls in a small rectangle around (a,b).
rubric_items: Full credit: States that P(X=a,Y=b)=0 for continuous joint variables.; Explains that f_{X,Y}(a,b) is a density, not a probability.; Describes probability over a region as a double integral, or as approximately density times small area for a tiny rectangle.

Partial credit: Says the claim is false but gives only a vague reason.; Mentions integration but does not connect it to a 2D region.; Confuses density with relative likelihood but still notes point probabilities are zero.
Common mistakes: Saying f_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X=a,Y=b).; Using a single integral instead of a double integral.; Claiming the PDF must be less than or equal to 1 at every point.

questions.text: Suppose a joint density is proposed as g(x,y)=xy on the support 0<=x<=1 and 0<=y<=2, and 0 otherwise. Without rushing to the final answer, explain the two conditions you must check for a valid joint PDF, and then verify them in this case.
rubric_items: Full credit: Names nonnegativity and normalization as the two checks.; Sets up the correct double integral over the stated support.; Evaluates correctly to 1 and concludes validity.

Partial credit: Checks only the integral but omits explicit nonnegativity.; Sets up the right integral but makes a minor arithmetic slip.; Explains the idea of integrating over the support but is imprecise about bounds.
Common mistakes: Checking only that the function is nonnegative.; Integrating over the wrong bounds, such as y from 0 to 1.; Assuming a valid PDF must have maximum value at most 1.

questions.text: You roll two fair six-sided dice and define X as the first die and Y as the second. Explain how to construct the joint PMF, then derive the marginal PMF of X from it. Finally, say what feature of the setup makes the marginal simple.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies 36 equally likely ordered pairs.; States the correct joint PMF on the 6x6 grid.; Obtains the marginal by summing over y and gets 1/6.

Partial credit: Gets the marginal right but does not clearly explain summing over the other variable.; States independence informally without writing the joint PMF.; Confuses ordered and unordered outcomes but still reaches the right table shape.
Common mistakes: Using 1/21 or another value based on unordered pairs.; Averaging instead of summing to obtain the marginal.; Forgetting the support outside {1,...,6}x{1,...,6} has probability 0.

questions.text: A classmate sees a joint PMF table for the number of Macs X and PCs Y in a household, with the constraint X+Y<=3, and says: "The marginal of X is found by summing down a column because columns correspond to X-values." How would you respond? Give a careful explanation that does not depend on one particular table orientation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the general marginalization rule p_X(x)=sum over y of p_{X,Y}(x,y).; Explains that row/column direction depends on table layout, not probability theory.; Mentions the support restriction only changes which terms are nonzero.

Partial credit: Says 'sum over the other variable' without making the row/column clarification.; Explains the table orientation issue but omits the formula.; Understands the idea but is confused about which variable is fixed.
Common mistakes: Treating row/column direction as universal across all tables.; Summing over x when asked for the marginal of X.; Ignoring impossible states created by X+Y<=3.

questions.text: For two jointly continuous random variables, define the joint CDF F_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X<=a,Y<=b). Explain how this object differs from the joint PDF conceptually, and then describe how you would recover the joint PDF from the CDF if enough smoothness is present.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the CDF as accumulated probability up to thresholds a and b.; Contrasts it with the PDF as a density whose integral gives probability.; States the mixed-partial relationship under appropriate smoothness.

Partial credit: Knows one direction, such as integrating the PDF to get the CDF, but does not clearly contrast meanings.; Mentions derivatives but not that the CDF is a probability over a rectangle.; Gives a correct formula but poor conceptual explanation.
Common mistakes: Saying the CDF and PDF are both probabilities at a point.; Using a single derivative instead of a mixed partial.; Forgetting that the CDF applies to discrete variables too.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y have joint density f_{X,Y}(x,y)=3e^{-3x} for x>0 and 1<y<2, and 0 otherwise. Determine whether X and Y are independent, but do it by reasoning through marginals rather than by assertion. Then compute E[X+Y].
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes both marginals correctly.; Uses factorization into marginals to justify independence.; Computes E[X]=1/3, E[Y]=3/2, and sums to 11/6.

Partial credit: Correctly identifies independence by factorization but computes one expectation incorrectly.; Finds marginals but does not explicitly connect them to independence.; Gets E[Y]=3/2 by symmetry of a uniform interval but leaves E[X] vague.
Common mistakes: Claiming independence just because the support is rectangular.; Forgetting to check normalization of f_Y(y).; Using E[XY] instead of E[X]+E[Y] for the sum.

questions.text: In a medical screening system, four binary variables are tracked: flu status, undergrad status, tiredness, and fever. A naive analyst proposes specifying all 2^4=16 joint probabilities directly. Give a reasoned argument for why that may be a poor modeling strategy, and explain how thinking in terms of causal or conditional structure can simplify the description of the joint distribution.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why direct enumeration is unwieldy or nontransparent.; Describes using causal/conditional relationships to factor the joint distribution.; Makes clear that the factorized model still implies a full joint distribution.

Partial credit: Says 'use Bayes net ideas' or 'use causality' without explaining the simplification.; Mentions conditional probabilities but not why they help.; Focuses only on computational convenience and not interpretability.

Common mistakes: Claiming the structured model is exactly the same as assuming independence everywhere.; Thinking factorization loses information automatically.; Saying a joint distribution cannot be built from conditionals.

questions.text: For continuous random variables X and Y with joint density f_{X,Y}, explain the formula for the marginal density f_X(a). Why is it an integral over y rather than an evaluation at one y-value?
rubric_items: Full credit: States the correct marginalization formula for continuous variables.; Explains that we integrate over all possible y values because Y is continuous.; Connects the integral to collapsing a 2D distribution into a 1D one.

Partial credit: Gives the formula but little conceptual explanation.; Explains 'sum over the other variable' without adapting to continuous variables.; Understands the collapse idea but writes incorrect bounds.

Common mistakes: Using a sum instead of an integral for continuous variables.; Evaluating at a single y instead of integrating over y.; Forgetting that the support may restrict which y values contribute.

questions.text: Let X and Y be independent Uniform(0,1) random variables, and define S=X+Y. Without quoting the known answer immediately, explain how convolution sets up f_S(\alpha), and then describe why the answer has one form for 0<\alpha<1 and another for 1<\alpha<2.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes or explains the convolution integral for independent continuous sums.; Translates the integrand into an interval-overlap problem.; Derives the piecewise density 0, \alpha, 2-\alpha, 0 on the correct ranges.

Partial credit: Knows the triangular shape but cannot justify it from convolution.; Sets up the convolution but mishandles overlap bounds slightly.; Explains overlap qualitatively but not with enough precision.
Common mistakes: Multiplying densities without integrating.; Forgetting that support of S is [0,2].; Giving the CDF instead of the density.

questions.text: A student says: "If two random variables have the same E[X], E[Y], Var(X), and Var(Y), then their joint distributions are basically the same." Explain why that statement is false, and identify what kind of information about the pair is still missing.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that equal marginal summaries do not determine the joint distribution.; Explains that dependence structure can differ dramatically.; Mentions covariance/correlation or more general dependence as missing information.

Partial credit: Says the statement is false but gives only one vague sentence.; Mentions correlation but not that even that may not fully specify the joint distribution.; Focuses on one example without stating the general principle.
Common mistakes: Claiming equal marginals imply equal joint distributions.; Thinking covariance alone always determines dependence.; Confusing the pair's joint behavior with the marginals.

questions.text: You are given a table and told it is either P(Y=y|T=t) or P(T=t|Y=y), but the labels have been erased. How can you determine which interpretation is correct just by inspecting which sets of entries sum to 1? Then explain why a conditional PMF is still a 'real' distribution once the condition is fixed.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the row/column sum test relative to what is conditioned on.; States that conditioning fixes one event and leaves a valid PMF over the other variable.; Mentions nonnegativity and summing to 1.

Partial credit: Knows to look for sums to 1 but is unclear about whether rows or columns correspond to the conditioned variable.; Explains only one of the two possible interpretations.; Uses intuition correctly but not formal enough.
Common mistakes: Saying all rows and columns must both sum to 1.; Confusing the conditioned-on variable with the variable being distributed.; Treating a conditional table as not a true distribution.

questions.text: Compare the roles of a PMF and a PDF when describing random variables. Then extend your explanation to the joint case: what changes when we move from one variable to two variables, and what stays conceptually the same?
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly distinguishes PMF from PDF in one dimension.; Extends the distinction to joint PMF versus joint PDF.; Mentions region probabilities in 2D and marginalization by sum/integral.

Partial credit: Gets the 1D comparison right but is weak on the joint extension.; Mentions double integrals but not the key point that PDFs are densities, not probabilities.; Gives examples without articulating the conceptual commonality.
Common mistakes: Saying PDFs give probabilities at points.; Not distinguishing discrete from continuous in the joint setting.; Forgetting the normalization requirement.

questions.text: Suppose F_{X,Y}(a,b)=P(X<=a,Y<=b) is known for a jointly continuous pair. How would you express P(a_1<X<=a_2, b_1<Y<=b_2) using only values of the joint CDF? Explain the inclusion-exclusion logic, not just the formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives the correct four-term formula.; Explains the inclusion-exclusion reasoning with the geometry of rectangles.; Uses the thresholds in the correct positions.
Partial credit: Remembers the formula but cannot explain why it works.; Explains inclusion-exclusion conceptually but swaps one term.; Has the correct sign pattern except for the final add-back term.
Common mistakes: Using only two terms.; Forgetting to add back the doubly subtracted corner.; Confusing upper and lower thresholds.

questions.text: A student argues: "If the support of (X,Y) is a rectangle and the formula for f_{X,Y}(x,y) looks separated into a function of x times a function of y, then independence is automatic." Is that always safe? Give a careful answer that distinguishes what must be checked from what may merely be suggestive.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the formal independence criterion f_{X,Y}=f_Xf_Y.; Explains why rectangular support helps but is not by itself enough.; Notes that non-rectangular support rules out independence in many cases even if the formula looks factorized.

Partial credit: Says 'check marginals' but does not explain support issues.; Understands support matters but is vague about the exact criterion.; Answers yes for this specific example but not in general.

Common mistakes: Claiming rectangular support alone proves independence.; Ignoring the need to verify normalization/marginals.; Thinking any product-looking formula implies independence regardless of support.

questions.text: Imagine X is study hours and Y is sleep hours over a day. A joint CDF value F_{X,Y}(5,7)=0.62 is reported. Interpret this number in plain language, and then explain one common incorrect interpretation that students make.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly interprets the two-threshold event with 'and'.; Uses non-strict inequalities appropriately.; Identifies a plausible incorrect interpretation and explains why it is wrong.

Partial credit: Gets the idea of accumulation up to a point but omits the simultaneity.; Gives one wrong interpretation without explaining the difference.; Uses 'or' loosely but otherwise understands the region.
Common mistakes: Interpreting the CDF as point probability.; Replacing 'and' with 'or'.; Forgetting that the event is a lower-left rectangle in the plane.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are jointly continuous with density proportional to x+y on the triangular support 0<x<1, 0<y<1-x. Without computing the normalizing constant unless you need it, explain how you would obtain the marginal density of X. Your explanation should show that you understand how support affects the integration limits.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly states that the marginal is obtained by integrating over y values allowed by the support.; Uses bounds 0 to 1-x for y when x is fixed.; Emphasizes that non-rectangular support leads to x-dependent limits.

Partial credit: Knows to integrate but uses overly vague bounds.; Recognizes the support matters but incorrectly sets y from 0 to 1.; Focuses on normalizing constant and misses the main point about bounds.
Common mistakes: Integrating over the full square instead of the triangle.; Treating bounds as constants when they depend on x.; Forgetting to specify the range of x itself.

questions.text: Explain why the conditional density f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y) is considered a genuine density in x for each fixed y with f_Y(y)>0. Your explanation should include both intuition and the normalization check.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the formula and explains the slice-and-rescale intuition.; Performs the normalization integral correctly.; Mentions the requirement f_Y(y)>0.
Partial credit: Gives the normalization argument but little intuition.; Provides intuition but does not show why it integrates to 1.; Forgets to mention the denominator must be positive.
Common mistakes: Treating f_{X|Y}(x|y) as a probability at a point.; Not seeing why division by f_Y(y) is needed.; Integrating with respect to y instead of x.

questions.text: Someone says: "Since probabilities must be at most 1, any valid joint PDF must also be at most 1 everywhere." Evaluate that statement and justify your answer using the idea of area under the density.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the claim is false.; Explains that densities can exceed 1 while integrals over regions give probabilities.; Connects validity to nonnegativity and total integral 1.
Partial credit: Says false but gives only a 1D explanation, not connecting to the joint case.; Mentions normalization but not nonnegativity.; Uses an example idea without articulating the principle.
Common mistakes: Confusing PDF values with probabilities.; Thinking all density values must lie in [0,1].; Forgetting the integral criterion.

questions.text: Suppose a joint model for waiting time X and service score Y is known, and a manager asks for P(X<=2, Y<=4). Another analyst proposes first finding the two marginals and multiplying P(X<=2) by P(Y<=4). Under what condition is that shortcut justified, and how would you explain the danger if the condition fails?
rubric_items: Full credit: States independence as the required condition.; Explains why product of marginals can fail without independence.; Uses a dependence-based intuition or example.
Partial credit: Says 'if unrelated' or 'if independent' but does not explain why.; Explains dependence generally but does not connect to the specific event.; Thinks zero covariance is enough.
Common mistakes: Multiplying marginal event probabilities without independence.; Arguing from marginal shapes alone.; Confusing independence of variables with disjoint events.

questions.text: In the two-dice experiment, define M=max(X,Y). Explain how you would derive the distribution of M using the joint distribution of (X,Y). I am not asking for all arithmetic immediately; I want the setup and logic.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the joint sample space or joint CDF logic correctly.; Recognizes that M<=m means both X and Y are <=m.; Derives the PMF from the CDF by differencing or by equivalent counting.

Partial credit: Counts correctly but does not explain why the event is a square in the joint table.; Knows to use P(M<=m) but makes a minor setup slip.; Attempts counting outcomes with maximum m but is somewhat disorganized.
Common mistakes: Using P(M=m)=1/6 by symmetry.; Forgetting ordered pairs produce 36 outcomes.; Confusing max with sum.

questions.text: Why is the ratio f(10)/f(5) meaningful for a continuous random variable even though P(X=10)=P(X=5)=0? Give the local-interval interpretation that rescues the idea of 'more likely near one value than another.'
rubric_items: Full credit: States that point probabilities are zero for continuous variables.; Explains the small-interval approximation around each point.; Interprets the density ratio as a ratio of local probabilities or local likelihoods.

Partial credit: Says 'densities compare relative likelihood' but gives no interval argument.; Provides the interval argument informally but not clearly.; Confuses exact equality with approximation but has the right idea.
Common mistakes: Treating f(10)/f(5) as P(X=10)/P(X=5).; Saying 10 is literally f(10) times as probable as 5 at a point.; Forgetting the interval widths must match for the comparison.

questions.text: You are fitting a simulation model for two continuous measurements, and a teammate says, "As long as I choose any nonnegative function f(x,y), it works as a joint PDF." Give a complete response describing what else must be true, and explain how support enters the argument.
rubric_items: Full credit: States both nonnegativity and total integral 1 as required conditions.; Explains that normalization is performed over the support.; Mentions that support geometry determines integration limits.
Partial credit: States the two conditions but says little about support.; Understands support but forgets one condition.; Describes normalization vaguely without region language.
Common mistakes: Thinking any nonnegative function is automatically a PDF.; Integrating over the wrong region.; Ignoring that the function may be zero outside the support.

questions.text: Suppose you know a joint PMF p_{X,Y}(x,y) for discrete variables and are asked for P(X=2). Then someone else asks for P(X=2 | Y=1). Explain the difference in setup between these two calculations, and why students often confuse them.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly distinguishes marginalization from conditioning.; Provides the correct formulas for both quantities.; Explains the renormalization step in the conditional case.

Partial credit: Gets both formulas mostly right but does not explain the conceptual difference.; Understands renormalization but is shaky on which variable to sum over.; Uses row/column language correctly but without general formulas.
Common mistakes: Treating P(X=2|Y=1) as just p_{X,Y}(2,1).; Forgetting to divide by P(Y=1).; Summing over the wrong variable for the marginal.

questions.text: A joint density is proposed on the rectangular support 0  x  1, 0  y  2 by f_{X,Y}(x,y)=kxy, and f_{X,Y}(x,y)=0 elsewhere. Without rushing to compute, explain how you would verify this is a valid joint PDF, find the constant k, and then derive the marginal densities of X and Y. Finally, say whether X and Y are independent and justify your answer from the formulas, not from intuition about the picture.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the two validity conditions: nonnegativity and total integral 1.; Correctly sets up and evaluates the double integral to get k=1.; Correctly derives f_X(x)=2x on (0,1) and f_Y(y)=y/2 on (0,2), with 0 elsewhere.; Justifies independence by showing f_{X,Y}=f_X f_Y on the full support.

Partial credit: Correct integral setup but arithmetic slip in solving for k.; Correct marginals but weak or incomplete support statements.; Claims independence correctly but does not explicitly verify factorization.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the support limits when integrating.; Saying 'it looks separable so independent' without checking normalization or support.; Using point probabilities for a continuous distribution.; Computing marginals with reversed bounds or treating the density itself as a probability.

questions.text: A student says: 'For continuous random variables, conditioning on Y=y makes no sense because P(Y=y)=0, so f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/P(Y=y) is impossible.' Respond to this claim carefully. Explain what the correct conditional object is, when it is defined, and why it still behaves like a legitimate density in x.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly identifies the error of using P(Y=y) in the continuous case.; States the correct formula f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_{X,Y}(x,y)/f_Y(y) for f_Y(y)>0.; Explains the small-interval or density-ratio intuition.; Verifies that the conditional density integrates to 1 over x.

Partial credit: Knows the correct formula but gives little intuition.; Explains point probabilities are zero but does not clearly contrast discrete vs continuous conditioning.; Mentions the requirement f_Y(y)>0 but does not explain why.

Common mistakes: Saying conditioning on an event of probability zero is always impossible in continuous settings.; Using PMF language for PDFs.; Failing to note the domain restriction f_Y(y)>0.; Treating f(x) itself as a probability.

questions.text: A clinic tracks two binary symptoms, Fever F and Tired T, and a student proposes storing all four joint probabilities P(F=a,T=b) directly. Another student says it is often smarter to think in terms of causal structure and conditional distributions instead of listing every joint entry. Using this small example, explain what information a joint distribution gives you, how marginals would be extracted from it, and why a causal or conditional-factorized view can be more scalable as the number of variables grows.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the joint distribution as a complete description of the pair.; Correctly explains how to obtain marginals by summing over the other variable.; Discusses parameter growth of full joint tables and why factorization/causal structure helps.; Recognizes that conditional or causal representations and joint distributions are alternative representations of the same underlying probabilities.

Partial credit: Understands marginals from a joint table but gives only vague comments about scalability.; Mentions factorization but does not connect it back to the full joint.; Uses the symptom example correctly but without generalizing to more variables.

Common mistakes: Claiming marginals determine the joint without further assumptions.; Confusing conditional tables with joint tables because both contain probabilities.; Ignoring the sum-to-1 constraint on the joint table.; Saying causal structure changes the probabilities rather than representing them differently.

questions.text: Let X and Y be independent Uniform(0,1) random variables, and define S=X+Y. Rather than quoting the known answer, derive the density of S by reasoning about where both densities are nonzero in the convolution integral. I want you to explain why the formula changes at s=1 and what the density is on the different ranges of s.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up the convolution integral correctly.; Uses support-overlap reasoning rather than unsupported memorization.; Correctly derives the piecewise density: 0 for s\le0, s for 0<s<1, 2-s for 1\le s<2, 0 for s\ge2.; Explains conceptually why the breakpoint occurs at s=1.

Partial credit: Gets the triangular answer but cannot clearly justify the limits of integration.; Correct setup with minor endpoint or piecewise-boundary errors.; Explains overlap idea informally but not fully enough to derive all cases.

Common mistakes: Integrating from 0 to 1 without checking when f_Y(s-x) is nonzero.; Assuming the sum of two uniforms is uniform.; Forgetting support outside [0,2].; Giving only the graph shape without a derivation.

questions.text: Consider the continuous joint density f_{X,Y}(x,y)=3e^{-3x} on the support x>0 and 1<y<2, with 0 elsewhere. A classmate looks at the formula and says, 'Because the expression contains both x and y in the notation f_{X,Y}(x,y), the variables must be dependent.' Explain why that reasoning is wrong, determine whether X and Y are independent, and then use your answer to compute E[X+Y] efficiently.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the misconception that dependence is inferred from notation alone.; Correctly identifies factorization and rectangular support as evidence for independence.; Derives or states the correct marginals: 3e^{-3x} on x>0 and 1 on 1<y<2.; Uses linearity to compute E[X+Y]=11/6, with correct component expectations.

Partial credit: Correctly concludes independence but gives weak justification.; Finds marginals correctly but hesitates on one expectation.; Uses linearity correctly even if one expectation has an arithmetic slip.

Common mistakes: Thinking any joint density involving two variables must imply dependence.; Forgetting to include support when checking independence.; Claiming E[X+Y]=E[X]E[Y].; Treating f_Y(y)=1 on (1,2) as impossible because the density equals 1 rather than being less than 1.

questions.text: Suppose you are fitting a 1-D linear regression model to predict sea level from year using the model Y = aX + b. A classmate says, “If our real goal is prediction, there is no reason to talk about likelihood or random noise at all; just fit the best line by squared error.” Explain the modeling difference between the MSE view and the MLE view, and then state when they lead to the same fitted parameters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains MSE as minimizing squared deviation of prediction from Y; Explains MLE as modeling Y = aX+b+Z with random noise and maximizing conditional likelihood; States the Gaussian noise assumption clearly; Concludes that under Z ~ N(0, sigma^2), MSE and MLE give the same parameters

Partial credit: Mentions that MSE and MLE are related but does not explain the noise model; Says Gaussian errors make them equivalent but does not justify why; Describes one approach well but the other vaguely

Common mistakes: Claiming MLE never needs a distributional assumption; Saying MSE always equals MLE regardless of noise model; Confusing prediction error on one point with a probabilistic model for all observations

questions.text: You decide to train linear regression by gradient ascent on the objective h(a,b) = -Σ_i (y_i - (ax_i + b))^2. Without plugging in any numbers, derive the batch gradients with respect to a and b, and explain in words why the gradient for b does not involve x_i except through the residual.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines residual or equivalent quantity; Correctly gives ∂h/∂a = Σ 2(y_i-ax_i-b)x_i; Correctly gives ∂h/∂b = Σ 2(y_i-ax_i-b); Interprets derivative with respect to b as scaling by 1 because intercept affects all predictions equally
Partial credit: Gets one gradient right but misses a factor or sign on the other; Provides formulas without interpretation; Explains intercept idea informally but not mathematically
Common mistakes: Using gradient descent sign while claiming ascent; Omitting x_i from the gradient for a; Putting x_i into the derivative with respect to b

questions.text: A teammate implements batch gradient ascent for linear regression, but updates a immediately after computing gradient_a and then uses the new a while still computing gradient_b on the same pass through the data. They argue this should be even faster because the parameters are kept more current. Do you agree? Explain what quantity batch gradient ascent is supposed to approximate, and why mixing old and new parameter values changes the algorithm.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that all gradient components should be computed at the same old parameter vector; Explains that mixing updated and non-updated parameters means the result is not the true batch gradient at one point; Connects this to why updates should happen after gradient accumulation is complete
Partial credit: Says it is wrong or unstable but without a precise reason; Mentions consistency of parameters but not gradient evaluation at one point

Common mistakes: Claiming any update order is equivalent in batch gradient methods; Confusing this with stochastic gradient methods without noting the difference; Saying the issue is only computational speed, not mathematical correctness

questions.text: In a lecture, someone says, “We use log-likelihood only because computers cannot multiply many probabilities.” Give a more principled explanation for why optimization is usually done with the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood itself. Your answer should include both the argmax argument and the calculus advantage.
rubric_items: Full credit: States monotonicity of log implies same argmax; Explains product over IID datapoints becomes a sum under log; Explains that sums are easier to differentiate for gradient methods
Partial credit: Mentions numerical convenience only; Says log-likelihood is easier to optimize but omits why argmax is preserved
Common mistakes: Claiming log changes the maximizing parameter; Focusing only on underflow/overflow with no mathematical explanation; Confusing log of a sum with sum of logs

questions.text: You are modeling annual environmental measurements with a linear model Y = aX + b + Z and Gaussian noise. A student claims that because the model is linear in X, there must always be a closed-form analytic MLE, so using gradient ascent is unnecessary. How would you respond using both the specific linear-regression case and the broader optimization lesson the course is trying to teach?
rubric_items: Full credit: Acknowledges analytic solution exists for standard linear regression; Explains gradient ascent is taught for general optimization beyond this case; Connects the example to defining objectives and computing gradients
Partial credit: Says gradient ascent is useful in general but does not reconcile that with linear regression having a closed form; Mentions analytic solution vaguely

Common mistakes: Claiming linear regression has no analytic solution at all; Claiming analytic solutions make optimization methods irrelevant; Failing to distinguish the specific case from the general lesson

questions.text: Consider the one-parameter log-likelihood LL(α) whose derivative is n/α - Σ_i log(1+x_i). Explain aloud how you would find the optimizer without running gradient ascent, and then justify that the point you find is a maximum rather than a minimum or saddle point.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets first derivative to zero correctly; Solves α = n / Σ log(1+x_i); Uses second derivative test with -n/α^2 < 0; Interprets result as a maximum
Partial credit: Finds the stationary point but does not justify maximality; Mentions second derivative but not its sign reasoning
Common mistakes: Forgetting to set derivative to zero; Using gradient ascent language without solving analytically; Saying negative second derivative implies minimum

questions.text: A student says, “Gradient ascent always finds the global maximum, as long as I repeat many times.” Use the simple function f(x) = -x^2 + 4 to explain what is true in this example, and then carefully state what the algorithm can and cannot guarantee in general.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the specific example has derivative -2x and maximum at 0; Notes small enough step size allows uphill movement; Clarifies that general objectives may have local maxima or other issues, so global optimality is not guaranteed
Partial credit: Says gradient ascent can fail in general but does not explain why; Analyzes the parabola but overgeneralizes from it
Common mistakes: Claiming repetition alone guarantees the global maximum; Ignoring dependence on learning rate; Confusing local improvement with global optimality

questions.text: You fit a line to data where X is year and Y is temperature anomaly. After one gradient-ascent pass, you find gradient_a is strongly positive while gradient_b is near zero. Give a plausible interpretation of this pattern in terms of the residuals and the role of x_i, and explain what kind of parameter change the algorithm will prefer next.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses weighted residual interpretation for gradient_a; Uses unweighted residual interpretation for gradient_b; Concludes slope should increase more than intercept
Partial credit: Correctly says slope increases but gives weak reasoning; Discusses residuals without connecting to weighting by x_i

Common mistakes: Treating gradient_b near zero as meaning perfect fit; Ignoring that large x values affect slope gradient more strongly; Claiming intercept must decrease because slope gradient is positive

questions.text: Why is it meaningful in linear regression MLE to maximize the conditional likelihood Σ_i log f(y_i | x_i, θ) rather than the joint likelihood of x_i and y_i together? Explain what assumption about the inputs is implicit in this choice and why it is natural in supervised learning.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains focus on modeling Y|X for prediction; States that X is treated as given/fixed or not explicitly modeled; Connects this to supervised learning objectives
Partial credit: Says conditional likelihood is easier but not why it is conceptually appropriate; Mentions predicting Y from X without discussing the status of X
Common mistakes: Claiming joint and conditional likelihood are always the same objective; Saying we maximize P(X|Y) in regression; Ignoring the predictive meaning of conditioning

questions.text: For batch logistic regression training, the j-th gradient component is Σ_i (y_i - σ(θ^T x_i)) x_{ij}. Without doing a full derivation from scratch, explain the sign of this term. In particular, if the model predicts too low a probability on examples with large positive x_{ij} and y_i = 1, what effect does that have on θ_j?
rubric_items: Full credit: Interprets y_i - prediction as signed prediction error; Explains positive x_{ij} makes the contribution positive when underpredicting a positive example; States gradient ascent increases θ_j; Connects that increase to higher future predicted probabilities
Partial credit: Gets the sign right but gives little intuition; Discusses logistic regression generally without linking to the specific gradient term
Common mistakes: Using descent instead of ascent sign; Saying θ_j should decrease when the model underpredicts a positive case; Ignoring the role of x_{ij}

questions.text: A friend tries to use linear regression for a binary classification problem with labels 0 and 1, saying, “A line is simpler than a sigmoid, and I can just threshold the output at 0.5.” Give a principled critique of this idea, and contrast what linear regression and logistic regression are each trying to fit.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why linear regression outputs are not valid probabilities; Explains logistic regression outputs probabilities in [0,1] via sigmoid; Contrasts line fitting versus conditional probability / decision boundary modeling
Partial credit: Says logistic regression is better for classification but gives only one reason; Mentions thresholding issue without discussing probability interpretation

Common mistakes: Claiming linear regression cannot be thresholded at all; Saying logistic regression is nonlinear in the features rather than nonlinear only in output transformation; Ignoring the modeling objective difference

questions.text: In logistic regression training code, why do we initialize gradients[j] to zero at the start of each outer iteration rather than leaving the previous iteration’s values in place and continuing to add? Explain what quantity the gradient array is supposed to represent at one iteration.
rubric_items: Full credit: States gradient array should equal current iteration's gradient at current θ; Explains leaving old values mixes gradients from different parameter states; Connects reset-to-zero step to correct batch accumulation
Partial credit: Says resetting avoids double counting but without noting different θ values; Mentions implementation correctness vaguely
Common mistakes: Claiming accumulated old gradients help momentum automatically; Confusing the gradient array with the parameter vector; Thinking reset is only for memory reasons

questions.text: You are handed a dataset with one feature X and told to fit linear regression by MLE under Gaussian noise. During the oral exam, I ask you to justify why maximizing log f(y_i | x_i, θ) over all i becomes an optimization problem involving residuals y_i - (ax_i+b). Walk through that logic verbally without deriving every constant term.
