For one binary feature among patients with Y=1, you observe X'=0 exactly 0 times and X'=1 exactly 100 times. What is the MLE for P(X'=0|Y=1), and why can that be problematic when the classifier later multiplies many such probabilities together?
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes the MLE as 0 and 1 from observed counts.; Explains the zero-probability problem in multiplicative classifiers.; Connects the issue to sparse data and extreme MLE estimates.
Partial credit: States the estimate correctly but gives only a vague reason it is problematic.; Recognizes a zero in the product is bad without tying it to future prediction.

Common mistakes: Claiming the true conditional probability must be zero.; Discussing smoothing methods without first stating the plain MLE.; Forgetting conditioning on Y=1 restricts which data are counted.

questions.text: Explain why the iid assumption is so convenient in MLE derivations. Then tell me what part of the derivation would break if the observations were dependent, even if each marginal distribution looked the same.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the iid product factorization clearly.; Explains that logs turn the product into a sum.; Describes what fails under dependence: the factorization and hence the derivation.; Mentions the need for a correct joint or conditional model under dependence.
Partial credit: Mentions independence helps simplify multiplication but does not explain the consequence if it fails.; Says dependence 'makes it harder' without stating the mathematical issue.
Common mistakes: Thinking identical marginals alone are enough for product factorization.; Saying MLE cannot be done with dependent data at all.; Ignoring the role of the joint distribution.

questions.text: For the normal model with unknown μ and σ^2, explain why solving the μ equation first simplifies the σ equation. In other words, why is it natural to plug μ̂=x̄ into the likelihood before solving for σ̂^2?
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that μ̂=x̄ comes from the first-order condition.; Explains why replacing μ by x̄ simplifies the squared-error term.; Derives or states the resulting σ̂^2 formula correctly.; Shows understanding that one parameter can be solved and substituted into the other optimization.
Partial credit: States 'plug in x̄' as a procedure but does not justify it.; Gets the final σ̂^2 formula right with limited reasoning.
Common mistakes: Treating μ and σ as completely independent without explanation.; Plugging in the unbiased variance formula instead of the MLE.; Not recognizing that ∑(xi-μ)^2 depends on μ.

questions.text: Someone says, "Since likelihoods can be bigger than 1 for continuous models, they are not meaningful." How would you respond, using the distinction between density and probability and the role of likelihood in MLE?
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains density versus probability correctly.; States that likelihood need not be a probability distribution over θ.; Explains that MLE uses relative comparison of θ values.
Partial credit: Says densities can exceed 1 but does not connect this to likelihood.; States likelihood is meaningful for comparison without clarifying density/probability.
Common mistakes: Insisting all likelihood values must lie in [0,1].; Confusing PDF values with probabilities of points.; Claiming continuous-model MLE is invalid.

questions.text: You are given a likelihood optimization problem with a parameter constraint, and a student tries to differentiate the unconstrained log-likelihood and solve independently for each parameter. Use the multinomial example to explain why that can fail and how Lagrange multipliers repair the issue.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why the parameters are constrained and not independently free.; Describes the failure of naive unconstrained differentiation.; Sets up the Lagrangian correctly in words or formulas.; Obtains or explains the solution pi=Xi/n.
Partial credit: Mentions the sum-to-one constraint and Lagrange multipliers but not why ignoring the constraint fails.; States the final answer without showing the role of λ.
Common mistakes: Differentiating as if each pi could increase independently.; Using a separate normalization afterward without justification.; Forgetting λ or the sum-to-one constraint.

questions.text: Imagine two candidate Bernoulli parameters, p=0.5 and p=0.8, for the same sample with 8 successes and 2 failures. Without multiplying out large decimals, explain how you would compare them efficiently and why your method is preferable.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the correct log-likelihood comparison.; Explains why logs simplify the comparison.; Concludes correctly that p=0.8 is preferred.
Partial credit: Compares using the likelihoods directly but explains the same logic correctly.; States 0.8 is better because it matches the sample proportion but does not write the objective.
Common mistakes: Comparing only p values to the sample proportion without mentioning the likelihood.; Using 8 log(1-p)+2 log p.; Claiming logs could change which parameter is better.

questions.text: Suppose you are handed a black-box optimization problem for MLE where the score equations are too messy to solve by hand. Describe how gradient ascent fits into the standard MLE workflow, what quantity it updates, and one thing you would monitor to know whether it is working.
rubric_items: Full credit: Places gradient ascent correctly within the MLE workflow.; States that parameters are updated using the gradient of the log-likelihood.; Explains why ascent rather than descent is used here.; Mentions a sensible diagnostic such as increasing log-likelihood, shrinking gradient, or parameter validity.
Partial credit: Describes iterative optimization generally but not specifically for maximizing log-likelihood.; Mentions gradient ascent but not what is being updated or monitored.

Common mistakes: Using gradient descent on the log-likelihood without changing the sign.; Saying numerical optimization replaces the need to define a likelihood.; Not considering parameter constraints during updates.

questions.text: A student says, "Because the sample mean is the MLE for Bernoulli p, Poisson λ, and Normal μ, the sample mean must be the MLE for any one-parameter distribution." Critique this claim and give a principled reason why it fails.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the generalization clearly.; Explains that MLE depends on the full likelihood form of the chosen model.; Uses the sample-mean examples as special cases rather than a universal rule.; Mentions a contrasting family such as Uniform.
Partial credit: Says it is false and names a counterexample but gives little principled explanation.; Explains model dependence vaguely without a concrete contrast.

Common mistakes: Treating one-parameter families as automatically mean-parameterized.; Assuming MLE must equal a familiar summary statistic.; Failing to provide a reason beyond 'because the notes say so.'

questions.text: If I tell you that MLE 'fits the curve to match the data,' what is a more mathematically precise version of that statement? Answer using the language of observed data, a parametric family, and an optimization problem.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the parametric family and observed data setup.; States the optimization problem θ̂=argmax L(θ) or argmax LL(θ).; Uses iid factorization if appropriate.; Translates the informal phrase into mathematical language about model fitting.
Partial credit: Gives the argmax idea but omits the role of the model family or observed sample.; Uses informal language with only partial mathematical precision.
Common mistakes: Saying MLE maximizes the probability of θ.; Failing to specify that the optimization is over parameter values.; Ignoring the observed-data conditioning.

questions.text: A student says: "For a Bernoulli sample with 8 ones and 2 zeros, the likelihood is the probability that p equals 0.8, so MLE tells us the most probable value of the parameter." Explain carefully what is wrong with that statement, then use the sample to describe what the likelihood function actually is and why its maximizer is p-hat = 0.8.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly states that MLE does not maximize the probability of the parameter itself in the frequentist setup.; Writes the Bernoulli likelihood or log-likelihood correctly for 8 ones and 2 zeros.; Explains why log-likelihood can be used instead of likelihood.; Derives or justifies p-hat = 0.8 and interprets it as the parameter making the observed data most likely.

Partial credit: Recognizes the difference between likelihood and posterior probability but explains it imprecisely.; States p-hat = 0.8 from intuition without showing the likelihood setup.; Uses the sample proportion correctly but does not explain the role of log-likelihood.

Common mistakes: Saying MLE computes P(p|data) rather than maximizing L(p).; Treating the likelihood as p^10 or as 0.8^8 0.2^2 without keeping p variable.; Claiming likelihood values across different models are probabilities that sum to 1 over p.

questions.text: You observe iid counts from a 6-sided die rolled 12 times: 3 ones, 2 twos, 0 threes, 3 fours, 1 five, and 3 sixes. Derive the multinomial MLE for the face probabilities using the constraint that the probabilities sum to 1, and explain why the combinatorial coefficient does not affect the optimizer. Then interpret what the zero count does to the MLE.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the multinomial likelihood correctly with the sum-to-one constraint.; Explains that the multinomial coefficient is constant in the parameters and therefore irrelevant to the argmax.; Uses Lagrange multipliers or an equivalent constrained optimization argument to derive p_i-hat = X_i/n.; Interprets the zero-count category correctly as yielding an MLE of zero and comments on its practical implication.

Partial credit: Gets the final estimator p_i-hat = X_i/n from intuition without a clear derivation.; States that the coefficient can be ignored but does not explain why.; Identifies the zero-count issue but does not connect it to small-sample behavior.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the sum-to-one constraint.; Treating X_i as probabilities instead of counts.; Claiming the combinatorial factor changes the maximizer.; Being uncomfortable with p_3-hat = 0 because 0! appears in the coefficient; 0! is just 1.

questions.text: In a simple linear regression setting, you model Y = aX + b + Z and decide to estimate a and b by maximum likelihood through the conditional likelihood of y given x. Explain what additional assumption about the noise Z is needed to recover the same objective as minimizing mean squared error, and then show verbally how the log-likelihood turns into an expression involving squared residuals.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the iid Gaussian noise assumption with mean 0 and common variance.; Connects the conditional density of Y|X to a normal centered at ax+b.; Explains how the log-likelihood becomes constants minus a scaled sum of squared residuals.; Concludes clearly that maximizing likelihood is equivalent to minimizing squared error only under that model assumption.

Partial credit: Mentions 'normal errors' but does not write or explain the conditional likelihood clearly.; Says MLE equals MSE in linear regression without emphasizing the needed assumptions.; Recognizes squared residuals appear in the log-likelihood but does not explain why constants and sigma matter.

Common mistakes: Claiming MLE always equals least squares regardless of noise model.; Maximizing likelihood of predicted values rather than conditional likelihood of observed y given x.; Ignoring the iid assumption on the noise terms.

questions.text: For iid Normal data with both mean and variance unknown, explain how the MLE for the mean is obtained from the log-likelihood, and then compare that result to the sample mean as an estimator you may already know. Why is this an example where MLE behaves nicely, in contrast to some small-sample problems mentioned for other families?
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes or describes the Normal log-likelihood in terms of sum of squared deviations.; Differentiates with respect to mu and obtains mu-hat = X-bar.; Compares the result to the known sample mean estimator and notes that it is unbiased.; Contrasts this with small-sample pathologies in less well-behaved MLE settings.

Partial credit: States mu-hat = X-bar correctly but with limited derivation.; Mentions unbiasedness of X-bar but does not connect it to the likelihood derivation.; Notes that some MLEs can be problematic without giving a meaningful contrast.

Common mistakes: Confusing the MLE of variance with the unbiased sample variance and mixing denominators without being asked.; Differentiating incorrectly and concluding mu-hat depends on sigma in a more complicated way.; Claiming all MLEs are unbiased because this one is.

questions.text: You are given positive-valued data that are modeled as iid from a truncated normal with density proportional to exp(-(x-mu)^2/2) for x>0, normalized by Phi(mu). Explain how MLE changes compared with the ordinary Normal case, derive the score equation with respect to mu, and say why a closed-form estimator is not generally available.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the role of the truncation-induced normalizing factor Phi(mu).; Writes the log-likelihood and differentiates it correctly to obtain the score involving phi(mu)/Phi(mu).; States clearly why no closed-form solution is generally available.; Mentions a numerical optimization method such as gradient ascent or another iterative solver.

Partial credit: Recognizes that truncation changes the likelihood but does not derive the derivative fully.; Writes the ordinary Normal score and forgets the Phi(mu) term, but notices some extra correction is needed.; Says 'use numerical methods' without explaining the source of the difficulty.

Common mistakes: Treating the truncated normal exactly like an untruncated normal and setting mu-hat equal to the sample mean.; Forgetting that d/dmu log Phi(mu) = phi(mu)/Phi(mu).; Missing the factor n in front of the truncation term when summing over observations.

questions.text: A classmate says: 'Naive Bayes assumes the features are independent, so if two words in an email are correlated in the raw data, the model is invalid.' Do you agree? Explain carefully what independence assumption Naive Bayes actually makes, and describe a situation where two features are dependent marginally but conditionally independent given the class label.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that the assumption is conditional independence given Y, not marginal independence.; Writes or verbalizes the factorization P(X1,...,Xm|Y)=∏P(Xi|Y).; Explains that marginal dependence can coexist with conditional independence.; Gives a plausible example grounded in class labels or a hidden cause.
Partial credit: Mentions 'given Y' but explanation is vague.; Gives the right intuition but no formal factorization.; Confuses events and random variables but overall idea is correct.

Common mistakes: Saying Naive Bayes assumes Xi are independent unconditionally.; Claiming any observed correlation between features makes Naive Bayes unusable.; Describing P(Y|X)=∏P(Y|Xi), which is not the Naive Bayes assumption.

questions.text: Suppose you are building a binary spam classifier with binary word-presence features X1,...,Xm. Walk me through exactly which probabilities must be estimated during training under Naive Bayes, and contrast that with the brute-force Bayes approach that estimates the full conditional distribution P(X1,...,Xm | Y). Why does the parameter count change so dramatically?
rubric_items: Full credit: Lists the prior(s) and per-feature conditional probabilities needed for Naive Bayes.; Explains that binary features allow one probability per feature per class as a free parameter.; Contrasts with exponential-size full joint conditional table for brute-force Bayes.; Mentions tractability/data sparsity motivation.
Partial credit: Correctly identifies the needed Naive Bayes quantities but weakly explains the brute-force case.; Says 'fewer parameters' without describing linear versus exponential growth.
Common mistakes: Saying Naive Bayes estimates P(Y|Xi) directly during training.; Forgetting the class prior.; Claiming the full joint needs only m parameters.

questions.text: You train a Naive Bayes classifier on a large text dataset, and at test time you must score an email with thousands of features. A teammate multiplies all the estimated probabilities directly and gets numerical underflow, producing zeros for both classes. Explain a principled fix, justify why it preserves the argmax decision, and mention any interpretation change in the resulting score.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies underflow as the issue with multiplying many small probabilities.; Replaces the product by a sum of log-probabilities.; Justifies unchanged argmax using monotonicity of log.; Notes that P(X) can be dropped for classification because it is common across classes.
Partial credit: Suggests logs but does not justify why decision is preserved.; Mentions numerical stability but not how to score classes.
Common mistakes: Taking log after the product is already rounded to zero.; Believing log changes the predicted class.; Dropping terms incorrectly, such as omitting the prior P(Y).

questions.text: A student says: 'Since Bayes’ rule divides by P(X), we need to estimate P(X) for every possible test point in order to classify with Naive Bayes.' Evaluate this claim. In your explanation, be precise about when P(X) matters and when it does not.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that P(X) cancels in the argmax because it is common across classes.; Distinguishes prediction of the class label from computing normalized posterior probabilities.; Uses Bayes' rule correctly.
Partial credit: Says 'it cancels' without clearly explaining why.; Correctly discusses argmax but ignores the case of wanting calibrated probabilities.
Common mistakes: Claiming P(X) depends on Y in the denominator during argmax.; Saying Naive Bayes never needs P(X) for any purpose.; Confusing P(X) with P(X|Y).

questions.text: Consider binary Naive Bayes with class Y in {0,1}. In the training set, feature X7 never appears as 1 among examples with Y=1, but the test point has X7=1. Compare what happens under MLE versus Laplace smoothing, both numerically in the class score and conceptually in the classifier’s behavior.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains zero probability under MLE and its multiplicative/log consequence.; Explains Laplace smoothing formula qualitatively or explicitly for binary features.; Interprets smoothing as avoiding impossible predictions from unseen events.; Compares the effect on the class decision.
Partial credit: Understands that Laplace avoids zeros but gives no detail.; Describes the issue only qualitatively without linking to the class score.
Common mistakes: Saying Laplace changes only the prior P(Y).; Claiming MLE is always preferable because it uses the data more 'exactly'.; Forgetting that one zero factor kills the whole product.

questions.text: You are asked to extend a binary-feature Naive Bayes model to a four-class problem where Y can be {Like, Love, Haha, Sad}. A new user has X1=1, X2=1, X3=0. Explain how you would write the prediction rule as an argmax over classes and how you would estimate each term using counts with Laplace smoothing.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the multiclass argmax structure correctly.; Uses the Naive Bayes factorization over the three features.; Gives correct Laplace-smoothed count formulas for binary features.; Explains evaluation across all four classes.
Partial credit: Correct argmax but missing smoothing details.; Correct formulas for conditionals but omits the prior or the class comparison.

Common mistakes: Using one-vs-rest logistic-regression style reasoning instead of multiclass Naive Bayes.; Applying Laplace smoothing with the wrong denominator.; Forgetting to use X3=0 rather than X3=1 in the score.

questions.text: Compare Naive Bayes and logistic regression as models for binary classification. I do not want just the slogan 'generative versus discriminative'—explain what each model learns, whether each can generate new (x,y) pairs after fitting, and how each naturally handles continuous or non-binary discrete features.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains generative vs discriminative in terms of modeled distributions, not just names.; States whether each can generate new (x,y) pairs and why.; Addresses continuous features and non-binary discrete features for both models.; Keeps the comparison tied to model assumptions rather than implementation trivia.
Partial credit: Correctly says generative vs discriminative but gives limited consequences.; Mentions Gaussian Naive Bayes or categorical features but not both.
Common mistakes: Claiming logistic regression models P(X|Y).; Saying Naive Bayes cannot handle continuous features.; Confusing feature encoding issues with probability-model structure.

questions.text: Suppose you have m binary features and a binary label. During testing, a student writes the score for class y as product over i of P(Xi=1 | Y=y), regardless of whether the observed Xi is 0 or 1. Explain what is wrong with this, and give the correct per-feature contribution to the Naive Bayes score.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies mismatch between observed Xi and the factor used.; States the correct factor as P(Xi=xi|Y=y).; Notes that Xi=0 can also carry information.
Partial credit: Recognizes the error but gives only an informal correction.; Mentions using 1-P(Xi=1|Y=y) for zeros but not the general rule.
Common mistakes: Treating only present words/features as part of the model by default.; Writing P(Y|Xi) instead of P(Xi|Y).; Forgetting that the product runs over all modeled features.

questions.text: Someone argues: 'Because Naive Bayes factorizes P(X|Y), the features must be pairwise conditionally independent, and that is the same as full conditional independence of all features given Y.' Is that statement fully correct? Explain the subtlety between pairwise and mutual conditional independence and which version Naive Bayes uses.
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes pairwise from full mutual conditional independence.; States that Naive Bayes assumes the full factorization.; Notes that pairwise independence alone is insufficient in general when m>2.
Partial credit: Senses there is a distinction but cannot articulate it fully.; Correctly states the Naive Bayes factorization but not the pairwise subtlety.
Common mistakes: Saying pairwise independence always implies mutual independence.; Talking only about unconditional independence.; Failing to mention the joint factorization.

questions.text: Imagine you are classifying users as liking or disliking a TV genre using many binary indicators of preferences for individual shows. Explain why the brute-force Bayes classifier becomes impractical as the number of shows grows, and why Naive Bayes offers a useful compromise even if its independence assumption is not exactly true.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains exponential state space for brute-force Bayes.; Connects that to data sparsity and unstable estimates.; Explains the linear-parameter simplification in Naive Bayes.; Gives a sensible reason Naive Bayes can still work when assumptions are approximate.
Partial credit: Mentions 'too many combinations' but not the 2^m growth.; Says Naive Bayes is simpler without explaining why.
Common mistakes: Claiming Naive Bayes is exact whenever m is large.; Failing to connect parameter count to sample-size needs.; Saying brute-force Bayes is fine if you use logs.

questions.text: In Gaussian Naive Bayes, suppose for each feature Xi and class y you model Xi as Normal with mean μi,y and variance σ^2_i,y. For a test point with two features x=(5,3), explain how to decide whether Y=1 or Y=0 without computing any integrals, and write the comparison in terms of Gaussian densities and the prior p=P(Y=1).
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses class-conditional Gaussian densities, not discrete probabilities, in the comparison.; Includes both features under the Naive Bayes product and the class prior.; Recognizes that logs may be used for stability.; Explains why no integral is needed.
Partial credit: Correct comparison idea but forgets the prior or one feature.; Says 'use Gaussian probability' without distinguishing density evaluation.
Common mistakes: Trying to compute P(X=5) for a continuous variable directly as a positive probability.; Using a single joint Gaussian without invoking Naive Bayes.; Omitting the class prior.

questions.text: After training a spam classifier, you evaluate it on a separate test set with known labels. Explain what precision and recall mean for the spam class, and describe a realistic situation in which a Naive Bayes system could have high precision but lower recall, or vice versa.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines precision and recall correctly for a chosen class.; Distinguishes denominator for each metric.; Provides a coherent scenario for precision-recall tradeoff.
Partial credit: Gets the intuition right but swaps denominators.; Provides only one of the two scenarios.
Common mistakes: Confusing precision with overall accuracy.; Defining recall using predicted positives instead of actual positives.; Ignoring the class-specific nature of the metrics.

questions.text: A teammate says: 'Because Naive Bayes uses Bayes’ theorem, it must be estimating P(Y|X) directly during training.' Explain why this is misleading, and identify what is typically estimated from the training data instead.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that training estimates P(Y) and class-conditional feature distributions.; States Bayes' theorem is used at prediction/inference time to obtain posterior scores.; Contrasts this with direct conditional modeling.
Partial credit: Says Naive Bayes is generative but does not spell out what is estimated.; Mentions P(X|Y) but omits P(Y).

Common mistakes: Claiming Naive Bayes optimizes conditional log-likelihood directly by default.; Confusing Naive Bayes training with logistic regression training.; Ignoring the role of Bayes’ theorem at test time.

questions.text: Suppose you have two highly redundant binary features: X1 indicates whether the word 'free' appears in an email, and X2 indicates whether the exact same tokenization pipeline also marks a nearly identical feature for that same word. Under Naive Bayes, what risk does this redundancy create in the posterior score, and how would you explain the issue without saying the classifier is automatically wrong?
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies double-counting of evidence due to correlated/redundant features.; Explains impact on overconfidence or calibration.; Avoids overstating the consequence as inevitable misclassification.
Partial credit: Recognizes dependence problem but not the overconfidence effect.; Says 'it violates assumptions' without explaining practical consequences.

Common mistakes: Claiming Naive Bayes cannot be used at all with correlated features.; Saying duplicate features have no effect because each feature is treated separately.; Confusing redundancy with class imbalance.

questions.text: For binary Naive Bayes, explain how you would estimate P(Xi=0 | Y=y) from training data in two different ways, and under what assumptions those two ways agree. Then comment on whether it is ever necessary to estimate both P(Xi=1|Y=y) and P(Xi=0|Y=y) as independent free parameters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives both direct counting and complement methods.; States that for binary features the two probabilities sum to 1.; Explains that they are not independent free parameters.
Partial credit: Only gives one estimation approach but correctly notes complementarity.; Mentions that outcomes sum to 1 but not the implications for parameter count.
Common mistakes: Treating P(Xi=0|Y=y) and P(Xi=1|Y=y) as unrelated parameters.; Using P(Xi=0|Y=y)=1-P(Y=y).; Ignoring smoothing consistency.

questions.text: Why is conditioning the right lens for understanding Naive Bayes? Answer by connecting the general conditional probability identities to the Naive Bayes derivation, starting from Bayes’ theorem and ending at the class-score factorization.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from Bayes’ theorem correctly.; Drops P(X) only in the argmax context and explains why.; Applies conditional independence inside P(X|Y).; Connects the reasoning to conditioning as fixing Y.
Partial credit: Gives the right equations but weak conceptual explanation.; Explains conditioning but does not connect all the derivation steps.
Common mistakes: Applying independence to P(Y|X).; Dropping P(X) without noting the argmax context.; Describing unconditional rather than conditional independence.

questions.text: You are handed a dataset where the training set was taken as the first 1538 emails in time and the test set as the next 251 emails. Explain why we still need a separate test set after training Naive Bayes, and describe one risk specific to time-ordered splitting that you would mention in an oral exam.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the purpose of a held-out test set for generalization assessment.; Mentions optimistic bias if evaluating on training data.; Identifies a time-order-specific issue such as distribution shift or concept drift.; Optionally notes realism of temporal evaluation.
Partial credit: Explains test-set purpose but not the temporal risk.; Mentions overfitting vaguely without tying it to evaluation.
Common mistakes: Saying the test set is used to estimate the Naive Bayes parameters.; Assuming random and time-based splits always answer the same question.; Ignoring temporal drift.

questions.text: A student says: 'Since continuous random variables satisfy P(X=x)=0, Gaussian Naive Bayes cannot classify a point x because every exact observation has probability zero.' Diagnose the mistake and repair the statement precisely.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes probability from density.; States that Gaussian Naive Bayes uses class-conditional densities evaluated at the observed x.; Explains why zero point probability does not prevent classification.
Partial credit: Says 'use densities' but does not explain the conceptual error.; Recognizes continuous-variable issue but remains imprecise.

Common mistakes: Saying Gaussian Naive Bayes approximates probabilities of tiny intervals and that is the only valid approach.; Claiming exact-point classification is impossible for continuous features.; Using the word probability when density is required.

questions.text: Suppose a binary Naive Bayes model has learned priors P(Y=1)=0.9 and P(Y=0)=0.1. For a particular test point, the product of conditional feature likelihoods is 10^-8 under Y=1 and 10^-6 under Y=0. Without doing elaborate arithmetic, reason out which class wins and explain why priors and likelihoods must both be considered on the same scale.
rubric_items: Full credit: Combines prior and likelihood correctly for both classes.; Chooses the correct winning class.; Explains the conceptual need to balance prior and evidence, ideally in log-space.
Partial credit: Gets the winner right but explanation is weak.; Mentions priors matter but does not combine them correctly with likelihoods.
Common mistakes: Picking Y=1 solely because its prior is larger.; Comparing only likelihoods or only priors.; Forgetting that posteriors are proportional to prior times likelihood.

questions.text: Explain why Naive Bayes can be seen as a model of the joint distribution over X and Y, even though at prediction time we usually write an argmax over P(Y|X). Then say what extra thing this generative view gives you that a purely conditional model may not give directly.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the joint factorization P(X,Y)=P(X|Y)P(Y).; Connects prediction via Bayes’ theorem to the posterior P(Y|X).; Mentions at least one consequence of the generative view, such as sampling new data.
Partial credit: States generative meaning correctly but gives limited consequences.; Describes prediction only, without mentioning the joint.
Common mistakes: Saying Naive Bayes models only P(Y|X).; Failing to explain why P(X,Y) is available.; Giving a consequence unrelated to generative modeling.

questions.text: A medical screening team wants to use Naive Bayes on a mix of binary symptoms and one continuous lab value. They ask whether Naive Bayes forces all features to be binary. Answer their question, and outline a coherent modeling strategy for the mixed feature types while preserving the basic Naive Bayes idea.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that Naive Bayes is not restricted to binary features.; Describes a mixed-feature strategy using different class-conditional models by feature type.; Preserves the conditional independence/product structure.
Partial credit: Says continuous features are allowed but gives no modeling detail.; Mentions Gaussian Naive Bayes without explaining how it combines with binary features.

Common mistakes: Claiming all features must be converted to binary for Naive Bayes.; Using one joint Gaussian for all features without connecting to the Naive Bayes factorization.; Forgetting the class prior.

questions.text: A classmate says: 'If Naive Bayes predicts the class by argmax over products, then adding more features can only improve the classifier because you are multiplying in more information.' Do you agree? Explain the best argument against this claim within the Naive Bayes framework.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the claim and explains why more features can hurt.; Mentions at least one of redundancy, noise, dependence violations, or estimation error.; Frames the argument within Naive Bayes scoring/assumptions.
Partial credit: Says more features are not always better but gives only a generic machine-learning answer.; Mentions overfitting vaguely without tying it to Naive Bayes.
Common mistakes: Agreeing unconditionally because 'information never hurts'.; Ignoring estimation error and assumption mismatch.; Assuming independence violations have no effect.

questions.text: Without plugging in numbers, derive the log-odds form of binary Naive Bayes for binary features: explain why comparing class 1 to class 0 can be written as a prior log-odds term plus a sum of per-feature contributions. I want the structure and the reasoning, not a memorized formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from the two class scores and forms a ratio or comparison.; Uses logs to convert the product ratio into a sum.; Identifies a prior log-odds term and per-feature log-likelihood-ratio terms.; Notes dependence on observed xi for binary features.
Partial credit: Gets the overall idea of log-odds but not the derivation.; States a sum of terms without explaining where it comes from.
Common mistakes: Writing posterior odds without conditioning on observed xi.; Forgetting to divide class-1 and class-0 scores before taking logs.; Using P(Y|Xi) instead of P(Xi|Y).

questions.text: A classmate says: “Naïve Bayes assumes the features are independent, so if two words in an email are correlated in the overall population, Naïve Bayes is invalid.” Respond to that claim carefully. In your answer, distinguish ordinary independence from conditional independence given the label, and explain why the Naïve Bayes factorization is still written in terms of P(X_i | Y) rather than P(X_i).
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly states the assumption is conditional independence given Y, not marginal independence.; Gives or paraphrases the factorization P(X_1,...,X_m | Y)=∏_i P(X_i | Y).; Explains how marginal dependence can still occur even if conditional independence holds.; Connects the assumption to simplifying P(X|Y) in Bayes classification, not simplifying P(X_i) or P(Y|X) directly.

Partial credit: Says 'independent given the class' but does not clearly contrast with unconditional independence.; Mentions Bayes rule and argmax_y P(X|Y)P(Y) but gives little interpretation.; Recognizes that correlated features do not automatically break the model, without explaining why.

Common mistakes: Claiming Naïve Bayes assumes full independence of features in the dataset.; Writing P(X_1,...,X_m)=∏_i P(X_i) as the model assumption.; Confusing conditional independence with pairwise independence only.; Saying the model directly learns P(Y|X) rather than P(X|Y) and P(Y).

questions.text: You are building a binary spam filter with binary word-presence features. In the training set, 90 of 100 emails are ham and 10 are spam. A particular word, 'lottery', appears in 0 of the 90 ham emails and 3 of the 10 spam emails. For a test email whose only active feature is lottery = 1, compare the MLE-based Naïve Bayes decision with the Laplace-smoothed decision, and explain the role of log-probabilities in the test-time computation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes or correctly sets up priors and class-conditional probabilities under MLE and Laplace.; Explains that MLE gives zero likelihood for ham, forcing the decision.; Uses correct Laplace denominator for a binary feature: count(Y=y)+2.; Compares the smoothed class scores and identifies the predicted class.; Explains that log-probabilities preserve the argmax because log is monotone and improve numerical stability.

Partial credit: Gets the intuition of zero counts causing brittleness, but mishandles one denominator.; Correctly describes smoothing conceptually without fully comparing scores.; Mentions logs for stability but does not connect to the argmax computation.

Common mistakes: Adding 1 only to the numerator but not adjusting the denominator.; Using denominator +1 instead of +2 for binary features.; Claiming logs change the predicted class.; Ignoring the class prior when comparing classes.

questions.text: A product team wants to predict a 4-class reaction to a book: {Like, Love, Haha, Sad}, using three binary taste indicators X1, X2, X3. You are given only a count(query) interface that returns training-set counts with equality constraints. For a new user with X1=1, X2=1, X3=0, state the Naïve Bayes prediction rule in a form you could actually evaluate from counts, and explain exactly where Laplace smoothing is applied. Then say whether the denominator P(X1=1, X2=1, X3=0) is needed for choosing the predicted class.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the multiclass argmax over the four labels.; Correctly factors the likelihood into three conditional terms using the Naïve Bayes assumption.; Expresses each term in evaluable count form with Laplace smoothing and correct binary-feature denominator +2.; States that P(X) is not needed for argmax because it is constant across labels.; Notes that the denominator would be needed only to produce calibrated posterior probabilities, not just the predicted label.

Partial credit: Gives the correct argmax but not the count-based formulas.; Uses counts correctly but omits smoothing or is vague about where it enters.; States that P(X) cancels without explaining why.

Common mistakes: Trying to estimate P(X1=1,X2=1,X3=0|Y=y) directly from counts despite being asked for Naïve Bayes.; Applying Laplace smoothing to the prior in an inconsistent way without explanation.; Using count(X1=1)/N instead of count(X1=1,Y=y)/count(Y=y)-type class-conditional probabilities.; Saying the denominator is needed to compare labels.

questions.text: A student says: “Naïve Bayes and logistic regression are basically the same because both output a class probability, so once trained they can both generate new (x, y) samples from the same learned model.” Evaluate this statement. Compare what distribution each model is trying to learn, and use that comparison to explain which model is naturally generative and what that implies for handling different feature types.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes generative modeling of P(X|Y) and P(Y) from discriminative modeling of P(Y|X).; Explains why Naïve Bayes can generate (x,y) samples and logistic regression cannot do so without an extra model for X.; Connects the comparison to handling continuous or non-binary discrete features via chosen class-conditional distributions in Naïve Bayes.; Avoids claiming the models are identical just because both can output class probabilities.

Partial credit: Correctly says Naïve Bayes is generative and logistic regression is discriminative, but gives little explanation.; Mentions sample generation but not how it follows from the modeled distribution.; Discusses feature types only vaguely.

Common mistakes: Saying logistic regression learns P(X,Y).; Saying both models can equally generate X once they output P(Y|X).; Confusing the ability to classify continuous features with having a generative probabilistic model for them.; Claiming Naïve Bayes cannot handle continuous features.

questions.text: Consider Gaussian Naïve Bayes with two continuous features. You have already estimated: for feature 1, if Y=0 then X1~N(5,1) and if Y=1 then X1~N(0,1); for feature 2, if Y=0 then X2~N(0,1) and if Y=1 then X2~N(3,4); and P(Y=1)=0.6. For a test point x=(5,3), explain how to decide between Y=1 and Y=0 without plugging through every decimal, and argue qualitatively which class is favored.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the correct Gaussian Naïve Bayes inequality or equivalent log-score comparison.; Explains that each class score is the product of two class-conditional Gaussian densities times the prior.; Correctly identifies feature 1 as strongly favoring Y=0 and feature 2 as favoring Y=1.; Comments on the effect of larger variance for class 1 on feature 2's density peak.; Gives a defensible qualitative conclusion that class 0 likely wins because feature 1 is overwhelmingly more informative here.

Partial credit: Sets up the inequality correctly but does not reason qualitatively about means and variances.; Identifies which feature favors which class but misses the role of the prior or variance.; States a class choice without enough justification.

Common mistakes: Using probabilities P(X_i=value|Y) for continuous variables instead of densities.; Ignoring the prior entirely.; Assuming the feature at the class mean always dominates regardless of variance.; Multiplying raw z-scores instead of Gaussian densities or log-densities.

questions.text: A student says, 'A normal distribution is just any bell-shaped curve, so if two datasets look roughly symmetric, they are basically the same normal distribution.' Do you agree? Explain using the roles of mean and variance, and describe how changing each parameter changes the graph.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that a normal distribution is determined by mean and variance.; Explains that mean changes location/center.; Explains that variance changes spread/height.; Explicitly rejects the idea that all bell-shaped curves are the same normal.
Partial credit: Mentions mean and variance but does not clearly tie them to graph shape.; Says distributions can differ in center or spread but gives only one parameter correctly.
Common mistakes: Confusing variance and standard deviation.; Saying taller means larger mean.; Treating symmetry alone as enough to identify a normal distribution.

questions.text: Suppose adult reaction times in milliseconds are modeled as X ~ N(250, 40^2). Without plugging in table values, explain how you would compute the probability that a randomly chosen person has a reaction time between 220 and 300 milliseconds, and interpret the result in terms of areas under a curve.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses correct standardization formula.; Sets up probability as difference of two CDF values.; Interprets answer as area/probability, not density height.
Partial credit: Gets one z-score correct but not the other.; Knows to use Phi but does not clearly show interval subtraction.
Common mistakes: Using the PDF instead of the CDF.; Forgetting to subtract the lower-tail probability.; Using variance 40^2 incorrectly as if standard deviation were 1600.

questions.text: A factory measures the diameter of a part, and past data suggest diameters are approximately normal with mean 10 mm and variance 0.04. The quality manager wants the probability a part falls between 9.8 and 10.1 mm. Describe the full modeling and computation steps aloud, including whether you would use variance or standard deviation when standardizing.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies sigma = 0.2 from variance 0.04.; Sets up both z-scores correctly.; Uses Phi difference correctly.; Explicitly notes standard deviation is used in standardization.
Partial credit: Correct method with arithmetic slip.; Understands interval probability but is vague about variance vs standard deviation.
Common mistakes: Dividing by 0.04 instead of 0.2.; Confusing variance notation with standard deviation notation.; Using symmetry without computing both endpoints.

questions.text: You are modeling student heights from one classroom. Someone argues that using a normal model is justified because 'this classroom histogram looks nice and smooth,' while another person argues it is useful because the model generalizes through mean and variance. Compare these justifications and say which is stronger.
rubric_items: Full credit: Contrasts empirical visual fit with modeling/generalization reasoning.; States that the normal is specified by mean and variance.; Explains why generalization is a stronger argument than a single histogram looking smooth.
Partial credit: Says both are valid without comparing their strengths.; Mentions bell shape but not mean/variance or generalization.

Common mistakes: Claiming a single classroom histogram proves exact normality.; Saying maximum entropy means every dataset should be normal.; Ignoring the distinction between sample histogram and population model.

questions.text: Let X1, X2, and X3 be independent Gaussian random variables with means 5, -2, and 1 and variances 4, 9, and 16 respectively. Without deriving from scratch, give the distribution of S = X1 + X2 + X3 and explain why the variance adds the way it does.
rubric_items: Full credit: States sum is Gaussian under independence.; Computes mean 4 correctly.; Computes variance 29 correctly.; Explains role of independence/covariance.
Partial credit: Gets form right but confuses variance and standard deviation.; States parameters correctly without explanation of independence.
Common mistakes: Adding standard deviations instead of variances.; Forgetting the result is Gaussian.; Using 5-2+1 for mean but then also subtracting variances.

questions.text: Suppose X ~ N(100, 15^2), and you take an independent sample of size 10. Explain the distribution of the sample mean, and then set up the probability that the sample mean lies between 95 and 105. Do not just state the answer; explain where the new standard deviation comes from.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly states distribution of sample mean.; Uses variance divided by n or standard deviation divided by sqrt(n).; Sets up probability with correct standardized bounds.; Explains why averaging reduces variability.
Partial credit: Correct setup but vague explanation of why spread changes.; States CLT-like result without noting exact normality here.
Common mistakes: Using standard deviation 15/10 instead of 15/sqrt(10).; Leaving sample mean with same variance as original X.; Confusing variance 15^2/10 with standard deviation 15^2/sqrt(10).

questions.text: A classmate says, 'Whenever I see a binomial random variable with large n, I will use a normal approximation.' Give a careful response. Your answer should discuss when a normal approximation is reasonable, when a Poisson approximation is more appropriate, and what independence assumption matters for the normal case.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects 'large n alone' as sufficient.; States a normal-approximation criterion involving np(1-p).; States a Poisson-approximation regime with large n and small p.; Mentions independence for the normal approximation.
Partial credit: Identifies one approximation regime correctly but not the comparison.; Mentions p near 0 or 1 is problematic but gives no criterion.
Common mistakes: Saying Poisson is always better when n is large.; Ignoring p entirely.; Forgetting continuity correction if using normal for a discrete variable.

questions.text: Consider three binomial distributions: Bin(100, 0.5), Bin(100, 0.04), and Bin(100, 0.96). A student claims that Poisson should approximate all three because n is 100 in every case. Evaluate each case separately, and for the third one explain the useful trick if you still want a Poisson-style approximation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly rejects Poisson for Bin(100,0.5).; Correctly accepts Poisson for Bin(100,0.04).; Explains complement/failure-count trick for Bin(100,0.96).
Partial credit: Gets two of three cases right.; Recognizes that Bin(100,0.96) is problematic but cannot articulate the failure-count trick.
Common mistakes: Using Poisson directly for Bin(100,0.96) successes.; Thinking lambda large automatically helps Poisson approximation.; Not distinguishing rare failures from common successes.

questions.text: Let X ~ Bin(100, 0.5). You want an approximate value for P(48 <= X <= 56) using a normal approximation. Set up the approximation carefully, including the mean, variance, and the continuity correction, and explain why the correction is needed.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies mu = 50 and variance = 25.; Uses continuity-corrected bounds 47.5 and 56.5.; Explains why correction is used for discrete-to-continuous approximation.
Partial credit: Correct normal parameters but no continuity correction.; Applies some correction but with one bound wrong.
Common mistakes: Using bounds 48 and 56 directly without explanation.; Using standard deviation 25 instead of 5.; Forgetting that both endpoints must be shifted by 0.5.

questions.text: In a web-service setting, the number of requests landing in one bucket of a large hash table is only approximately independent across items, and the success probabilities vary slightly from item to item. A teammate says this invalidates all approximations based on rare events. Using the course guidance, explain whether a Poisson approximation can still be reasonable and what caveat you would mention.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that mild dependence/slight p variation can still permit Poisson approximation.; Explains the rare-event intuition.; Mentions approximation is not exact and assumptions are only approximately satisfied.
Partial credit: Says 'yes, maybe' but without specifying the mild-violation conditions.; Mentions rare events but not the caveat.
Common mistakes: Claiming any dependence makes Poisson impossible.; Claiming heterogeneity in p always invalidates the model.; Treating the result as exact rather than approximate.

questions.text: You are told that the number of floods in a 500-year period is modeled as Poisson with parameter 1. Explain how to compute the probability of at least 3 floods in 500 years, and then describe why summing the lower counts is preferable to summing the infinite upper tail.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies X ~ Poi(1).; Uses complement 1 - P(X <= 2).; Writes the finite Poisson sum correctly.; Explains why the complement is computationally convenient.
Partial credit: Gets the distribution and idea right but omits one Poisson term.; Says 'use complement' without explicit finite sum.
Common mistakes: Using a binomial model with arbitrary n.; Computing P(X=3) instead of P(X>=3).; Forgetting the e^-lambda term.

questions.text: A region is called a '500-year floodplain,' meaning the average flood rate is 1 per 500 years. A student concludes that after 499 years without a flood, a flood is now almost guaranteed next year. Respond to this claim by connecting the counting model and the waiting-time model.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the misconception clearly.; Connects Poisson counts to exponential waiting time.; Mentions memorylessness or equivalent reasoning.; Gives correct next-year probability expression or interpretation.
Partial credit: Correct intuition without naming memorylessness.; Uses long-run average rate correctly but does not connect models.

Common mistakes: Interpreting '500-year floodplain' as exactly one flood every 500 years.; Confusing average waiting time with certainty after that time.; Using P(T>499)=0.5 or similar unsupported claim.

questions.text: Suppose there are 10 independent floodplains, each with annual flood count modeled as Poisson(1/500). You care about the event that more than 2 of the floodplains have at least 3 floods in a given year. Explain the two-stage modeling strategy and write the final probability expression.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines single-floodplain event probability p* correctly.; Uses binomial model across 10 independent floodplains.; Writes correct upper-tail binomial sum for more than 2.
Partial credit: Understands two-stage structure but gets the threshold wrong.; Uses p* conceptually but leaves it poorly defined.
Common mistakes: Using Poisson directly for the number of floodplains.; Confusing 'in 500 years' with 'in a given year.'; Forgetting that the first stage is P(X>=3), not P(X=3).

questions.text: A botanist thinks a population of rose bushes is actually a mixture of two visually identical species. Species A occurs with probability 2/3 and has flower count approximated by N(4, 4); species B occurs with probability 1/3 and has flower count approximated by N(2, 9). Explain how to compute the probability that a randomly chosen bush has more than 3 flowers, and justify any continuity correction you use.
rubric_items: Full credit: Conditions on species correctly with weights 2/3 and 1/3.; Uses continuity correction with threshold 3.5.; Sets up both Gaussian tail probabilities correctly.; Explains why continuity correction is needed.
Partial credit: Gets mixture weighting right but omits continuity correction.; Uses correction conceptually but on only one component.
Common mistakes: Averaging means first and treating mixture as one normal.; Using 3 instead of 3.5 without justification.; Reversing species weights.

questions.text: Using the same two-species rose model, a bush is observed to have exactly 3 flowers. Explain how to compare how likely species B is relative to species A. Do not just say 'use Bayes'; describe why densities appear and how the ratio simplifies.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses posterior odds or Bayes ratio correctly.; Explains why density values are used for a point observation under continuous models.; Includes prior weights for A and B.; Explains cancellation of the small interval width/epsilon idea.
Partial credit: Invokes Bayes correctly but does not explain density-vs-probability distinction.; Sets up ratio but forgets one prior weight.
Common mistakes: Saying P(X=3)=0 for continuous variables so Bayes cannot be used.; Using CDF values instead of PDF values at the observed point.; Ignoring the prior species proportions.

questions.text: A program first samples X ~ Bernoulli(0.3). If X=0 it returns Y ~ N(-1, 2^2); if X=1 it returns Y ~ N(1, 1^2). Explain how to compute P(Y < 0), and then comment on why treating Y as a single normal with mean equal to the weighted average would be a conceptual mistake.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses law of total probability over X.; Correctly standardizes each conditional normal.; Explains why a Gaussian mixture is not generally one Gaussian.
Partial credit: Sets up conditional decomposition but with minor sign error in one z-score.; Recognizes mixture issue but explains vaguely.
Common mistakes: Averaging the two means and variances and using one normal directly.; Forgetting the Bernoulli weights 0.7 and 0.3.; Using Phi(1) instead of Phi(-1) for the second term.

questions.text: In the same Gaussian-mixture program, suppose the output value observed is y = 0.1. Explain how to compute the posterior probability that the Bernoulli variable was X=1. Your answer should distinguish clearly between probabilities and densities.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes Bayes formula with densities in numerator and denominator.; Uses correct priors 0.3 and 0.7.; Explains why densities rather than probabilities appear for continuous observations.
Partial credit: Correct Bayes structure but omits one denominator term.; States 'use PDF' without explaining why.
Common mistakes: Writing P(Y=0.1|X=1) as a nonzero probability mass.; Using CDFs instead of PDFs.; Ignoring the mixture denominator.

questions.text: Suppose a painting feature is defined as the average number of neighboring brushstrokes across all brushstrokes in a painting. Why might a normal model be appropriate for this average even if the individual neighbor counts are not normal? Explain the theorem and the assumptions you would want.
rubric_items: Full credit: Invokes the central limit theorem.; Explains that the feature is an average/sum of many terms.; Mentions some assumptions such as independence or finite variance.
Partial credit: Says 'averages are normal' without naming CLT or assumptions.; Mentions CLT but not why it applies here.
Common mistakes: Claiming every average is exactly normal.; Confusing the distribution of individual counts with the distribution of the average.; Ignoring assumptions entirely.

questions.text: An art historian has prior probability 0.75 that a painting is by Van Gogh. A measured feature value is x = 19, and under the two hypotheses the feature is modeled as N(20, 9) if Van Gogh and N(12, 25) otherwise. Explain how to update the belief using Bayes' rule, and say whether you should compare CDF values or PDF values at x = 19.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correct Bayes update with PDFs.; Includes prior 0.75 and complementary prior 0.25.; Explains why densities, not CDFs, are used for an exact observed value.
Partial credit: Gets Bayes structure right but forgets denominator expansion.; Recognizes use of likelihoods but is vague about density vs probability.
Common mistakes: Using Phi-based tail probabilities instead of densities at 19.; Ignoring the prior.; Saying the posterior equals the prior because 19 is near 20.

questions.text: A random variable X has mean 0.01 and variance 0.482, and you collect 100 independent samples and average them. State the approximate distribution of the average and explain why the variance changes by a factor of 1/100 rather than staying the same.
rubric_items: Full credit: States approximate mean 0.01 and variance 0.482/100.; Explains variance scaling under averaging.; Mentions CLT or independent-sum reasoning.
Partial credit: Correct distribution form but no explanation of variance scaling.; Uses standard deviation form correctly but not variance form.
Common mistakes: Leaving variance unchanged.; Dividing standard deviation by 100 and calling that variance.; Forgetting the average has same mean as individual draws.

questions.text: A student approximates X ~ Poi(1000) by N(1000, 1000) and then computes P(990 < X < 1000) using the bounds 990 and 1000 directly. Critique this method carefully. What parts are right, what part needs refinement, and what would the corrected setup look like?
rubric_items: Full credit: Approves the normal approximation for large lambda.; Identifies need for continuity correction.; Translates strict inequalities to corrected bounds 990.5 and 999.5.; Notes matching mean and variance.
Partial credit: Mentions continuity correction but gets one bound slightly wrong.; Gets normal approximation right but vague about discrete-to-continuous issue.
Common mistakes: Using 989.5 and 1000.5 for this strict-inequality event.; Matching variance incorrectly as standard deviation 1000.; Rejecting normal approximation altogether despite large lambda.

questions.text: Someone says, 'The standard normal is a completely different distribution from the normal distribution.' Give a careful response that includes its parameters, its CDF notation, and why standardization is useful.
rubric_items: Full credit: States Z ~ N(0,1).; Identifies standard normal as a special case, not a separate family.; Defines Phi(z) correctly.; Explains purpose of standardization.
Partial credit: Knows parameters 0 and 1 but not CDF notation or use.; Explains standardization mechanically without the conceptual purpose.
Common mistakes: Calling 1 the standard deviation when asked for variance without clarification.; Saying Phi is the PDF.; Treating standardization as changing the shape to a different family.

questions.text: A factory produces light bulbs, and the lifetime of a single bulb is modeled as a normal random variable with mean 1200 hours and standard deviation 300 hours. An engineer tests 25 bulbs independently and wants the probability that the sample mean lifetime is at least 1300 hours. Explain which random variable you would model, what its distribution is, and how you would express the probability in terms of the standard normal CDF.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the sample mean as the random variable of interest.; States that the sample mean is normal with mean 1200 and variance \(300^2/25\) or standard deviation 60.; Correctly standardizes to a Z-score and writes the answer using \(\Phi\).; Explains why the sample mean has smaller spread than an individual observation.

Partial credit: Correct setup but uses the single-observation standard deviation 300 instead of 60.; Gets the right distributional idea but leaves the probability only partially standardized.; States CLT-type reasoning without recognizing that exact normality already holds because the original distribution is normal.

Common mistakes: Treating the sample mean as \(N(1200,300^2)\).; Using \(\Phi(z)\) instead of \(1-\Phi(z)\) for an upper-tail probability.; Confusing variance and standard deviation when scaling by sample size.

questions.text: A student says: 'For any large-count discrete random variable, if I approximate it with a normal distribution, I never need a continuity correction because the normal is already continuous.' Do you agree? Use a concrete example such as approximating a binomial probability like \(P(X \le 50)\) for \(X \sim \text{Bin}(100,0.5)\), and explain what correction should be used and why.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly disagrees with the claim.; Explains the discrete-versus-continuous mismatch.; Uses a correct continuity correction such as 50.5 for \(P(X\le 50)\), or 49.5 and 50.5 for exact-point events converted to intervals.; Mentions that normal approximation is reasonable here because binomial conditions are met.

Partial credit: Knows a continuity correction is needed but gives the wrong boundary direction.; Explains the idea verbally without a concrete example.; Correctly computes mean and variance but omits why the half-unit adjustment matters.

Common mistakes: Saying continuity correction is only needed for Poisson and not binomial.; Using \(P(Y\le 50)\) directly for \(P(X\le 50)\).; Applying a correction in the wrong direction, such as 49.5 for \(P(X\le 50)\).

questions.text: You are modeling the total score from two independent measurement devices. One device’s error is \(X \sim N(2,4)\), the other’s is \(Y \sim N(-1,9)\), independently. Without doing any integration, explain the distribution of the combined error \(X+Y\), and then explain what assumption would break if the devices were strongly dependent.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the sum is normal.; Correctly gives mean 1 and variance 13.; Explains that independence justifies adding variances directly.; Identifies covariance as the missing term under dependence.

Partial credit: Correct mean and variance but weak explanation of why normality is preserved.; Mentions dependence matters but cannot state how.; Uses standard deviations instead of variances when combining spread.
Common mistakes: Adding standard deviations to get 5.; Saying the sum is only approximately normal rather than exactly normal here.; Claiming dependence changes the mean formula.

questions.text: A call center tracks the number of successful upsells per day. Historically, each of 400 calls independently leads to an upsell with probability 0.03. A manager proposes two approximations for the distribution of the daily upsell count: Poisson and Normal. Which approximation would you recommend first, which would you avoid, and how would you justify your choice using the problem parameters rather than just intuition?
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the exact distribution as binomial with \(n=400, p=0.03\).; Computes \(\lambda=np=12\) for Poisson and recognizes why Poisson is plausible.; Computes or discusses \(np(1-p)\approx 11.64\) and recognizes why normal is also plausible.; States the preference for normal when both are available, and mentions continuity correction for normal approximation to a discrete RV.

Partial credit: Correctly identifies one valid approximation with justification but does not discuss the other.; Recognizes both approximations but gives no parameter-based threshold argument.; Chooses normal but forgets continuity correction.

Common mistakes: Rejecting normal solely because \(p\) is small, without checking \(np(1-p)\).; Using Poisson with parameter \(p\) instead of \(np\).; Claiming continuity correction is unnecessary because the sample size is large.

questions.text: A data scientist builds a classifier using a mixture model. With probability 0.7, a measurement comes from \(N(-1, 2^2)\); with probability 0.3, it comes from \(N(1,1^2)\). You observe a value of 0.1. Explain aloud how to compute the posterior probability that it came from the second component, and why you must use densities rather than probabilities at the single point 0.1.
rubric_items: Full credit: Introduces a latent component variable and states the prior probabilities.; Uses Bayes' rule with densities, not point probabilities.; Writes the posterior as density times prior over total evidence.; Explains why densities are appropriate for a continuous observation at a single point.

Partial credit: Correct Bayes setup but omits one of the Gaussian density normalizing constants.; Gets the idea of weighting components by likelihood but does not justify the use of densities.; Uses informal proportionality correctly but does not normalize.
Common mistakes: Writing \(P(X=0.1\mid C=i)\) as an ordinary nonzero probability.; Ignoring the prior weights 0.7 and 0.3.; Using CDF values instead of density values for the observed point.

questions.text: A student says: 'Whenever a Binomial random variable has large n, I can approximate it by a Poisson with parameter np.' Do you agree? Give a careful response using the roles of n, p, and λ=np, and explain why Bin(100,0.5) and Bin(100,0.04) should be judged differently.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that large n alone is insufficient; Identifies the needed regime: large n, small p, moderate λ=np; Correctly distinguishes Bin(100,0.5) from Bin(100,0.04); Mentions why Normal is better for mid-range p or the limiting argument for Poisson
Partial credit: Says p must be small but gives weak justification; Correctly classifies one example but not the other; Mentions λ=np without explaining why it matters
Common mistakes: Saying Poisson is always good when n is large; Using only λ moderate and ignoring p; Claiming Bin(100,0.5) is well approximated by Poi(50)

questions.text: A quality-control machine inspects 2000 chips, and each chip independently has probability 0.0015 of being defective. You want the probability of finding exactly two defectives. Explain whether a Poisson approximation is appropriate, state the approximating distribution, and write the approximation for the probability.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes λ=np=3; Justifies Poisson by large n and small p; Writes P(X=2)=e^{-3}3^2/2!; Makes clear this approximates the Binomial probability
Partial credit: Gets λ correct but does not justify approximation; Justifies approximation but makes a minor formula slip; Writes the Binomial expression but does not transition to Poisson
Common mistakes: Using Normal instead of Poisson here without justification; Using λ=p instead of np; Forgetting the factor 2!

questions.text: Someone argues that Bin(100,0.96) cannot be approximated by a Poisson because p is not small. Is that the end of the story? Explain how to rescue a Poisson approximation if the quantity of interest is the number of failures, and describe what parameter you would use.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects direct Poisson on successes; Introduces failures with q=0.04; States failure count ~ Bin(100,0.04) ≈ Poi(4); Explains that the random variable being counted matters
Partial credit: Mentions using 1-p but does not clearly define the new random variable; Recognizes failures are rare but omits the parameter 4; States approximation without explaining why
Common mistakes: Approximating Bin(100,0.96) by Poi(96); Saying Poisson cannot be used at all; Confusing successes and failures in the event definition

questions.text: A call center receives a very large number of independent potential customer calls in an hour, each person calling with a tiny probability. Suppose the expected number of calls is 4. Using a Poisson model, derive the probability of getting at least one call, and then explain in words why subtracting from 1 is natural here.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines X~Poi(4); Uses complement correctly; Computes P(X=0)=e^{-4}; Explains why the complement is the efficient route
Partial credit: Gets 1-e^{-4} with little explanation; States the complement idea but not the zero-event formula; Minor notation issue but correct logic
Common mistakes: Summing only P(X=1); Using 1-P(X>1); Forgetting that Poisson support starts at 0

questions.text: Explain aloud why the Poisson can be viewed as a limit of the Binomial. I do not need a full proof, but I do want the key conditions, what remains fixed, and the intuition for why the Binomial mass function turns into e^{-λ} λ^k / k! for fixed k.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the limiting regime correctly; Identifies λ=np as fixed; Explains the two key limiting pieces: combinatorial term and exponential term; Gives intuition of many rare opportunities
Partial credit: States the conditions without describing the pmf transition; Mentions e^{-λ} but not how it arises; Gives intuition only
Common mistakes: Saying both n and p go to infinity; Holding p fixed instead of np; Claiming the result without any mechanism

questions.text: In a large hash table, each of n keys is sent to a bucket, almost independently, and each key has approximately the same tiny probability of landing in a given bucket. Why might a Poisson approximation still be useful for the number of keys in one bucket, even though the assumptions are not perfectly satisfied?
rubric_items: Full credit: Mentions many trials and tiny success probability; Explains mild dependence or slightly varying probabilities are acceptable; Connects the mean to approximately np; Frames the result as an approximation, not exact
Partial credit: Says Poisson still works approximately but gives little reason; Mentions rare events but not the dependence issue; Correct intuition without explicit mean parameter
Common mistakes: Claiming exact Poisson despite imperfect assumptions; Refusing Poisson because independence is not perfect; Ignoring the role of rarity

questions.text: A website averages 1000 requests in a minute, and you model the request count X by a Poisson random variable. Use a Normal approximation to estimate P(990 < X < 1000). Be explicit about the mean, variance, and continuity correction you would apply.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses N(1000,1000) as the approximation; Applies continuity correction correctly; Standardizes both bounds correctly; Gives a reasonable numerical approximation near 0.11
Partial credit: Gets the Normal mean and variance right but omits continuity correction; Uses continuity correction but makes a small standardization error; Sets up correctly without numeric finish
Common mistakes: Using variance sqrt(1000) instead of 1000; Ignoring that Poisson variance equals mean; Using bounds 990 and 1000 directly without continuity correction

questions.text: You are given Bin(100,0.04). Two students propose two approximations: one says Poisson(4), the other says Normal with mean 4 and variance 3.84. Compare the two choices and explain which the course guidance would prefer, and why.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies Poisson(4) as the preferred approximation; Explains small p and skew/small-count behavior; Mentions the Normal condition involving mid-range p or np(1-p)>10; Shows awareness that approximation choice depends on shape, not just mean
Partial credit: Chooses Poisson but with limited justification; Notes p is small but does not compare with Normal; Says both could work without explaining preference
Common mistakes: Choosing Normal just because n is large; Ignoring the skewness at small means; Using N(4,4) without considering the Binomial variance or context

questions.text: A student says, 'The Poisson distribution models the time until the next event.' Give a response that untangles the random variable being modeled, and use the earthquake example to explain the distinction between counting events and waiting time.
rubric_items: Full credit: Distinguishes count vs waiting-time random variables; Uses the earthquake example correctly; Associates Poisson with counts in intervals and Exponential with waiting time; Notes the importance of defining the random variable
Partial credit: States Poisson counts events but does not mention Exponential; Mentions the example but mixes up the variables; Correct intuition with weak terminology

Common mistakes: Saying Poisson directly models waiting time; Treating 'zero events next year' and 'time to next event exceeds one year' as different probabilities in the Poisson-process setup without explanation; Not defining the random variable

questions.text: Suppose a web server gets requests from many users. The probability any one user sends a request in a given second is tiny, but it fluctuates slightly over the day rather than being exactly constant. Defend or critique using a Poisson approximation for the number of requests in one second, and explain what feature of the approximation is robust here.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why rare-event structure still supports Poisson approximation; Notes slight variation in probabilities does not necessarily break it; Identifies mean as approximately the sum of small probabilities; States that the result is approximate and assumption-sensitive
Partial credit: Says Poisson is okay because p is small but ignores variation; Mentions robustness without explaining why; Correct idea but no explicit mean parameter
Common mistakes: Insisting identical p is absolutely required for any approximation; Claiming exact Poisson despite changing probabilities; Ignoring the 'slight fluctuation' qualifier

questions.text: A security system records the number of failed login attempts per minute, and historical data suggest an average of 0.8 failed attempts per minute. Model the count by a Poisson random variable. What is the probability of exactly three failed attempts in the next minute, and how would you interpret the result operationally?
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the Poisson model with λ=0.8; Writes the exact pmf value for k=3; Interprets the event in context; Recognizes that λ is the expected count per minute
Partial credit: Correct formula with no interpretation; Interpretation is present but formula has a minor mistake; Defines the model but omits the pmf
Common mistakes: Using λ=3 because k=3; Confusing exactly three with at least three; Forgetting the factorial

questions.text: In an oral exam, I ask you to justify why E[X]=Var(X)=λ is especially useful when moving from a Poisson model to a Normal approximation. Explain the logic and what matching 'mean and variance' means in practice.
rubric_items: Full credit: States E[X]=Var(X)=λ for Poisson; Explains that Normal approximation uses N(λ,λ); Connects mean and variance to center and spread; Mentions the discrete-to-continuous issue and continuity correction
Partial credit: Gives N(λ,λ) without much explanation; States the moment matching but omits continuity correction; Correct concept but weak practical interpretation
Common mistakes: Using N(λ,sqrt(λ)) as parameterization without clarifying variance vs standard deviation; Saying only the mean needs to match; Forgetting the Poisson variance equals its mean

questions.text: Two independent sensors each produce rare false alarms. In one hour, the first sensor's false alarm count is Poi(1.2) and the second's is Poi(0.8). Without doing a long calculation, determine the distribution of the total false alarms and explain why this result is useful in systems design.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the total is Poisson with parameter 2.0; Uses independence as the key condition; Explains usefulness in aggregating rates; Avoids unnecessary computation
Partial credit: Gets the parameter sum right but does not mention independence; Mentions adding rates but not the resulting distribution; Correct idea with weak application comment
Common mistakes: Adding standard deviations or variances instead of rates; Claiming the sum is Binomial; Forgetting independence matters

questions.text: A population study tracks a rare mutation. Out of 50,000 births, each independently has probability 0.00004 of showing the mutation. Use a Poisson approximation to estimate the probability of at least two cases, and explain your setup before simplifying.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes λ=2; Justifies the Poisson approximation; Uses the complement for at least two; Obtains 1-3e^{-2}
Partial credit: Gets λ correct but sums probabilities awkwardly; Correct complement idea with small algebra slip; States approximation without justification
Common mistakes: Using P(X=2) instead of P(X≥2); Using λ=0.00004; Forgetting to include P(X=1) in the complement

questions.text: A student writes, 'X=3' and then says 'that is a random variable.' Correct the language carefully. Then explain why this distinction matters when you say P(X=3) under a Poisson model.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that X is the random variable and X=3 is an event; Explains why P(X=3) is the probability of an event; Connects this to the Poisson pmf; Uses precise language
Partial credit: Distinguishes variable and event but not clearly; Gives a correct example but weak explanation; Understands notation but explains imprecisely
Common mistakes: Calling X=3 the random variable; Treating P(X=3) as the variable itself; Using event and random variable interchangeably

questions.text: Suppose Y~Bin(n,p) with λ=np fixed at 5. Compare the quality of a Poisson approximation in two regimes: n=50,p=0.1 and n=5000,p=0.001. Both have the same mean. Why is one typically more trustworthy than the other?
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes that equal mean does not imply equal approximation quality; Identifies n large and p small as improving factors; Prefers the n=5000,p=0.001 regime; Relates to the Poisson limit with fixed λ
Partial credit: Chooses the better regime without explaining why; Mentions p small but ignores n; Says same mean so both are equal-quality approximations
Common mistakes: Thinking matching λ alone guarantees equal closeness; Preferring n=50,p=0.1 because it is easier to compute; Ignoring the limiting argument
