questions.text: A hospital tracks rare adverse reactions to a treatment. Historically, the average is 0.2 adverse reactions per day. If you model the count per day by a Poisson random variable, how would you compute the probability of zero adverse reactions over the next 3 days, and why is the parameter 0.6 rather than 0.2 in your final expression?
rubric_items: Full credit: Scales the mean to λ=0.6 for 3 days; Defines the 3-day count random variable; Computes P(X=0)=e^{-0.6}; Explains why λ depends on interval length
Partial credit: Gets e^{-0.6} with little explanation; Correct scaling but weak modeling statement; Uses the right intuition but not formal notation

Common mistakes: Using e^{-0.2} for the 3-day interval; Multiplying probabilities of daily zero counts without recognizing this gives the same result; Confusing rate per day with total expected count over 3 days

questions.text: For a large Poisson mean λ, suppose you want K such that P(X≤K)≈0.99 for X~Poi(λ). Explain how a Normal approximation leads to an expression involving the probit function Φ^{-1}, and state the approximate formula including continuity correction.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from the Normal approximation N(λ,λ); Uses continuity correction K+0.5; Standardizes and invokes Φ^{-1}(0.99); Solves for K correctly
Partial credit: Gets the general form without continuity correction; Uses z_{0.99} correctly but not explicit probit notation; Correct idea with algebraic slip
Common mistakes: Using variance sqrt(λ) instead of λ; Using K-0.5 for a ≤ event without explanation; Forgetting to standardize by sqrt(λ)

questions.text: If I say 'Poisson approximates Binomial when λ is moderate,' what does 'moderate' mean in practice? Give a response that avoids treating the word as a strict theorem and instead explains the rule-of-thumb nature of the criterion.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that 'moderate' is a rule of thumb; Provides at least one practical threshold from context; Connects moderation to rare events and manageable expected count; Avoids portraying the criterion as exact law
Partial credit: States a threshold but treats it as absolute; Mentions λ=np without explaining moderation; Gives only vague intuition
Common mistakes: Claiming one universal exact cutoff; Ignoring n and p and discussing only λ; Saying any moderate λ guarantees a good approximation

questions.text: A manufacturing line produces 10,000 items. Defects occur independently, but the defect probability on one shift is 0.0008 and on another is 0.0012, with 5,000 items from each shift. You are asked whether a single Poisson approximation for the total number of defects is reasonable. Explain your reasoning and identify the approximate mean.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes rare-event approximation despite unequal probabilities; Computes mean 4+6=10; Optionally decomposes into two Poisson pieces and sums them; Explains why the approximation is still reasonable
Partial credit: Gets mean 10 but gives weak justification; Mentions unequal probabilities but is unsure about approximation; Correct intuition without decomposition
Common mistakes: Rejecting Poisson solely because p is not identical across all items; Using a Binomial with one common p without comment; Adding probabilities incorrectly instead of expected counts

questions.text: A student sees Bin(100,0.04) and says, 'Since both the Poisson and the Binomial have mean 4, they must also have the same variance, so the approximation is exact enough.' Respond carefully. What is right in this statement, and what is misleading?
rubric_items: Full credit: Confirms same mean 4; Computes or states Binomial variance 3.84 and Poisson variance 4; Explains why the approximation may still be good; Distinguishes approximation quality from exact equality
Partial credit: States variances differ but does not compute them; Explains means match but not why that is insufficient; Correct idea with weak nuance
Common mistakes: Claiming exact equality because means match; Forgetting the Binomial variance factor 1-p; Saying variance mismatch alone makes the approximation unusable

questions.text: A reliability engineer models the number of component failures in a month by X~Poi(12). Without summing many terms, explain how you would approximate P(X>20) and defend whether you would stay with Poisson calculations or switch to a Normal approximation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes Normal approximation as practical here; Uses N(12,12); Applies continuity correction with 20.5; Explains the tradeoff between exact Poisson and convenient approximation
Partial credit: Chooses the Normal route but omits continuity correction; Prefers exact Poisson but explains setup inadequately; Correct standardization idea with arithmetic slip
Common mistakes: Using N(12,sqrt(12)) without clarifying parameters; Using threshold 21.5 instead of 20.5 for X>20 without justification; Saying Poisson approximation to Poisson is needed

questions.text: A student says: 'Poisson is a good approximation to any Binomial distribution as long as n is large.' Evaluate that claim using the three examples Bin(100, 0.5), Bin(100, 0.04), and Bin(100, 0.96). For each one, explain whether a Poisson approximation is appropriate, and if not, what adjustment or alternative approximation you would suggest.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly rejects the claim that large n alone is sufficient.; States the key conditions: n large, p small, lambda = np moderate.; Correctly identifies Bin(100, 0.04) as suitable for Poisson with lambda = 4.; Explains that Bin(100, 0.5) is not suitable for Poisson and is better handled by a normal approximation.; Explains that Bin(100, 0.96) is not directly Poisson-approximable but that the number of failures can be approximated by Poi(4).

Partial credit: Correctly classifies at least two of the three examples.; Mentions p small as important, but gives incomplete justification.; Recognizes the complement idea for p = 0.96 without fully articulating the transformed variable.

Common mistakes: Saying Bin(100, 0.5) is fine for Poisson because n is large.; Approximating Bin(100, 0.96) by Poi(96) without discussing why that is inappropriate.; Ignoring the role of p and focusing only on lambda.

questions.text: A website receives a very large number of independent opportunities for a request to fail during one minute. Each opportunity fails with a tiny probability p, so the total number of failures in a minute is modeled as approximately Poisson with mean 4. Give an approximate expression for the probability of at most 2 failures in a minute, then explain how you would approximate the probability of between 990 and 1000 events when X ~ Poi(1000), including any correction you would use and why.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly writes the Poisson cumulative expression for P(Y <= 2) with lambda = 4.; States that a large-lambda Poisson is approximated by a normal with mean lambda and variance lambda.; Correctly identifies N(1000, 1000) as the approximating normal.; Uses an appropriate continuity correction for the discrete-to-continuous approximation.; Correctly standardizes the interval in terms of a standard normal.

Partial credit: Gets the Poisson setup right but not the normal approximation details.; Identifies the normal approximation but omits continuity correction.; Uses the right mean and standard deviation conceptually but makes minor endpoint errors.

Common mistakes: Using variance 1 instead of 1000 for the approximating normal.; Forgetting the continuity correction.; Replacing P(990 < X < 1000) by P(990 < Y < 1000) with no translation to integer values.

questions.text: A systems engineer is analyzing a large hash table and wants to model the number of entries in a particular bucket. She says, 'The bucket count is not exactly Binomial because the placements are only almost independent, so Poisson is invalid.' Based on the lecture guidance, explain whether you agree. Your answer should discuss what assumptions are being mildly violated and why the approximation may still be useful.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes that Poisson need not be exact to be useful.; Explains the two mild violations mentioned in the notes: slight dependence and slight variation in success probabilities.; Connects the approximation back to the usual regime of tiny probabilities and moderate expected count.; Frames the conclusion as 'approximately valid under mild violations,' not 'always valid.'

Partial credit: States that Poisson may still work under slight dependence but does not mention varying probabilities.; Says approximation is okay when p is small, without discussing the violated assumptions.; Gives the right conclusion with weak justification.
Common mistakes: Claiming any dependence immediately invalidates Poisson approximation.; Claiming Poisson remains exact under dependence.; Ignoring the need for small probabilities and moderate mean.

questions.text: A classmate argues: 'If requests arrive according to independent Poisson counts from two services, with means 2 and 3 per second, then the total is approximately Binomial because we are combining two random variables.' Diagnose the mistake and replace it with the correct statement. Then compute the probability of exactly 4 total requests in one second.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly identifies the claim 'sum is Binomial' as incorrect.; States the correct closure property: independent Poissons add to a Poisson with summed rates.; Correctly gives the resulting distribution as Poi(5).; Correctly computes or sets up P(total = 4) = e^{-5} 5^4 / 4!.

Partial credit: Gets the right final distribution but gives a vague explanation.; Understands the means add but cannot justify why the family stays Poisson.; Sets up the probability correctly but does not explicitly diagnose the Binomial misconception.

Common mistakes: Multiplying means instead of adding them.; Calling the total approximately normal or binomial without justification.; Using P(X = 4) + P(Y = 4) instead of the distribution of the sum.

questions.text: Derive, in words rather than a fully formal proof, why Bin(n, p) approaches a Poisson distribution when n becomes large and p becomes small with np = lambda fixed. I want you to explain what happens separately to the combinatorial term, the factor p^k, and the factor (1-p)^(n-k), and to state what this says about when the approximation is appropriate in practice.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rewrites p as lambda/n and starts from the Binomial pmf.; Explains the approximation of the combinatorial factor for fixed k.; Explains how the p^k term combines with the combinatorial factor to give lambda^k / k!.; Explains why the remaining factor tends to e^{-lambda}.; Connects the limit argument to practical approximation conditions.

Partial credit: States the limiting pmf correctly but gives only partial reasoning.; Explains the e^{-lambda} term correctly but not the combinatorial term.; Knows the practical rule of thumb but cannot connect it to the limiting argument.

Common mistakes: Treating k as growing with n in the limit explanation without qualification.; Saying only 'because np = lambda' with no decomposition of the pmf.; Confusing the Poisson approximation conditions with those for normal approximation.

questions.text: A student says: "Axiom 3 is just a special case that almost never matters, because in real problems events usually overlap." Do you agree? Explain by giving one reason Axiom 3 is foundational even when events are not mutually exclusive, and show how it leads to a useful formula for general unions.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that arbitrary events can be partitioned into mutually exclusive components.; Derives or clearly motivates inclusion-exclusion from Axiom 3.; States why the axiom is analytically useful beyond the mutually exclusive case.
Partial credit: States inclusion-exclusion correctly but does not explain the disjoint decomposition.; Says Axiom 3 is important for unions but gives only a vague justification.
Common mistakes: Claiming P(E ∪ F) = P(E) + P(F) for all events.; Confusing mutually exclusive with independent.; Subtracting P(E ∩ F) without explaining double counting.

questions.text: In a course platform, event A is "student watched the lecture" and event B is "student attempted the quiz." Suppose P(A) = 0.7, P(B) = 0.6, and P(A ∪ B) = 0.9. Without assuming independence, compute P(A ∩ B), then explain whether the data are consistent with A and B being mutually exclusive.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly applies inclusion-exclusion to obtain 0.4.; Explains why mutually exclusive would require zero intersection.; Interprets the result in context.
Partial credit: Gets the intersection correct but gives only a minimal explanation.; Recognizes they are not mutually exclusive but makes a small arithmetic slip.
Common mistakes: Computing P(A ∩ B) as P(A)P(B) without independence.; Saying they are mutually exclusive because A ∪ B is less than 1.; Forgetting to subtract the union rather than the intersection.

questions.text: A classmate argues: "If P(E) = 0.4, then the probability of not E must also be 0.4, because one just mirrors the other." Respond to this claim using the axioms. Then explain what additional axiom or corollary you are implicitly using.
rubric_items: Full credit: States P(E^c) = 1 - P(E).; Explains that E and E^c partition the sample space.; References Axiom 2 and Axiom 3 or the complement corollary.
Partial credit: Gives 0.6 correctly but does not justify from axioms.; Mentions complement rule but not why it is valid.

Common mistakes: Saying complement probabilities are equal unless P(E)=0.5.; Using symmetry language with no relation to the actual sample space.; Treating E and E^c as independent rather than disjoint and exhaustive.

questions.text: A device has three mutually exclusive operating modes on startup: safe mode, normal mode, and recovery mode. You are told P(safe) = 0.1 and P(normal) = 0.85. Use the axioms to determine P(recovery), and explain what hidden assumption makes this deduction possible.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes 0.05 correctly.; Explains both mutual exclusivity and that the modes partition the sample space.; Connects the sum-to-one conclusion to the axioms.
Partial credit: Gets 0.05 with weak explanation.; Mentions probabilities sum to 1 but does not articulate exhaustiveness.
Common mistakes: Subtracting from something other than 1.; Assuming mutual exclusivity alone implies completeness.; Allowing overlap among operating modes.

questions.text: Explain why the statement "if E is a subset of F, then P(E) ≤ P(F)" should be true from the axioms rather than accepted as obvious. Your explanation should explicitly use a disjoint decomposition.
rubric_items: Full credit: Decomposes F into E and F \ E.; Uses mutual exclusivity and Axiom 3 to add probabilities.; Invokes nonnegativity to conclude P(E) ≤ P(F).
Partial credit: States the result correctly with an intuitive explanation but no formal decomposition.; Uses a Venn diagram argument without connecting to axioms.
Common mistakes: Claiming strict inequality must always hold.; Using independence language.; Forgetting that F \ E might have probability 0.

questions.text: Suppose P(A) = 0.55 and P(B) = 0.65. A student claims that P(A ∩ B) could be as small as 0.05 because intersections can always be tiny. Is that possible? Give the sharpest lower bound you can justify from the axioms and explain the reasoning aloud.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses P(A ∪ B) ≤ 1 together with inclusion-exclusion.; Derives the lower bound 0.20.; Explains that 0.05 is impossible.
Partial credit: States the bound correctly but does not justify sharpness.; Recognizes 0.05 is impossible but gives an incomplete argument.
Common mistakes: Using P(A)P(B) as the minimum intersection.; Thinking intersections can be arbitrarily small regardless of marginals.; Forgetting the union cannot exceed 1.

questions.text: You roll a fair six-sided die once. Let E be the event "the outcome is even" and F be the event "the outcome is at least 4." Compute P(E), P(F), P(E ∩ F), and P(E ∪ F) using equally likely outcomes, and explain where Axiom 3 does and does not apply directly.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly enumerates the sample space and relevant events.; Computes all four probabilities correctly.; Explains that direct addition fails because E and F are not mutually exclusive.
Partial credit: Gets most probabilities right but gives a thin explanation.; Correctly computes union by counting outcomes even if the axiom discussion is partial.
Common mistakes: Adding 1/2 + 1/2 to get 1 for the union.; Forgetting 4 and 6 are in both events.; Treating equally likely outcomes as optional rather than the basis for the count.

questions.text: A student says: "Mutually exclusive events are a kind of strong independence, because they do not affect each other." Critique this statement carefully. Include the special case where both events have positive probability.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes mutually exclusive from independent.; Uses the equations P(E ∩ F)=0 and P(E)P(F).; Notes the probability-0 exception.
Partial credit: States they are different but gives only an intuitive explanation.; Mentions that disjoint positive-probability events cannot be independent without formal support.

Common mistakes: Saying mutually exclusive implies independent.; Thinking 'not affecting each other' is the definition of independence without checking the product rule.; Ignoring the probability-0 edge case.

questions.text: Imagine a randomized function returns True in one of two ways: either event M happens and then event B happens, or M does not happen and then event G happens. Explain why those two ways are mutually exclusive, and write an expression for the total probability that the function returns True. You may assume M happens with probability 0.3, B given M has probability 0.5, and G given not M has probability 0.76.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the two path events correctly.; Explains mutual exclusivity via M versus M^c.; Writes the total probability expression using chain rule factors.
Partial credit: Gets the expression mostly right but does not justify exclusivity.; Recognizes a case split but omits conditional notation.
Common mistakes: Adding P(B|M) and P(G|M^c) directly.; Multiplying all terms together as if all must happen.; Failing to distinguish M from M^c.

questions.text: Suppose a probability assignment on a sample space S claims P(S) = 0.9, while still keeping all event probabilities between 0 and 1 and using additivity for disjoint events. Explain why this is not considered a valid probability model under the standard axioms. Then say what kinds of derived rules would immediately break.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the violation of Axiom 2.; Explains at least one corollary that fails, such as the complement rule.; Shows understanding of normalization over the whole sample space.
Partial credit: Says it is invalid because the total should be 1 but gives little further discussion.; Mentions normalization without tying it to a specific axiom.

Common mistakes: Arguing that any total less than 1 is fine if all other probabilities look reasonable.; Thinking Axiom 2 is just a convention rather than a defining property.; Confusing sample space with an event of probability less than 1.

questions.text: A museum tracks visitors by hour. Let p_i be the probability that a randomly selected visitor arrives i hours after midnight, for i = 0 through 23. How would you express the probability that a visitor arrives before noon, and why is it legitimate to add those hourly probabilities directly?
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the sum over i=0 to 11.; Explains the hourly events are mutually exclusive.; Notes that the hours form a partition of the day.
Partial credit: Writes the correct sum but gives only minimal justification.; Explains exclusivity but not the partition idea.

Common mistakes: Summing to 12 instead of 11 when 'before noon' excludes noon to 1 pm.; Treating hourly bins as overlapping.; Normalizing by dividing by the sum of all p_i even though it already equals 1.

questions.text: In a fair coin experiment with two flips, define E as "at least one head" and F as "exactly one head." Use the equally likely outcomes idea to compute P(E), P(F), and P(E \ F). Then explain why P(E) = P(F) + P(E \ F) is an instance of Axiom 3.
rubric_items: Full credit: Enumerates the four equally likely outcomes.; Computes the three probabilities correctly.; Explains the disjoint decomposition E = F ∪ (E \ F).
Partial credit: Gets values right but gives little explanation of the set difference.; Explains Axiom 3 correctly but makes a minor counting slip.
Common mistakes: Counting (H,T) and (T,H) as the same outcome.; Confusing 'at least one head' with 'exactly one head'.; Forgetting that E \ F excludes the exactly-one-head outcomes.

questions.text: A student claims that for any events A and B, if P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B), then A and B must be independent. Is that right? Give a careful counterargument and say what condition the equation actually implies.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses inclusion-exclusion to deduce zero intersection.; Identifies the correct implication: mutual exclusivity.; Explains why this differs from independence.
Partial credit: Says the claim is false and mentions mutual exclusivity but does not justify well.; Provides a correct verbal distinction without the formula.
Common mistakes: Equating 'just add' with independence.; Forgetting that independence concerns intersections, not unions directly.; Missing the positive-probability caveat.

questions.text: Why does the formula P(E) = |E| / |S| require more than just knowing the sample space is finite? Give an example of a finite sample space where this formula would fail if used blindly, and state the missing assumption.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the missing assumption of equally likely outcomes.; Gives a concrete finite counterexample such as a biased coin.; Explains why counting alone fails there.
Partial credit: Mentions equal likelihood but gives no example.; Gives an example but does not articulate the assumption clearly.

Common mistakes: Believing all finite sample spaces are automatically uniform.; Confusing 'possible' with 'equally probable'.; Using a continuous example when the question is about finite sample spaces.

questions.text: Suppose events A, B, and C are pairwise mutually exclusive. Explain how the probability of 'exactly one of them occurs' simplifies, and contrast that with the case where they are not mutually exclusive. Then, if P(A)=0.2, P(B)=0.15, and P(C)=0.05, compute the probability in the mutually exclusive case.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why exactly one equals the union in the mutually exclusive case.; Uses repeated additivity to compute 0.4.; Contrasts with the overlapping case conceptually.
Partial credit: Computes 0.4 but gives little contrast with the non-exclusive case.; Correctly states repeated addition without explaining 'exactly one'.

Common mistakes: Thinking pairwise mutually exclusive is irrelevant.; Using inclusion-exclusion terms when all intersections are zero.; Confusing 'at least one' and 'exactly one' without noticing they coincide here.

questions.text: In a quality-control pipeline, let D be the event a part is defective. The engineer has verified P(D)=0.02. Without any other information, what can you say about the probability a part is not defective, and what can you not say about the probability it passes a second independent inspection? Explain the difference in what is and is not justified from the axioms alone.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes P(D^c)=0.98.; Explains this comes from complement structure.; Clearly says why no further product-type probability follows without more assumptions.
Partial credit: Gets the complement right but only vaguely addresses the second part.; Recognizes that more information is needed without naming independence or conditioning.

Common mistakes: Assuming a second inspection pass probability equals 0.98 automatically.; Multiplying probabilities without defining the relevant event.; Treating complements and independent repeat events as the same idea.

questions.text: Give an oral proof that probabilities cannot be negative using the axioms and corollaries already available. Your argument should not simply quote Axiom 1; instead, explain how nonnegativity is used in proving other facts such as monotonicity or inclusion-exclusion bounds.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes nonnegativity is an axiom, not something proved from the others in this setup.; Explains how it is used to prove at least one corollary or inequality.; Shows structural understanding rather than merely quoting formulas.
Partial credit: States that it is an axiom but gives limited discussion of consequences.; Mentions monotonicity or bounds without a clear proof sketch.
Common mistakes: Claiming nonnegativity can be derived from P(S)=1 alone.; Failing to distinguish axioms from corollaries.; Using undefined notions instead of event decompositions.

questions.text: A friend says: "Since P(A ∩ B) is always less than or equal to both P(A) and P(B), it follows that P(A ∩ B) must equal the smaller of the two." Diagnose the mistake and give conditions under which equality does hold.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the confusion between inequality and equality.; Uses subset reasoning for the upper bound.; States a correct condition for equality, such as one event contained in the other.
Partial credit: Says the claim is false and gives an example but no general condition.; States the equality condition but weakly explains the upper bound.
Common mistakes: Claiming equality holds whenever events overlap.; Using independence as the equality condition.; Ignoring that the intersection can be much smaller than both.

questions.text: You are told that a random visitor to a website either arrives from search, from social media, or from a direct link, and these categories are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. Later, an analyst reports P(search or social) = 0.8 and P(search) = 0.5. What is P(direct), and what additional step would let you recover P(social)? Explain carefully.
rubric_items: Full credit: Finds P(direct)=0.2.; Uses mutual exclusivity to find P(social)=0.3.; Explains both the complement and disjoint-addition steps.
Partial credit: Gets one of the two probabilities right with incomplete reasoning.; Understands the partition but forgets to invoke exclusivity for search and social.
Common mistakes: Subtracting 0.5 from 1 to get direct.; Using inclusion-exclusion with an unnecessary overlap term.; Not using the exhaustive-category information.

questions.text: On a two-child family problem, let E be the event 'both children are girls' and F be the event 'at least one child is a girl born on Tuesday.' Without doing all arithmetic, explain how inclusion-exclusion appears in the setup of P(F), and why a naive answer of 1/2 for P(E|F) ignores the new sample space.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the two subevents used to build F.; Explains why they overlap and inclusion-exclusion is required.; Explains that conditioning changes the effective sample space.
Partial credit: Recognizes conditioning matters but does not clearly describe the overlap.; Mentions Tuesday information changes the answer without explaining why.
Common mistakes: Saying the answer must be 1/2 because one child is known to be a girl.; Treating the two child-specific Tuesday events as disjoint.; Ignoring the role of conditional probability.

questions.text: The lecture notes say that 'the challenge of probability is in defining events.' Give an example where the same real-world question can be represented by two different event decompositions, one of which makes Axiom 3 easy to use and the other of which obscures the solution. Explain your choice.
rubric_items: Full credit: Provides a concrete example with two different decompositions.; Shows which decomposition yields disjoint events and why that helps.; Connects the idea explicitly to Axiom 3.
Partial credit: Gives an example but only one decomposition.; States that event definition matters without a clear illustration.
Common mistakes: Giving only abstract statements with no example.; Claiming all decompositions are equally easy.; Not distinguishing disjoint and overlapping cases.

questions.text: For a fair six-sided die, let A be 'roll is 1 or 2 or 3 or 4' and B be 'roll is 3 or 4 or 5.' Compute P(A), P(B), P(A ∩ B), and verify both inequalities P(A ∩ B) ≤ P(A ∪ B) ≤ P(A)+P(B). Then state when each inequality would become equality in general.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes all four probabilities correctly.; Checks both inequalities numerically.; States correct equality conditions in general.
Partial credit: Gets the event probabilities right but only vaguely addresses equality cases.; Verifies inequalities with a minor arithmetic slip.
Common mistakes: Confusing intersection with union.; Forgetting that 3 and 4 belong to both A and B.; Claiming P(A∩B)=P(A∪B) whenever the events overlap at all.

questions.text: A student says: “If two events cannot happen together, they are basically independent, because knowing one happened tells you the other probably did not.” Evaluate that claim carefully using the axioms. In your answer, compare the formulas for mutually exclusive events and independent events, and explain whether both properties can hold at once.
rubric_items: Full credit: States mutually exclusive implies P(A ∩ B) = 0.; States independence implies P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).; Shows both can hold only if P(A)=0 or P(B)=0.; Explains verbally why mutual exclusivity usually creates dependence rather than independence.

Partial credit: Correctly says the claim is false but gives only an intuitive explanation.; Writes one of the two formulas correctly but does not connect them.; Mentions the degenerate zero-probability exception without fully justifying it.
Common mistakes: Saying mutually exclusive events are independent because they ‘do not overlap’.; Using P(A ∪ B) = P(A)P(B).; Forgetting that independence concerns intersections, not unions.

questions.text: In a class of equally likely final grades, suppose the sample space is the 10 letter outcomes {A+, A, A-, B+, B, B-, C+, C, C-, D}. Let E be the event “grade is at least B” and F be the event “grade is plus or minus, not a plain letter.” Compute P(E), P(F), and P(E ∪ F), but do it in two different ways: first by counting equally likely outcomes, and then by using inclusion-exclusion. I care at least as much about the setup as the final number.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses equally likely outcomes rule P(E)=|E|/|S|.; Correctly identifies E, F, and E ∩ F.; Computes P(E ∪ F) both by direct counting and by inclusion-exclusion.; Notes that the two methods agree.

Partial credit: Gets the right final probability for the union but with incomplete event descriptions.; Correctly counts E and F but makes a minor slip in the intersection.; Uses only one method correctly.
Common mistakes: Adding P(E)+P(F) without subtracting the overlap.; Treating ‘plus or minus’ as mutually exclusive from ‘at least B’.; Counting plain A or plain B inside F.

questions.text: Without quoting it as a memorized fact, derive the monotonicity property: if E ⊆ F, then P(E) ≤ P(F). Your derivation should start from the axioms and the idea of decomposing F into disjoint pieces. Then explain why this result is not obvious from Axiom 1 alone.
rubric_items: Full credit: Represents F as E ∪ (F \ E).; States these pieces are mutually exclusive.; Uses Axiom 3 to write P(F)=P(E)+P(F\E).; Uses nonnegativity to conclude P(E)≤P(F).; Explains why Axiom 1 by itself is insufficient.

Partial credit: States monotonicity correctly and gives the right intuition but not the full derivation.; Mentions disjoint decomposition but omits explicit use of Axiom 1 or Axiom 3.; Gives a Venn-diagram explanation without a formal algebraic argument.

Common mistakes: Arguing only that ‘bigger sets should have bigger probabilities’ without justification.; Using inclusion-exclusion unnecessarily and incorrectly.; Forgetting to note that F \ E has nonnegative probability.

questions.text: A startup classifies daily server incidents into three categories: hardware failure H, software bug S, and human error U. On a given day, exactly one of these three root causes can occur, or there may be no incident at all. You are told P(H)=0.08, P(S)=0.11, and P(U)=0.05. A teammate concludes that the probability of no incident is 1 - 0.08 - 0.11 - 0.05 = 0.76, and then says this same subtraction would still work even if incidents could have multiple causes at once. Assess both parts of that statement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly uses mutual exclusivity to sum H, S, and U.; Uses the complement rule to get probability of no incident.; Separately evaluates the second statement and says it is false in the non-mutually-exclusive case.; Explains that overlap causes double-counting and motivates inclusion-exclusion.

Partial credit: Gets 0.76 correctly but does not fully explain why the same subtraction can fail.; Recognizes the need for inclusion-exclusion but gives only a vague explanation.; Discusses complement correctly but omits mutual exclusivity.

Common mistakes: Assuming any list of event probabilities can always be added.; Confusing ‘exactly one can occur’ with independence.; Forgetting that complement applies to the union of all incident types.

questions.text: A lecturer picks one of two quiz formats at random: format A with probability 0.4 and format B with probability 0.6. Under format A, the probability a student answers a target question correctly is 0.9; under format B it is 0.5. Let C be the event the student answers correctly. Compute P(C) using a partition of the sample space, and then explain why the two cases can be added directly even though ‘correct under A’ and ‘correct under B’ sound like different events about correctness.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies A and B as a mutually exclusive, exhaustive partition.; Writes C as (C ∩ A) ∪ (C ∩ B).; Uses P(C ∩ A)=P(C|A)P(A) and similarly for B.; Computes P(C)=0.66.; Explains why the addition works through disjoint partitioning, not because of independence.

Partial credit: Gets the numeric answer but does not justify the decomposition.; Uses the weighted-average structure correctly but cannot explain why the terms can be summed.; Recognizes law of total probability without connecting it back to disjoint events.

Common mistakes: Adding 0.9 and 0.5 directly.; Multiplying 0.9 and 0.5 as if both formats occur together.; Saying the two correctness events are mutually exclusive without mentioning the conditioning events A and B.

questions.text: A student says, "An event is just one outcome, so in two coin flips the event 'at least one head' is not really an event because it contains several outcomes." Do you agree? Explain by identifying the sample space for two fair flips and then describing how events relate to that sample space.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the sample space correctly as {HH, HT, TH, TT} or equivalent.; Explains that an event is any subset of the sample space.; Correctly identifies 'at least one head' as {HH, HT, TH}.
Partial credit: Gives the right sample space but only vaguely explains what an event is.; Says 'at least one head' has multiple outcomes but does not explicitly connect this to subsets.
Common mistakes: Saying an event must be a single outcome.; Leaving out HT or TH from 'at least one head'.; Confusing sample space with event.

questions.text: For two fair coin flips, compare the events A = 'two heads' and B = 'at least one head'. Compute P(A), P(B), and P(A|B), and explain in words why the conditional probability differs from the unconditional one.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes P(A)=1/4, P(B)=3/4, and P(A|B)=1/3.; Uses or explains the reduced sample space under conditioning.; Notes that A is a subset of B.
Partial credit: Gets the three probabilities right but gives little interpretation.; Uses enumeration correctly but does not articulate why conditioning changes the probability.
Common mistakes: Saying P(A|B)=1/4 because the coin is fair.; Using denominator 4 instead of 3 after conditioning on B.; Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A).

questions.text: Someone argues: "The events 'first flip is heads' and 'at least one head' are independent because knowing the first flip is heads does not change whether at least one head happened." Evaluate this claim carefully using the formal definition of independence.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the events correctly.; Checks independence via P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) or equivalently P(B|A)=P(B).; Concludes correctly that the events are not independent and explains why.
Partial credit: States they are not independent with correct intuition but incomplete calculation.; Calculates one or two probabilities correctly but does not finish the formal test.
Common mistakes: Arguing independence from a verbal intuition without checking the definition.; Confusing logical implication with independence.; Using disjointness as if it implied independence.

questions.text: A medical screening test returns positive. Let D be the event that a patient has a disease and T+ the event of a positive test. Without plugging in numbers, explain how Bayes' rule combines prior information and the test's accuracy to produce P(D|T+). Then describe one reason why a positive test does not automatically mean the patient probably has the disease.
rubric_items: Full credit: States Bayes' rule in correct form or equivalent verbal decomposition.; Explains prior, likelihood, and posterior roles.; Mentions the denominator as all ways to get a positive result.; Identifies low base rate / false positives as a key reason a positive test need not imply high disease probability.
Partial credit: States Bayes' rule but gives only partial interpretation.; Mentions priors matter but does not explain the denominator.
Common mistakes: Treating P(D|T+) as the same as P(T+|D).; Ignoring the prior prevalence.; Saying posterior depends only on test accuracy.

questions.text: Explain why the axioms of probability force P(A^c) = 1 - P(A). Your explanation should rely on the ideas of sample space, mutually exclusive events, and total probability 1, rather than just quoting a formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies A and A^c as disjoint and exhaustive.; Uses P(S)=1.; Derives P(A^c)=1-P(A) from additivity.
Partial credit: States the formula correctly with limited justification.; Mentions complement but not the role of disjoint union or total probability.
Common mistakes: Saying complements are independent by default.; Failing to note that A and A^c cover the sample space.; Using unsupported algebra without the axioms.

questions.text: In two fair coin flips, let A be 'exactly one head' and B be 'the second flip is heads.' Compute P(A), P(B), P(A∩B), and decide whether A and B are independent. Explain your conclusion aloud rather than just naming it.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies A, B, and A∩B correctly.; Computes probabilities correctly.; Uses the formal criterion for independence and interprets it.
Partial credit: Gets most probabilities right but does not clearly conclude independence.; Gives correct conclusion with incomplete explanation.
Common mistakes: Listing A∩B as {HT}.; Thinking shared outcomes automatically mean dependence.; Confusing independence with disjointness.

questions.text: A classmate says, "If two events cannot happen together, they are independent because they do not affect one another." Assess this statement in general, and then test it on the two-flip coin experiment using A = 'two heads' and B = 'two tails.'
rubric_items: Full credit: States the general principle that disjointness does not imply independence.; Explains the exception when one event has probability 0.; Verifies with the concrete coin-flip example numerically.
Partial credit: Correctly rejects the statement for the example but does not give the general reasoning.; Explains disjointness versus independence but omits the zero-probability exception.
Common mistakes: Saying disjoint events are always independent.; Confusing 'cannot occur together' with 'no influence.'; Failing to compare 0 with P(A)P(B).

questions.text: Suppose a spam filter labels an email as spam. Let S be 'email is actually spam' and F be 'filter flags spam.' Explain how you would compute P(S|F) using Bayes' rule, and then argue qualitatively how that posterior changes if the inbox suddenly receives far fewer spam emails while the filter's true-positive and false-positive rates stay unchanged.
rubric_items: Full credit: States Bayes' rule with a correct denominator decomposition.; Explains the role of prevalence as the prior.; Correctly predicts that the posterior decreases when spam becomes rarer, all else equal.
Partial credit: States Bayes' rule but does not expand P(F).; Gives the right qualitative conclusion with weak justification.
Common mistakes: Confusing P(F|S) with P(S|F).; Ignoring the effect of the base rate.; Claiming unchanged filter accuracy implies unchanged posterior.

questions.text: Let X be the number of heads in two fair coin flips, and let Y be the indicator that the first flip is heads, so Y=1 if the first flip is heads and 0 otherwise. Are X and Y independent? Answer by comparing at least one joint probability with the product of the corresponding marginals, and explain the dependence in words.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines X and Y correctly from the experiment.; Computes a valid counterexample showing P(X=x,Y=y) ≠ P(X=x)P(Y=y).; Explains dependence conceptually.
Partial credit: Concludes dependence correctly with a weaker or less explicit calculation.; Computes marginals correctly but uses incomplete reasoning.
Common mistakes: Saying X and Y are independent because the coin flips themselves are independent.; Confusing random variables with the underlying flips.; Not computing joint probability correctly.

questions.text: In the two-coin-flip experiment, a student reasons: "There are three outcomes with at least one head, so P(at least one head)=1/3." Diagnose the mistake and give a correct method for finding the probability.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the specific counting mistake.; Uses the full sample space of four equally likely outcomes.; Gives the correct probability 3/4 and explains either direct counting or complement.
Partial credit: Gets 3/4 correctly but only says 'because there are 3 outcomes' without emphasizing denominator 4.; Recognizes the mistake vaguely but does not articulate the correct principle.
Common mistakes: Using number of favorable outcomes as denominator.; Ignoring the equally likely assumption.; Mixing up 'at least one' with 'exactly one'.

questions.text: A teacher says, "Bayes' rule is just algebra, so it does not really say anything conceptual." Respond to that claim. Your answer should connect Bayes' rule to updating beliefs from prior to posterior after observing evidence.
rubric_items: Full credit: Acknowledges the algebraic basis.; Explains prior, likelihood, posterior, and normalization conceptually.; Emphasizes that the rule formalizes updating beliefs with evidence.
Partial credit: Says Bayes updates beliefs but gives little detail.; Mentions prior and posterior without explaining the role of evidence or normalization.
Common mistakes: Calling Bayes' rule merely a formula with no interpretation.; Confusing the posterior with the likelihood.; Omitting the role of the denominator.

questions.text: For two fair coin flips, explain the difference between the statements 'exactly one head' and 'at least one head' in terms of events. Then discuss why students often confuse them and how you would distinguish them systematically from the sample space.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly lists both events.; Explains the inclusion of HH in 'at least one' and its exclusion from 'exactly one'.; Describes a systematic sample-space method to avoid confusion.
Partial credit: Gets the event sets right but gives little discussion of the distinction.; Explains verbally but does not enumerate the outcomes.
Common mistakes: Treating the two events as the same.; Including TT in one of the events.; Failing to distinguish 'exactly' from 'at least'.

questions.text: In two fair coin flips, let A be 'the two flips match' and B be 'at least one head.' Compute P(A), P(B), and P(A|B). Then decide whether A and B are independent and justify your answer both numerically and intuitively.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies A, B, and A∩B correctly.; Computes P(A)=1/2, P(B)=3/4, P(A|B)=1/3.; Concludes non-independence using a valid criterion and gives intuition.
Partial credit: Gets the main probabilities right but does not explicitly connect them to independence.; Concludes they are not independent with only one type of justification.
Common mistakes: Forgetting TT is in A.; Using P(A∩B)=1/2.; Saying conditioning should not matter because flips are fair.

questions.text: A student claims: "If P(A|B) is bigger than P(A), then B causes A." Give a careful response from the perspective of probability basics. Your answer should explain what the inequality really tells us and what it does not justify.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that the inequality indicates association or information, not causation.; Connects it to lack of independence when P(B)>0.; Explains that causal interpretation needs more than conditional probability.
Partial credit: Rejects causal conclusion but provides only general caution.; Mentions dependence but not the distinction from causation.

Common mistakes: Equating increased conditional probability with causation.; Ignoring the requirement P(B)>0 for conditional probability.; Saying probability statements can never inform us, which is too strong.

questions.text: Suppose A is an event with P(A)=0.7 and B is a subset of A. Without choosing specific outcomes, explain what must be true about P(B) relative to P(A), and justify your answer using the axioms or basic properties of events.
rubric_items: Full credit: States P(B) ≤ P(A).; Justifies via disjoint decomposition A = B ∪ (A\B) and nonnegativity.; Connects to a basic property derived from the axioms.
Partial credit: States the inequality correctly with intuitive but incomplete reasoning.; Mentions subsets should not be more likely but lacks formal justification.
Common mistakes: Saying subset events can have larger probability because they are more specific.; Using unsupported intuition only.; Confusing subset with complement.

questions.text: For two fair coin flips, compute the probability of 'at most one head' in two different ways: first by listing outcomes directly, and second using a complement argument. Then explain why both methods must agree.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies the event and computes 3/4 by direct counting.; Computes 3/4 again via complement.; Explains why the two methods are equivalent.
Partial credit: Gets the answer right by one method only.; Uses both methods but does not explain why agreement is guaranteed.
Common mistakes: Confusing 'at most one' with 'exactly one'.; Omitting TT from the direct-counting method.; Using complement of the wrong event.

questions.text: You are told that in a certain population, an observed symptom E is common even among healthy people. Explain, using Bayes' rule in words, why seeing E may provide only weak evidence for a disease D even if most diseased people show the symptom.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains the distinction between P(E|D) and P(D|E).; Identifies disease prevalence and nonspecific symptoms as key factors.; Uses Bayes' rule conceptually to argue why evidence can be weak.
Partial credit: States that common symptoms are weaker evidence but gives limited Bayesian explanation.; Mentions one of prevalence or false positives but not both.
Common mistakes: Equating 'most diseased have the symptom' with 'most with the symptom are diseased'.; Ignoring the denominator or alternative causes of E.; Treating the symptom as decisive evidence.

questions.text: Describe a strategy for computing a probability from a worded problem before doing any arithmetic. Your strategy should mention the sample space, event identification, and whether conditioning is present, and then illustrate it briefly on the phrase 'probability of at least one head in two fair flips given that the first flip is tails.'
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives a clear general strategy involving sample space, event translation, and conditioning.; Correctly applies it to the example.; Obtains P(A|B)=1/2 and explains the restricted sample space.
Partial credit: Provides a reasonable strategy but applies it incompletely.; Gets the example right but does not extract a general method.

Common mistakes: Computing the unconditional 3/4 instead of the conditional 1/2.; Forgetting to restrict the sample space under conditioning.; Skipping event definitions and relying on intuition only.

questions.text: In two fair coin flips, let A be 'exactly one head' and B be 'at least one head.' Compute P(A|B) and P(B|A), and explain why one of these conditional probabilities equals 1 while the other does not.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies A and B correctly.; Computes P(A|B)=2/3 and P(B|A)=1.; Explains asymmetry through subset relation A⊆B.
Partial credit: Gets both numbers right but gives weak explanation.; Recognizes one direction is 1 but mishandles the other slightly.
Common mistakes: Confusing P(A|B) and P(B|A).; Saying both are 1 because the events are related.; Forgetting HH when conditioning on B.

questions.text: A student says, "Because each flip is independent, any two events built from the two flips must also be independent." Challenge this claim by giving a concrete counterexample from the two-flip experiment and explaining where the reasoning breaks down.
rubric_items: Full credit: Provides a valid counterexample from two fair flips.; Shows non-independence with a correct calculation or conditional probability.; Explains why independence of trials does not automatically transfer to arbitrary derived events.
Partial credit: Gives a plausible counterexample but weak verification.; States the principle correctly with limited example detail.
Common mistakes: Assuming event independence follows automatically from trial independence.; Using an example that actually is independent.; Explaining only verbally without any check.

questions.text: Imagine you are explaining probability to someone who keeps asking, "What are we taking probability of?" Using the language of sample space and events, answer that question in a way that would help them correctly interpret both 'two heads' and 'at least one head' in the two-flip coin experiment.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that probability is assigned to events, which are subsets of the sample space.; Gives the correct sample space and event sets for both phrases.; Explains why this viewpoint helps interpretation.
Partial credit: Gives correct examples but only a minimal explanation of events.; Defines sample space correctly but is vague about events as subsets.
Common mistakes: Saying probability is taken only of outcomes, not events.; Misstating one of the event sets.; Leaving out the sample-space perspective.

questions.text: A student says: "If two events cannot happen at the same time, then they must be independent." Do you agree? Answer by comparing the axioms of probability for disjoint events with the definition of independence, and give a concrete example using a simple sample space.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that disjointness and independence are different concepts; Uses the equations P(A∩B)=0 for disjoint events and P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B) for independence; Explains the special case that disjoint events can only be independent if one has probability 0; Gives or analyzes a correct example
Partial credit: Says the claim is false but gives only an informal explanation; Provides an example without connecting it to the formal definitions; Mentions the probability-0 exception vaguely

Common mistakes: Saying disjoint events are automatically independent; Confusing 'cannot occur together' with 'one does not affect the probability of the other'; Forgetting the probability-0 exception

questions.text: A fair coin is flipped twice. Let A be the event "the first flip is heads" and B be the event "at least one head occurs." Compute P(A), P(B), and P(A|B), and then decide whether A and B are independent. Explain your conclusion in words, not just with arithmetic.
rubric_items: Full credit: Lists or uses the correct sample space for two fair flips; Computes P(A)=1/2 and P(B)=3/4 correctly; Uses conditional probability correctly to get P(A|B)=2/3; Concludes non-independence and explains why conditioning changes the probability

Partial credit: Gets most probabilities right but makes a minor arithmetic slip; Correctly concludes non-independence using P(A∩B)≠P(A)P(B) without computing P(A|B) fully; Uses verbal reasoning that is mostly sound but incomplete
Common mistakes: Treating A and B as independent because they both involve heads; Computing P(B) as 1/2 instead of 3/4; Forgetting that A is contained in B, so A∩B=A

questions.text: A medical screening test is used in a population where 1% of people have a disease. The test is positive 95% of the time when the disease is present, and it is falsely positive 10% of the time when the disease is absent. A person tests positive. Using Bayes' rule, explain how to compute the probability the person actually has the disease, and interpret the result for someone who confuses it with 95%.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines relevant events and identifies prior, likelihood, and false-positive rate; Applies Bayes' rule with the correct denominator using total probability; Obtains a posterior of about 8.8%; Explains the base-rate effect and why 95% is the wrong interpretation

Partial credit: Sets up Bayes' rule correctly but makes a minor arithmetic mistake; Computes the numerator correctly but is incomplete on the denominator; Gives a qualitatively correct interpretation of why the posterior is much smaller than 95%
Common mistakes: Answering 95% by confusing P(+|D) with P(D|+); Ignoring false positives in the denominator; Using 10% as P(D|+) directly

questions.text: For two discrete random variables X and Y, a classmate claims: "If knowing Y does not change the probability of one event about X, then X and Y are independent." Is that enough? Explain what must be true for independence, and describe how you would check it in principle without relying on a specific numerical table.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that one matching conditional probability is not sufficient; Gives the correct all-values condition for independence of discrete random variables; Mentions either factorization of the joint distribution or equality of conditional and marginal probabilities for every value; Explains why a single case can be misleading

Partial credit: Knows the formal definition but does not explicitly address why one case is insufficient; Explains the need to check multiple values but not clearly 'all' relevant values; Uses event-based language that is mostly correct

Common mistakes: Saying one successful check proves independence; Defining independence only for one pair of events rather than the whole variables; Confusing zero correlation or a single unchanged probability with independence

questions.text: A fair coin is flipped twice. Without listing only the final numbers, compare the events A='two heads' and B='at least one head.' Compute P(A), P(B), and P(A|B), then explain why the conditional probability makes sense from the reduced sample space.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the correct four-outcome sample space; Computes P(A)=1/4 and P(B)=3/4 correctly; Computes P(A|B)=1/3 either by ratio or reduced sample space; Explains the interpretation of conditioning on B

Partial credit: Gets the unconditional probabilities right but struggles to explain the conditional sample space; Finds P(A|B) correctly with limited verbal interpretation; Minor arithmetic or notation slips with otherwise correct reasoning
Common mistakes: Answering P(A|B)=1/4 by ignoring the condition; Using only two outcomes after conditioning instead of three; Confusing 'at least one head' with 'exactly one head'

questions.text: A student says: “If X and Y are discrete random variables, independence just means P(X=2 and Y=5)=P(X=2)P(Y=5).” Do you agree? Explain carefully what the full definition requires, and why checking only one pair of values is not enough.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the universal quantifier: the equality must hold for all x,y.; Distinguishes a single event from independence of random variables.; Explains why one matching product does not imply full independence.
Partial credit: Gives the correct formula but forgets to say it must hold for all values.; Says 'not enough' without explaining why.
Common mistakes: Treating independence as something that can be checked from one pair of values.; Confusing X and Y with events rather than random variables.

questions.text: Suppose X is the number of heads in 3 fair coin flips. A classmate says “X=2 is a random variable.” Explain what is wrong with that sentence, and then state what X is, what the event X=2 is, and what probability would be attached to that event.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes random variable from event.; Identifies the event X=2 as a set of outcomes.; States or derives P(X=2)=3/8.
Partial credit: Knows X=2 is an event but does not describe the sample-space set.; Gets the event right but not the probability.
Common mistakes: Saying X=2 is a random variable value rather than an event.; Confusing the probability P(X=2) with the event X=2 itself.

questions.text: You generate 10 independent values from Uniform(0,1). Let I be the indicator that the first generated value is less than 0.3, and let N be the number of the remaining 9 values that are less than 0.3. First identify the distributions of I and N. Then say whether I and N are independent, and justify your answer from the sampling process.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies I as Bernoulli(0.3).; Correctly identifies N as Binomial(9,0.3).; Justifies independence using independent underlying draws, not just 'they look unrelated.'
Partial credit: Gets the distributions right but gives weak justification for independence.; States independence without connecting it to disjoint independent samples.
Common mistakes: Calling N geometric.; Thinking I and N cannot be independent because both refer to the same threshold 0.3.; Forgetting that uniform probabilities come from interval length.

questions.text: A server makes 8 independent requests to a backup service. Each request succeeds with probability 0.9. Let X be the total number of successes. Give the distribution of X, then express the probability that the first failure occurs on request 4. Finally, explain why these are modeled by different random variables even though they come from the same underlying Bernoulli trials.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies X~Bin(8,0.9).; Correctly gives probability of first failure on request 4 as 0.9^3*0.1.; Explains count-vs-waiting-time distinction.
Partial credit: Gets the formula but not the interpretation.; Correct intuition but uses incorrect RV name for the waiting-time event.
Common mistakes: Using Binomial for the first-failure timing event without conditioning on order.; Writing 0.1^3*0.9.; Forgetting that geometric counts trial number until first success/failure.

questions.text: Two students debate the statement: “If Cov(X,Y)=0, then X and Y must be independent.” Give a response that addresses both directions: when independence does imply something about covariance, and why the converse fails in general. If you can, give or describe a concrete counterexample.
rubric_items: Full credit: States independence implies zero covariance.; States converse is false in general.; Provides a valid counterexample or explains nonlinear dependence.
Partial credit: Gets the true/false status right but lacks explanation.; Mentions dependence can be nonlinear without a concrete example.
Common mistakes: Claiming zero covariance is equivalent to independence.; Using correlation 0 as if it proved independence.

questions.text: A museum stores a prior belief that a newly found painting is by Artist V with probability 0.7. If it is by V, a measured feature X is Normal with mean 20 and variance 9; otherwise X is Normal with mean 12 and variance 25. You observe X=19. Without doing all the arithmetic, explain how to set up the posterior probability that the painting is by V, and say qualitatively whether the posterior should be above or below 0.7.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes Bayes rule using densities, not point probabilities for a continuous RV.; Uses the correct priors 0.7 and 0.3.; Correctly argues posterior should increase above 0.7.
Partial credit: Has the right Bayes structure but uses probability notation loosely for X=19.; Qualitative direction correct but no justification from likelihoods.
Common mistakes: Using P(X=19|V) for a continuous variable without clarifying density.; Ignoring the prior.; Assuming the posterior must equal whichever mean is closer without Bayes structure.

questions.text: Let X be Uniform(a,b). A student claims that P(X is between the midpoint and b) depends on the length b−a. Is that right? Explain using the pdf or geometry of the interval, and then give the probability.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses constant density or interval-length argument.; Shows dependence cancels out.; States probability is 1/2.
Partial credit: Correct answer 1/2 with weak justification.; Mentions symmetry but does not connect to uniform density.
Common mistakes: Thinking a wider interval changes the fraction.; Using discrete reasoning for a continuous interval.

questions.text: Consider random variables X1, X2, ..., Xn. Someone says, “They are iid because each Xi is exponential.” Give at least two distinct reasons why that statement may fail, and contrast iid with merely independent or merely identically distributed.
rubric_items: Full credit: States iid means both independent and identically distributed.; Gives a non-identical-parameter example.; Gives a dependent example such as Xi all equal.
Partial credit: Defines iid correctly but gives only one failure mode.; Explains independent vs identical but not both.
Common mistakes: Saying same family of distributions automatically means identical.; Forgetting dependence can occur even when each marginal is exponential.

questions.text: A parent says, “I have two children, and at least one is a daughter born on Tuesday.” Many people immediately answer that the probability both children are daughters is 1/2. Explain why conditioning changes the sample space, and outline a correct method for finding the conditional probability.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that the conditioning event changes the sample space.; Sets up P(B|T)=P(B∩T)/P(T).; Mentions inclusion-exclusion or an equivalent careful counting argument.; Recognizes the result is not 1/2.
Partial credit: Knows it is not 1/2 and invokes Bayes/conditional probability, but explanation is incomplete.; Describes the sample-space change informally without a formal setup.
Common mistakes: Treating 'at least one daughter born on Tuesday' as equivalent to 'one specified child is a daughter.'; Answering 1/2 by symmetry without conditioning correctly.

questions.text: You repeatedly flip a biased coin with P(H)=0.2 until the first head appears. Let T be the trial number of the first head. Write the pmf of T and then explain in words why the support starts at 1 rather than 0.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives the correct geometric pmf.; States support is {1,2,...}.; Explains why 0 is impossible.
Partial credit: Correct formula but vague about support.; Knows support starts at 1 but does not explain.
Common mistakes: Using k starting at 0.; Using p^(k-1)(1-p) instead of (1-p)^(k-1)p.

questions.text: Why is a normal model often reasonable for an average of many small contributions, even if the individual contributions are not normal? Give a concrete explanation rather than just naming a theorem, and state any assumptions you need.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains averaging/summing many contributions leads to approximate normality.; Mentions assumptions such as independence and finite variance.; Connects to a real aggregate measurement rather than pure theorem citation.
Partial credit: Names CLT correctly but gives little intuition.; Mentions sums become normal without assumptions.
Common mistakes: Claiming each individual variable must be normal.; Ignoring the role of aggregation.

questions.text: Let N be a nonnegative integer-valued random variable, independent of iid random variables X1, X2, ... each with mean μ. Define S = X1 + X2 + ... + XN. Before doing algebra, say what you think E[S] should be, and then justify it using conditional expectation.
rubric_items: Full credit: States E[S]=μE[N].; Uses E[S]=E[E[S|N]].; Explains why E[S|N=n]=nμ and notes the independence role.
Partial credit: Gets μE[N] with heuristic explanation only.; Uses summation reasoning but omits the conditioning step.
Common mistakes: Assuming S has mean E[N]+μ.; Forgetting that random upper limits require conditioning carefully.

questions.text: A random variable X takes values 1,2,3,... with pmf p(x). What is one quick validity check you should always perform on a proposed pmf, and why does that check matter before doing any further calculations with X?
rubric_items: Full credit: States nonnegativity and total probability 1.; Explains why validity matters before computing other quantities.
Partial credit: Mentions only that probabilities sum to 1.; Gives the check but no explanation.
Common mistakes: Only checking that each probability is less than 1.; Forgetting nonnegativity.

questions.text: A registrar models the counts of freshmen, sophomores, juniors, and seniors in a class of 600 chosen uniformly from 7000 students without replacement. A student calls this multinomial. Do you agree? Explain what feature of the sampling design breaks the multinomial assumption, and what the correct style of joint probability expression looks like.
rubric_items: Full credit: States it is not multinomial.; Explains dependence caused by sampling without replacement.; Identifies the correct structure as multivariate hypergeometric / combination ratio.
Partial credit: Knows without replacement breaks independence but cannot name the distribution family.; Says 'not multinomial' without explaining why.
Common mistakes: Calling every count-across-categories problem multinomial.; Saying large population size makes it exactly multinomial rather than approximately.

questions.text: A function returns the sum of 1000 independent Uniform(0,1) samples. Without computing a final numerical probability, explain how you would approximate P(sum > 501), including the mean and variance you would use and why a normal approximation is appropriate.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the sum of iid uniforms.; Uses mean 500 and variance 1000/12.; Explains CLT justification and standardization step.
Partial credit: Gets CLT idea but misses mean or variance.; States normal approximation without parameter derivation.
Common mistakes: Using variance of one uniform as 1/2.; Forgetting variances add for independent sums.; Using exact uniform support endpoints as if S were uniform.

questions.text: Why are random variables often more useful than event-only descriptions when analyzing repeated experiments? Give an answer that compares what each framework makes easy or hard.
rubric_items: Full credit: Contrasts binary events with numeric random variables.; Explains how RVs unify many related events.; Mentions useful summaries like mean/variance or easier algebra.
Partial credit: Says RVs are 'more general' without concretely comparing frameworks.; Gives an example but no conceptual comparison.
Common mistakes: Saying events and random variables are the same thing.; Focusing only on notation, not analytic advantages.

questions.text: Suppose X and Y are independent Binomial random variables with X~Bin(10,0.5) and Y~Bin(10,0.5). Without deriving the full pmf from scratch, explain why X+Y has a simple named distribution, and state it. Then say which assumption is essential for that conclusion.
rubric_items: Full credit: States X+Y~Bin(20,0.5).; Explains the interpretation as 20 Bernoulli trials.; Identifies equal p and independence as essential.
Partial credit: Gets the result but weak explanation.; Mentions only independence but not equal p.
Common mistakes: Adding variances or means and assuming that alone proves the distribution.; Claiming any two binomials add to a binomial regardless of parameters.

questions.text: You observe 30 successes and 20 failures for an unknown success probability p, and someone models p itself as a Beta random variable. They want to report an estimate in the form m ± b, where m is the expectation of p and b is the smallest half-width giving at least 95% posterior probability. Explain how you would describe m and how you would find b in words or pseudocode, even if you do not know closed forms for the interval endpoints.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains m as posterior mean of the Beta.; Describes numerical search or inverse-CDF style method for the smallest b with central mass at least 95%.; Recognizes this is about posterior uncertainty in p, not sample proportion alone.
Partial credit: Knows mean formula idea but not how to find b.; Describes a 95% interval without emphasizing smallest symmetric half-width around m.

Common mistakes: Using a normal approximation without justification as the only method.; Confusing the random variable p with future counts.; Reporting m=30/50 without explaining the Beta posterior context.

questions.text: For multiple random variables X1, X2, ..., Xn, what does mutual independence require? Explain why pairwise independence alone is a weaker statement, and say how the definition differs in the discrete and continuous cases.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the all-variables factorization definition.; Distinguishes pairwise from mutual independence.; Notes discrete uses probabilities / pmf, continuous uses density or CDF.
Partial credit: Gives pairwise definition only.; States 'all combinations' vaguely without formulas.
Common mistakes: Assuming pairwise independence implies mutual independence.; Using pmf notation for continuous variables without qualification.

questions.text: Let Z be exponential with rate 1/8267, representing the lifetime of one C14 molecule in years. In a sample of 100 independent molecules, define M as the number that have decayed by time t. Derive the distribution of M in terms of t and explain each step from the single-molecule model to the 100-molecule model.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes single-molecule decay probability as 1-exp(-t/8267).; Defines Bernoulli success clearly.; Uses independence to conclude M is Binomial(100,p(t)).
Partial credit: Gets Binomial structure but not the exact p(t).; Computes p(t) correctly but does not connect to Binomial reasoning.
Common mistakes: Using p(t)=exp(-t/8267) for 'decayed' instead of 'survived'.; Forgetting independence across molecules.; Using Poisson without justification.

questions.text: Someone says, “If two random variables each have marginal distribution N(0,1), then their correlation must be 1 because they look the same.” Respond to this claim, and separate the ideas of sharing the same marginal distribution, being perfectly correlated, and being independent.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the claim clearly.; Distinguishes marginals from joint dependence structure.; Explains what correlation 1 actually means.
Partial credit: Says the claim is false but explanation is vague.; Mentions independence and correlation are different without defining either.
Common mistakes: Thinking identical marginals determine the joint relationship.; Confusing same distribution with perfect dependence.

questions.text: A phone lifetime model has density f(x|a)=(1/a^2) x^{a-1} e^{-x^2/a^2} for observed lifetimes x1,...,xN assumed independent. Explain how maximum likelihood estimation would choose a, and why people usually maximize the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood directly. You do not need to solve for a numerically, but you should describe the derivative step.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines likelihood as product over independent observations.; Explains why log-likelihood is used and why maximizer is unchanged.; Describes differentiate-set-to-zero procedure and identifies main terms.
Partial credit: Understands MLE qualitatively but omits the derivative step.; Mentions log-likelihood for convenience only, without monotonicity argument.
Common mistakes: Adding densities instead of multiplying.; Thinking MLE matches sample mean by default.; Forgetting independence in the likelihood product.

questions.text: A student says: “If two discrete random variables X and Y are independent, then once I know X=x, that itself is an event, so X and Y stop being random variables and independence no longer matters.” Respond to this claim carefully. In your answer, distinguish random variables from events, state the correct definition of independence for discrete random variables, and explain what independence implies about P(Y=y | X=x).
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes random variables from events such as X=x.; States the discrete independence condition P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x)P(Y=y) for all x,y.; Derives or explains that P(Y=y | X=x)=P(Y=y) when P(X=x)>0.; Addresses the misconception that conditioning on an event makes variables 'stop being random'.

Partial credit: Gives the correct independence definition but does not explain the event-vs-variable distinction.; Explains event-vs-variable distinction but gives only an informal definition of independence.; States conditional equality without showing how it follows from independence.
Common mistakes: Saying 'X is an event' instead of 'X=x is an event'.; Claiming independence means P(X=x | Y=y)=P(X=x,Y=y).; Forgetting the condition P(X=x)>0 when writing conditional probabilities.

questions.text: Ten i.i.d. random values are sampled from Uniform(0,1), and let M be their maximum. Without doing heavy integration, derive the CDF of M and then use it to compute P(M < 0.8). Explain exactly where independence enters your argument.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines M as the maximum and recognizes M<m iff all Xi<m.; Uses independence to factor the joint probability into a product.; Uses the Uniform(0,1) CDF P(Xi<m)=m on [0,1].; Gives the piecewise CDF and computes P(M<0.8)=0.8^10.; Comments on the role of independence.

Partial credit: Gets P(M<0.8)=0.8^10 with limited explanation.; Correct reasoning on [0,1] but omits piecewise behavior outside the support.; Uses <= instead of < without discussing that it makes no difference for a continuous distribution.
Common mistakes: Using 10·0.8 instead of 0.8^10.; Confusing the maximum with the number of samples below 0.8.; Failing to mention that independence justifies the product.

questions.text: A classmate claims: “If Cov(X,Y)=0, then X and Y must be independent, because zero covariance means no relationship.” Give a careful response. Your answer should say what implication is true, which converse fails, and provide a concrete counterexample using a random variable X and a transformed variable Y.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the true implication independence => covariance 0.; Explicitly says the converse covariance 0 => independence is false.; Provides a valid counterexample such as X~N(0,1), Y=X^2.; Explains why the variables are dependent and why covariance is nevertheless zero.

Partial credit: Correctly says the converse is false but gives only an informal counterexample.; Gives a counterexample idea but does not justify why covariance is zero.; States only that covariance measures linear relationship without tying it to the formal claim.

Common mistakes: Claiming normality alone makes zero covariance imply independence without specifying a jointly normal setting.; Using Y=3X as a counterexample for zero covariance.; Saying 'uncorrelated means independent' with no qualification.

questions.text: A call center receives a random number N of customers in an hour, and conditional on N=n, the waiting times X1,...,Xn of those customers are i.i.d. with mean 4 minutes. Assume N is independent of the sequence X1,X2,.... Let T=Σ_{i=1}^N Xi be the total waiting time accumulated in that hour. What is E[T], and explain your reasoning in a way that makes clear why the independence assumption matters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Introduces conditioning on N or an equivalent argument.; States E[T|N=n]=4n and therefore E[T]=4E[N].; Explains that independence of N from the Xi ensures the conditional mean of each Xi remains 4.; Mentions what could go wrong without independence.

Partial credit: Gets 4E[N] but with minimal explanation.; Uses linearity of expectation correctly but does not discuss conditioning or independence.; Explains the idea informally without clear notation.
Common mistakes: Treating N as a constant instead of a random variable.; Writing E[T]=E[N]+E[X].; Assuming independence is unnecessary without explaining why E[Xi|N]=4 still holds.

questions.text: You repeatedly flip a biased coin with probability p of heads until the first heads appears. Let G be the trial on which the first heads occurs. A student models G as Binomial because 'we are counting successes.' Explain why that model is wrong, identify the correct random variable, and derive P(G>7) in words and notation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why Binomial is inappropriate: fixed number of trials versus waiting time to first success.; Identifies G as Geometric(p).; Interprets G>7 as seven consecutive failures before the first success.; Derives P(G>7)=(1-p)^7 using independence.

Partial credit: Names the Geometric distribution correctly but does not clearly contrast it with Binomial.; Gets the right probability with limited explanation.; Explains the event verbally but omits notation.

Common mistakes: Using Binomial with n=7 and saying P(G>7)=P(X=0) without connecting it to the waiting-time variable.; Using support starting at 0 without clarifying the convention.; Writing P(G>7)=1-p^7.

questions.text: You are given a sample of 200 commute times from a much larger population of commuters. Explain, in words, how the bootstrap replaces the unknown population distribution with something you can actually compute from, and why that replacement is plausible at all. Then state one key assumption under which this logic is defensible.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains empirical/sample distribution as estimate of unknown population distribution; Connects repeated resampling to approximating the sampling distribution of a statistic; States and justifies iid as a key assumption
Partial credit: Mentions resampling from the sample but not why that approximates the population; States iid without explaining its role; Describes histogram/PMF vaguely
