Common mistakes: Saying bootstrap samples from the true population; Confusing the sample distribution with the sampling distribution; Omitting the iid assumption

questions.text: A student says: 'When bootstrapping a sample of size n, we should resample without replacement, because that better preserves the original data.' Do you agree? Give a careful argument using what distribution the bootstrap is trying to simulate.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that bootstrap resamples with replacement; Explains empirical PMF interpretation; Explains why without replacement understates variability or nearly reproduces the original sample
Partial credit: Says 'with replacement' is correct but gives only a procedural reason; Mentions variability but not independence or empirical PMF

Common mistakes: Arguing that preserving the original sample exactly is the goal; Confusing bootstrap with train/test splitting or permutation testing; Saying replacement is only to allow larger samples than n

questions.text: You have one iid sample of 80 observations and you care about the sample mean. Describe the bootstrap algorithm step by step, but for each step explain what probabilistic object is being approximated. Do not just list code-like instructions.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives the three steps in correct order; Interprets empirical distribution, bootstrap samples, and bootstrap statistic distribution probabilistically; Mentions size of resamples equals original sample size
Partial credit: Gives algorithm steps without interpretation; Explains some objects correctly but confuses sample distribution vs sampling distribution

Common mistakes: Saying each resample is drawn from a fitted normal by default; Using sample size different from n without justification; Calling the histogram of bootstrap means the empirical distribution of the raw data

questions.text: A team has a single sample of daily website revenue that contains a few extremely large days due to viral events. They want to bootstrap the sample mean. Based on the lecture caveat, explain why you might worry about the result even if the data are iid, and what aspect of the underlying distribution causes the concern.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies long/heavy tails as the issue; Explains that empirical distribution may poorly capture extreme tail behavior; Connects this to unreliable bootstrap approximation for the mean
Partial credit: Mentions outliers or extremes but not the tail assumption explicitly; Says bootstrap may be 'less accurate' without explaining why

Common mistakes: Claiming iid is sufficient in all cases; Saying bootstrap fails only because mean is a bad statistic, with no mention of tail behavior; Treating one or two outliers as automatically violating iid

questions.text: Suppose your original sample is [1, 1, 4, 10]. Without doing exhaustive arithmetic, describe the empirical PMF that the bootstrap uses, and give two different bootstrap resamples of size 4 that are possible. Then explain why one of those resamples may contain repeated values not repeated in the original positions.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correct empirical PMF from observed frequencies; Provides valid bootstrap resamples of size 4; Explains repetition via with-replacement iid draws from empirical PMF
Partial credit: Gets the idea of frequencies right but muddles one probability; Provides one valid resample but weak explanation of repetition

Common mistakes: Assigning equal probability to all distinct values rather than frequency-weighted values; Thinking 10 cannot appear twice because it appeared once originally; Confusing value repetition with index repetition

questions.text: Why does bootstrapping help especially when there is no convenient closed-form distribution for a statistic, such as the sample variance? Answer by comparing what you would like to know mathematically with what the bootstrap constructs computationally.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the target as the sampling distribution of the statistic; Explains that closed forms may be unavailable or inconvenient; Explains simulation via many resamples and recalculated statistic
Partial credit: Says bootstrap is useful when math is hard but does not name the sampling distribution; Mentions sample variance example without explaining the computational substitution
Common mistakes: Saying bootstrap gives the exact distribution; Confusing population variance with sampling distribution of sample variance; Claiming bootstrap only works for the mean

questions.text: A classmate says: 'The bootstrap distribution of the sample mean is just the histogram of the original sample values, because both come from the sample.' Explain precisely why this is false. Your explanation should distinguish three different distributions that students often blur together.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly distinguishes empirical distribution of data, bootstrap distribution of statistic, and true sampling distribution; Explains that the bootstrap distribution is over recalculated means, not raw values; Connects bootstrap distribution to an approximation target
Partial credit: Separates raw data from means but omits the true sampling distribution; Uses correct intuition but vague terminology
Common mistakes: Saying both are the same because they use the same data; Ignoring the role of the statistic; Calling the sample histogram the sampling distribution

questions.text: A pollster cannot survey an entire population and asks, 'What can we safely infer from a sample, and how do we express confidence in those conclusions?' Use this prompt to explain how sampling and bootstrapping answer two different parts of that question.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains sampling as producing estimators for population quantities; Explains bootstrap as quantifying uncertainty in those estimators; Links bootstrap output to confidence/variability/probability statements
Partial credit: Discusses only estimation or only uncertainty; Gives a generic statement about confidence without saying how bootstrap provides it
Common mistakes: Treating bootstrap as a way to collect more real data; Saying sampling alone gives confidence without variability assumptions; Equating a point estimate with a confidence statement

questions.text: You run 10,000 bootstrap resamples of an iid sample and compute the sample variance each time. The resulting bootstrap distribution is quite spread out. Give two different interpretations of that spread, one correct and one incorrect, and explain why the incorrect one is a misunderstanding.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly interprets spread as sampling variability of the statistic; Identifies and refutes the mistaken idea that the parameter itself varies; Uses sample variance example specifically
Partial credit: States that wider spread means 'more uncertainty' but does not clarify what is uncertain; Identifies incorrect interpretation but weakly explains why
Common mistakes: Confusing parameter variability with estimator variability; Calling the bootstrap distribution the distribution of the raw data; Saying wide spread proves the bootstrap failed

questions.text: An analyst has two independent datasets from two user interfaces and wants a p-value for whether the interfaces differ in a chosen statistic. The lecture notes mention creating a 'universal sample' by combining the two samples to recreate the null hypothesis. Explain the logic of that bootstrap-style testing strategy and why pooling is connected to the null.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains pooling as empirical implementation of the null hypothesis of a common distribution; Describes resampling two groups and computing a difference statistic; Explains p-value as comparison of observed statistic to null resampled distribution
Partial credit: Mentions pooling and p-value but not why pooling reflects the null; Describes permutation-like logic vaguely

Common mistakes: Pooling under the alternative rather than the null; Using separate-group bootstraps to generate the null distribution without modification; Defining p-value as probability the null is true

questions.text: In one sentence, a lecture says bootstrapping works for any statistic, with caveats. I now ask you to unpack that sentence carefully. What is powerful about the 'any statistic' claim, and what are the main limitations that stop it from being literally universal?
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains flexibility across many statistics; Names iid and long-tail caveats; Frames limitations as failures of approximation rather than arbitrary exceptions
Partial credit: Mentions flexibility and one caveat only; Says 'works for any statistic' without discussing why
Common mistakes: Claiming bootstrap requires only large sample size and nothing else; Interpreting 'any statistic' as 'any dataset and any sampling design'; Omitting the caveats entirely

questions.text: Someone says, 'If my bootstrap resamples are all the same size as the original sample, then every bootstrap sample should contain every original observation exactly once, just shuffled.' Diagnose the error and relate your correction to the phrase 'generated with replacement.'
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies confusion with permutation/shuffling; Explains repeated or omitted observations in a bootstrap sample; Defines with replacement correctly
Partial credit: Says duplicates are allowed but gives weak reasoning; Corrects the claim without distinguishing permutation from bootstrap
Common mistakes: Saying sample size n forces each point to appear once; Believing with replacement only matters if resample size exceeds n; Using 'replacement' to mean replacing missing values

questions.text: You sample 1,000 iid observations from a NegBin(10, 0.5) population and compute the sample mean and the usual 'divide by n' sample variance. Without calculating exact numbers, compare the roles of the Central Limit Theorem and the bootstrap if your goal is to understand uncertainty in those two statistics.
rubric_items: Full credit: Contrasts CLT for mean with bootstrap for variance; Mentions approximate normality of sample mean under CLT; Notes divide-by-n variance is biased low and separates bias from variability
Partial credit: Mentions CLT for mean and bootstrap for variance but ignores bias issue; Discusses only one of the two statistics

Common mistakes: Using CLT as if it directly gives the exact distribution of sample variance; Claiming bootstrap automatically corrects the divide-by-n bias; Confusing estimator bias with spread of its sampling distribution

questions.text: You use code like np.random.choice(sample, n, replace=True) inside a bootstrap routine. Explain what random variable that code is effectively sampling from, and why the probabilities are not necessarily uniform over the distinct observed values.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies empirical distribution as the sampled-from random variable; Explains frequency weighting of duplicated values; Distinguishes uniform over positions from nonuniform over distinct values
Partial credit: Says it samples from the sample with replacement but not how probabilities are induced; Mentions duplicates vaguely
Common mistakes: Assuming all distinct values have equal probability; Calling the code a draw from a fitted parametric model; Ignoring repeated observations in the original sample

questions.text: A researcher says, 'I only have one sample, so it makes no sense to talk about the distribution of my sample mean.' Give a response that uses the repeated-sampling idea and then explain how the bootstrap approximates that thought experiment from the one sample actually observed.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains sampling distribution as distribution over hypothetical repeated samples; Clarifies that one observed value of the mean does not eliminate underlying randomness; Explains bootstrap as computational approximation from empirical distribution
Partial credit: Mentions repeated sampling but weakly connects it to bootstrap; Explains bootstrap without defining sampling distribution

Common mistakes: Saying the mean is not random once observed, therefore no distribution exists; Treating bootstrap draws as new real-world data rather than pseudo-samples; Confusing posterior uncertainty with sampling uncertainty

questions.text: Imagine you are comparing rejection sampling from a known joint distribution with bootstrap resampling from an observed dataset. Both involve generating many samples on a computer. Explain the fundamental difference in what source distribution you are sampling from in each case.
rubric_items: Full credit: Contrasts known/model joint distribution with empirical distribution from observed data; Notes both are simulation methods but with different sources; Uses correct terminology about unknown population in bootstrap
Partial credit: Says one uses a model and one uses data, but not clearly; Brings up rejection steps without addressing source distribution
Common mistakes: Claiming bootstrap requires a known joint distribution; Equating rejection sampling and bootstrap because both 'sample a ton'; Ignoring the role of the empirical distribution

questions.text: A student argues: 'Because the sample is only an approximation to the population, bootstrap can never tell us anything about uncertainty.' Give the best rebuttal you can, but also acknowledge the valid caution hidden inside the statement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defends bootstrap as an uncertainty-estimation tool; Explains why it can work under representativeness/iid; Acknowledges legitimate limitations and failure modes
Partial credit: Defends bootstrap but gives no caveats; Lists caveats but does not explain why bootstrap is still useful
Common mistakes: Saying approximation means uselessness; Saying bootstrap is always reliable if sample size is large; Treating assumptions as minor technicalities with no practical impact

questions.text: Suppose you bootstrap the sample mean from a dataset of size n and obtain 10,000 bootstrap means. How would you use those 10,000 numbers to answer the oral question, 'What is the estimated probability that a fresh sample mean exceeds the observed sample mean by at least 2 units?' Explain the approximation carefully.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses fraction of bootstrap means beyond threshold as probability estimate; Defines threshold relative to observed mean; States approximation is with respect to empirical/bootstrap distribution
Partial credit: Says to count exceedances but not what threshold is being compared; Forgets to mention this is an estimate under the bootstrap approximation

Common mistakes: Comparing raw data values instead of bootstrap means; Calling the resulting fraction the exact population probability; Using the original sample histogram rather than the bootstrap statistic distribution

questions.text: Why is the empirical distribution often described as 'just a histogram of your data,' and what important mathematical simplification does that phrase hide when the data are discrete?
rubric_items: Full credit: Connects histogram to empirical PMF for discrete data; States probability as relative frequency; Explains why this matters for computation/resampling
Partial credit: Mentions histogram and relative frequencies loosely; Understands it is an estimate of the distribution but not how it becomes a PMF
Common mistakes: Treating histogram as merely visual and not probabilistic; Assuming a smooth density is required before bootstrapping; Ignoring discreteness and frequency counts

questions.text: A scientist has time-series data observed across consecutive days and wants to use the standard bootstrap described in lecture. She argues, 'I can just treat the days as my sample and resample them iid.' Critique this plan using the lecture’s assumptions, but keep your answer focused on first principles rather than specialized time-series methods.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies violation of iid due to dependence across days; Explains why independent resampling from empirical distribution is then misaligned with the data-generating process; Keeps critique at principle level
Partial credit: Says time series may be problematic but not why; Mentions dependence without linking it to bootstrap validity

Common mistakes: Saying bootstrap only fails for long tails, not dependence; Treating ordered observations as automatically iid because sample size is large; Jumping to advanced remedies without first identifying the assumption failure

questions.text: After seeing a bootstrap distribution of the sample mean, a student concludes, 'This shows where future individual observations will lie.' Explain why that interpretation is wrong, and say what kind of random quantity the bootstrap distribution is actually about.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects confusion between distribution of observations and distribution of a statistic; Identifies the statistic as the sample mean over resamples; Explains why individual observations and means have different variability
Partial credit: Says 'wrong distribution' without specifying which two are confused; Identifies means versus observations but does not explain the consequence

Common mistakes: Treating all distributions built from the sample as interchangeable; Saying bootstrap mean distribution predicts next observation directly; Ignoring the role of sample size in averaging

questions.text: You have 25 observations and want to compare bootstrapping the mean versus bootstrapping the variance. Without invoking formulas, explain why the bootstrap distribution for the variance might look qualitatively more irregular than the one for the mean, even when both are based on the same resamples.
rubric_items: Full credit: Contrasts sensitivity of variance vs mean to extremes and duplicate draws; Explains qualitative irregularity in bootstrap distribution of variance; Mentions role of same resamples leading to different statistic behavior
Partial credit: Says variance is 'more variable' without explaining why; Attributes difference only to sample size

Common mistakes: Assuming all statistics have similarly shaped bootstrap distributions; Confusing raw data spread with spread of bootstrap statistic distributions; Claiming variance bootstrap is irregular because algorithm changes

questions.text: A classmate says: "If I have a sample of size 200, then a bootstrap resample should contain each of the 200 original observations exactly once, just in a different order. Otherwise we are changing the data." Explain carefully why this statement is wrong, and why bootstrap resampling is done with replacement rather than without replacement.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that the sample is used to estimate the population PMF/distribution.; States that bootstrap draws are with replacement.; Explains that duplicates and omissions in a resample are expected, not errors.; Justifies why without-replacement resampling would fail to capture sampling variability when resample size equals original size.

Partial credit: Mentions with replacement but gives only an intuitive reason.; Says duplicates can occur but does not connect this to estimating a sampling distribution.; Recognizes that without replacement would just shuffle the data, but does not explain why that is a problem.

Common mistakes: Claiming bootstrap resamples should be permutations of the original data.; Saying replacement is used only so the resample can be larger than the original sample.; Confusing the sample distribution with the sampling distribution of a statistic.

questions.text: You observe the sample [2, 2, 5, 9]. Without doing 10,000 simulations, describe exactly what empirical PMF the bootstrap uses, and explain how you would estimate the sampling distribution of the sample mean from it. Then compare the center of that bootstrap distribution to the original sample mean and justify your claim.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly constructs the empirical PMF from observed frequencies.; Describes resampling 4 observations with replacement from that PMF.; Explains that repeating this many times yields an approximate distribution of the sample mean.; Correctly computes the original sample mean as 4.5 and explains why the bootstrap mean distribution is centered there.

Partial credit: Gets the PMF right but is vague about the simulation procedure.; Describes the algorithm correctly but does not justify the center of the bootstrap distribution.; Computes the sample mean correctly but gives only an intuitive, not probabilistic, explanation of centering.

Common mistakes: Using probabilities 1/4,1/4,1/4 for the distinct values and ignoring the duplicate 2.; Sampling without replacement.; Saying the bootstrap distribution is centered at the population mean, which is unknown.

questions.text: A startup measures daily spending per user. The data are iid, but a few users spend vastly more than everyone else, producing an extremely long right tail. A teammate says, "Bootstrap works for any statistic, so let's use it to estimate uncertainty for the sample mean." Based on the lecture caveat, how would you respond? Give a nuanced answer: what assumption is satisfied here, what assumption is questionable, and what practical consequence might that have for the bootstrap estimate.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies iid as satisfied in the scenario.; Identifies the long-tail caveat as the problematic assumption.; Explains why long tails are troublesome for bootstrap approximation of the mean.; Discusses the practical impact: unstable or misleading uncertainty estimates, especially for the mean.

Partial credit: Mentions long tails are bad but does not explain why.; Says only that outliers are a problem, without connecting to the empirical distribution approximation.; Suggests caution but provides no reasoning about assumptions.
Common mistakes: Claiming iid alone is sufficient for bootstrap validity in all cases.; Saying bootstrap never works with skewed data of any kind.; Confusing long tail issues with dependence issues.

questions.text: Explain the difference between these two objects in the bootstrap story: the sample distribution and the sampling distribution of a statistic. Your answer should use the phrase "estimate the PMF using the sample" and should make clear why students often confuse the two.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the sample distribution as the empirical distribution/histogram/estimated PMF of observed values.; Defines the sampling distribution as the distribution of a statistic over repeated samples.; Explains that bootstrap uses the first to simulate the second.; Explicitly distinguishes distributions over data values versus distributions over statistics.

Partial credit: Gives partially correct definitions but blurs the distinction.; States the algorithm but does not explain the conceptual difference.; Recognizes one is about means/variances and the other about data, but lacks precision.

Common mistakes: Saying the sample distribution and sampling distribution are the same thing.; Describing the bootstrap output as another estimate of the population distribution rather than of the statistic's distribution.; Failing to distinguish values from statistics computed from values.

questions.text: You are comparing two small classes' exam scores and want a p-value for the difference in their average scores. A peer proposes bootstrapping each class separately from its own data and then checking how often the bootstrapped mean difference is as large as the observed one. Another peer says you should first combine the two samples into one 'universal sample' before resampling. Which approach is appropriate for testing the null hypothesis of equal means, and why?
rubric_items: Full credit: Chooses the combined or universal sample approach for the hypothesis test.; Explains that combining recreates the null hypothesis of no group difference.; Explains that separate bootstrapping preserves the observed difference and therefore does not generate the correct null distribution.; Distinguishes between estimating sampling variability and computing a p-value under a null.

Partial credit: Chooses the combined approach but gives only an intuitive explanation.; Recognizes that separate resampling is wrong for a p-value but cannot explain what distribution it estimates instead.; Mentions the null hypothesis but does not connect it to the resampling scheme.

Common mistakes: Bootstrapping each group separately for a null-hypothesis p-value.; Thinking any bootstrap procedure automatically gives a valid p-value.; Failing to distinguish a confidence-style bootstrap from a hypothesis-test null simulation.

questions.text: In the flu Bayes net, suppose a student is an undergrad and is tired. Without using the precomputed answer, explain aloud how you would compute the probability they have the flu, and identify which hidden variable must be summed out. Then say what feature of the network makes the computation manageable.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up conditional probability correctly as numerator over denominator.; Explicitly sums over the hidden Fever node.; Uses the Bayes net factorization with the correct local terms.; Explains why factorization reduces complexity.

Partial credit: Identifies the target conditional probability but omits one summation.; Gets the factorization mostly right but mixes up the role of Fever and Tired.; Explains conceptually that hidden variables are marginalized without fully writing the expression.
Common mistakes: Conditioning on Fever even though it is unobserved.; Forgetting the denominator normalization.; Assuming Tired is independent of Flu once U is known, which is false in this network.

questions.text: A classmate says: 'Because 80% of students are undergrads and undergrads are often tired, observing U=1 and T=1 should make the flu probability close to 0.8.' Critique this statement using the flu network. Your answer should distinguish a prior from a posterior and explain why a common base rate cannot simply be reused as the answer.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly identifies the confusion between P(U=1) and P(F_flu=1|U=1,T=1).; Explains prior versus posterior correctly.; Explains that evidence must be weighted by likelihoods under competing hypotheses and normalized.; Mentions base-rate effects, especially the low prior flu probability.

Partial credit: Says the statement is wrong but gives only an intuitive reason.; Mentions Bayes' rule or normalization without connecting it to the specific variables.; Recognizes that U=1 is not the queried event.
Common mistakes: Saying undergrad status causes flu directly.; Ignoring the prior probability of flu.; Treating Tired as evidence only for flu and not for being an undergrad without flu.

questions.text: You are asked to estimate P(flu | undergrad, tired) by simulation rather than exact summation. Describe a rejection sampling procedure using samples from the joint distribution of the Bayes net, and explain both how the estimate is formed and when the method becomes inefficient.
rubric_items: Full credit: Describes ancestral sampling from the joint in network order.; States the rejection criterion based on the observed evidence.; Forms the estimator as an accepted-sample frequency.; Explains inefficiency in terms of low acceptance probability for rare evidence.

Partial credit: Describes simulation but not clearly from the joint distribution.; Explains acceptance but not how the final ratio is computed.; Mentions inefficiency vaguely without tying it to evidence rarity.

Common mistakes: Sampling directly from the posterior without explaining how.; Counting all samples instead of accepted ones in the denominator.; Rejecting on the wrong variables or in the wrong order.

questions.text: The lecture claims that with enough samples from the joint distribution, you can answer 'any probability inference question.' Defend that statement carefully, but also say what 'enough' really means in practice and what quantity becomes difficult when the event of interest is rare.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains how sample frequencies approximate probabilities, conditional probabilities, and expectations.; States the asymptotic nature of the claim.; Explains that sample size needs depend on rarity/variance of the queried event.; Identifies rare-event estimation as especially difficult.

Partial credit: Repeats the claim correctly but without discussing practical limits.; Mentions law of large numbers informally without application to conditional queries.; Says 'more samples are better' without identifying what drives the required number.

Common mistakes: Claiming a small sample can answer any query accurately.; Ignoring the denominator instability in conditional probability estimation when conditioning event is rare.; Confusing model error with Monte Carlo error.

questions.text: In the SFO arrival-time distribution, let p_i be the probability a visitor arrives i hours past midnight. A student says the expected fraction arriving before noon is an average of the numbers p_0 through p_11, so it should be (1/12) times their sum. Is that right? Explain what quantity is actually being asked for and why the correct expression does or does not involve dividing by 12.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the target as a probability of a union of hour bins.; Gives the expression sum_{i=0}^{11} p_i.; Explains why dividing by 12 changes the meaning to an average of probabilities rather than total probability mass.
Partial credit: Provides the correct summation with minimal explanation.; Recognizes that p_i are already probabilities but does not articulate the difference between total and average.
Common mistakes: Averaging instead of summing.; Treating p_i as counts rather than probabilities.; Forgetting that the bins are mutually exclusive.

questions.text: A distribution is X ~ Geo(p=0.8), and an instructor defines an outlier as a value x for which P(X >= x) <= 0.05. A student argues that to check whether 7 is an outlier, you should compute P(X > 7) because '7 itself is not larger than 7.' Evaluate this reasoning and state the correct tail event under the given definition.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly identifies the tail event as X >= 7.; Explains that the wording '7 or larger' includes 7.; Notes that one may express it via a survival function or 1-CDF, subject to the geometric convention.
Partial credit: Says the student is wrong but gives little explanation.; Uses the right tail event but does not discuss inclusion of 7.
Common mistakes: Using X > 7.; Getting distracted by the exact geometric support convention and failing to answer the event-definition issue.; Confusing outlier definition with a two-sided criterion.

questions.text: A random sample of 20 students gives a mean course rating. The population mean is 4.5 and the population variance is 1.0. Explain how to approximate the probability that the sample mean is at least 4.7, and justify why a normal approximation is appropriate here even though individual ratings may not be normal.
rubric_items: Full credit: States mean and variance of the sample mean correctly.; Uses a normal approximation with the correct z-score.; Justifies the approximation via the CLT on the sample mean.; Distinguishes the distribution of individual ratings from the distribution of the sample mean.
Partial credit: Sets up the z-score correctly but gives a weak CLT justification.; Knows variance shrinks by n but makes a minor algebra error.; Mentions CLT without stating the assumptions.

Common mistakes: Using variance 1.0 instead of 1.0/20.; Saying ratings themselves must be normal for CLT to work.; Using a t distribution despite known population variance and a setup framed around CLT.

questions.text: At a party, someone says: 'I have two children, and at least one is a daughter born on Tuesday.' Many people answer 1/2 for the probability that both are daughters. Give a careful oral explanation of why 1/2 is not correct, and describe the conditioning event in a way that makes the correct sample space visible.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly rejects 1/2 because the conditioning event is more specific.; Describes the conditional sample space in terms of gender-weekday combinations.; Explains that probabilities must be recomputed within the new sample space.; States or motivates the result 13/27.

Partial credit: Recognizes that 1/2 is wrong and mentions conditional probability.; Explains qualitatively that Tuesday information changes the denominator but does not fully articulate the sample space.; Gives 13/27 with limited reasoning.

Common mistakes: Arguing symmetry implies 1/2.; Conditioning only on 'at least one daughter' instead of 'at least one daughter born on Tuesday.'; Forgetting inclusion-exclusion when counting families with at least one qualifying child.

questions.text: In the Van Gogh brushstroke problem, the average number of brushstrokes in a neighborhood is modeled as normal. Explain why a normal model is plausible for this average, but also give one limitation of using the central limit theorem here without further thought.
rubric_items: Full credit: Connects normality to the fact that the feature is an average.; Mentions the CLT appropriately.; Notes at least one assumption or limitation, such as dependence or insufficient sample size/effective independence.; Distinguishes plausibility from certainty.

Partial credit: States 'by CLT' without explaining why averaging matters.; Mentions that many terms are involved but not the assumptions.; Provides a generic caveat without linking it to this feature.
Common mistakes: Saying the original brushstroke counts themselves must be normal.; Using CLT as an unconditional guarantee.; Ignoring dependence among brushstroke-level quantities.

questions.text: You have prior belief 0.75 that a discovered painting is by Van Gogh. The observed average neighborhood brushstroke count is 19, with one normal model if Van Gogh painted it and another if not. Explain how to update your belief and why you must use densities rather than probabilities at the observed value.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes or states Bayes' rule with class-conditional densities.; Uses the prior 0.75 and complement prior 0.25.; Explains why densities are used for continuous observations.; Interprets the update as likelihood times prior, then normalization.

Partial credit: Gives the correct formula idea but says 'probability' instead of 'density.'; States that Bayes' rule applies but does not explain the continuous-observation issue.; Explains weighting by prior and likelihood qualitatively.
Common mistakes: Using P(X=19|Y) as an ordinary probability mass.; Forgetting the normalization denominator.; Ignoring the non-Van-Gogh class in the denominator.

questions.text: You observed 30 successes and 20 failures, and model the unknown success probability p with a Beta distribution. You want to report a claim of the form m ± b, where m is the posterior mean and b is the smallest half-width giving at least 95% posterior probability. Explain an algorithmic strategy for finding m and b, and justify why 'smallest' matters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies m as the posterior mean of the Beta posterior.; Defines b through a posterior probability statement centered at m.; Describes a valid search procedure, such as binary search or incremental search using the Beta CDF.; Explains why the minimal qualifying b gives the tightest symmetric interval around m.

Partial credit: Knows m is a posterior mean but is vague on how to find b.; Suggests simulation from the Beta posterior as an approximation route.; States the 95% condition but not the minimization idea.

Common mistakes: Using the sample proportion as the full answer without uncertainty.; Choosing any interval with 95% mass but ignoring the requirement of smallest symmetric half-width.; Confusing a frequentist confidence interval with the posterior probability interval requested.

questions.text: For carbon dating, a single C14 molecule has decay time T ~ Exp(lambda = 1/8267). Explain how to compute the probability that it decays within 500 years, and then interpret the complement event in words.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses the exponential CDF correctly.; States the complement as survival beyond 500 years.; Interprets the event in the decay context.
Partial credit: Writes the formula but gives little interpretation.; Gets the complement idea right without the exact expression.

Common mistakes: Using e^{-500/8267} as the decay-within-500 probability instead of the survival probability.; Confusing the exponential waiting time with a Poisson count directly.; Misstating the rate parameter as 8267 instead of 1/8267.

questions.text: A dead sample started with 100 independent C14 molecules. Using your result for the probability that one molecule decays within 500 years, explain why the number remaining after 500 years leads to a binomial model, and write the expression for exactly 95 molecules remaining.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies independent Bernoulli trials for each molecule.; Chooses a consistent binomial parameterization.; Connects '95 remaining' with either 5 decayed or 95 survived.; Writes the correct binomial probability expression.

Partial credit: States binomial correctly but is slightly inconsistent about whether the success event is decay or survival.; Gives a binomial expression without the combinatorial factor but explains the setup well.

Common mistakes: Using a Poisson distribution directly for the number remaining.; Forgetting independence or common probability across molecules.; Mixing up p and 1-p when switching between decayed and remaining.

questions.text: You observe m = 95 surviving molecules and want a posterior distribution over the sample age A, where A can be any whole number from 500 to 600 and is otherwise impossible. Describe, in words or pseudocode, how to compute the normalized list of posterior probabilities P(A=i | M=95) for all i in that range.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes likelihood for each discrete age candidate.; Uses the stated uniform prior on 500 through 600 inclusive.; Forms unnormalized posterior weights as likelihood times prior.; Normalizes across all candidate ages to get a valid posterior distribution.

Partial credit: Describes Bayes' rule conceptually but omits the normalization step.; Knows to loop over ages and compute likelihoods but is vague on the prior.; Uses the right support but does not explain why outside ages get zero.

Common mistakes: Choosing the age with maximum likelihood only, instead of computing the full posterior distribution.; Forgetting to normalize the weights.; Treating age as continuous despite the problem specifying whole years.

questions.text: In a reliability model with density f(x|a) = (1/a^2) x^{a-1} exp(-x^2/a^2), you observe independent lifetimes x_1,...,x_N. Explain how maximum likelihood estimation would choose a, why we typically maximize the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood directly, and what role the derivative plays.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines MLE as maximizing likelihood over a.; Explains why log-likelihood is used and that it preserves the argmax.; States that the derivative is set to zero to locate critical points.; Mentions the need to verify a maximum, not just any critical point.

Partial credit: Knows to maximize log-likelihood but gives only computational convenience as justification.; Mentions taking derivatives without explaining what is being optimized.; Defines MLE correctly but omits the critical-point verification step.
Common mistakes: Thinking log changes the maximizing parameter.; Stopping after writing the likelihood without discussing optimization.; Assuming every derivative-zero point is automatically the MLE.

questions.text: True or false, with justification: if two random variables X and Y are independent, it is still possible that for some assignments x and y, the events {X=x} and {Y=y} are dependent. Your answer should address the relationship between independence of variables and independence of events generated from them.
rubric_items: Full credit: Answers false.; Explains that random-variable independence implies factorization for all events based on X and Y separately.; Applies that principle to singleton events {X=x} and {Y=y}.

Partial credit: Answers false with a correct but informal statement like 'all such events must be independent.'; Mentions the product rule for independent variables without explicitly tying it to assignments.

Common mistakes: Answering true because dependence can appear 'for special values.'; Confusing independence of variables with zero correlation.; Forgetting the event-level interpretation of variable independence.

questions.text: A student says: 'The log-likelihood is always nonpositive, so likelihoods are always at most 1.' Use the Bernoulli example to explain why the first part can be true in that setting, but the general conclusion is false in statistics more broadly.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why Bernoulli point probabilities force log-likelihood <= 0.; Distinguishes discrete probabilities from continuous densities.; States that densities may exceed 1, so the general claim fails.
Partial credit: Recognizes the Bernoulli-specific nature of the statement.; Mentions continuous distributions but not densities explicitly.; States the conclusion correctly with limited explanation.
Common mistakes: Claiming all likelihoods are probabilities.; Saying densities cannot exceed 1.; Failing to distinguish model type.

questions.text: You compare two samples from unknown populations and, via bootstrap under a null model, obtain a p-value of 0.99 for the difference in their modes. Explain what this says and what it does not say. In particular, address the common mistake of interpreting 0.99 as a 99% probability that the null hypothesis is true.
rubric_items: Full credit: Interprets the p-value as a tail probability under the null.; States that the observed difference is not unusual under the null.; Explicitly rejects the '99% chance the null is true' interpretation.; Notes that failing to find evidence against the null is not proof of equality.

Partial credit: Says the result is not significant but does not explain the conditioning on the null.; Identifies the posterior-probability confusion but not the rest of the interpretation.; Explains bootstrap only loosely.
Common mistakes: Interpreting the p-value as P(null | data).; Saying a large p-value proves the null hypothesis.; Ignoring the role of the chosen test statistic.

questions.text: A statement claims: if X_1,...,X_n are iid, then the sample mean tends toward a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 0 as n grows. Give a careful critique. Your answer should separate what remains fixed, what changes with n, and what extra assumptions the central limit theorem quietly needs.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the claim is false.; Explains that the sample mean's expectation is mu, not automatically 0.; Explains variance sigma^2/n and its shrinkage.; Notes the CLT gives approximate normality under conditions such as finite variance.
Partial credit: Identifies the mean error or the variance behavior but not both.; Mentions CLT but not the required assumptions.; Explains the statement is false but only partially justifies why.
Common mistakes: Saying the sample mean itself converges to N(0,0).; Confusing a standardized mean with the raw sample mean.; Ignoring finite-variance assumptions.

questions.text: Explain why P(X=0) for X ~ Poi(lambda=5) equals P(Y>1) for Y ~ Exp(lambda=5). Give both an intuitive explanation in terms of arrivals and a short mathematical verification.
rubric_items: Full credit: Gives the Poisson-process intuition linking zero arrivals and waiting time beyond 1.; Computes both probabilities as e^{-5}.; Explains that the equality reflects the same event viewed two ways.

Partial credit: Provides only the mathematical verification or only the intuition.; Gets the event correspondence right but omits one formula.; Mentions memorylessness incorrectly but still lands on the right equality.
Common mistakes: Treating Poisson and exponential as unrelated distributions here.; Using P(Y<=1) instead of P(Y>1).; Forgetting the time interval length in the exponential tail.

questions.text: Suppose X_1,...,X_n are not necessarily independent, but each has mean 1. Explain why it must still be true that P(X_1+...+X_n >= n) > 0. Your explanation should avoid the central limit theorem and should directly use expectation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines the sum S and applies linearity of expectation correctly.; Uses a contradiction: if P(S>=n)=0 then S<n almost surely.; Concludes that would imply E[S]<n, contradicting E[S]=n.; Notes independence is unnecessary.

Partial credit: Uses linearity of expectation correctly but gives a less rigorous final step.; States the contradiction informally without clearly explaining why E[S] would then be less than n.; Mentions CLT but does not rely on it.
Common mistakes: Invoking the CLT or large-sample normality.; Arguing each X_i must individually be at least 1 with positive probability.; Ignoring dependence issues.

questions.text: In the A-B-C Bayes net example, A and B are independent marginally, but not independent given C=1. Explain this seeming paradox. Your answer should reference the graph structure and also describe how conditioning on a common effect can create dependence.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that A and B are marginally independent but conditionally dependent given C=1.; Explains the collider/common-effect structure.; Describes explaining away in intuitive terms.; Connects the graph structure to the conditional dependence.

Partial credit: Recognizes conditioning can induce dependence but does not name the collider structure.; Gives only a table-based or only a graph-based explanation.; States explaining away without making it intuitive.

Common mistakes: Assuming conditioning always preserves or increases independence.; Treating C as a common cause rather than a common effect.; Failing to distinguish marginal from conditional relationships.

questions.text: In the Fish Sticks model, hidden demand D determines two conditionally independent Poisson counts A and B. Explain how to compute P(D=0 | A=6), and then say why observing B as well would generally change the answer even though A and B are independent given D.
rubric_items: Full credit: Sets up Bayes' rule with the two class-conditional Poisson terms and priors.; Explains the normalization over D=0 and D=1.; Correctly states that A and B are conditionally independent given D.; Explains why B still informs D when D is hidden.

Partial credit: Gets Bayes' rule idea right but is vague about the Poisson likelihoods.; Recognizes that B provides extra information without fully articulating the conditional-independence point.; Explains independence incorrectly but still reaches the right conclusion.
Common mistakes: Claiming B is irrelevant because A and B are independent given D, forgetting D is unobserved.; Forgetting to normalize the proportional expression.; Using P(D=0|A=6)=P(A=6|D=0).

questions.text: You are asked to simulate P(A+B=12) in the Fish Sticks model by rejection sampling. Describe a correct simulation algorithm, then explain why this particular task does not actually require rejection in the strict conditional-evidence sense.
rubric_items: Full credit: Describes sampling D, then A and B conditional on D, then checking A+B=12.; Forms the estimate as the fraction of trials with total 12.; Explains that no conditioning event is imposed, so this is direct Monte Carlo rather than true rejection sampling.; Shows awareness of the conceptual distinction.

Partial credit: Gives a valid simulation algorithm but calls it rejection sampling without discussion.; Explains event-frequency estimation correctly but not the terminology issue.; Mentions that no samples are discarded unless one artificially does so.

Common mistakes: Trying to reject on A+B=12 and then estimate a conditional probability that was never asked.; Sampling A and B marginally without reference to D.; Confusing direct estimation of an event probability with conditional inference by rejection.

questions.text: In the flu Bayesian network, suppose a student tells you only that they are an undergrad and they are tired. Explain how you would compute the probability they have the flu, and then say whether that probability should be larger or smaller than the prior 0.1. You do not need to multiply every decimal out fully, but you should set up the numerator and denominator clearly and justify the direction of the update.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the correct conditional probability target P(F=1|U=1,T=1).; Uses Bayes rule or equivalent ratio of joint to marginal.; Correctly sums out the unobserved Fever variable or explains why it drops out.; Recognizes that U=1 and T=1 increase the probability only modestly, yielding about 0.122.

Partial credit: Sets up Bayes rule correctly but forgets to marginalize Fever explicitly.; Computes the numerator correctly but is incomplete on the denominator.; Gives the right qualitative conclusion that the posterior exceeds 0.1, with reasonable justification.
Common mistakes: Treating Tired and Flu as independent once Undergrad is known.; Conditioning on Fever even though it is unobserved.; Using P(T=1|U=1)=0.8 directly without averaging over Flu status.

questions.text: A classmate says: 'If two variables A and B are independent, then learning C can never make them dependent.' Use the three-variable Bayes-net example with A and B marginally independent but both influencing C to evaluate this claim. Your answer should explain both the marginal independence and why conditioning on C=1 can break it.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that the claim is false.; Explains why A and B are marginally independent in the unconditioned network.; Explains that conditioning on a common effect C induces dependence.; Uses the idea of explaining away or an equivalent conditional-probability comparison.

Partial credit: Recognizes the claim is false but gives only intuition without tying it to factorization or conditionals.; States explaining away correctly but does not explain the original marginal independence.; Provides a numerical comparison but not the conceptual reason.

Common mistakes: Saying independence is preserved under all conditioning.; Confusing 'no edge between A and B' with conditional independence given every other variable.; Claiming C screens off A and B in this collider structure.

questions.text: You have two samples from unknown populations and you observe a difference in their sample means. A teammate proposes estimating a p-value by pooling the data into one 'universal sample,' repeatedly resampling two groups of the original sizes, and counting how often the resampled mean difference is at least as large as the observed one. Explain what null hypothesis this procedure is approximating, why pooling is appropriate under that null, and what it would mean if the estimated p-value were 0.99.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the null as no real difference between the underlying populations in the target statistic.; Explains why pooling follows from the null and the idea of exchangeability/common source.; Describes the resampling distribution as an estimate of chance variation under the null.; Interprets p=0.99 correctly as weak evidence against the null, not proof the null is true.

Partial credit: Describes the mechanics of bootstrapping/resampling correctly but is vague on the null hypothesis.; Interprets a large p-value as 'not significant' but without explaining why pooling is justified.; Recognizes that p=0.99 means the observed difference is common under chance.

Common mistakes: Saying the p-value is the probability the null hypothesis is true.; Claiming p=0.99 proves the means are equal.; Ignoring the need to compare the observed statistic to a resampled null distribution.

questions.text: In the Van Gogh brushstroke problem, you start with prior probability 0.75 that the painting is by Van Gogh. You then observe an average neighborhood brushstroke count of 19, where the count is modeled as Normal with mean 20 and variance 9 if Van Gogh painted it, and Normal with mean 12 and variance 25 otherwise. Set up the posterior probability that the painting is by Van Gogh, and explain aloud why the answer should be quite high even before doing exact arithmetic.
rubric_items: Full credit: Writes the correct Bayes-rule expression using normal densities.; Uses the correct priors 0.75 and 0.25.; Explains qualitatively why x=19 favors the Van Gogh model strongly.; Mentions or correctly handles the continuous-variable issue by using densities.

Partial credit: Sets up Bayes rule correctly but writes P(X=19|V) instead of a density, while reasoning is otherwise sound.; Gets the correct qualitative conclusion without a full formula.; Recognizes that the prior and likelihood both favor Van Gogh.

Common mistakes: Comparing only distances from the means and forgetting different variances entirely.; Using the posterior formula without the denominator normalization.; Treating density values as probabilities without acknowledging continuity.

questions.text: A student says: 'Since the sample mean of i.i.d. data becomes approximately normal by the central limit theorem, its mean must go to 0 and its variance must go to 0 as n grows.' Critique this statement carefully. Your answer should distinguish what stays fixed, what changes with n, and any assumptions needed for the approximation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explicitly rejects the claim that the mean goes to 0 in general.; States E[\bar X]=mu and Var(\bar X)=sigma^2/n under independence.; Explains the CLT approximation as Normal(mu, sigma^2/n) for large n.; Mentions needed assumptions such as i.i.d. and finite variance.

Partial credit: Correctly identifies only one of the two errors, such as variance shrinking but mean staying at mu.; States the CLT informally without formulas but with correct direction.; Mentions dependence or infinite-variance caveats even if details are incomplete.

Common mistakes: Confusing convergence in distribution with convergence of the mean to 0.; Saying the CLT always applies regardless of variance assumptions.; Forgetting the factor 1/n in the variance of the sample mean.

questions.text: Two discrete random variables each have expectation 3. One student says that means they are 'equally concentrated around 3.' Explain why that conclusion is wrong, and describe what variance adds that expectation alone does not capture. In your answer, say how two distributions can share the same mean but still look very different.
rubric_items: Full credit: States that equal expectation does not imply equal spread; Explains variance as expected squared deviation from the mean; Describes qualitatively how two distributions with same mean can differ in shape/spread
Partial credit: Says variance measures spread but does not clearly contrast it with expectation; Gives an intuitive but incomplete explanation without mentioning distance from the mean

Common mistakes: Claiming the mean determines the whole distribution; Saying variance is just the average deviation instead of average squared deviation; Confusing variance with probability of extreme events only

questions.text: Let Y be the outcome of a fair six-sided die roll. Without listing all six squared deviations one by one, explain how you would compute Var(Y) using the second-moment formula, and then interpret the units of your final answer.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses Var(Y)=E[Y^2]-(E[Y])^2 correctly; Computes or states E[Y]=7/2 and E[Y^2]=91/6; Gets Var(Y)=35/12; Interprets variance units as squared units
Partial credit: Correct setup but arithmetic slip; Correct numerical answer with little explanation; Understands units only partially
Common mistakes: Averaging absolute deviations instead of squared deviations; Forgetting to square E[Y]; Saying variance has the same units as Y

questions.text: A classmate claims, 'Expectation is linear, so variance should also be linear: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y) for any random variables.' Respond to this claim carefully. State when such an additivity statement is valid in the binomial setting and why the general claim is too broad.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly rejects the claim that variance is always linear; States a correct condition such as independence for additivity of variance; Connects this to binomial as a sum of independent Bernoullis
Partial credit: Says 'only if independent' but does not explain why; Mentions covariance vaguely without connecting to the claim
Common mistakes: Saying variance is linear because expectation is linear; Using the binomial formula without mentioning independence; Confusing independent with mutually exclusive

questions.text: An ad is shown to 20 users independently, and each user clicks with probability 0.2. Define a natural random variable for the number of clicks, name its distribution, and then give both its expectation and variance. Finally, explain in one sentence what each of those two numbers means in context.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines X as count of successes; Identifies X~Bin(20,0.2); Computes E[X]=4 and Var(X)=3.2; Interprets both quantities in context
Partial credit: Correct distribution and formulas but weak interpretation; Correct mean but incorrect variance arithmetic
Common mistakes: Using Bernoulli instead of binomial for the count over 20 trials; Using np^2 or n(1-p) for the variance; Interpreting variance as a probability

questions.text: For X~Bin(n,p), keep n fixed and vary p. Without doing calculus, explain where the variance np(1-p) is largest and why that makes intuitive sense from the story of counting successes. Your explanation should combine the formula with a verbal interpretation of trial uncertainty.
rubric_items: Full credit: States the maximum occurs at p=0.5; Uses symmetry or equal factors reasoning on p(1-p); Provides intuitive Bernoulli-trial explanation
Partial credit: Correctly identifies p=0.5 but explanation is formula-only or intuition-only; Mentions symmetry but not uncertainty

Common mistakes: Claiming variance is largest when p is near 0 or 1 because outcomes are more extreme; Confusing mean np with variance np(1-p); Giving a calculus-based answer only without interpretation

questions.text: A random variable X has mean 10 and variance 4. Define Z=(X-10)/2. Compute E[Z] and Var(Z), but also explain why centering and scaling affect expectation and variance differently. I want the properties you use stated out loud.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes E[Z]=0; Correctly computes Var(Z)=1; States and applies linearity of expectation and Var(aX+b)=a^2Var(X); Explains why constants affect mean and variance differently
Partial credit: Correct numerical answer with limited explanation; Correct use of one property but not both
Common mistakes: Saying Var(aX+b)=aVar(X); Thinking subtracting 10 changes variance; Computing E[Z] as 10/2=5

questions.text: A data center has 1000 disk drives, each crashing independently during a day with probability 0.001. Let X be the number of crashed drives that day. Give a binomial model for X, then compute its expectation and variance, and comment on whether the variance is larger or smaller than the mean.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies Bin(1000,0.001); Computes mean 1 and variance 0.999; Explains why variance is slightly below the mean
Partial credit: Correct setup with small arithmetic error; Correct numerical results without comparison
Common mistakes: Using Bernoulli instead of binomial; Computing variance as np; Claiming variance must exceed mean

questions.text: A student sees X~Bin(10,0.3) and says, 'Since the expected number of successes is 3, the most likely outcome must be exactly 3, and the variance should also be 3.' Evaluate both parts of this statement. Be careful to separate what is always true from what only happens in some cases.
rubric_items: Full credit: Rejects the claim that the mean must equal the most likely value; Computes variance 2.1 correctly; Distinguishes mean, mode, and variance
Partial credit: Gets variance right but is vague about the mode issue; Explains expectation versus variance but ignores the 'most likely outcome' claim
Common mistakes: Saying the mean always equals the mode; Saying variance equals mean for every count model; Confusing average outcome with most probable single outcome

questions.text: Compare standard deviation and variance as summaries of spread. Why might an analyst report standard deviation when discussing temperatures, even if variance is often easier to manipulate algebraically? Use the units issue in your explanation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains variance uses squared units; Explains standard deviation returns to original units; Mentions variance is often algebraically easier
Partial credit: Mentions units but not interpretability; Mentions square root relationship only

Common mistakes: Saying variance and standard deviation have the same units; Claiming standard deviation is always easier to compute algebraically; Defining SD without explaining why it may be preferred in reporting

questions.text: Suppose X is a discrete random variable with PMF p(x), and you know only that E[X]=mu. Derive aloud the shortcut formula Var(X)=E[X^2]-mu^2 starting from the definition Var(X)=E[(X-mu)^2]. I care more about the logic than the notation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Starts from the definition and expands the square correctly; Uses linearity of expectation correctly; Treats mu as a constant and substitutes E[X]=mu; Arrives at E[X^2]-mu^2
Partial credit: Correct result with incomplete derivation; Minor algebra slip with otherwise correct reasoning
Common mistakes: Writing E[(X-mu)^2]=E[X-mu]^2; Forgetting that expectation is linear but variance is not; Dropping the cross term incorrectly

questions.text: You flip a fair coin 10 times and let X be the number of heads. Another student flips a fair coin 5 times and lets Y be the number of heads. Compare E[X] to E[Y] and Var(X) to Var(Y), and explain why the PMFs should have different spread even though both use p=0.5.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly computes both means and variances; Explains increased spread via larger n; Mentions support or accumulation of independent trial variability
Partial credit: Correct calculations but weak explanation; Correct qualitative comparison only
Common mistakes: Assuming equal p means equal variance regardless of n; Confusing probability of heads with expected count of heads; Saying the fair-coin PMFs are identical except shifted

questions.text: A student says, 'Because X and Y have the same variance, they must have the same distribution.' Give a careful rebuttal. Your answer should explain what information variance preserves and what information it throws away.
rubric_items: Full credit: Clearly states same variance does not imply same distribution; Explains variance captures only spread around the mean; Mentions missing features such as mean, shape, support, or skew
Partial credit: Says it is false but gives only one example-free sentence; Focuses on mean alone without broader explanation
Common mistakes: Treating variance as a complete description; Claiming same variance implies same standard deviation and therefore same distribution; Mixing up mean and variance

questions.text: Let X be Bernoulli with parameter p, taking values 1 for success and 0 for failure. Compute Var(X) from first principles using either the definition or E[X^2]-(E[X])^2, and then explain why this same quantity appears inside the binomial variance formula.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes E[X]=p and E[X^2]=p using X^2=X; Derives Var(X)=p(1-p); Connects Bernoulli variance to binomial variance via sum of independent indicators
Partial credit: Gets p(1-p) but does not justify X^2=X; Understands the binomial connection only vaguely
Common mistakes: Computing E[X^2] as p^2; Forgetting Bernoulli support is {0,1}; Claiming binomial variance is n times the mean

questions.text: You are shown two unlabeled binomial PMF plots with n=10: one is centered near 3 and the other near 7, and they appear to have the same spread but mirrored shapes. Identify plausible parameter values for each and explain why their variances match even though their means differ.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies p=0.3 and p=0.7 as plausible values; Computes means 3 and 7; Computes equal variances 2.1; Explains symmetry under p and 1-p
Partial credit: Correct pair but weak explanation of equal variance; Correct symmetry explanation without explicit calculations
Common mistakes: Assuming different means must imply different variances; Using p=0.5 for one of the plots; Not connecting the mirror image to swapping success and failure

questions.text: Explain why independence matters in the usual derivation of Var(X)=np(1-p) for a binomial random variable. I do not want just the formula; I want you to describe what breaks if the trials are no longer independent.
rubric_items: Full credit: Expresses binomial count as sum of Bernoulli indicators; States independence is needed to add variances without covariance terms; Explains non-independence can preserve the mean but alter the variance and even the distribution family
Partial credit: Says independence is needed but does not explain what breaks; Mentions covariance without tying it to the derivation
Common mistakes: Claiming only the mean formula needs independence; Saying dependence never affects variance; Thinking identical marginal probabilities alone guarantee a binomial model

questions.text: Suppose X has variance 9. Compute Var(3X+4) and Var(-2X+100), and explain why one transformation leaves no trace of the added constant. Then compare what happens to standard deviation in the same two cases.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes 81 and 36 correctly; Explains constants do not affect spread; Explains SD scales by absolute value of multiplier
Partial credit: Correct variances but no interpretation; Correct idea about shift invariance with arithmetic slip
Common mistakes: Using a instead of a^2 in the variance formula; Letting the constant affect variance; Giving negative standard deviation for -2X+100

questions.text: A simulation returns R=Y-X, where X~Bern(p) and Y~Bern(p+k), and in one construction R can only take values 0 and 1 with E[R]=k. Explain why that immediately determines Var(R), without using the general covariance formula. Then interpret what this says about the simulation's variability when k is small.
rubric_items: Full credit: Recognizes a 0-1 variable with mean k is Bernoulli(k); Computes Var(R)=k(1-k); Interprets the variance for small k
Partial credit: Gets the variance formula but does not justify Bernoulli identification; Gives intuition but no clear derivation
Common mistakes: Trying to use Var(Y)-Var(X) mechanically; Missing that support {0,1} plus mean identifies Bernoulli; Saying variance is exactly k for all k

questions.text: A student computes Var(X)=E[X-E[X]]^2 and concludes variance is always 0 because E[X-E[X]]=0. Diagnose the mistake precisely. Then give the correct formula and explain in words why the placement of the square matters.
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the confusion between E[(... )^2] and (E[...])^2; States the correct variance formula; Explains cancellation of signed deviations
Partial credit: Says the square is in the wrong place but gives little explanation; Correct formula only
Common mistakes: Treating expectation as if it distributes over squaring; Saying variance can be negative; Writing E[X-E[X]^2]

questions.text: In the temperature example, one city had nearly the same mean high temperature as another but much larger variance. Explain how that can happen in practical terms. Then say whether a larger variance automatically means the city is 'worse' or just more variable.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains same mean with different day-to-day spread; Links larger variance to less consistency around the mean; Avoids normative claims and frames variance as variability
Partial credit: Good intuition but weak connection to the formal meaning of variance; States only that the distributions are 'different'
Common mistakes: Equating mean climate with predictability; Treating larger variance as automatically bad in a mathematical sense; Ignoring spread and talking only about averages

questions.text: You are told X is a discrete random variable with support {0,1,2} and PMF P(X=0)=a, P(X=1)=a, P(X=2)=1-2a, where 0<=a<=1/2. Compute E[X] and Var(X) in terms of a, and describe qualitatively how the spread changes as a increases.
rubric_items: Full credit: Computes E[X]=2-3a; Computes E[X^2]=4-7a; Derives Var(X)=5a-9a^2; Provides a sensible qualitative interpretation of how spread changes
Partial credit: Correct moments with algebra slip in variance; Correct formula but little interpretation
Common mistakes: Forgetting probabilities must sum to 1; Using E[X]^2 in place of E[X^2]; Treating variance as linear in a automatically

questions.text: A quality-control engineer records whether each manufactured chip passes a test. For one chip the result is Bernoulli, but for a batch of n chips the number of passes is binomial. Explain this relationship clearly, including the role of indicator variables, and use it to justify the formulas for the mean and variance of the batch count at a high level.
rubric_items: Full credit: Defines Bernoulli indicators for individual chips; Explains the batch count as a sum of indicators; Justifies mean via linearity of expectation; Justifies variance via independence and Bernoulli variance
Partial credit: Identifies Bernoulli vs binomial but does not justify formulas; Gives formulas without the indicator interpretation
Common mistakes: Saying the batch count is Bernoulli; Using independence for expectation even though it is unnecessary there; Forgetting the identical-p assumption for binomial

questions.text: Suppose someone wants to compare variability across two discrete random variables measured in different units, one in dollars and one in counts. Explain why comparing raw variances can be misleading, and connect your explanation to the fact that variance has squared units. Then suggest a more interpretable quantity from the same family if the goal is to speak in original units.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains why squared units make raw variance comparisons misleading; Mentions that the units differ across variables; Suggests standard deviation as the original-unit alternative
Partial credit: Mentions squared units only vaguely; Names standard deviation but does not explain why
Common mistakes: Claiming variance is unit-free; Saying variance and standard deviation are interchangeable in interpretation; Ignoring the different-unit issue

questions.text: Two discrete random variables both have expectation 3. A classmate says that means they are 'equally predictable' and should have about the same spread. How would you respond using the definition of variance, and can you explain why two distributions can share the same mean but still look very different? Give a concrete kind of example in words, not necessarily with full arithmetic.
rubric_items: Full credit: States clearly that equal means do not imply equal spread.; Uses the variance definition or equivalent interpretation involving squared distance from the mean.; Explains that probability mass farther from the mean increases variance.; Provides a sensible example or verbal comparison of concentrated versus dispersed distributions.

Partial credit: Says variance measures spread but does not connect it to the formula or squared distance.; Gives an example without clearly explaining why the means can match.; Confuses variance with range but still recognizes that distributions with same mean can differ.

Common mistakes: Claiming the mean determines the whole distribution.; Saying two variables with the same expected value must have the same variance.; Describing variance only as 'how big the values are' rather than distance from the mean.

questions.text: Let Y be the outcome of a fair six-sided die roll, and define X = 2Y - 1. Without writing out the full PMF of X, compute Var(X) and explain each property you use. Then interpret why the variance changes the way it does under this transformation.
rubric_items: Full credit: Correctly obtains Var(Y)=35/12 or cites it with valid justification.; Applies Var(aX+b)=a^2 Var(X) correctly to get 35/3.; Explains why the additive constant does not affect variance.; Interprets scaling in terms of distances from the mean being squared.

Partial credit: Computes the correct final value but gives weak explanation.; Uses the right transformation rule but has arithmetic errors.; Understands that shifting does not matter but is unsure why scaling contributes a square.
Common mistakes: Using Var(2Y-1)=2Var(Y)-1.; Confusing expectation rules with variance rules.; Forgetting that variance scales by a^2, not by a.

questions.text: A system has 1000 disk drives, and each drive crashes independently during a day with probability 0.01. One student models the number of crashes as Bin(1000, 0.01) and says the variance is 1000(0.01)(0.99). Another student says, 'variance is linear, so it should just be 1000 times the variance of one Bernoulli, and independence is irrelevant.' Evaluate both statements carefully. Which parts are right, which parts are incomplete, and where does independence matter?
rubric_items: Full credit: Identifies the count as binomial and gives the correct variance formula.; States that variance is not generally linear, unlike expectation.; Explains that the sum-of-variances step requires independence here.; Connects the binomial proof idea to indicator variables Xi for each drive.

Partial credit: Gets the formula right but does not explain why independence matters.; Says variance is not linear but cannot articulate the role of covariance or independence.; Recognizes the Bernoulli-sum representation but leaves the critique of the second student incomplete.
Common mistakes: Saying independence is unnecessary for Var(sum Xi)=sum Var(Xi).; Claiming 'variance is linear' because expectation is linear.; Using np for the variance instead of np(1-p).

questions.text: You observe a random variable X with X ~ Bin(n,p), but you are only told that E[X] = 3. An engineer claims this is enough information to conclude Var(X) = 3(1-p). Do you agree? Explain what can and cannot be determined from the mean alone, and then characterize all possible binomial variances consistent with E[X]=3.
rubric_items: Full credit: Uses np=3 correctly and substitutes into the variance formula.; Explains that the variance is not numerically identifiable from the mean alone because p is unknown.; Recognizes the binomial constraint p=3/n with integer n>=3.; Characterizes the family of possible variances and interprets the endpoints or trend.

Partial credit: States that more information is needed but does not fully characterize the possibilities.; Correctly writes Var(X)=3(1-p) but misses the need for p=3/n.; Gives examples such as Bin(3,1) and Bin(6,0.5) to show different variances, even without a full general characterization.
Common mistakes: Treating E[X]=3 as enough to determine p.; Forgetting the integer constraint on n in the binomial model.; Assuming all random variables with mean 3 have the same or similar variance.

questions.text: A team is comparing two Monte Carlo estimators that both return a discrete random value with the same expectation. One estimator has outcomes tightly clustered near its mean, while the other occasionally makes larger deviations. Without appealing to asymptotics, explain how variance helps decide which estimator is more stable, and then distinguish that from standard deviation in terms of interpretation and units.
rubric_items: Full credit: Explains that smaller variance means less variability around the same mean and thus greater stability.; Uses the variance definition or second-moment identity appropriately.; Correctly distinguishes variance from standard deviation by square root and units.; Mentions that equal expectation alone is not enough to compare estimator reliability.

Partial credit: Says lower variance is better but gives limited reasoning.; Correctly distinguishes SD from variance but does not connect back to estimator stability.; Discusses spread informally without using the formal definition.

Common mistakes: Saying two estimators with the same mean are equally good regardless of variance.; Confusing variance with bias or expected value.; Ignoring the units issue and interpreting variance on the original measurement scale.
